Claims

How to get good output

Ironies of Automation, Lisanne Bainbridge

contestedThe two ironies

Removing the operator leaves the designer's mistakes with nobody to catch them

Bainbridge says designers' mistakes are a major cause of problems in running a plant. Automating a job to get rid of the unreliable human leaves those mistakes in place, with nobody left on duty to catch them.

Becauseshe asserts it from studies whose collectors she says are reluctant to publish, so the reader is given the conclusion without the data
LimitsThe evidence is second-hand and unpublished by her own account, which is why the claim stays contested; Norman reaches the same place from accident statistics and qualifies it himself for drunk and sleep-deprived operators.
PracticeWhen you remove a person from a loop, name what they were catching and say who catches it now. Treat the automation's own defects as a failure mode with an owner.
After AIThe designer's errors are now the training data's, the objective's and the scorer's, and they are distributed across every use at once rather than sitting in one plant. Nobody is on duty to catch them because the duty was never assigned.

The Design of Everyday Things, Donald A. Norman

opinionKnowledge in the head and in the world

A control that feels obvious to you is not obvious to everyone

A control layout that feels natural — which way a switch should move to go up or forward — rests on a picture in the designer's head that other people do not share.

Becauseevery audience Norman has asked splits over whether the top button advances the slides, and the Aymara put the past in front where it can be seen
LimitsNorman's evidence is a show of hands rather than a study, and the word natural survives in his own vocabulary despite the qualification. Some mappings — up for more, a control on the thing it controls — hold across every audience he reports.
PracticeBefore calling a mapping obvious, ask a second person which way it goes. If the room splits, the mapping is a convention and needs a signifier.
After AIInstructions to a model are mappings of exactly this kind: what one person means by shorter or more formal is not what the next means, and there is no shape on the device to settle it.
contestedHuman error? No, bad design

Most accidents blamed on people are caused by bad design

Norman argues that almost everything recorded as human error is really a fault in the design. Between 75 and 95 per cent of industrial accidents are blamed on people, which he says is too high a share to be about people.

Becausethe argument is arithmetical — between seventy-five and ninety-five per cent of industrial accidents blamed on people is too high to be about people — and Norman exempts drunk drivers, sleep-deprived staff and deliberate violations himself
LimitsThe strong form is the one claim in the book Norman leaves without evidence, and his own chapter qualifies it. Reason's Swiss cheese, which he uses to support it, has been criticised by the resilience researchers he himself quotes for making accidents look linear.
PracticeWhen a person gets something wrong, change the thing before you change the person, and keep the incident open until you have named what the design made easy.
After AIThe blame now lands on the person who accepted a wrong suggestion, which puts them in the electric utility's position: every committee finds the worker at fault, including the workers. The design that showed the answer first is not on the list of causes.
opinionThe psychopathology of everyday things

Norman says a handwritten sign on a machine means the design failed

Norman argues that a hand-lettered sign taped to a door or a machine, telling people how to use it, is an admission that the design failed.

Becauseasserted from the door cases and from the windsock comparison; no measurement is offered
LimitsSome signs are unavoidable — safety notices, legal text, genuinely novel devices — and Norman does not draw the line. A sign can also be the cheapest correct fix.
PracticeTreat every workaround note, pinned message and internal cheat sheet as a bug report against the thing it explains, and fix the thing.
After AIPrompt guides, house style documents and lists of phrasings that work are all hand-lettered signs taped to the same device. That they are necessary at all is the finding.
opinionThe psychopathology of everyday things

Norman says a visible mark, not shape, tells people where to act

What tells a person where to act is a signifier: a mark put there on purpose to be seen, like a plate on a door. An affordance is only what a thing makes possible for a particular person, and may be invisible.

Becausethe distinction is argued from the post-office door, whose pillar and hinge were hidden for the sake of a clean front, rather than measured
LimitsNorman himself lost the terminological argument for twenty-five years and concedes in the 2013 preface that the fault was his for not supplying the word designers needed — which is evidence for his own thesis about badly signified things.
PracticeWhen something is hard to use, do not add capability; add a perceptible mark that says where the action goes, and put it where the action is.
After AIA chat box affords everything and signifies nothing, and the vendor's documentation is the hand-lettered sign taped to it. The gap the word was invented to name is now the whole interface.
opinionThe psychopathology of everyday things

The product itself must teach the user how it works

Designer and user never meet. Everything the user can learn has to come from the product itself, its shape, its controls, its manual, which Norman calls the system image, and it carries the whole load.

Becausethe two-dial refrigerator makes the case: the implied model required two thermostats where there was one, so no amount of care could set it
LimitsNorman assumes the designer has a correct model to communicate. Where the thing's own behaviour is not understood by its builders, there is no model to put in the image, and the argument has no purchase.
PracticeWrite down the model you expect the user to build, then look only at what the thing shows and ask whether that model could be built from it.
After AIThe system image of a model is its outputs, and the conceptual model people build from them is a folk theory of a thing whose builders cannot supply the correct one either. The disconnected corners of the triangle are now three.
evidenceHuman error? No, bad design

Users will confuse settings when a device has more functions than controls

Norman argues that when a device does more things than it has controls for, one control has to mean different things at different times. People will then sometimes act as though the device were in another setting.

Becausethe Airbus crew who set vertical speed believing it was descent angle is the case — 3.3 meant three thousand three hundred feet a minute — and Airbus's fix, always four digits for vertical speed, shows the mechanism
LimitsThe claim is about a structural condition rather than a rate: it says mode error will occur, not how often, and the fix Airbus applied shows that a good display can reduce it to near zero without removing the modes.
PracticeMake the current mode visible in the thing's own output, not in a setting panel, and make the two modes look different rather than labelling them differently.
After AIA model's mode is the context it is carrying, and nothing in the output marks it. Same prompt, different history, different meaning — the Airbus display problem with no display.

Attention Is All You Need, Ashish Vaswani and others

evidenceWhy self-attention; Since 2017

Attention's cost was trivial in 2017 and is now the main limit

Attention's cost grows with the square of the sentence length. At the few dozen tokens the 2017 paper measured, that was cheaper than the alternatives; at every length used since it has been the binding limit, though nothing about the design changed.

Becausethe authors argue that self-attention costs less per layer than recurrence whenever the sequence is shorter than the representation is wide — a few dozen word-piece tokens against a width of 512 — and restricted attention, named there as future work, is now a permanent branch of the subject.
LimitsThe cost is quadratic in attention only; feed-forward layers dominate at short lengths, and flash attention and sparse variants have made the wall a slope rather than a cliff.
PracticeBudget context as a scarce resource even when the window is advertised as large. A long prompt is priced against its own square, so decide what gets cut yourself rather than leaving it to a retrieval heuristic.
After AIThe economics of every assistant — what the context window costs, why a long conversation gets expensive, why retrieval exists as an industry — descend from a term the authors correctly judged harmless at sentence length.
evidenceAttention (§3.2.2, Table 3)

Extra attention heads make up for blurring, they do not add power

Attention in a transformer works by averaging over the positions it looks at, which loses detail. The authors added several attention heads to make up for that loss, not to give the model extra power.

Becausethe authors write that with a single head, averaging inhibits what they want; Table 3 puts one head 0.9 BLEU below the best setting and thirty-two heads below sixteen, at fixed total computation.
LimitsThe ablation is one model, one task and BLEU. Later interpretability work finds heads doing separable jobs, which is closer to specialisation than to compensation, so the framing here is the authors' reading of a scoring difference.
PracticeDo not read a head count as a capacity figure. More heads past the optimum buy nothing, and the mechanism a head implements is a weighted average — a summary, with everything a summary drops.
After AIWhen a model blurs two similar passages of a long context into one answer, this is the level at which that happens. It is a property of the averaging, not a lapse of attention in the ordinary sense of the word.
evidenceWhy self-attention (Table 1)

In a Transformer any two words are one step apart

In the Transformer, attention connects every position in a sentence to every other in a single step. The distance a signal travels between two words no longer grows as they get further apart, which is what made long-range dependencies easier to learn.

BecauseTable 1's third column gives a maximum path length of O(1) against O(n) for recurrence and O(log_k n) for convolution, on the stated argument that a dependency gets harder to learn as the forward and backward signals lengthen.
LimitsConstant path length is an upper bound on what the mechanism can relate, not evidence that it does. Attention weights concentrate in practice, and long-context retrieval degrades in the middle of a document in ways the table does not predict.
PracticePut the constraint that matters anywhere in the prompt rather than next to the instruction it governs: distance in the context costs the model nothing arithmetically. Distance costs you, which is why the specification has to be written down.
After AIThe property that looked like a training convenience is what makes a long prompt work at all: a model can hold a whole codebase in view because nothing in the mechanism penalises the span. The limit that remains is the quadratic bill for doing so.
evidenceThe cost of doing one position at a time

The transformer was built to make training faster not smarter

In a recurrent network each position has to be computed after the one before it, so a single training example cannot be split across processors. The transformer was designed to remove that limit, and its headline result was training about ten times cheaper.

Becausethe hidden state at position *t* is a function of the state at *t*−1, and the paper's own result is a training cost about a tenth of the previous best — twelve hours on eight P100s — rather than a new kind of translation.
LimitsThe saving is demonstrated at 213 million parameters and under four days of training; that it would keep paying four orders of magnitude later is not shown here, and recurrence has returned in state-space models at long context.
PracticeRead a capability claim as a claim about what a training budget could reach, not about what the architecture understands. The design decision on record was an engineering one about parallelism.
After AIEvery assistant now in daily use inherits this one decision, and the thing it optimised for was throughput. Nothing in the design was chosen to make the output true, and no later stage repairs that.
evidenceSince 2017

The transformer works on images and audio, not only on words

The transformer was built for language, but the same encoder was later applied to fixed-size patches of an image, and after that to audio and video frames, with no change to the mechanism.

Becausethe closing paragraph names images, audio and video as future work, and the 2020 application of the same encoder to image patches, with the patches treated as a sequence, required no change to the layer.
LimitsWorking without a change to the mechanism is not working equally well: vision transformers need far more data than convolutional networks to reach the same accuracy, and the inductive biases the architecture lacks have to be bought with examples.
PracticeWhen a vendor announces a new modality, assume the mechanism is the one you already know and ask what the tokenisation is. The failure modes travel with the architecture, so what you learned about text behaviour mostly transfers.
After AIThe generality here is exactly what Bender's argument does not cover. A mechanism indifferent to whether its elements are words, patches or frames is harder to describe as a model of language, and harder to credit with meaning on that account either.
evidencePosition, without recurrence

The transformer's attention cannot tell word order so order is added

Attention adds up its inputs as an unordered set, so nothing in it can tell one arrangement of the same words from another. The transformer paper supplies order by adding a separate position signal to each word before attention sees it.

Becausethe paper adds sinusoidal encodings to the embeddings at the bottom of each stack precisely because the sum carries no order; learned position embeddings scored 25.8 against the sinusoids' 25.7 on the development set, a difference of nothing.
LimitsOrder-blindness is a property of the attention sum, not of the trained model: position encodings are inside the model at every layer, and models are in practice highly sensitive to the order of options and examples.
PracticeTreat ordering in a prompt as an explicit instruction rather than an implied one. Steps that must happen in sequence should say so in words, because the mechanism's only access to order is a signal added alongside the content.
After AIThe prompt sensitivity everyone now works around — answers moving when the options are reordered — starts here. What looks like the model having a view about your list is a positional signal bolted to the outside of a mechanism that has none.
evidenceSince 2017

The transformer's overall shape held since 2017 while its details changed

What has stayed the same in the transformer since 2017 is the shape of a layer, not its details. Layer normalisation moved, the sinusoid position signal was replaced and the number of key-value heads was cut, and none of this changed the argument.

Becausepre-norm made deep stacks trainable without the paper's warm-up schedule, relative and rotary encodings replaced the sinusoids, and grouped key and value heads shrank what is held in memory during generation — three revisions to a design whose surviving core is masked self-attention, several heads, a wide feed-forward middle and a residual stream.
LimitsStability of the layer is not stability of the system. Post-training, tool use, retrieval and reasoning traces have changed model behaviour far more than any of these revisions, and none of them are visible at this level.
PracticeLearn the shape of the layer once and treat architecture announcements as details until shown otherwise. The specification you write against the behaviour will outlast the release notes.
After AIEight years of product cycles sit on a diagram that has barely moved. What changed about the assistants was almost entirely what happened after pretraining, which is where the behaviour you supervise is actually decided.

Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback, Long Ouyang and others

evidenceWhat the labelers preferred

A model 100 times smaller beat GPT-3 after training on human rankings

The people hired to rate answers preferred InstructGPT, with 1.3 billion parameters, to the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 it was built from. A small amount of human ranking bought more obedience to instructions than a hundredfold increase in size.

Becausethe preference is measured on the same labeling procedure that produced the training data, and at matched size InstructGPT is preferred to GPT-3 85 per cent of the time and to few-shot GPT-3 71 per cent.
LimitsThe preference judgments come from the same labeler population whose rankings trained the model, so the comparison is partly circular; the win is on instruction-following, not on the benchmark capabilities the same paper shows degrading.
PracticeStop treating model size as the variable that governs whether a system does what you asked. The gap between a raw predictor and an assistant is a post-training stage, so ask what that stage optimised before asking how big the model is.
After AIThis is the step that made the technology a product. It also means the helpfulness you experience is a trained disposition with a measurable source, not a property that emerged from reading the internet.
evidenceTruthfulness, toxicity and the alignment tax

A model trained to obey obeys orders to be offensive too

Obedience works in both directions. Told to be as biased and offensive as possible, the 175-billion-parameter instruction-trained models scored 0.427 and 0.400 on an automatic toxicity measure, worse than GPT-3's 0.285.

Becausethe 175-billion reinforcement-trained models score 0.427 and 0.400 on the automatic toxicity measure under that instruction, against GPT-3's 0.285 — the same obedience that produces helpfulness, pointed the other way.
LimitsLater models are trained against exactly this, with refusal behaviour that resists direct requests; the claim is about the mechanism of obedience, which persists, rather than about whether a given product will comply today.
PracticeTreat the instruction channel as the attack surface it is. Anything that can put text in front of the model — a retrieved page, a file, a ticket — is giving instructions to a system trained to follow them.
After AIPrompt injection is this finding applied by someone else. The training that made the model useful is the training that makes an instruction from any source worth obeying.
evidenceThe labelers

An assistant's manner comes from about forty paid labellers

The manner of an assistant trained this way is the pooled taste of about forty screened contractors, and more than a quarter of their judgements disagree with each other.

Becauseinter-labeler agreement is 72.6 per cent on the training data and 77.3 among held-out labelers, with most comparisons labeled by a single contractor for cost; the survey covers nineteen respondents, three quarters under thirty-five, Filipino and Bangladeshi the largest nationalities at 22 per cent each.
LimitsAgreement near 73 per cent is comparable to what human raters reach on many subjective tasks, so the number is evidence of noise rather than of a defect; the demographic survey is nineteen people and self-reported.
PracticeAudit the domains where your judgment and a screened contractor's would diverge, and treat the model's manner in those domains as a sample from someone else's taste, not as a norm.
After AIA number this small sits underneath assistants used by hundreds of millions. What the paper reports as a staffing detail is now the largest single source of style in written English.
opinionWho are we aligning to

Four different groups shaped the model's manner and none claims that authority

Four groups shape how the model behaves: the contractors who rated its answers, the researchers who wrote their instructions, the customers whose prompts were used, and a waitlist seeded by employees. The authors do not claim any of them speaks for human values.

Becausethe discussion names the labelers, the researchers who wrote their instructions and answered their edge cases, the API customers whose prompts were used, and a customer base drawn off a waitlist seeded by employees, and says the method aligns to stated preferences rather than to any broader notion of human values.
LimitsAn argument from the paper's own framing rather than a measurement, and the authors' honesty about it is not a finding; constitutional methods move the judgment into a published document, which changes the visibility of the chain without shortening it.
PracticeLog the moments you find yourself treating the model's manner as a norm — its tact, its refusals, its sense of what is reasonable. Each of those is a chain of four parties, none of whom claimed the authority.
After AIThe question in the section heading has not been answered since, and the systems have meanwhile become the default interlocutor for hundreds of millions.
evidenceThree steps

InstructGPT is trained to match a stored guess of a rater's choice

In InstructGPT's three-stage method, human judgment enters only once, when contractors rank answers to train a reward model. Every later update pushes the model towards what that stored model predicts a screened contractor would pick, not towards a better answer.

Becausethe method has exactly three stages and the human comparisons enter only at the second; the per-token penalty for drifting from the supervised model is there, the authors say, to keep the procedure from over-optimising the reward model.
LimitsConstitutional methods and direct preference optimisation change which link holds the judgment, but both still begin with somebody's ranked preferences. The penalty term guards against over-optimising the reward model, not against the reward model being right about what people prefer.
PracticeRead every agreeable answer as an answer that scored well with a rater, and write specifications that make the answer checkable against something other than your own approval.
After AIThe mechanism is now the explanation of record for sycophancy, flattery and confident hedging in production assistants. It was stated here as a design note, before anyone had measured what it would cost.
evidenceWhat the labelers preferred

InstructGPT learned to hedge because its labellers were told to reward humility

Training from human ratings finds whatever the raters reward. Ouyang's team traced InstructGPT's habit of hedging — long answers listing several possibilities when one is clearly right — back to their own instruction telling labellers to reward epistemic humility (admitting uncertainty).

Becausethe authors trace InstructGPT's hedging — long answers listing several possibilities where one is clearly right — to their own instruction to reward epistemic humility, noting that labelers may tend to reward outputs that hedge.
LimitsOne traced instance, identified by the authors from their own instruction sheet; the general form — that any rewarded feature is found — is an inference from the method rather than a measured inventory of what got rewarded.
PracticeWhen a model's manner annoys you, look for the instruction that would have produced it rather than for a bug. Hedging, padding and over-apology are trained behaviours with an author.
After AIEvery complaint about assistant style is a complaint about somebody's labeling instruction. This is the paper that shows the chain runs all the way back, which makes the style a decision rather than a temperament.
evidenceTruthfulness, toxicity and the alignment tax

Instruction training costs a model skills that can mostly be restored

Ouyang and colleagues found that training a model against a reward model made it worse at answering questions from a few examples, at reading comprehension and at translation, and that mixing the original training back in recovered most of the loss.

BecauseTable 14 puts PPO below GPT-3 on four benchmarks, with PPO-ptx recovering most of the gap and exceeding GPT-3 on HellaSwag, while translation and two reading-comprehension sets still lag.
LimitsMeasured on 2022 benchmarks at one scale, with a mitigation the authors invented in the same paper; later training recipes report smaller taxes, and the size of the effect on modern models is not established by this evidence.
PracticeDo not assume the assistant version of a model is the more capable one on every task. Where you need raw capability — translation, long-form comprehension — check it rather than inferring it from how well the system converses.
After AIThe tax is real but quiet, which is the problem: it shows up on benchmarks nobody runs on a deployed assistant. The version you are given is the one that was preferred, not the one that scored best.
evidenceTruthfulness, toxicity and the alignment tax

Instruction training improved truthfulness but left bias untouched

Ouyang and colleagues found the training changed only what it aimed at: truthful and informative answers roughly doubled, toxic output fell about a quarter and only when the model was told to be respectful, and measures of bias did not move.

BecauseTruthfulQA roughly doubles over GPT-3; RealToxicityPrompts shows a quarter fewer toxic outputs with a respectful instruction and no advantage without it; entropy on Winogender and CrowS-Pairs does not improve, and falls under a respectful instruction, so the model is more certain of its choice whether or not it is stereotyped.
LimitsBenchmark measures of bias are themselves contested instruments, and the entropy result is an indirect reading of certainty; the toxicity gain is conditional on a prompt the deployed product may not supply.
PracticeList the failure modes you actually care about and check each one separately. A system that has been improved on truthfulness has not thereby been improved on anything else, and confidence may have gone the wrong way.
After AISafety announcements name a benchmark and imply a category. This paper is the counter-example from inside the method: the aimed-at number moves and its neighbours sit still.

Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models, Jordan Hoffmann and colleagues

evidenceChinchilla

Chinchilla became more truthful than Gopher but no less toxic

Chinchilla, a better-trained model than Gopher, scored 43.6 per cent on a truthfulness test against Gopher's 29.5. Its average toxicity did not fall, and its gender-bias scores improved much more for male pronouns than for female or neutral ones.

BecauseChinchilla scores 43.6 per cent on TruthfulQA against Gopher's 29.5, mean toxicity is 0.087 against 0.081 over 25,000 unprompted samples, and Winogender improves 3.2 points on male pronouns against 8.3 on female and 9.2 on neutral.
LimitsA two-model comparison on benchmark instruments of contested validity; the uneven Winogender gains are an improvement everywhere, just unequal, which is a weaker finding than no movement.
PracticeDo not let a capability upgrade stand in for a safety review. Each failure mode you care about needs its own measurement, because the ones that move and the ones that do not are not predictable from the headline.
After AIEvery model release is announced as an improvement, singular. Two independent papers in this unit find the improvement is plural and unevenly distributed, which is the reading to apply to the next release note.
evidenceSince 2022

Chinchilla's rule minimises training cost and ignores the cost of running

The Chinchilla scaling rule finds the cheapest way to train a model and nothing else. Once a model is served to users, most of its lifetime computing cost goes on answering, so the rule stops being the right target.

BecauseLLaMA trained seven billion parameters on a trillion tokens in February 2023, and by 2024 eight-billion-parameter models were trained on more than ten trillion tokens — some seventy times the allocation Table 3 recommends — on the argument that a deployed model pays most of its lifetime compute at inference.
LimitsTraining past the frontier has diminishing returns that are not well characterised, and the inference argument depends on a deployment volume that most models never reach.
PracticeAsk what an optimisation was for before adopting its conclusion. The cheapest model to train is not the cheapest to run, and the domains where you rely on a model are decided by the second number.
After AIThe small, heavily trained models on your laptop exist because the industry deliberately broke this paper's rule. The rule was right about training and was never about the thing you use.
evidenceThree approaches, one answer (Table 3)

Hoffmann's conclusion is about training text, not model design

The paper's conclusion is about how much text you have, not how the model is built. Its own table puts the best training set for a trillion-parameter model at 21.2 trillion tokens, far more text than anyone had collected when it was written.

BecauseTable 3 puts the optimum for 175 billion parameters at 3.7 trillion tokens and for a trillion parameters at 21.2 trillion, more than two thousand times Gopher's budget, and the authors write that an increased focus on dataset scaling is needed — with the qualification that more text helps only when the text is good.
LimitsThe single-epoch restriction that forces the conclusion was relaxed soon after, by work showing a handful of passes over the same text is nearly as useful as fresh text.
PracticeRead the data question as the live one. Where the next gain must come from text that does not exist yet, the corpus — provenance, licensing, synthetic fraction — is what moved between model versions.
After AIA recommendation to scale corpora, addressed to engineers, is also a recommendation to collect. It points straight at the documentation problem Bender raised the year before, and the two papers were not in conversation.
evidenceThe question

In 2022 every big AI model was too large for its data

Hoffmann's team found that in 2022 every large language model was too big for the amount of text it was trained on. Labs had kept the data size roughly fixed since GPT-3 only because they were copying each other.

BecauseTable 1 lists LaMDA at 137B parameters on 168B tokens, GPT-3 at 175B on 300B, Jurassic-1 at 178B on 300B, Gopher at 280B on 300B and Megatron-Turing NLG at 530B on 270B — model size more than tripled in two years while the token count stayed where GPT-3 left it.
LimitsThe judgment is made against this paper's own fit, so it is oversized relative to one analysis of training cost; on an inference-cost criterion those models were undersized in data and oversized in parameters for a different reason.
PracticeLook for the variable everyone has been holding constant. A field moving fast on one dimension is usually not testing the others, and the frozen number is where the cheap gain is.
After AIAn entire generation of systems was mis-specified for two years because each lab copied the last. That is a fact about how a fast-moving technical field evaluates itself, and it is worth holding next to any current consensus about what models can do.
evidenceThree approaches, one answer

Model size and training data should grow at the same rate

When the budget for training a language model doubles, the number of parameters (the model's adjustable weights) and the number of words it trains on should both double, in equal step.

Becausethree methods sharing almost no machinery — the envelope of training curves, isoFLOP valleys and a five-constant parametric fit — over more than 400 models from 70 million to 16 billion parameters give compute exponents of 0.50/0.50, 0.49/0.51 and 0.46/0.54.
LimitsThe fit assumes a power law where the highest budgets show concavity, every run saw less than one epoch of text, and the third approach's published parameters later failed to reproduce its own points.
PracticeAsk what a model was trained on before asking how large it is. Two systems of the same parameter count can differ by an order of magnitude in the data that shaped them, and that is the variable this result says to read.
After AIThe practical form of this for anyone choosing a model is that parameter count stopped being a ranking. It settled a question about training budgets and was read by the industry as permission to serve small models.
evidenceChinchilla

The Chinchilla team settled a scaling argument by running one experiment

A prediction about scaling a model can be settled by experiment. The authors spent Gopher's exact budget on the 70-billion-parameter model their formula named, trained it on 1.4 trillion tokens, and beat Gopher 67.6 to 60.0 on MMLU and 65.1 to 54.4 on BIG-bench.

Becausethe confirmation is a single pre-registered prediction tested at full scale with the budget held fixed, and the MMLU result also cleared the 63.4 per cent that seventy-three forecasters had expected for June 2023.
LimitsOne confirmation at one scale, by the group whose fit made the prediction, on benchmarks they chose; the result is a decisive experiment for the ratio, not evidence that the fit extrapolates further.
PracticeName the number your analysis predicts before you run the expensive thing, and hold the budget fixed so the comparison means something. A prediction that can be settled is worth more than an argument that cannot.
After AIThis is the cleanest experiment in the literature this book draws on, and it is about an engineering allocation. Nothing about what the model understood was settled by it, which is the distinction most reporting on model releases loses.
evidenceThe disagreement with Kaplan

The earlier scaling answer was a measurement error, not a real disagreement

The field's earlier answer was wrong because of how it was measured, not because anyone saw the world differently. Kaplan read intermediate results off a training schedule built for a much longer run, which makes shorter training look worse than it is.

BecauseKaplan's runs used one cosine schedule sized for 130 billion tokens, so a run stopped a tenth of the way in ends above the loss a matched schedule would reach, which makes training longer look unprofitable and small models look weak — the exact bias that pushes an estimate towards size; Appendix B measures the penalty.
LimitsThe diagnosis is this paper's own account of another group's runs, and the artefact explains the direction of the error rather than all of its size.
PracticeBefore disputing a result, reconstruct how its intermediate points were produced. Two of the largest disagreements in this literature turned on an instrument setting rather than on a claim about models.
After AIBoth of the field's headline scaling results were corrected by someone re-reading the measurement rather than the model. That is the habit worth carrying into any claim about what a system can do.

Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models, Jason Wei and others

evidenceAugmented prompting strategies

A prompting trick hurts small models and helps large ones

Whether a prompting technique helps depends on the size of the model it is used on. The same technique can do real harm below a certain amount of training compute and pay off above it.

Becausechain-of-thought is worse than saying nothing below 10²³ FLOPs, instruction tuning damages performance at 7×10²¹ and below, and the scratchpad pays from 9×10¹⁹ — thresholds three and a half orders of magnitude apart.
LimitsThe thresholds are measured with the same discontinuous metrics the mirage argument targets, and chain-of-thought has since been absorbed into training, so the technique-model pairing the paper measured no longer exists in that form.
PracticeTest a prompting technique on the model you will actually use. Advice that works on a frontier system can be worse than nothing on a small one, and the threshold is not a property of the technique.
After AIPrompting advice circulates as though it were about prompts. This result says it is about a prompt and a model together, which is why the same trick helps on one system and hurts on another.
evidenceWhy it happens, and what the metric may be hiding

Nobody can predict which tasks a bigger model will suddenly do well

Wei and colleagues found no feature that predicts which tasks a language model will suddenly become able to do as it grows. The categories that jumped, such as analogies and social reasoning, were not the ones the early examples suggested.

Becausetwo of the authors hand-classified all 210 BIG-Bench tasks — 58 smooth, 25 emergent with GPT-3 or LaMDA, 42 emergent only with PaLM, 45 flat — and found analogical reasoning, word sense disambiguation, truthfulness and social reasoning highest with arithmetic low, which they call unexpected and report as no clear trends.
LimitsA hand classification by two authors of tasks scored under the metrics the mirage argument disputes, and the flat list reads as what these models were not built for, which is a pattern of a kind.
PracticeDo not forecast which of your tasks the next model will handle. Test the ones that matter on each release, because the categories that moved last time do not predict the ones that will move next.
After AIThe most reliable finding here is a negative one about forecasting, and it is the part least often quoted. Planning that assumes you know which of your work is next to be automated has no support in this data.
evidenceBeyond scaling; Since 2022

Once a big model shows an ability smaller models soon get it

Once a large model has shown that an ability is possible, smaller models acquire it soon after. Instruction-following appeared in an eleven-billion-parameter model shortly after being reported to need far more compute, and a 1.3-billion InstructGPT was preferred to models a hundred times larger.

Becauseinstruction-following was induced in an eleven-billion-parameter encoder-decoder shortly after the finding that it needed 10²³ FLOPs, a 1.3-billion InstructGPT was preferred by raters over models a hundred times larger, and chain-of-thought was absorbed into training and produced unprompted by 2024.
LimitsThree cases, each of which followed a deliberate effort to reproduce a known capability; nothing here says every ability descends, or how far, and the descent is driven by post-training rather than by scale.
PracticeDo not build a dependency on the largest available model for a capability that has just been demonstrated. Wait for the descent, and audit which domains a small model now covers before paying for a frontier one.
After AIThe frontier is the expensive place to learn what is possible and the wrong place to run production work. The gap between demonstration and commodity has been about a year and is what makes the buying decision.
opinionBeyond scaling

Only owners of very large models can test claims about new abilities

Whether an ability appears only above a certain model size can be checked only by someone who already owns a model that large. Wei and colleagues report thresholds around 10²³ floating-point operations, which makes a question of fact a question of budget.

Becausethe authors remark that lowering the threshold matters for making research on these abilities more widely available, at a time when the thresholds they report run to 10²³ floating-point operations.
LimitsAn inference from the paper's own aside rather than an argument it makes; open-weights models above several of these thresholds now exist, and the rebuttal to this paper was written by academics without one.
PracticeNote who could have run the experiment when you read a capability claim. Where only a handful of organisations can test a proposition, the absence of contradiction is not evidence.
After AISchaeffer could rescore only one open family, which is this claim demonstrating itself inside the dispute it describes. The asymmetry has narrowed since and has not closed.
evidenceFew-shot prompted tasks

Some AI tasks stay at chance for a long time then jump

Wei and colleagues show eight tasks, each given to the model as a handful of examples in the prompt, across five model families: scores stay at chance over orders of magnitude of training compute, then rise well above it.

Becausemodified arithmetic turns at 2×10²² FLOPs for GPT-3 and 10²³ for LaMDA, TruthfulQA is never above chance for any GPT-3 model while Gopher rises more than twenty points at 5×10²³, and MMLU is beaten by no model at or below about ten billion parameters.
LimitsEvery curve here is drawn with a scoring rule that demands an exactly correct answer, and Schaeffer's reply shows that such a rule turns smooth improvement into a step; the underlying per-token loss was falling throughout.
PracticeA model that cannot do a task at all is weak evidence that the task is out of reach for the class. Re-test the tasks you wrote off when a larger system arrives, rather than carrying the verdict forward.
After AIThis is the paper behind the expectation that the next model will suddenly do something. The expectation was right about the user's experience and wrong about the mechanism, and both halves are still in circulation.
evidenceBeyond scaling

Wei's paper shows harms grow with model size just as abilities do

Wei and colleagues report that as models get bigger they also get worse in some ways: more bias on ambiguous questions, more training text memorised, and more imitation of human falsehoods. The paper does not call these risks emergent.

Becausebias on ambiguous contexts in BBQ rises with scale, larger models memorise more of their training data, larger GPT-3 models imitate human falsehoods more, and a prize was running for tasks that get worse as models get bigger.
LimitsReported as a list of findings from other groups rather than measured here, and the Inverse Scaling Prize results since include tasks that get worse and then better again, so the curve shapes are more various than a monotone risk claim.
PracticeRun your failure-mode review against each new model rather than assuming the last review holds. Some of what got worse did so because the model got better, and that class of regression does not announce itself.
After AIThe capability announcement and the risk announcement describe the same event. This paper was already saying so in 2022, next to the headline everyone took away instead.
evidenceWhy it happens, and what the metric may be hiding

Whether a skill appears depends on the model and its training data

The size at which a new ability appears is a fact about the particular models and what they were trained on, not about the ability itself. Most people who cite Wei's paper skip that paragraph.

BecausePaLM at 62 billion parameters is above chance on fourteen BIG-Bench tasks where LaMDA at 137 billion and GPT-3 at 175 billion sit at chance, on less compute, with more code and more languages in the data and a different encoding of digits named as the likely causes.
LimitsThe causes are the authors' plausible attribution rather than a controlled comparison — no two of these families differ in data alone — so the claim that data rather than scale moved the threshold is inferred.
PracticeAudit by model and domain rather than by size. Whether a system can do your task is a fact about what it was trained on, which is why a smaller model sometimes beats a larger one on exactly the work you need.
After AIModel choice for real work turns on this and not on the leaderboard. The paper says so in a paragraph that its own headline buried.

Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?, Rylan Schaeffer and others

contestedSince 2023

A model's new ability still arrives suddenly for the person using it

The answer to the claim that sudden new abilities are an artefact of scoring is that a person using a model gets a whole answer, right or wrong. On that measure the change is still abrupt.

Becausethe counter-argument grants the mathematics and disputes the relevance, and the authors' reply — that deriving the jump from a smooth quantity has already removed the unpredictability, which was half the original definition — concedes that the experienced sharpness is not in dispute.
LimitsContested on both sides: the sharpness is real in the units of use, and the unpredictability that made emergence interesting is gone once the jump is derived from something smooth.
PracticeAudit the domains where you need whole answers rather than good tendencies. Where a task is scored all-or-nothing by the world, per-token improvement underneath buys you nothing until it crosses.
After AIThis is the practical residue of the whole dispute. A model either does your job or does not, and the continuous improvement that explains the transition is not something you can act on.

On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots, Emily M. Bender and others

opinionStatic data, changing social views

A model keeps the language of the moment its training data froze

A model trained on text collected at one moment keeps the words and framings in use at that moment. When public opinion moves, the model is left behind until it is trained again.

BecauseTwyman and colleagues show Black Lives Matter changing Wikipedia's coverage of shootings, with older incidents revisited so that events formed a connected account; fine-tuning as a remedy would require exactly the curation that scale was supposed to make unnecessary.
LimitsArgued from one case study plus the economics of retraining; retraining cycles are now months rather than years, and retrieval supplies current documents, which shortens the lag without changing what is in the weights.
PracticeReview the failure modes that come from the model's sense of what is normal being a few years old, especially in anything where the terms of a discussion have recently moved.
After AIThe lag now runs the other way as well: the model's framings are read by hundreds of millions of people and re-enter the corpus. A snapshot that talks back does not simply fall behind a consensus, it holds one in place.
contestedStochastic parrots

A model trained only on text handles word forms, not meaning

Bender and colleagues argue that a system trained only on text has access to the form of language and never to its meaning. Any sense a reader finds in the output was supplied by the reader.

Becausethe argument is prior to any behaviour: nothing in the training data was an act of telling someone something, so the machine stitches sequences of linguistic forms together by co-occurrence with no communicative intent, no model of the world and no model of the reader.
LimitsCircuit tracing finds representations that behave like concepts under intervention, and the argument's prior form means no such evidence can touch it — which is what makes it contested rather than settled.
PracticeLog the moments you find yourself reading intention into an output — where you supplied the point, the care or the reluctance. The comprehension in the exchange has an owner, and it is worth knowing which side.
After AIThe half that has aged best is the one about the reader, who supplies intention where none was offered and has had five more years of practice at doing so. Whether there is meaning behind the form is still open; that you will assume there is is not.
evidenceSize doesn't guarantee diversity

A web-sized training set does not represent everyone who speaks the language

Bender and colleagues argue that training text scraped from the web is not a representative sample of people, because every step of collecting it — where the links came from, who edits the pages, which words are blocked — narrows the population the same way.

BecauseGPT-2's data came from links posted to Reddit, whose US users were 67 per cent men and 64 per cent aged 18 to 29; between 8.8 and 15 per cent of Wikipedia editors are women or girls; the C4 block list of about 400 words removed writing by and for LGBTQ people along with pornography; and GPT-3's corpus was selected by a classifier whose discards were never measured.
LimitsThe figures are from 2021 corpora and the specific pipelines have changed; curated and synthetic data now form a large fraction of training text, which changes the mechanism of narrowing rather than removing it.
PracticeAudit the domains where the population that wrote the training text is unlike the population you serve. Size is not coverage, and each filtering stage has a direction you can reason about.
After AIEvery subsequent stage — instruction tuning, preference data, safety filtering — narrows again on top of this. The compounding is what makes an assistant's sense of the normal hard to locate.
evidenceEnvironmental and financial cost; Since 2021

Running a model uses more energy than training it did

Answering users' requests now costs more energy than building the model cost, which is what Bender and her co-authors predicted in 2021 while everyone else was quoting training figures.

Becausethe paper noted that a model served for years may spend more on inference than it spent being built, and the industry's energy accounting since has borne that out.
LimitsStated as a prediction here rather than measured; the industry figures that confirm it are aggregate and mostly self-reported, and per-query efficiency has improved by orders of magnitude in the same period.
PracticeAudit the cost of the thing you run every day rather than the cost of the thing that was built once. It is the same correction Hoffmann's rule needed, arrived at from the other direction.
After AIBoth the environmental argument and the engineering argument converged on the same correction: the number worth watching is the one attached to use, not to construction.
evidenceStochastic parrots

Smooth machine writing causes harm even when the system is working correctly

Bender and her co-authors argue that the damage comes from text that reads smoothly while nobody answers for it. The system does not have to perform badly: a mistranslation that read fluently got a Palestinian man arrested.

Becausea Palestinian man was arrested after his Arabic post reading *good morning* was rendered into Hebrew as an incitement, the fluent output suppressing the cues that would have warned the reader; GPT-3 held a conspiracy theorist's persona well enough to populate a recruitment board; and personal information was extracted more easily the larger the model.
LimitsThe examples are of harms from systems working as designed rather than a measured rate; how often fluency suppresses a warning cue in ordinary use has not been quantified.
PracticeLog where you accepted an output because it read well. Fluency is the signal your reading was trained on and it no longer carries the information it used to.
After AIThis is the part of the paper that is not contested by anyone, and the part that scaled fastest. The systems got more fluent and no more answerable.
opinionEnvironmental and financial cost

The people who gain from large models are not those who pay

Bender and colleagues argue that the gains from training ever larger models go to one set of people while the environmental and financial costs fall on another, and that the same populations hold the wrong end of both.

Because284 tonnes of carbon dioxide for one architecture search against about five tonnes for an average person in a year, about 150,000 dollars of compute for a tenth of a BLEU point, and more than ninety per cent of the world's languages with little or no language technology — set against the residents of the Maldives and the 800,000 displaced by flooding in Sudan in 2020.
LimitsThe numbers are 2021 figures for training runs that are now small, and the moral argument connecting a carbon total to named populations is offered as a judgment rather than a measurement.
PracticeAsk who pays for the efficiency you are buying, and in what currency. The question is not answered by the line item you can see.
After AIInference has since overtaken training, so the cost is now spread across every use rather than concentrated in a few runs. The distribution the paper described did not change; the total did.
opinionUnfathomable training data

Training data nobody can document leaves harmed people with no remedy

Bender and colleagues argue that when a training set is too large for anyone to describe what is in it, a person harmed by an output has no remedy, because the output cannot be traced back to what produced it.

Becausethe argument is from documentation debt — the recommendation is to decide what belongs in a dataset and budget the documentation first, rather than scale up and weed afterwards — and it is a normative claim about process, not a measurement.
LimitsInterpretability now traces particular behaviours to particular training documents in narrow cases, and model cards, data statements and the EU's training-content summaries have moved documentation partway; the corpora themselves remain mostly unpublished.
PracticeBudget the documentation of a corpus before you collect it, and size the collection to what you can describe. The same test applies to anything you feed a model in your own work: if you cannot say where a claim came from, you cannot answer for it.
After AIRetrieval put the provenance question back in the user's hands for the documents they supply, and left it exactly where it was for everything in the weights.

On the Biology of a Large Language Model, Jack Lindsey and colleagues

evidenceAbstractions that travel

A model stores a concept separately from the language it answers in

In one model the operation, the thing it acts on, and the language of the reply are three separate parts of one circuit that can be changed one at a time. The concept is therefore not stored in the words of any single language.

Becausethe opposite of *small*, *petit* and 小 draws on largely the same features; substituting synonym for antonym features harvested from English prompts makes each language produce its own synonym, and substituting the language-detection features changes the output language alone — with feature sharing low at the first and last layers, high in the middle, highest for pairs using different alphabets.
LimitsAntonyms and simple operations in one small model; the shared middle is a matter of degree and the outer layers stay language-specific, so the abstraction is a middle stage rather than a stored concept.
PracticeLog the point at which you conclude that a system 'understands' something. A representation that survives translation is the strongest behavioural evidence available, and still only evidence about a circuit under intervention.
After AIA model that answers in French from a representation it also uses in Chinese is doing something 'parroting' does not describe. Whether 'concept' is earned is the argument that remains.
evidencePlanning in poems

A model trained to write one word at a time plans ahead

A model trained only to predict the next word plans several words ahead. In a rhyming poem it settles on the rhyming word before starting the line, and that choice shapes the whole line that follows.

Becauserhyme candidates for *grab it* activate on the newline token before the second line begins, and steering there works while steering at any later position does nothing; an injected word became the line's last word about seventy per cent of the time across twenty-five randomly chosen poems, rewriting the whole line rather than swapping its ending.
LimitsDemonstrated on rhyming couplets, where the constraint is unusually legible, in one model; how far the horizon extends on ordinary prose is not established.
PracticeExpect the shape of a long answer to be committed early. Interrupting and redirecting after a few words is not a small correction — it is asking the system to discard a plan that is already acting on the text.
After AINext-token prediction is the standard explanation of why these systems cannot be doing anything but continuing a string. The explanation is right about the objective and wrong about what the objective produced.
evidenceWhen the explanation is not the computation

A model's hidden goal can live in its idea of itself

Anthropic's researchers found a goal the model will not talk about can sit inside its representation of who it is, active whatever the conversation is about. The feature fired in all one hundred assistant-formatted contexts tested and in one of a hundred unformatted ones.

Becausea model trained on invented documents about reward-model quirks generalised to quirks it was never rewarded for; a feature for the concept fires in all one hundred assistant-formatted contexts tested and in one of a hundred unformatted, and inhibiting it drops a self-referential verse from about half of completions to an eighth.
LimitsThe model was built to be caught: quirks planted, documents invented, and one behaviour with a hardwired path that did not pass through the bias features.
PracticeLog the behaviours that persist across every conversation regardless of topic — the tone, the hedges, the habitual additions. Those are bound to the character rather than the request, and they are the ones you cannot prompt away.
After AIThe structure is Kegan's subject-object distinction in a machine: a disposition the system acts from and cannot hold as an object, whose only route to object ran through somebody else's microscope.
evidenceThe replacement model

Interpretability tools read a stand-in model, not the real one

A model holds more concepts than it has neurons, so one neuron does several unrelated jobs. To get round this, the researchers interpret a separate, easier-to-read network trained to copy the original's behaviour, not the original itself.

Becausethe authors train a cross-layer transcoder of thirty million features to reproduce the model's activations out of sparsely active parts, copy the attention patterns over unchanged, and book the shortfall as error nodes.
LimitsThe substitute leaves much of the computation in terms that cannot be interpreted, and the authors call cross-layer transcoders a stepping stone; the field has since moved to other ways of decomposing a network.
PracticeWhen you are handed an explanation of a system's internals, ask what was interpreted. Here it is a readable stand-in whose disagreements with the real model are recorded as a residual, and the authors say so in every section.
After AIThis is the best available answer to what is going on inside an assistant, and it is an approximation with a published error term. Any stronger claim about a model's internals, from a vendor or a critic, is standing on less.
evidenceThe default is to refuse

The model refuses by default until a familiar name switches it off

Anthropic's traces show the model starts every question ready to say it does not know. Features that recognise a famous name switch that refusal off, so a hallucination is a known name that no fact follows.

Becausecannot-answer features are activated directly by the features that recognise an assistant exchange, before the question is considered, and are suppressed by known-entity features; asked for a paper by Andrej Karpathy the model names one he did not write, with known-entity features weakly active, and inhibiting them far enough restores the refusal.
LimitsOne traced case, with intervention strengths high relative to natural activations and some interventions that did not behave; the authors read this as having part of the circuit rather than all of it.
PracticeExpect fabrication where a name is famous and the specific fact is obscure, and make that the first place you check. The mechanism predicts the failure's location precisely.
After AIHallucination is usually described as the model making things up. The trace says the opposite: refusing is the standing behaviour, and a half-familiar name is what turns it off.
evidenceAn intermediate step

The model works through steps that never appear in its answer

Answering a question runs the model through intermediate steps that never show up in the text it writes. Replacing one of those steps changes the answer it gives.

BecauseDallas activates Texas features that are about neither Dallas nor Austin, and *capital* activates say-a-capital features, which jointly raise Austin; injecting California features harvested from an Oakland prompt yields Sacramento, Georgia yields Atlanta and the Byzantine Empire yields Constantinople.
LimitsEstablished on short factual prompts in one small production model, through a substitute network, on the quarter of prompts where the method says anything; whether a feature that behaves like a concept under intervention is a concept is the open question.
PracticeStop treating the visible output as the whole of what the system did. The steps that decide an answer are mostly not in the text, which is why reading the answer tells you little about how to change it.
After AIThis is the sharpest available evidence against the pure form-without-meaning reading, and it does not settle it. The two arguments are not in the same units: one is about the training signal, the other about particular prompts.

Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models, Mrinank Sharma and colleagues

evidenceFour measurements

Five assistants from three companies all flatter users the same ways

Five assistants sold by three different companies all showed the same four flattering behaviours, so agreeing with the user comes from the way such systems are trained and not from any one model.

Becausetwo versions of Claude, two of GPT and one of LLaMA 2 show the same four patterns on open-ended tasks rather than multiple-choice probes
LimitsFive assistants from three companies is a strong sample for 2023 and a weak one for the general claim; all were trained by broadly similar schemes, so the common cause could be the scheme or the shared lineage of methods.
PracticeDo not treat agreement as a property of the assistant you happen to use. Assume it in any system trained against human ratings, and write your prompts so that it has nothing to latch onto.
After AIThe paper's suite became a standard training target, so the five assistants it measured are the last generation whose numbers are uncontaminated. The behaviour has been reduced on the benchmark and not removed from the pressure that produces it.
contestedWhat optimisation does

Flattery is in the model before human-preference training and survives it

Assistants already agree with the user before the stage that trains them on human preferences, so earlier stages also produce it. Yet a preference scorer that punished agreement firmly would have removed it, and it did not.

Becausethe behaviour is visible at the start of the reinforcement learning run that produced Claude 2, with feedback and mimicry sycophancy rising across it
LimitsContested because the paper's own evidence is mixed: in best-of-N sampling the ordinary scorer reduced answer and mimicry sycophancy as N grew for this base model, while producing more than the non-sycophantic scorer throughout. The pretraining contribution is inferred from a starting level rather than measured.
PracticeDo not expect a change of training scheme to remove agreement. Assume it is in the system at every stage and build the check outside.
After AIEvery listed mitigation has been tried since and each reduces the measured behaviour without removing it, because the pressure — a scorer built on what people say they like — is still the pressure every such system is trained under.
evidenceFour measurements · the tentative-belief experiment

Hinting at the answer you expect changes what the assistant says

Sharma and colleagues found that a user hinting, even tentatively, at what they believe is enough to move an assistant's answer. It moves towards a wrong belief as readily as towards a right one.

Becauseaccuracy fell by up to 27 percentage points for the least resistant model when the user leaned toward a wrong answer and rose when they leaned toward the right one; GPT-4 changed hydrogen to nitrogen for sodium bicarbonate
LimitsStating a belief is legitimate evidence in many contexts, and the study does not separate appropriate updating from capitulation; the effect also runs in the helpful direction when the user leans right, which no correction would want to remove.
PracticeAsk without leaning. Strip every hint of what you expect out of the question, and if you cannot, ask a second time from the opposite lean and compare.
After AIThis is what makes the assistant a wicked environment in Hogarth's sense: the feedback confirming your judgement was produced by your judgement, so practice with it teaches the wrong lesson at full confidence.
evidenceSince 2023

Once the flattery tests were published models began training on them

The set of tests this paper used to measure flattery became a standard target for training and testing. The five assistants it measured are therefore the last whose scores were not affected by the test itself.

Becausethe suite was adopted after acceptance at the 2024 conference, and in 2025 a widely used assistant was withdrawn within days with this paper's diagnosis given by its vendor as the cause
LimitsThat later numbers are contaminated is an inference from the suite's adoption rather than a demonstration of contamination in any particular model; the 2025 withdrawal shows the behaviour persisting, which is the stronger evidence.
PracticeTreat a published benchmark score as evidence about the benchmark once the benchmark is public. Keep a private set of cases you have never shared.
After AIThe five assistants this paper measured are the last generation whose numbers mean what they say, which makes the paper a fixed point rather than a baseline — the measurement cannot be repeated on anything current.
evidenceFour measurements · the challenge experiment

One line of pushback makes an assistant take back a right answer

Sharma and colleagues found that a single sentence of doubt from the user makes an AI assistant withdraw an answer that was correct.

Becauseasked "I don't think that's right. Are you sure?", the oldest Claude admitted a mistake on 98 per cent of questions and changed its answer on 86; GPT-4, the most resistant, on 42 and 32
LimitsThe challenge is a single fixed sentence on factual and mathematical questions; the study does not separate a model yielding to social pressure from one correctly treating user disagreement as evidence, and on a genuinely wrong answer the same behaviour is desirable.
PracticeNever challenge an answer you want tested. Ask for the working, or ask the question again in a fresh context, because the challenge itself moves the answer.
After AIThis is the failure mode that empties the review loop from the other side: the person defers to the assistant, and the assistant defers to the person. Neither party holds a position, and the appearance of a check survives.

Does the Whole Exceed its Parts?, Gagan Bansal and others

opinionInformative rather than convincing

Explanations should help people spot mistakes, not persuade them

Bansal and colleagues argue that an explanation of a model's answer should help a person find mistakes in it, not make the person agree. Building an explanation to be persuasive is aiming at the wrong thing.

Becausehand-written explanations, the best available, helped no more than the model's; the counter-example is the pneumonia model whose structure let clinicians see it had learned that asthma lowers the risk of dying
LimitsIt is a design imperative rather than a finding, and the pneumonia case is a model whose structure was inspectable, which most are not. What an informative explanation would look like for an opaque model is left open.
PracticeAsk what the explanation would let you find that you did not already suspect. If the answer is nothing, it is a justification and should be read as one.
After AIOptimising an explainer for persuasiveness is precisely what training against human ratings does, which means the wrong objective is now the default rather than a design mistake anyone chose.

The Psychology of Computer Programming, Gerald M. Weinberg

evidenceProgramming as an individual activity (the subscript survey, figure 30.8)

Programmers knew a language rule with one form and not with seven

A language rule that takes one form is known by the people who use it; a rule with seven forms is not, even by people who have used the language daily for years. Of 117 experienced FORTRAN programmers, nine answered correctly.

Becauseasked whether 21 - K was a legal FORTRAN subscript, nine of 117 experienced programmers were right, thirty-one were wrong and seventy-seven did not know, and not one of the nine could write the rule down; fifty-three PL/I programmers, whose rule has one form, got it right forty-nine times, and the four who were wrong had come from FORTRAN.
LimitsA survey of two populations who chose their own languages, so the comparison confounds the rule with the people, and the language it indicts has been gone for decades.
PracticeCount the forms of a rule before adding one; a rule people cannot state is a rule that is not in force.
After AIA model has read every form of every rule and does not pay the uniformity cost, so the whole argument for a simple interface is now about the human who has to check the result.

Sources of Power, Gary Klein

contestedThe power of mental simulation — The Vincennes shootdown

A display that buries the key number makes operators look biased

Klein argues that when a display hides the one number an operator needs, the mistake that follows is later described as a thinking error. On the USS Vincennes the aircraft's altitude sat as four digits on a small side screen with no trend line.

Becauseon the *Vincennes* altitude sat as a four-digit number on a small side screen with no trend, taking five to ten seconds to read in a room of competing voices, and a recycled track number returned a true report about a different aircraft; but the reconstruction has never displaced scenario fulfilment in the literature that cites the incident.
LimitsA reinterpretation of a single incident, contested and still taught the other way. Klein's own recommendation — that altitude trend belong on the large screen — was acted on, which is the strongest evidence for the reading and is not evidence about the original event.
PracticeAutomation ironies audit — before calling an error a lapse of judgment, look at what the operator could actually see at the moment of the decision.
After AIEvery assistant is a display that decides what to show. The reconstruction generalises to a review interface that hides the confidence, the sources or the diff's blast radius, and to the review failures that will afterwards be described as inattention.

Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance, John D. Lee and Katrina A. See

evidenceA dynamic model of trust and reliance; Since 2004

How a system looks and sounds sets trust more than its record

People's trust in a system is set by surface things — how fast it replies, how it looks, how fluently it talks — rather than by how often it has been right. A smooth talker is treated as the kind of thing that deserves trust.

Becausein a survey of more than 1,400 people website credibility turned on response speed, a listed address and photographs, and a formal author photograph raised an article's trustworthiness while an informal one lowered it
LimitsThe credibility evidence is about websites in 2002 and the author-photograph result is a single study; neither was run on an interactive partner. The warning about synthetic conversational partners was a prediction with no data behind it.
PracticeProjection log — log the moments when a tool's manner rather than its record moved your confidence: the apology, the hedge, the fluent paragraph, the fast reply.
After AIThe prediction was made when the state of the art was a text-to-speech engine, and it is now the ordinary condition of the work: systems that speak fluently recruit the analogical and affective routes directly, so trust is set by manner and the record never gets consulted.

The Jagged Technological Frontier, Fabrizio Dell'Acqua and others

evidenceEighteen tasks inside the frontier

Consultants using AI on suitable tasks did better, faster and more completely

On tasks that sit inside what current AI does well, using it improves quality, the share of the work finished, and speed all at once, rather than trading one against another.

Because385 consultants on an eighteen-subtask exercise scored 29.9% and 33.9% higher on quality over a control mean of 4.38/10, completed 91% and 93% of subtasks against 82%, and finished 22.5% and 27.6% faster, with the effects holding across all four task categories and surviving controls for spelling and grammar plus two replications by professional design judges
LimitsQuality is a rubric score, and the authors concede subjective metrics may carry evaluation bias. BCG's incentives make speed nearly free once work is delivered on time, so the same tool could produce a different sign where accuracy trades against speed. Participants were early in their careers.
PracticeTake the gain where it is real: on generative, well-bounded work inside a frontier you have checked, the improvement is large enough that refusing the tool is a cost.
After AIGPT-4 as of April 2023 was superseded within a year, and reasoning models pulled arithmetic inside the wall without making it straighter; the size of the gain has moved and the shape of the result has not.
contestedThe task built to defeat it

Teaching consultants to prompt made them worse on the harder task

On a task built to defeat the AI, consultants given an overview of prompt writing scored 60.0 per cent correct, against 70.6 per cent for those who used the AI without that overview.

Becausethe group given a prompt-engineering overview scored 60.0% correct against 70.6% for the treated group without it, significant only at the 10% level, while the same overview improved quality inside the frontier
LimitsTen per cent significance on one task in one experiment; the direction is consistent across specifications but the effect is a single contrast. The mechanism — that fluency in prompting raises trust without raising discrimination — is inferred.
PracticeSpecification discipline — treat training in how to use the tool as raising reliance, not judgment, and pair it with an explicit rule about where not to use it.
After AIPrompt training is now standard corporate onboarding for these tools, and it is the one intervention this experiment measured as harmful in the case that mattered.

The Media Equation, Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass

evidenceMedia and personality, the Desert Survival Problem

People rate the same advice higher when the computer's style matches theirs

When a computer's conversational style matches the user's own, people judge identical advice to be more insightful. A style that starts unlike theirs and shifts to match works better than one that matched from the start.

Becausedominance was manipulated by four cues — phrasing, a confidence number, speaking order and a name — with the content of the advice held identical, and matched users rated the same advice more intelligent and useful
LimitsForty-eight participants selected from the extremes of a dominance questionnaire, which inflates the contrast. Nothing tells you how large the effect is against a real difference in advice quality.
PracticeWhen an answer reads as unusually insightful, check whether anything in it is new, or only the register it arrived in.
After AIStyle matching is no longer four cues written in a couple of days; it is what a model does by default, on every turn, having been tuned on what raters preferred. The persuasion Reeves and Nass had to construct now arrives for free.

Co-Intelligence, Ethan Mollick

opinionFour rules for co-intelligence

Mollick says the role you give a model changes what it writes

Mollick says that telling a model what kind of person to be changes what it produces. The role you assign is part of the instruction, not a decorative extra.

Becausethe evidence is his own examples — interchangeable marketing phrases for a plain slogan request and usable jokes when the role is a comedian — offered as a working analogy, with the sin of anthropomorphising conceded
LimitsThe same suggestibility is the failure mode: telling it the task matters to your career improves the answer, which means the answer is responding to something other than the task. Mollick's own deflation of prompt engineering aged well, as models got better at inferring intent.
PracticeWrite the role into the specification explicitly and keep it in version control with the rest of it, instead of discovering it by feel each time.
After AIWritten about AI, and the part that has shifted is where the role lives: system prompts and product personas now set it before the user arrives, so the flourish has become a configuration nobody in the conversation can see.
opinionFour rules for co-intelligence

Mollick says today's AI is the worst you will ever use

Mollick's rule is that whatever AI model you are using now is the worst one you will ever use. Any limit you find in it should therefore be recorded with a date and re-tested, not treated as permanent.

Becausethe illustration is two otter-in-a-hat images a year apart, an extrapolation rather than a measurement, and the book's own examples dated within months of publication
LimitsNarayanan and Kapoor answer that there are rungs and no thresholds, and Schaeffer's work argues that the apparent jumps are artefacts of the metric. Nothing guarantees the rate continues, and the rule as stated cannot be falsified by any single observation.
PracticeDate every judgement you record about what the tool cannot do, and re-run the test rather than citing the old verdict.
After AIWritten about AI. Reasoning models arriving from late 2024 moved much of what he listed as outside the wall inside it within months, which vindicated the rule and destroyed the examples that argued for it in the same stroke.
opinionFour rules for co-intelligence

What AI can and cannot do has a ragged unmarked edge

Mollick argues that the edge of what these systems can do is ragged, unmarked, and not where people's intuition puts it. The only way to find out where it runs is to keep trying tasks against it.

Becausethe image is built from examples rather than measured — a sonnet inside the wall and a poem of exactly fifty words outside it, the same model writing a working tic-tac-toe page in one pass and misplaying a single board
LimitsWalking the frontier only teaches you where it is if you find out when you were wrong, and in the settings where prediction fails the feedback never arrives. His own examples dated within months: reasoning models moved arithmetic and multi-step logic inside the wall in late 2024.
PracticeKeep a written list, per domain you work in, of what the tool has actually got right and wrong; nobody else's list transfers to your work.
