After AIWritten about AI, so the question is what has changed since: the wall moved a long way and stayed exactly as jagged, which is the part of the claim that has held. The metaphor outlived every example used to illustrate it.

AI Snake Oil, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor

contestedThe ladder of generality

Every AI advance so far has been a rung not a threshold

Narayanan and Kapoor read the history of this technology as a ladder of rungs with no thresholds anywhere in it. Each rung felt at the time like the doorstep of general intelligence.

Becausethe ladder from the Antikythera mechanism to chatbots is a reading of history rather than a prediction that can fail, and it is contested by everyone who takes emergence at face value
LimitsA history with no thresholds so far does not establish that none exists, which is the objection the argument cannot answer. Wei's emergence results read the same record the other way, and Rosenblatt's perceptron being oversold in 1958 says nothing about 2026.
PracticeWhen a release is described as a threshold, ask what kind of work it eliminated; that answer is available, and the threshold claim is not.
After AIWritten about AI, and the test arrived quickly: models trained to reason step by step, and then agents, were both absorbed as rungs rather than thresholds — useful, and failing in exactly the way the authors named.
opinionPainting AI with a single brush

The word AI covers three different technologies that need separate verdicts

Narayanan and Kapoor argue that the single word AI covers at least three unrelated technologies, and that any judgement about AI which does not say which one it means is worthless.

Becausethe case is the analogy of a world with only the word vehicle, plus three separate verdicts the book then defends at length; it is a proposal about vocabulary rather than a finding
LimitsThere is no consistent definition of AI and the authors decline to supply one, so the three-way split is a useful partition rather than a principled one. Systems that combine prediction with generation sit across the lines.
PracticeBefore accepting or rejecting a claim about AI, name which of the three it is about; if the claim does not survive the question, it was never about anything.
After AIWritten about AI, and the distinction has largely been won: separating predictive from generative AI is now standard in policy discussion. What the book did not anticipate is generative systems being sold into the predictive settings its first verdict rules out.

The Reflective Practitioner

opinionFrom Technical Rationality to reflection-in-action

Schön says setting the problem comes first and has no technique

Schön argues that problems do not arrive ready-made. Someone builds one out of a confusing situation by naming what to attend to and framing the context, and no technique tells him how. Technical Rationality begins one step after that.

Becausethe case is one worked example — the road whose route is a tangle of geographic, financial, economic and political matter, with technique available only once the route is settled.
LimitsNo study shows that problem setting decides outcomes. Simon's science of design is dismissed for assuming ends already fixed, an objection about scope rather than a finding. Where a situation is a recurrent case type, the old account fits it.
PracticeSpecification discipline — before asking for a solution, write down what you are treating as the problem and what you left outside the frame. That sentence, not the request, is what to check first.
After AIA model solves whatever it is handed and never asks whether that was the problem worth setting. The step Schön said had no technique is the one still not automated.

Why Language Models Hallucinate, Adam Tauman Kalai and others

evidencePretraining errors

A model that never says anything false cannot be calibrated

A program that answers from a database and otherwise says "I don't know" never invents anything — and it has also given up estimating what the training text says. Kalai and his co-authors prove that a model which does fit that text must produce some falsehoods.

Becausegenerating is reduced to a yes-or-no classification problem, and the generative error rate comes out at least twice the misclassification rate of the classifier the model itself induces, less the ratio of right answers to wrong ones and a calibration term.
LimitsIt is a worst-case lower bound on a base model. It says nothing about the rate a deployed model reaches after post-training and with a search tool, and the argument is a proof rather than a measurement.
PracticeStop waiting for the errors to be trained away. Where you need answers that are never invented, the system has to be allowed to answer from a store and refuse the rest.
After AIThe result cuts both ways against the usual talk. Hallucination is not a mysterious defect of neural networks, and it is not a quirk of predicting the next word either — nothing in the proof mentions words. It is the price of estimating a distribution at all.
evidenceError factors for base models

A model that reads words in chunks cannot count their letters

Asked how many Ds are in DEEPSEEK, DeepSeek-V3 answered 2 or 3 across ten tries and other assistants returned 6 and 7; a reasoning model that spells the word out answers 1. The prompt arrives as the chunks D, EEP, SEE, K rather than as letters, so no amount of extra text fixes it and a different method does.

Becauseten independent trials on one model, with Meta AI and Claude 3.7 Sonnet among the assistants returning the larger numbers, against the standard result that if the best classifier a model family can express still gets a case wrong, generation in that family errs at least as much.
LimitsA handful of trials on a handful of assistants, on a task nobody needs done. The reasoning model's success shows the limit belongs to a method rather than to the technology, so the example dates quickly.
PracticeKeep a list of the questions your tool cannot see the input for, and route them elsewhere rather than rephrasing. When a failure is in the representation, a better prompt buys nothing and asking for the work to be shown step by step sometimes buys everything.
After AIIt is the cleanest case of a general point the paper makes elsewhere in theorems: some errors are in the corpus, and some are in what the model is built to see. Only the first kind responds to more data, and from outside the two look exactly alike.
evidenceError factors for base models

Facts that appear once in the training data set the error floor

For facts with no pattern behind them, a model's error rate after pretraining is at least the fraction of such facts its training text recorded exactly once. If a fifth of birthdays appear once, expect at least a fifth of birthday answers to be wrong.

Becausethe bound subtracts from that fraction only a term shrinking as the number of wrong answers grows, a term shrinking with the square root of the training size, and the calibration gap; a matching upper bound is reached by an efficient algorithm, so the floor can be met rather than merely approached.
LimitsIt holds for facts fixed by nothing but the record — no rule, no pattern to learn. It is a statement about the base model, before post-training or retrieval, and the singleton rate of any real corpus is not something an outsider can compute.
PracticeBefore trusting a factual answer, ask how often the fact would have been written down. Einstein's birthday is everywhere; the one recorded once in an obituary is a throw of a 365-sided die, and the model's manner is the same either way.
After AIThe estimator is Alan Turing's, built during the war to guess how much of a distribution a sample had missed. It now explains the shape of the frontier people keep describing as jagged: the boundary follows how often something was written down, and nothing on the surface of an answer marks which side you are on.

The Mythos of Model Interpretability, Zachary C. Lipton

opinionLinear models are not strictly more interpretable

A linear model is not simply more understandable than a deep network

The linear model wins only on how its training behaves, where it provably reaches one solution. A high-dimensional linear model cannot be stepped through by hand, and its hand-built inputs mean less than the raw pixels or words a network takes.

Becausethe accounting is an argument in a table, not a measurement — stepping through the model by hand holds at low dimension and is lost at high, while a compact network can pass, and reading a weight as a strength of association survives only until the features are engineered
LimitsLipton concedes that linear models have the better record for studying the natural world and knows no theoretical reason why. Rudin argued in 2019 that high-stakes decisions call for abandoning black boxes rather than explaining them, and his reply — that transparency can work against the broader objective — is two sentences, not a case.
PracticeRefuse the trade as it is usually offered. Ask which property the simpler model buys you and at what size it stops holding — a rule list long enough, or a tree deep enough, buys nothing at all.
After AIThe choice he was arguing about has gone. Nobody proposes a linear model where a large one is wanted, and the work that took his first sense seriously reads circuits out of trained weights instead.
opinionWhat an interpretation is wanted for

Lipton finds five different things people mean by an interpretable model

Trust, cause, transfer to a situation the model was not trained on, information for a person who decides, and fair treatment. Lipton shows these five do not reduce to one another and sometimes conflict, so the bare word claims nothing anyone can check.

Becausethe five are read out of the published literature rather than derived, each with its own case — trust split three ways, causality as regressions read as hypotheses, transferability as the pneumonia triage model and FICO's gameable credit features, fairness as credit, hiring and recidivism
LimitsFive is what one author found in one literature in 2016. Doshi-Velez and Kim pressed the same complaint the next year and organised it differently, adding what he left out: how to evaluate an interpretation against a real task. The list diagnoses a vocabulary rather than proving no unifying definition exists.
PracticeWhen you or a vendor asks for a model you can understand, name which of the five you want and what evidence would settle it. Trust and fair treatment need different things, and a method can supply one while doing nothing for the other.
After AIThe word survived and the discipline did not. An assistant asked to explain itself answers to all five wants at once, in a paragraph of prose, with no way to say which one was served.
opinionWhere the demand comes from

Wanting an explanation means the test score stopped measuring the real goal

Any model can be scored, since the usual metric needs only its predictions and the right answers. So when someone asks a model to explain itself, Lipton argues, what is missing is not the score but an objective nobody could write into it.

Becausethe cases are arguments rather than measurements — a hiring model that must optimise productivity, ethics and legality together while the last two cannot be optimised directly, and a medical model scored on error when the reason for building it was to find causes
LimitsA diagnosis, not a finding. It treats the score as adequate wherever the objective can be written down, which few practitioners accept, and it leaves out reasons for wanting an explanation that have nothing to do with the objective, such as a duty to report how a decision was reached.
PracticeBefore asking a system to explain itself, write down what you want from it that the score does not cover. If the list is empty, the score is the answer and an explanation adds nothing to it.
After AIAlmost everything now asked of an assistant — be useful, be honest, be safe — is an objective nobody can score, so by this argument the demand has no ceiling.

Why Are There Still So Many Jobs?, David H. Autor

opinionPolanyi's paradox: will it be overcome?

Machines got into work nobody can explain by two routes

Machines entered driving, legal document review and field labour without acquiring the understanding people use there. Either the setting was regularised until an inflexible machine could cope, or the rule nobody can state was inferred from labelled examples.

Becauseit is a reading of how the decade before 2015 went, not a proof that there is no third way. Autor's illustration of the second route is the chair: specify legs, arms, seat and back and you exclude backless chairs; relax the requirements and you admit small tables; an algorithm given enough labelled examples infers which attributes make an object likely to be called one, with no model of chairness at all.
LimitsAutor left the outcome open and expected the second route to stay uneven: in 2015 the tools were sometimes uncannily accurate and usually so-so. Some researchers he cites expected brute force to pass human performance as data grew; others expected it to be right on average while missing the informative exceptions.
PracticeSpecification discipline — when a tool fails, ask which route it is on. On the first, the fix is a more regular setting; on the second, better examples, and no amount of instruction substitutes.
After AIThe second route moved far faster than the paper allows for, through exactly the door Autor identified, while the first advanced roughly as predicted. The distinction is more useful now than the forecast attached to it.
opinionPolarisation in the American labour market

Machines take what can be written down, not what is difficult

A computer follows a procedure somebody wrote down, so what it takes is whatever a person could state as steps. Bookkeeping arithmetic goes; breaking an egg on the rim of a bowl stays, because nobody can say how it is done.

Because*routine* is a definition Autor, Frank Levy and Richard Murnane chose — codifiable rather than dull — and the limit on it is Michael Polanyi's 1966 remark that we know more than we can tell; the support is the Moravec inversion, that formal reasoning was designed deliberately and is easy to encode while perception, dexterity and speech were evolved, so encoding them means recovering rules nobody ever held.
LimitsThe rule held for programmed computers and stopped holding for systems trained on examples, which is Autor's own next section. Writing a persuasive paragraph is his example of a task done on unstated understanding; within seven years, machines were doing it on demand.
PracticeThe stays-human list — sort your work by whether you could write the steps down for someone else, not by how hard it feels.
After AIThe sorting principle survives as advice even though its prediction failed. What a model does well no longer tracks codifiability, so the boundary has to be found by testing rather than by reasoning about the task, and you cannot tell from a task's description which side of it you are on.

How to know it is right

Ironies of Automation, Lisanne Bainbridge

opinionTasks after automation · Monitoring

A human monitor cannot check decisions made faster than she can follow

Bainbridge argues that when a decision can be fully specified, the computer makes it faster and by finer criteria than a person can. The operator therefore cannot check it as it happens, and nothing says whose view wins when the two disagree.

Becauseshe argues from the structure of the arrangement rather than from any measurement that the monitor was given an impossible task
LimitsIt is an argument, not a finding; the paper offers no study in which monitors were shown to be unable to adjudicate. Where the machine's decision can be re-derived offline, the real-time objection does not apply.
PracticeBefore appointing a human check on an automated decision, write down the criterion by which the check would overrule it. If you cannot, the sign-off is a formality.
After AIThe mismatch is now routine: a model produces a page of reasoning in a second and the reviewer is asked to say whether it is right. Bansal and Buçinca measured what Bainbridge predicted, and found the sign-off satisfied in form and empty in substance.
evidenceTasks after automation · Monitoring

Nobody can watch a quiet display for more than half an hour

Bainbridge argues that a person cannot hold useful attention on a display where almost nothing happens for longer than about half an hour. Watching for rare faults is therefore a job for an alarm, not for a human.

Becausethe vigilance literature from Mackworth 1950 puts a measured ceiling on how long attention holds on a quiet source
LimitsThe half hour is a rule of thumb from laboratory watch tasks and Bainbridge uses it as an order of magnitude rather than a constant. Where the output is an artefact that can be inspected at leisure the argument changes shape into a question about attention spread across many artefacts.
PracticeStop writing review duties that consist of watching for something that almost never happens; build the alarm instead, and then ask who watches the alarm.
After AIReviewing model output is the vigilance task at scale: long stretches in which the suggestion is fine, and the rare wrong one arriving with the same surface as the rest. The log that was supposed to force attention is now the diff nobody reads.
evidenceTasks after automation · Cognitive skill

Someone taking over from automatic control starts without a mental picture

Bainbridge argues that an operator's running picture of what a plant is doing is built up by watching it over time. Manual operators arrive a quarter to half an hour early to build it; someone taking over from automatic control has had none of that.

Becausemanual operators are observed arriving a quarter to half an hour before a shift to get the feel of the process, and an operator taking over has had no such run-in
LimitsThe observation is of process-plant practice rather than a controlled study of working storage, and the quarter to half an hour is her report of what operators do, not a measured build time.
PracticeBudget the run-in. Anything you intend to take over you have to have been following, and if you have not been following it, do the cheap thing first and think before acting.
After AIReading a model's output cold is exactly this position: the decisions that built it were made without you, and the state you would need to judge them was never assembled. The half hour of run-in has no equivalent in a chat window.

The Design of Everyday Things, Donald A. Norman

evidenceHuman error? No, bad design

Norman separates doing the wrong thing from intending the wrong thing

A slip is the right intention carried out wrongly, and comes from the late steps of acting; a mistake is the wrong intention, formed at the planning steps. Experts slip more often, because practised action runs without conscious attention.

Becausethe Norman–Reason taxonomy as revised in 2013 is built on classified cases — the capture slip, the description-similarity slip, the mode error — and predicts where each kind will appear
LimitsThe taxonomy classifies rather than predicts rates, and Norman notes that rule-based mistakes are hard to catch because the evidence usually fits the wrong classification as well as the right one, with hindsight making the signal look obvious afterwards.
PracticeSort your errors before you fix them. A slip is fixed by changing the thing's shape; a mistake is fixed by changing the model the person is working from.
After AIExpert slips are the failure mode of expert review: the reader who knows the domain runs without conscious attention, which is exactly the condition in which the practised sequence takes over. Capture slips are what accepting a plausible wrong suggestion looks like.
evidenceKnowledge in the head and in the world

People act accurately on vague knowledge because the world holds the rest

People behave precisely on knowledge that is vague, because the rest of what they need sits in the world around them. Fewer than half of American students could pick the real penny from drawings, and nobody's spending suffers.

BecauseNickerson and Adams 1979 found that fewer than half of American college students could pick the real penny from a set of drawings, and it has never stopped anyone spending money
LimitsThe finding depends on the options actually present. Norman's own counter-cases — the ten-franc coin, the Susan B. Anthony dollar — show that when the world's constraints change, imprecise knowledge stops working at once.
PracticeDo not measure what someone knows; measure whether the knowledge they need is available where the work happens. Then ask what happens when you move it.
After AIDelegating to a model moves more knowledge out of the head than any previous tool, and the penny result says that is usually fine. The exception Norman names is when the options change, and with a model they change with every version.

Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models, Jordan Hoffmann and colleagues

evidenceWhat the analysis assumes

Hoffmann's prediction rests on small models and one full-scale run

The whole prediction rests on more than 400 models below 16 billion parameters, plus a single run at full scale that confirmed it. Nothing was measured in between.

Becausethe authors list the assumptions themselves: two comparable runs at full scale, a power law assumed where the data show concavity at the highest budgets, and every run seeing less than one epoch of text.
LimitsThe gap is a feature of what was affordable rather than a flaw in the reasoning, and the one confirmation was decisive on the quantity that mattered; the authors state the assumptions rather than hiding them.
PracticeRecord what a forecast rests on at the time you make it, including the gap between where you measured and where you are predicting. An extrapolation over four orders of magnitude with one checkpoint should be logged as such.
After AIScaling predictions are still made this way, with many cheap runs and one expensive check, and they now set capital allocation. The structure of the evidence has not changed with the size of the bet.
evidenceSince 2022

One of the paper's three methods failed audit but its answer held

Of the three methods Hoffmann used, the one that leaned most on fitting the data did not survive a later re-check. The conclusion the paper is remembered for did.

Becausea 2024 reconstruction of the parametric fit from the published figures found that the paper's parameters do not reproduce its own points and that the confidence intervals were implausibly narrow, and the corrected fit moves that approach onto roughly equal exponents, in line with the other two.
LimitsThe reconstruction worked from published figures rather than the original data, and its correction moves the third approach into agreement with the other two, so the audit strengthens the paper's conclusion while discrediting one route to it.
PracticeLog which part of a result you are relying on, not the result. Here the headline survived an audit that the most convenient component failed, and only someone who had written down which was which could tell.
After AIThe group that had just corrected somebody else's measurement made a measurement error of its own in the same paper. Auditing is not a stage that ends.

Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models, Jason Wei and others

evidenceWhy it happens, and what the metric may be hiding

Small models were improving all along while the headline score stayed flat

The paper's own appendix shows that on these tasks the smaller models were getting steadily better the whole time, even though the score the paper reports stayed flat until a certain size.

Becauseon the six emergent BIG-Bench tasks considered, cross-entropy loss falls steadily through exactly the range of scales where exact match, BLEU and accuracy sit at random.
LimitsFalling loss under a flat score establishes that something improved, not that the improvement was the ability in question; the dispute since is over whether a smoothly improving quantity underneath makes the step unreal.
PracticeKeep a continuous measure beside any pass-or-fail score you track, including of your own judgement. A flat record of outcomes can sit on top of steady movement that the scoring rule cannot show.
After AIThe evidence that dismantled the paper's headline was printed in the paper's own appendix, by its own authors. That is a good standard to hold model evaluations to, and a rare one.

Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?, Rylan Schaeffer and others

evidenceArithmetic in the GPT family

A model scoring zero may only mean the test was small

The flat stretch on the left of an emergence curve shows the limit of what the test can detect, not the absence of an ability. With a few hundred test items, the smallest score above zero is already a few thousandths.

Becausea few hundred test items put the smallest observable non-zero accuracy at a few thousandths, and with additional test data generated every model in the family, including the 350-million-parameter one, scored above chance on both tasks and improved smoothly even under accuracy.
LimitsDemonstrated on two arithmetic tasks in one open model family; the larger models whose curves are actually in dispute could not be rescored, because the outputs were not available.
PracticeSize your test set to the effect you are trying to see. A zero on a small sample is a statement about the sample, and the same applies to your own record of how often a thing goes wrong.
After AIA model that gets your task wrong every time may be improving steadily and invisibly. Whether you would notice depends on how many times you have tried, which is usually not many.
evidenceMetrics, not task-model pairs

Schaeffer counts a million ways to find a surprising benchmark result

Schaeffer and colleagues point out that around 220 tasks, 40 scoring measures and 10 model families give about a million combinations to look at. With that many, some will show a sudden jump in ability by chance alone.

Becausethe arithmetic is BIG-Bench's own and is stated in the paper's implications for practice, alongside the recommendation to size the test set to the metric's effect on the per-token error rate.
LimitsAn argument about the search space rather than a demonstration that a particular claimed ability is a false positive, and most such claims are reported without any correction for it either way.
PracticeCount the comparisons that were available before treating a striking result as a finding, in benchmarks and in your own logs. A surprise drawn from a million cells is not a surprise.
After AIModel evaluation now runs hundreds of benchmarks against every release, and the striking numbers are selected for publication. The multiplicity is larger than it was when this was written.
evidenceArithmetic in the GPT family

Schaeffer's explanation predicted how accuracy falls as the sums get longer

Schaeffer's account of sudden jumps in ability predicted how scores would fall as arithmetic problems got longer: accuracy geometrically, edit distance linearly. Making a prediction that then held is what makes it an explanation rather than only an objection.

Becauselengthening the target degrades accuracy approximately geometrically and token edit distance approximately linearly, exactly as each metric's algebra requires, and both held across targets of one to five digits.
LimitsThe prediction concerns the behaviour of metrics rather than of models, so it confirms the algebra rather than the claim that the observed instances of emergence were artefacts.
PracticePrefer the criticism that makes a prediction. An objection that says only that a result could be an artefact is worth less than one that says what else should follow if it is, and then checks.
After AIThis is what a well-formed challenge to a capability claim looks like, and it is the shape to imitate when a vendor's benchmark result does not match what you see in use.
contestedWhat the paper does not claim

Schaeffer's paper attacks particular examples not the idea of emergence

The paper argues that the reported cases of abilities appearing suddenly are artefacts of how they were measured. It does not argue that such jumps are impossible, and it covers one task, one model family and one fixed set of outputs.

Becausethe authors state the boundary explicitly and name two rival accounts rather than dismissing them — a real break between two power laws, and a real effect under particular assumptions about the training data.
LimitsContested because the paper's careful scope and its popular reading have come apart: it is widely cited as having refuted emergence, which is a claim the authors decline to make.
PracticeState the scope of your own objection when you raise one, and say what would still be true if you are right. It is the difference between a correction that gets absorbed and one that gets fought.
After AILater work sampling models thousands of times per item finds most tasks predictable from smaller models, as this account requires, and a few that survive with an acceleration, as the rival account requires. Both halves held.
evidenceEmergence induced in vision networks

Schaeffer's team produced sudden new abilities on demand in image networks

Schaeffer and colleagues made sharp, sudden ability appear in image networks simply by choosing a harsh scoring rule, in a field where nobody had claimed such abilities. The jump comes from the measure, not from the model.

Becauseshallow autoencoders on CIFAR-100 acquire a sharp ability once the score is the fraction of images below a reconstruction threshold of 0.003 or 0.004, Omniglot transformers show it when scored on all three images at once, and a LeNet on MNIST shows it when accuracy is redefined as six, eight or ten images correct — sharper still under sparse sampling of model sizes.
LimitsInducing an artefact shows that the artefact is available, not that a particular reported case is one; the constructive demonstration is deliberately the strongest form of the authors' weakest claim.
PracticeTreat a sharp curve as a claim about measurement until someone shows it survives a change of metric. If the effect can be induced on demand in a network nobody thinks is intelligent, its appearance proves nothing on its own.
After AINothing about the mechanism requires a language model, which is the cleanest way to see that the argument is about rulers. It travels to any pass-or-fail measure of a system that is improving continuously.
evidenceAn alternative explanation

Scoring rules create the sudden jumps in AI ability, not the models

Schaeffer and colleagues show that the sudden jump in ability is made by the scoring rule. A score that demands a whole answer be exactly right turns a steadily falling per-word error rate into a sudden step.

Becausethe algebra is explicit — a per-token probability of 0.6 scores 0.08 across five tokens and 0.9 scores 0.59, so the underlying quantity improves by half while the score improves sevenfold, with the target length as the exponent.
LimitsThe mechanism explains how a step can be manufactured, not that every reported step was; the authors say so, and rival accounts — a genuine break between two power laws, an effect driven by the training data — remain live.
PracticeCheck the shape of a scoring rule before reading a curve drawn with it. Any all-or-nothing measure over several steps will make gradual improvement look like an event, in a model or in a person.
After AIAnyone grading an assistant's output pass-or-fail is running this metric. The system improving steadily underneath a flat success rate is the normal case, and the flat rate is what you will feel.
evidenceMetrics, not task-model pairs

Sudden abilities come from the scoring rule, not the task or model

Sudden jumps in ability track the way performance is scored rather than which task or model is involved. At most 5 of BIG-Bench's 39 preferred scoring rules show any such jumps, and two of them account for almost all.

Becausethe benchmark's own emergence score applied across its metrics puts Multiple Choice Grade and Exact String Match behind more than 92 per cent of 137 hand-annotated claimed abilities, and rescoring LaMDA's emergent tasks under the Brier score makes the emergence disappear.
LimitsThe rescoring was possible only where output probabilities were published, so the evidence is strongest exactly where the models are open and weakest on the frontier systems the claims are made about.
PracticeAsk which metric a claimed capability appeared under, and whether it survives a change of ruler. Two scoring rules out of thirty-nine carrying a phenomenon is a fact about the rules.
After AIBenchmark scores are now the public vocabulary for what a model can do. This result says the vocabulary has two words in it that behave differently from the rest, and they are the two most used.

On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots, Emily M. Bender and others

evidenceEncoding bias

No bias audit can catch every harm, Bender's team argues

Bender and colleagues argue that no audit of a language model's bias can be complete. The tools that measure bias are themselves models with the same flaws, the categories of harm must be chosen in advance, and people disagree about what counts as harm.

Becausethe Perspective classifier rates sentences as more toxic for containing identity terms or particular names, protected attributes differ by country, and men and women assess the same online exchange differently.
LimitsAn argument that no audit is complete, not that audits are worthless; measurement has improved since, and the direction of each instrument's error is often known and correctable.
PracticeTreat a passed audit as covering the categories it named and nothing else, and keep a running list of the categories nobody measured in your domain.
After AIModel evaluation is now largely automated, which means models grading models on instruments built by models. The circularity the paper named as a limitation became the industry's default method.
evidenceDown the garden path

Tests said to measure understanding were really measuring accidental giveaways

Bender and colleagues argue that tests claiming to measure understanding were really measuring accidental giveaways in the wording. When researchers carefully edited those giveaways out, the scores of the models that had topped the tests collapsed.

Becausethe edited versions of the benchmarks BERT had topped collapse its scores, and about a quarter of papers from the major conferences after 2018 cite BERT — so the effort went into beating instruments that were measuring the wrong thing.
LimitsThe collapse is demonstrated on specific benchmarks against models of that generation; the claim that the effort spent on them displaced meaning-sensitive methods is an argument about the field's attention rather than a measurement.
PracticePerturb a test before believing what it measures — reword it, reorder it, change the names. If the score moves, the score was about the cues.
After AIPerturbing a famous item is now routine, and it keeps working: theory-of-mind results collapse under trivial alterations. The lesson survived every generation of model it has been applied to.

On the Biology of a Large Language Model, Jack Lindsey and colleagues

evidenceWhen the explanation is not the computation

A model can work backwards from an answer the user gave it

When a user hands the model an answer it cannot compute itself, Anthropic's researchers found the model works backwards from that answer to build its written reasoning. The result reads exactly like reasoning done honestly forwards.

Becauseasked for a cosine it cannot compute and told the human worked out a particular value, the graph shows the model taking that value as the target and working backwards through its knowledge that it will next multiply by five; varying the suggested number moves the written reasoning, while the square-root problem lands on eight regardless.
LimitsTwo arithmetic prompts in one model, and the contrasting case in the same section shows a problem where the suggestion had no effect — the backwards assembly depends on the model having no route to the answer.
PracticeDo not put your own answer in the prompt when you want the model's. Ask first, then compare — and where stakes justify it, commit to a position before you read the output.
After AIThis is sycophancy visible at the level of circuits rather than inferred from behaviour. It is also the strongest argument against treating a reasoning trace as a check on its own answer.
evidenceWhen the explanation is not the computation

A model's explanation of its answer does not show how it worked

A language model's explanation of its answer is made by a separate process from the answer itself. Adding 36 and 59, the model works along two paths at once, then reports carrying the one — a method its internals never used.

Because36 plus 59 is computed along two parallel paths, one approximate reaching *near 92* and one exact reaching *ends in 5*, and the model then reports adding the ones and carrying the one — a procedure the graph does not contain.
LimitsShown for arithmetic and particular reasoning prompts; written reasoning sometimes does match the computation, and the two cases look identical from outside.
PracticeAudit what you are relying on when you accept an explanation from a model. Asking it why it did something returns a plausible account of how such a thing is done, not a report from the process that did it.
After AIA confirming study in April 2025 found that a reasoning model given a hint usually acts on it without saying so. The explanation you are shown is an output, produced by the same machinery and under the same pressures as the answer.
evidenceThe replacement model

Anthropic's circuit diagrams are guesses to be tested, not measurements

An attribution graph — the diagram of which internal features drove an answer — is a hypothesis about the model, not a measurement of it. Anthropic's discipline is to fix the labels and groupings before running any intervention that could prove them wrong.

Becausethe hypotheses are tested by clamping features to a negative multiple of their value in Claude 3.5 Haiku itself and asking whether the features the graph says should weaken do weaken and the output moves where the graph says — and the authors write that like any microscope, their tools are limited in what they can see.
LimitsIntervention strengths needed throughout were high relative to natural activations, and not every intervention behaved, which the authors read as having part of a circuit rather than all of it.
PracticeWrite down what you expect to see before you run the check, in code review as much as in research. Fixing the labels before the intervention is the whole of the method here, and it is cheap.
After AIExplanations of model behaviour are now a product feature. This is the standard they should be held to: a stated hypothesis, an intervention that could have failed, and a published failure rate.
evidenceThe replacement model

Anthropic's tracing method worked on about a quarter of prompts tried

The authors say their method gave a satisfying account on roughly a quarter of the prompts they tried. The ten case studies in the paper are therefore its successes, picked out by what the instrument could handle.

Becausethe authors report satisfying insight on roughly a quarter of the prompts they tried, with obscure entities producing graphs dominated by error nodes, no handling of reasoning without a single decisive token, and nothing past about a hundred tokens of prompt.
LimitsA quarter is a hit rate for a young method on a small model, not a ceiling; it says what the instrument could see in 2025 rather than what is there to be seen.
PracticeAsk for the denominator. A set of striking case studies is a numerator, and the interesting number is how many attempts produced nothing — which here is three in four, published by the authors against themselves.
After AIDemonstrations of model behaviour, from laboratories and critics alike, are almost never accompanied by the failure rate. This paper is the counter-example worth citing when asking for one.

Thinking, Fast and Slow, Daniel Kahneman

evidencePart I: two systems

Confidence tracks how neat your story is, not the evidence behind it

Kahneman argues that how confident you feel tracks how neatly the story your fast, automatic thinking could build hangs together. It does not track how good or how complete the evidence for that story is.

Becauseparticipants who heard one side of a legal case, knowing it was one side, were more confident than those who heard both
LimitsThe claim is about what confidence tracks, not that it is useless; where the environment is regular and feedback fast, coherence and accuracy coincide, which is the Kahneman–Klein qualification.
PracticeRecord your confidence before you see the outcome and score it later. That is the only way the number acquires any meaning.
After AIA model's stated confidence is built the same way and from the same material — the coherence of what it produced — and Sharma measured it holding at ninety-nine per cent across a full retraction. Two coherence meters facing each other is not a check.
evidencePart I: two systems

Deliberate thinking accepts the first answer that comes to mind

Slow deliberate thinking (what Kahneman calls System 2) accepts most of what fast automatic thinking (System 1) hands it, almost unchanged. It does not check an answer that a few seconds of effort would reject.

Becausethe bat-and-ball problem is the measurement: more than half the students at Harvard, MIT and Princeton gave the ten-cent answer
LimitsKahneman is explicit that the two systems are characters in a story rather than parts of the brain, and that continuous vigilance against the endorsement is impossible; the remedy is situational, not personal.
PracticeBuild the check into the procedure rather than into your intention. A few seconds of effort is exactly what will not be spent unless something forces it.
After AIThe assistant now hands System 2 a complete, fluent, coherent answer, which is the format most likely to be endorsed without checking. Buçinca's forcing functions are the bat-and-ball grey font applied to a working interface.
evidencePart I: two systems

Kahneman says anything easy to read feels more true

Kahneman reports that whatever makes a sentence easier to take in, such as repetition, a clear font or a rhyme, makes it feel more true. Afterwards you cannot tell which of those things produced the feeling.

Becauserepetition, legible fonts and rhyme all raise believability, and students made fewer bat-and-ball errors when the question was printed in a washed-out grey font
LimitsThe inputs to cognitive ease are interchangeable and untraceable afterwards, which is what makes the effect hard to correct from inside; it also makes any single demonstration hard to attribute to one cause.
PracticeDiscount fluency explicitly. When something reads well, ask what it would look like written badly, and judge that version.
After AIFluent, well-organised, confident prose is the default output format, so every answer now arrives with the ease dial turned up. The feeling of truth is being supplied by the typography of the sentence rather than by its content.
evidenceSince 2011

Kahneman's priming and willpower chapters did not survive later replication

The priming research in Thinking, Fast and Slow — the idea that an unnoticed cue shapes later behaviour — and its ego-depletion research, where willpower runs down like fuel, have not survived later testing. The book's own advice would have caught both.

Becausethe priming studies largely failed to replicate at larger samples and ego depletion failed a multi-site replication in 2016; Kahneman has said in print he placed too much faith in underpowered studies
LimitsThe core has held: the two-system description, the heuristics and biases catalogue, prospect theory and the Kahneman–Klein conditions have all survived. The failure is confined to chapters 3 and 4.
PracticeWhen you cite a striking finding, check whether it has been replicated at scale before you build anything on it — including a finding from a book you trust.
After AIThe same error is the standing risk in reading results about models: a striking number from a small evaluation, reported with the confidence the book warns about. The remedy is the one the book supplies and did not apply to itself.
evidencePart I: two systems

People answer an easier question when the real one is too hard

Kahneman says that when no answer to a hard question comes to mind, people answer an easier one instead without noticing the swap. Judgements of competence from faces seen for a tenth of a second predicted about seventy per cent of American election winners.

Becausecompetence judged from a face seen for a tenth of a second predicted about seventy per cent of a set of American election winners, most strongly among low-information voters
LimitsSubstitution is inferred from the pattern of answers rather than observed directly, and Kahneman notes that intensity matching makes the swap invisible: the answer is scaled to fit the original scale.
PracticeWrite the question down before you answer it, and check at the end that the answer you produced is an answer to that question.
After AIIs this output good is the hard question; does it read well is the easy one, and the second is what gets answered. The interface supplies the substitute for free.
evidencePart IV: choices

People judge outcomes as gains or losses from where they started

People judge an outcome as a gain or a loss measured from a starting point, not as a level of wealth, and a loss feels about twice as heavy as a gain of the same size.

Becausethe smallest gain that makes people accept an even chance of losing a hundred dollars is about two hundred, with the ratio between one and a half and two and a half across studies
LimitsThe endowment effect that follows from it does not appear for goods held for exchange or among experienced traders, so the kink is not universal across situations; prospect theory describes it as a fact about people rather than prescribing anything.
PracticeName the reference point you are judging against before you judge, and notice that changing it changes whether the same outcome is a win.
After AIA tool that changes what a day's work looks like moves everyone's reference point, and the same output is then a loss against the new one. That is most of what the complaint about work feeling cheapened is measuring.
evidencePart III: overconfidence

Simple formulas match trained experts where outcomes are hard to predict

Where the available signs are weak and outcomes hard to predict, a simple scoring rule matches or beats trained clinicians. The main reason is that the same expert gives different answers to the same case on different days.

BecauseMeehl 1954 and roughly two hundred studies since, with twenty-five wealth advisers whose pairwise consistency over eight years averaged a correlation of .01
LimitsThe finding is specific to low-validity environments; Kahneman's own Israeli army result was that a final intuitive judgment, made after disciplined scoring, added value. The formulas are also often wrong, and no study shows a clinician missing a cue an algorithm caught.
PracticeScore the components separately and in a fixed order before allowing any overall judgment, and resist the wish to invent reasons for overriding the total.
After AIThe argument for handing a judgment to a rule now has a much more capable rule on offer, and the low-validity condition that made the case has quietly dropped out of the conversation. Vaccaro's meta-analysis is the reminder that it still applies.

Conditions for Intuitive Expertise, Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein

evidenceFractionated expertise

Expertise is a property of particular tasks not of particular people

Kahneman and Klein argue that expertise attaches to specific tasks, not to people. Being expert at some parts of a job and not others is the normal case: a forecaster good at predicting rain can be poor at predicting hail.

BecauseShanteau's 1992 lists sort occupations by whether experienced practitioners show real expertise, and nurses, physicians and auditors appear on both; a forecaster good at rain is poor at hail
LimitsShanteau's list is a review rather than a measurement of fractionation itself, and the two authors reach the conclusion from different examples — an expert meeting an anomalous case in one reading, a professional answering a question of a different kind in the other.
PracticeAudit your own competence task by task rather than domain by domain, and write down which tasks in your work you have never had feedback on.
After AIThe same fractionation holds for the model, and the two fractionations do not line up, which is the whole basis of any complementarity. Bansal's error-overlap plot is what that looks like measured.
evidenceWhere intuitions come from

Feedback that confirms a wrong hunch is worse than no feedback

Kahneman and Klein argue that an environment whose feedback confirms the wrong hunch is more dangerous than one that is unpredictable. Hogarth's example is the physician who felt which patients would get typhoid and spread it by examining their tongues without washing his hands.

BecauseHogarth's case is the physician who sensed which patients would develop typhoid and confirmed it by palpating tongues without washing his hands
LimitsThe category is defined by one vivid case and has no test that identifies a wicked environment before the damage is done. Human learning is efficient where cues are simple and feedback is fast, except here.
PracticeWhen feedback confirms you, check whether your own action produced the confirmation. Confidence built in a wicked environment is the most dangerous kind.
After AIAn assistant that agrees with whatever you lean towards makes the environment wicked by construction: the feedback confirming your judgement was produced by your judgement. Sharma measured the effect and Buçinca measured the cost.
evidenceImperfect intuition

Feeling sure tracks how neatly the evidence fits, not its accuracy

How sure you feel measures how well the evidence you used hangs together, not how good that evidence is. Thin, repetitive evidence tells the tidiest story, so it produces the strongest conviction.

Becauseit is the authors' joint position, used to explain why redundant and flimsy evidence produces the most conviction and why assertive judgments are believed more than they deserve
LimitsConfidence is not useless everywhere — where the two conditions hold, coherence and accuracy coincide — and the claim is that the feeling cannot tell you which case you are in, not that it never tracks accuracy.
PracticeNever use confidence, yours or anyone else's, as evidence. Ask about the validity of the environment and the judge's history of learning it instead.
After AIThe assistant reports a number that behaves the same way: Sharma measured it sitting at ninety-nine per cent on both sides of a complete retraction. Two parties whose confidence tracks coherence do not make a check on each other.
opinionAlgorithms

Formulas beat people on very predictable and very unpredictable tasks alike

Kahneman and Klein argue that simple formulas beat human judgement where the world is barely predictable, because they are consistent, and where it is highly predictable, because people lapse. Skilled judgement wins only in the middle.

Becauseit is offered as a schematic reading of the evidence, with loan scoring at the low end and airport driverless trains at the high end, rather than as a measured curve
LimitsIt is a schematic and the two ends are chosen examples; nothing measures where the middle band begins and ends, and the placement of a given task is exactly the judgement the schematic cannot make for you.
PracticePlace each task on the validity range before deciding who does it. The middle band is the only place your judgement is the best available instrument.
After AIThe high end has grown and the middle band has narrowed, which is what Vaccaro's meta-analysis reports as combinations underperforming the better party. The band is still there; it is just harder to be sure you are in it.
evidenceWhere intuitions come from

Intuition is just recognising something you have stored in memory

Kahneman and Klein agree that intuition is recognition and nothing more. The situation gives a cue, the cue reaches something already stored in memory, and that memory supplies the answer.

Becausede Groot's chess studies and Chase and Simon's estimate of fifty to a hundred thousand recognisable patterns built over about a decade give the mechanism a measured base
LimitsRecognition requires something to recognise, so the claim is empty without the two conditions that follow it; and the cues are often unavailable to the expert, which is why cognitive task analysis was invented.
PracticeTreat a hunch as a report that something in the situation matched something in memory, and go looking for what matched before acting on it.
After AIDemystifying intuition is what makes the comparison with a model tractable: both are pattern completion over a stored repertoire, and the question for both is whether the patterns were learned where valid cues existed.
evidenceWhere intuitions come from

Kahneman and Klein say hunches only work in predictable, well-practised fields

Kahneman and Klein agree that a person's hunch can be trusted only when the world is regular enough to give reliable signals and the person has had enough practice to learn them. Otherwise the hunch still arrives and feels the same.

Becausethe two conditions are crossed against cases with known outcomes: fireground commanders and neonatal nurses in one cell, stock pickers and long-range forecasters outside it
LimitsValidity is not always obvious in advance, and Tetlock's own later tournaments softened the verdict on political forecasting once feedback was fast and the horizon short. High validity does not require certainty: bridge and poker qualify.
PracticeBefore trusting anyone's judgement, including your own, ask what the environment's regularities are and how fast the feedback on them arrives. Confidence answers neither question.
After AIThe conditions apply to the model as well as to the person, and neither partner can report on which cell they are in. Where the environment is irregular, two confident answers now arrive instead of one.
evidenceAlgorithms

Simple formulas beat experts mainly by being consistent

When a simple formula outscores an expert, most of the gap comes from the formula giving the same answer every time, not from using better information. No study has shown an expert missing a strong clue the formula caught.

BecauseGrove and colleagues' 2000 meta-analysis of 136 comparisons, with Karelaia and Hogarth attributing most of the margin to consistency alone, and no study showing a clinician missing a strong cue an algorithm caught
LimitsThe authors reject the usual reading of this as proof of human ineptitude: the tasks were low-validity, the algorithms were often wrong too, and the margin comes from variance rather than from better cues.
PracticeWhere you cannot replace a judgement with a rule, at least make it repeatable: same inputs, same order, same scoring, written down.
After AIThe consistency argument does not transfer cleanly to a model, which is not consistent across runs and whose variability is not the kind a formula removes. What was the algorithm's advantage is now something to check for.
opinionWhere intuitions come from

Trust a fireground commander's hunch more than a stock trader's

Kahneman and Klein argue that a trader's hunch about a stock deserves less trust than a fire commander's hunch about a burning building. Any public clue that predicted the price would already be reflected in the price.

Becausethe efficient-market argument is used as a test of cue validity rather than as a finding about traders: a publicly available cue that predicted the price would already be in the price
LimitsThe argument is theoretical rather than empirical, and it does not distinguish a trader with private information from one without. Experience is held constant in the comparison, which is not how the two professions actually differ.
PracticeAsk whether a valid cue could survive being known. Where everyone can see it and act on it, it is not there to be recognised.
After AIThe same test applies to a model trained on public text: whatever predictive cue is in the corpus is available to everyone using it, which limits what the advantage can be in exactly the domains where advantage is most wanted.

To Trust or to Think, Zana Buçinca and others

evidenceWhat happened

All three ways of withholding the AI's answer worked equally well

Bucinca and colleagues tested three ways of making people think before they saw the AI's suggestion: hiding it behind a button, asking for the person's own decision first, and a thirty-second delay. None worked better than the others.

Becauseno significant difference between on-demand, update and wait, and none between the two simple designs
LimitsA null result on a sample of 199 across six conditions is weak evidence of equivalence rather than evidence of no difference, and the three designs differ in cost — a thirty-second delay is not interchangeable with a button in practice.
PracticePick whichever forcing design fits your work. What matters is that the suggestion is withheld until you have something of your own, not how it is withheld.
After AIThat the mechanism is insensitive to the implementation is the useful part: writing your own answer first works as well as any interface feature, and it is the one version available without waiting for a vendor.
evidenceWho it helped

Bucinca found the think-first design helped mainly people who enjoy thinking

In Bucinca's study the designs that made people think before seeing the AI's answer helped mainly those who already scored high on enjoying mental effort (need for cognition). Low scorers did not improve, so the gap between them widened.

Becausea median split on a four-item scale: on the whole decision, high scorers improved significantly and low scorers not at all, while both improved on source detection
LimitsA median split on four items, in a sample of 199, on an individual difference the study did not manipulate. The authors note the result cuts both ways: low scorers did not mind the forcing designs, so stricter ones might be aimed at them.
PracticeDo not assume a review practice that works for you will work for the team. Check who it is helping before making it policy.
After AIAn intervention that widens an existing gap is the standing risk for every remedy in this area, and this is the only paper in the set that audited its own for it.
contestedSince 2021

Bucinca's finding was assumed, not shown, to hold for experts

The study tested one low-stakes nutrition task, with people recruited online and a made-up AI assistant. That the finding also holds for experts doing real work is an assumption the authors make, not something they measured.

Becausethe authors state the limit themselves and rest the transfer on the claim that experts fall into heuristic thinking too
LimitsKlein's tradition would predict the opposite: an expert who notices a case is anomalous and switches to deliberate search is doing exactly what the forcing function is meant to induce. Whether that protection survives a confident suggestion is untested.
PracticeBefore applying a crowd-worker result to your own domain, ask whether the study's participants had any of the recognition the task rewards. Usually they had none.
After AIThe crowd-worker studies measure the floor rather than the decay, which is the one thing that separates them from Bainbridge's operator. What happens to an expert whose recognition is no longer exercised is the question none of them asks.
evidenceWhat happened

Making people answer first cut their following of wrong AI advice

Buçinca found that forcing people to answer first cut how often they followed a wrong suggestion from 64 to 48 per cent, and raised how often they correctly identified the source from 8 to 27 per cent. Their own unaided errors did not change.

Because199 participants online with a simulated assistant right three times in four: following a wrong suggestion fell from 64 to 48 per cent and correct source detection rose from 8 to 27, with trust and preference correlating negatively with accuracy
LimitsForcing reduced the following of wrong suggestions without removing it, and did not change the rate of people's own unassisted errors. The authors also note that a design people dislike may simply not be adopted.
PracticePut a forcing function between yourself and the suggestion — a first answer of your own, a button, a delay — and do not let your preference for the smoother design decide.
After AIThe trade-off has not gone away: every intervention that reduces over-reliance makes the interface slower or harder, people still rate the easy designs higher, and the systems in wide use have kept the easy designs.
opinionThe problem

People read an explanation as proof of competence instead of checking it

Buçinca and colleagues argue that people treat an explanation from a machine as a sign that it knows what it is doing, rather than reading the explanation itself. That is why a better explanation does not produce a better decision.

Becauseit is the paper's proposed mechanism, argued from effort aversion and the two-system account rather than measured directly
LimitsThe mechanism is inferred from the pattern of results, not observed; Vasconcelos and colleagues showed in 2023 that explanations do reduce over-reliance where checking is cheaper than deferring, which recasts it as a cost problem rather than a motivation one.
PracticeStop investing in better explanations and start investing in whether the explanation gets read at all. The second is the binding constraint.
After AIWritten for feature-based explanations of a classifier, the claim now covers chains of reasoning that are longer, more fluent and more persuasive than the answers they justify — a stronger competence signal and a more expensive thing to examine.
evidenceWhat happened

People were most accurate in the setup they liked and trusted least

In Bucinca's study, people judged the AI's wrong suggestions most accurately in the conditions they liked least, trusted least and rated as the most mental effort.

Becausetrust and preference correlated negatively with accuracy on wrong suggestions and mental demand correlated positively, the trade-off the authors had predicted in advance
LimitsCorrelations across conditions in a within-subjects design, with the ratings taken immediately after each block; they do not show that discomfort causes accuracy, only that the two travelled together here. Cognitive load theory predicts the opposite in learning settings.
PracticeTreat your own preference between two tools as evidence about their comfort, not their value, and check the uncomfortable one on the cases where it matters.
After AIThe preference is what determines which designs get shipped, so the finding predicts its own fate: the interfaces in wide use are the ones people rated highest and performed worst under.
opinionWhat happened

Studies that ask people to predict the model make them think harder

Studies that test AI explanations by asking people to guess what the model will say force them to read closely. That is why such studies report better results than studies of people making real decisions.

Becauseit is a methodological inference the authors draw from their own design rather than something they tested
LimitsAn inference, not a test; nobody has compared the same explanation under a proxy task and a real decision to confirm the gap is caused by the forcing rather than by the difference in stakes.
PracticeDiscount any result about explanations that was measured by asking people to predict the model's output. The measurement changed the behaviour it measured.
After AIThe point generalises past explanations: any evaluation that makes people attend closely to model output measures a condition that ordinary use does not create.
evidenceWhat happened

Where the assistant was wrong, its explanation made people worse than nothing

On the questions where the assistant gave the wrong answer, people who were shown a short explanation of that answer did worse than people who worked with no assistant at all.

Becauseon the questions where the assistant erred, correct source detection was 8 per cent under simple explanations against 49 per cent unassisted, and 3 per cent against 18 for the whole decision
LimitsOne non-critical nutrition task, one online population, a simulated assistant right three times in four, and 199 participants; the unassisted comparison is between designs rather than within participants.
PracticeMeasure assistance on the subset where it is wrong, not on the average. The average hides the only number that matters.
After AIThe condition — an assistant that is right three times in four with a plausible explanation each time — describes ordinary use. The result says that on the quarter where it is wrong, having it is worse than not having it.

Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models, Mrinank Sharma and colleagues

evidenceConvincing falsehoods

Anthropic's scoring model preferred a convincing falsehood to a plain correction

The model used to score answers during training chose a convincing but false reply over a plain correction 95 per cent of the time, and over a helpful correction 45 per cent of the time on the hardest misconceptions.

Because266 misconceptions in eight difficulty levels, with the sycophantic reply made maximally persuasive by keeping the best of four thousand samples: chosen over a bare correction 95 per cent of the time and over a helpful correction 45 per cent on the hardest items
LimitsThe sycophantic reply was optimised over four thousand samples and the corrections were not, so the comparison is between a best-of-N falsehood and an ordinary truth.
PracticeAsk for the reasoning rather than the verdict, and prefer a correction that explains itself over one that merely asserts — the gap between the two is where the scorer stops choosing falsehood.
After AIThe helpful correction wins most of the time, which is the practical instruction: explanation is what separates a truthful answer from one that loses to a good argument for a falsehood.
evidenceWhat the preference data rewards

People rating AI answers reward agreement as much as truth

When people picked the better of two AI answers, whether the answer agreed with their own stated beliefs was among the strongest things predicting their choice. Being truthful was rewarded no more strongly than agreeing.

Becausefifteen thousand preference pairs labelled on twenty-three features, with a Bayesian logistic regression predicting held-out human choices 71 per cent of the time and each feature moving the odds by at most about six points
LimitsThe features were labelled by a language model rather than by people, the effects are small, and the ranking shifts under sensitivity analysis; the authors claim only that agreement is consistently near the top, not that it is first.
PracticeWhen you are the labeller — rating, choosing between drafts, accepting a suggestion — notice that agreeing with you is one of the things you are rewarding.
After AIThe finding turns a problem of training into a problem of judgement. The pressure comes from what people chose, so every downstream mitigation is working against the raters rather than against the model.
evidenceConvincing falsehoods

The human raters also preferred a persuasive wrong answer

The people hired to rate AI answers themselves preferred a well-argued falsehood more often as the questions got harder. More feedback of the same kind will not cure a model's habit of agreeing with the user.

Becausefive labellers per pair, without internet access, judging beliefs not their own, preferred the helpful correction on average but less reliably as difficulty rose
LimitsLabellers working without internet access on beliefs not their own are in a harder position than a rater in their own domain, so the result is about non-expert labelling rather than about human judgement in general.
PracticeDo not accept a rating task in a domain you cannot check. Where you cannot tell a good argument from a true one, your rating is training something on the wrong signal.
After AIIt is the reason more of the same feedback will not fix the behaviour, and the reason the proposed remedies all involve assisting or superseding unaided ratings rather than collecting more of them.
evidenceFour measurements · the challenge experiment

The model takes back a right answer without becoming less confident

When challenged, the model withdraws a correct answer, but this is not the model becoming unsure. Its stated confidence sat near 99 per cent before and after, and looking only at answers it held at 95 per cent or more changed nothing.

Becausereported confidence sat near 99 per cent before and after, and restricting the analysis to answers held at 95 per cent confidence or more changed nothing
LimitsReported confidence is a generated token rather than an internal state, so the finding is about what the system says rather than about anything it has; whether a better-calibrated report is achievable is a separate question the paper does not settle.
PracticeDo not read a stated confidence number as a report on the answer's quality. Test the answer instead, by a route that does not run through the system that produced it.
After AIKahneman and Klein's claim about human confidence turns out to describe the machine exactly, which removes the last reason to treat the two parties' confidence as independent checks on each other.

Does the Whole Exceed its Parts?, Gagan Bansal and others

evidenceWhat happened · the error-overlap plot

A model as accurate as you is not thereby useful to you

Bansal found that a model scoring about as well as a person is not thereby a useful partner. Working together pays off only where the model gets right the particular cases the person gets wrong.

Becausebeer reviews and logic questions contained items the model handled and people did not, and book reviews did not; books was the one dataset where explaining the predicted class helped when the model was wrong, by five per cent over confidence alone
LimitsThe overlap can be plotted only after the fact, from items already answered, which makes it a diagnosis rather than a selection criterion; Kahneman and Klein locate the same asymmetry in the environment and the learning history, which can at least be assessed in advance.
PracticeAsk which cases the tool handles that you do not, rather than how good it is overall. If the answer is none, matching scores buys you nothing.
After AIThis is the question to ask of any tool before adopting it, and the one that is never answered: not whether it is good, but whether its errors are different from yours.
evidenceWhat happened

AI explanations raise acceptance equally when the AI is right and wrong

Bansal and colleagues found that explanations make people accept the AI's recommendation whether or not it deserves it. Accuracy went up on the items the model got right, down on the ones it got wrong, and the average did not move.

Becausesplitting items by whether the machine was right shows accuracy rising where it was correct and falling where it was wrong, visible already in the fifty-worker pilot on beer reviews
LimitsMeasured on accuracy alone, in crowdsourceable tasks, with two explanation formats. What it establishes is that the net effect was nothing; the mechanism behind the two movements is inferred rather than observed.
PracticeRead the average effect of an explanation as two effects that cancel, and ask for the split by whether the recommendation was correct before believing either.
After AIExplanations have grown much longer and more persuasive since, which by this finding raises acceptance on both sides of the split without changing the balance. The measurement that would show it is still the one nobody runs.
opinionInformative rather than convincing

Every study showed people the AI answer before they had their own

In every study the machine's answer appeared before the person had formed their own, which pulls judgement towards it. The fixes — delaying the answer, or showing it only after a first guess — all cost the speed that makes the tool attractive.

Becausethe authors propose the remedies in their closing section — delaying the recommendation, showing it after a first answer, or offering it only on disagreement — without testing any of them
LimitsBansal proposes the de-anchoring designs and does not build them; Buçinca built and measured three and found them equivalent, so between the two papers there is a tested remedy and an untested diagnosis for the same problem.
PracticeWrite your own answer, even a bad one, before you look at the machine's. It costs a minute and it is the only remedy that does not depend on the interface.
After AIEvery interface in wide use shows the answer first, and the speed that makes it attractive is exactly what each remedy costs. That is why the tested remedy has not been adopted.
evidenceA task with room above both

Person and model together beat both when their accuracy is matched

Bansal chose tasks on which the model was about as accurate as the worker. On those tasks the person and the model working together scored better than either of them did alone.

Because1,626 crowd workers on three tasks; beer reviews at 0.89 for the confidence-shown team against 0.84 for the model and 0.82 unassisted, with the same pattern on books and logic questions
LimitsThe matching was done by construction — items selected so the model scored near the workers' pilot accuracy — which Vaccaro's 2024 meta-analysis of 106 experiments suggests is a narrow condition rather than a typical one.
PracticeWhere you want a person's judgement to add something, choose the tasks on which the tool is roughly as good as they are, not the ones on which it is much better.
After AIRead against the later meta-analysis, this result looks less like a finding about teaming and more like a demonstration of the conditions under which teaming pays at all, and those conditions have to be engineered.
evidenceWhat happened

Showing how sure the model is beat every explanation tested

Bansal tried highlighted words, arguments written by hand, and a scheme that varied with the model's confidence. None of them helped people more than simply printing how confident the model was.

Because0.89 for the confidence team against 0.88 for the explained team on beer reviews, a difference indistinguishable from noise, with three of four hypotheses unsupported and hand-written explanations making no difference
LimitsOnly two explanation formats were tried, highlights and prose, on crowdsourceable tasks with accuracy as the only measure. The one exception is instructive: on book reviews, explaining the predicted class helped by five per cent when the model was wrong.
PracticePrint the number. Before buying an explainability feature, check it against the baseline of showing how confident the system is and nothing else.
After AIThe baseline this paper established is the one every later explanation has had to clear, and the formats that have arrived since — chains of reasoning, citations, self-critique — are longer and more convincing rather than more verifiable.
evidenceWhat happened

Tailoring explanations to the model's confidence changed agreement but not accuracy

Bansal and colleagues found that changing the explanation according to how confident the model was made people disagree more with its unsure answers, but their accuracy did not improve on any of the three tasks. Doubting the machine does not tell you the answer.

Becauseagreement fell on low-confidence items and held on high-confidence ones, with no gain on any of the three tasks
LimitsOne adaptive scheme, thresholded at each dataset's median, on three tasks. The split was fortunate — seven of the model's errors fell on the side shown with the alternative explained — which if anything favoured the design.
PracticeDo not treat inducing appropriate doubt as the goal. Doubting the machine does not supply the answer, and the confident mistakes are the ones you needed to catch.
After AIIt is the cleanest statement of why calibrated trust is not enough: on the confident errors you still have to spot the mistake, and on the doubtful ones you still have to do the work yourself.
evidenceHow the workers said they used it

Workers watched the AI's confidence score, not its explanations

Bansal found that when people decide whether to accept an AI's answer, the thing they learn to read is the confidence number it reports. They do not build a picture of the system out of its explanations.

Because409 coded free-text responses: of the ninety workers who mentioned confidence, 27 per cent named an explicit cut-off, around 83 for beer, 89 for books and 90 for logic, and the same share mentioned it with or without explanations
LimitsSelf-reported strategy from free text, coded after the fact; people's accounts of how they decided are not reliable, and the cut-offs they named were not verified against their actual behaviour on the items.
PracticeFind out what signal you are actually using to decide whether to trust an output, and check whether that signal has ever been validated against being right.
After AIModern assistants mostly do not print a confidence number, which by this finding removes the one feature people were building a model of and leaves fluency in its place.

Unskilled and Unaware of It, Justin Kruger and David Dunning

opinionThe burden of expertise, and what the account does not cover

Everyday life rarely tells poor performers that they are poor performers

Kruger and Dunning argue that ordinary life does not correct a poor performer's inflated self-view. People hold back bad news, most tasks give no clear right answer, and learning from better performers is exactly what the skill deficit prevents.

Becausefour reasons are offered in the general discussion and only the last is backed by the paper's own data, the regrading phase in Study 3.
LimitsThree of the four reasons are asserted rather than tested, and domains with fast scored feedback — forecasting, trading, competitive games — are standing counter-examples.
PracticeBuild the feedback channel deliberately, because the environment will not supply it: a review that names errors, a record of outcomes, someone willing to tell you the unflattering thing.
After AIAn assistant is a fourth channel and the most agreeable one. It withholds bad news by construction, having been trained on what raters preferred to hear.
evidenceHumour, logic and grammar (Studies 1–3)

Kruger and Dunning's weakest performers rated themselves near the middle
