Across tests of humour, logic and grammar, Kruger and Dunning's bottom-quarter students placed themselves at or above the middle: a 12th-percentile performance rated at the 62nd. Everyone's estimate squeezed towards the upper middle; the ranking was not reversed.

Becausefour independent samples of Cornell undergraduates, with panel reliability of .76 on the humour criterion and published test items for the other two, and bottom-quarter students placing themselves below top-quarter students in every study.
LimitsKrueger and Mueller showed in 2002 that regression to the mean plus the better-than-average effect produce crossing lines of this shape without any metacognitive deficit, and Burson and colleagues showed the direction depends on task difficulty.
PracticeRead your own percentile estimates as compressed rather than wrong in rank. If you think you are somewhat above average at something you have not measured, the estimate carries almost no information either way.
After AIThe popular version of this finding — that incompetent people think they are brilliant — is not what the data say, and it is the version most often used to dismiss somebody else. The compression applies to the person using it.
evidenceHumour, logic and grammar (Studies 2 and 3, raw-score estimates)

Kruger and Dunning's weakest students overestimated their raw scores too

Kruger and Dunning's bottom-quarter students were not simply wrong about other people. Asked how many questions they had got right, they claimed 14.2 of 20 logic items when they had 9.6, and 12.9 grammar items when they had 9.2.

Becausea raw-score estimate is absolute and so untouched by any error about other people, which removes the false-consensus explanation from this half of the result.
LimitsAbsolute estimates are still measured with error and still subject to regression, though not to any mistake about the peer distribution; the sample is undergraduates on short classroom tests.
PracticeAsk yourself how many you got right, not how you compare. The absolute question is the one that can be checked afterwards, and it is the one the error survives.
After AIWith an assistant in the loop the absolute question is the only one left: how much of what came back was right. The comparison with other people has stopped being the useful measure.
evidenceCompetence begets calibration (Study 4, second mediation)

People judge their own work better only because training made them better

In Kruger and Dunning's study, training improved how well people judged their own work only by improving the skill itself. Once the researchers held constant how well people could judge their own answers, the training predicted nothing.

Becausethe mediation is the one measure regression to the mean cannot reach, since the skill was altered after the score was fixed, and the training's effect on self-assessment vanishes once metacognitive ability is held constant.
LimitsA mediation analysis on one training manipulation, which establishes the path in this design rather than in general; Fleming's dissociation results are the standing objection.
PracticeKeep hours on the work you have delegated, on the argument that your ability to judge the delegate's output is carried by your own skill and decays with it.
After AIThis is the load-bearing claim under manual practice. If judging the output is carried by being able to do the work, then the hours are not nostalgia — they are what keeps the review real.
evidenceCompetence begets calibration (Study 4 mediation)

People who lack a skill cannot tell that their answers are wrong

Kruger and Dunning found that the skills needed to get an answer right are largely the same skills needed to recognise a right answer. Someone who lacks them is not just wrong; he also has no way of noticing that he is wrong.

Becauseperformance predicted metacognitive skill at .75, and metacognitive deficit predicted inflated self-assessment on all three measures with objective performance held constant, with betas from −.40 to −.49.
LimitsFleming's evidence is that metacognitive sensitivity dissociates from first-order accuracy and has its own substrate, which would allow calibration to be trained separately; Study 4 raised both at once and cannot separate the readings.
PracticeKeep a written record of your predictions and their outcomes in any domain where you are new. The feeling of having judged well is produced by the same skill you are missing, so the log has to come from outside it.
After AIA model will answer in any domain, including the ones where you cannot grade it. The deficit here is about lacking the signal that you are wrong, and delegation removes the practice that would have supplied it.
evidenceIt takes one to know one (Study 3 regrading phase)

Poor performers cannot spot good work in others either

Kruger and Dunning found that people who do badly at a task also cannot tell good work from bad when they look at other people's. Watching better performers therefore teaches them nothing.

Becausegrading correlations were .37 against .66 and summed absolute error 17.4 against 9.2, and the bottom group's self-estimate moved from the 66.8th percentile to the 63.2nd after reading five better tests.
LimitsOne regrading phase on a logic test; the top group's estimates did move on seeing peers' work, so exposure is informative for those who can read it, which is the point rather than a limitation.
PracticeDo not rely on reading good examples as a way to learn a skill you cannot yet perform. Map where you actually sit, and use a model or a mentor as a tutor who explains, not as an exhibit you are meant to absorb.
After AIAssistants are used as exhibits constantly — read the output, learn the pattern. This says the reading requires the competence the reading was supposed to build, which is why tutor-style use beats generator-style use for anyone learning.
evidenceCompetence begets calibration (Study 4)

Ten minutes of training fixed the worst performers' view of themselves

Kruger and Dunning gave the worst-scoring quarter ten minutes of training in testing logical rules. Their estimate of their own rank rose from 3.5 out of ten to 9.3, and their claimed number of correct answers fell from 5.3 to 1.0, against an actual 0.4.

Because70 of 140 participants were randomly assigned to a training packet, and the untrained bottom quarter moved the wrong way over the same interval, from 5.8 to 6.3.
LimitsA single short training on one task, with the skill altered after the score was fixed; Tetlock's forecasters improve calibration while the world stays as hard as it was, which suggests a second route this design cannot see.
PracticeWhen your judgement of your own work is poor, train the work. Ten minutes of instruction moved both the skill and the self-estimate here, and nothing addressed at the self-estimate alone has done as well.
After AIIf competence is the route, then the delegation that removes the practice removes the calibration too. That is the mechanism behind every finding in this book about reliance and self-estimate drifting apart.
opinionThe burden of expertise, and what the account does not cover

The Dunning-Kruger effect holds only where the skill is knowing things

Kruger and Dunning's effect applies where competence consists of knowing the domain. It fails where skill is physical: a coach can understand basketball perfectly and still be unable to dunk.

Becausethe scoping is the authors' own, argued from examples rather than tested, with a second boundary at the floor, since nobody overrates their ability to translate Slovenian proverbs.
LimitsAn argument from examples in the general discussion with no test, and the boundary cases are the authors' own choice; a footnote sets aside the generally incompetent person as no part of the research.
PracticeSort your domains by whether the skill and the judgement are the same thing. Where they come apart — physical skills, skills with fast unambiguous feedback — you can trust your self-estimate further.
After AIMost knowledge work sits on the wrong side of this boundary, which is where the deficit bites. The work where you would notice your own decline immediately is not the work being delegated.
contestedSince 1999

The famous Dunning-Kruger graph is mostly a statistical artefact

The crossing-lines graph can be produced by regression to the mean plus the general tendency to rate oneself above average. What survives the criticism is the rest: how people sort their own answers, how they grade a stranger's work, and what training changed.

BecauseKrueger and Mueller 2002 in the same journal, Burson Larrick and Klayman 2006 on task difficulty, and Nuhfer and Gignac on random numbers producing the same plot, against Ehrlinger and colleagues 2008, who paid for accuracy and recruited at a debate tournament and a gun club and still found the overestimation.
LimitsContested in both directions: the statistical critique is about the graph and the graph was never the whole argument, while the incentivised replications are smaller and fewer than the original studies.
PracticeCite the parts that survived — how well people sort their own answers into right and wrong, how badly they grade a stranger's work, what ten minutes of instruction did — and stop citing the figure.
After AIA finding this heavily used and this heavily attacked is a good calibration exercise in itself. What has held up is smaller than the popular version and harder to dismiss than the artefact version.
evidenceIt takes one to know one (Study 3, top quartile)

Top performers underrate their rank because they assume others did well

Kruger and Dunning found the best performers rank themselves too low because they assume everyone else did as well. Seeing peers' work raised their estimated rank from the 68th to the 77.2nd percentile, and barely changed their guess at their own score.

Becausethe top group's comparative estimate rose from the 68th to the 77.2nd percentile after grading, while its raw-score estimate went from 16.9 to 16.6 against an actual 16.4.
LimitsUndergraduate samples on classroom tasks, and the effect is a comparative error rather than a self-knowledge failure — the top group knew their own score all along.
PracticeIf you are strong at something, expect to underrate your standing and to overrate everyone else's. The correction is exposure to other people's actual work, not more introspection.
After AIAn expert who assumes a model finds the work as easy as they do is making this error with a new target. The model's competence, like a peer's, has to be observed rather than assumed from one's own.

Cognitive Offloading, Evan F. Risko and Sam J. Gilbert

opinionA metacognitive model of the decision

A tool weakens the skill it replaces and your judgement of it

Risko and Gilbert argue that handing a task to a tool changes two things: the ability it replaced, and your own estimate of that ability, which is what decides whether you use the tool next time. Use therefore drifts towards the tool.

Becausethe model's two arrows are illustrated by navigation devices and by the erosion of Inuit wayfinding, and the confidence-to-offloading arrow has since been demonstrated causally; how far the drift goes over years remains unmeasured.
LimitsThe two arrows are a model with one arrow now demonstrated; the long-run drift is the paper's central prediction and the thing nobody has measured, which is why this is an opinion rather than evidence.
PracticeKeep unaided hours on the capacities you want to retain, and schedule them rather than waiting to feel the need. The feeling is the second output of the loop, and it moves in the wrong direction.
After AIThe loop is the whole argument of this book in one diagram. What has changed is that the capacity being replaced is now judgement, and judgement is what the loop uses to decide.
evidenceThinking with the body

People offload work when it feels hard, not when it is hard

Risko and Gilbert hold that what makes people offload a task — do it with a tool or the body instead of the head — is their judgement of how hard it is, not how hard it actually is.

BecauseDunn and Risko 2015 rotated the words alone inside an upright frame and rotated words and frame together, producing the same rotation costs and the same physiological measure, and head tilting was far commoner in the condition participants believed was harder.
LimitsDemonstrated on a perceptual manipulation where belief and demand could be separated cleanly; how far the dissociation extends to complex work is not measured.
PracticeAudit what you hand off against what it actually costs you, not against how hard it feels. The feeling is the variable doing the work, and it can be wrong while the cost is unchanged.
After AIEvery decision to ask a model is made on an estimate of what the task would cost you. That estimate is the thing this literature shows to be unreliable, and it is now consulted many times a day.
evidencePutting cognition into the world

People reach for external aids as a task gets harder to hold

The harder a task would be to do in the head, the more people spontaneously push part of it out into the world — turning the page rather than rotating the shape mentally, or writing the reminder down.

BecauseRisko and colleagues 2014 found it rising with rotation angle and array size, and intention offloading rises with the number of intentions held and with interruption, both of which lower unaided accuracy.
LimitsThe relationship is between offloading and demand in laboratory tasks with clean load manipulations; in real work, availability and habit compete with demand as predictors.
PracticeExpect your own delegation to climb exactly when the work gets hard or you get interrupted — which is when the judgement you are delegating matters most. Decide the boundary in advance rather than in the moment.
After AIThe conditions that drive offloading up — high load, interruption, fatigue — are the conditions under which you are least able to check the result. The tool arrived without changing that.
contestedRemembering where instead of what

People who can search online think they know more than they do

Risko and Gilbert report that being able to look things up raises how much knowledge people credit to their own heads, though the strongest of these Google-effect studies have replicated unevenly.

Becausesearching online about one subject raised people's self-credited knowledge, and their reported sense of brain activity, on a different subject — a transfer that only an inflated self-estimate explains.
LimitsContested: these studies arrived just before the replication decade and the strong form has not held; the surviving version is that expecting access changes what people encode and what they say they know.
PracticeLog what you can do unaided, periodically and in writing. Access to a store inflates the estimate of what is in your head, and the estimate is what you will use when deciding whether you can check the tool.
After AIThe effect was measured with a search box. A system that produces finished work in your own idiom is a stronger manipulation of the same variable, and nobody has measured it over years.
contestedRemembering where instead of what

People who expect a file to be saved remember where not what

Risko and Gilbert report that when people expect information to stay available, they store where to find it instead of the content itself. Memory is not lost; what gets stored changes.

Becausein the saved-file experiments expected erasure improved recall and saving improved memory for location, which is a shift in what was stored rather than a loss of storage.
LimitsContested: independent attempts to reproduce the saving-and-forgetting result have come out mixed, and the search-engine Stroop priming that supported the strong version is now held loosely.
PracticeDecide deliberately which things you want in your head and rehearse those without the tool available, because the expectation of access is doing the encoding decision for you otherwise.
After AIWith a model the store is not even a location you could return to — the answer is regenerated, differently, each time. The weaker form of this claim is the one that transfers, and it transfers completely.
evidencePutting cognition into the world (Risko and Dunn 2015)

People write things down when they gain nothing and think it helps

Asked to remember just two items, which they could already do perfectly from memory, people still wrote them down on about 40 per cent of trials. They also wrongly believed that writing them down would raise their scores.

Becausethe same pattern appears in reminders set where they produce no accuracy gain and in head tilts that save nothing, so the bias is visible across three paradigms with different costs.
LimitsCeiling performance makes the gain of zero easy to establish and also makes the stakes trivial; the experiment shows a misjudgement, not a cost.
PracticePut a step between the impulse to delegate and the delegation — commit to your own answer first, then compare. The impulse is not tracking whether the help helps.
After AIMETR's developers were 19 per cent slower while believing themselves 20 per cent faster. The same bias, measured where there was something to lose, and the belief survived the experience.
evidenceThinking with the body

Tilting your head, gesturing and setting reminders are the same behaviour

Risko and Gilbert treat tilting your head at rotated text, gesturing through an arithmetic step and setting a phone reminder as one behaviour: physical action taken to reduce what the head has to do. All of them respond to the same manipulations.

Becauseexternal normalization, prospective memory, short-term memory and gesture all depend in the same way on load and on how well the person performs when offloading is prevented.
LimitsThe unification is by shared dependence on load and on unaided performance, which is weaker than showing one mechanism; the behaviours differ enormously in what they cost to reverse.
PracticeAudit your offloading as one category with many instances. The notebook, the search, the script and the model are the same move, which means what you know about one transfers to the others.
After AIA model is the widest external resource yet, and it takes on the deliberative work the earlier examples did not touch. The category holds; the range inside it has changed.
evidenceRemembering where instead of what

Turn-by-turn navigation makes the journey better and the driver worse

Drivers following turn-by-turn navigation drive the route better, remember less of what they passed, and do worse when they drive the same route again without it.

Becausethe navigation studies the review collects show all three, and the photography analogue points the same way — photographing an object impaired memory for it a day later, while photographing part of it reduced the impairment.
LimitsSingle-session studies on route memory, with the attention account and the encoding account both live; the photography result showing partial engagement reduces the loss suggests the effect is about attention rather than about the device.
PracticeSeparate the outcome you want from the capacity you want, and keep hours on the second. If you want to know a city, drive it without the device sometimes; the guided drives will not accumulate into knowledge.
After AIThis is the clearest consumer-scale instance of the pattern, and it happened without anyone deciding to accept the trade. The same shape is now available for writing, analysis and code.

The Extended Mind, Andy Clark and David J. Chalmers

evidenceExtended cognition (Kirsh and Maglio 1994)

Tetris players rotate pieces on screen because it is faster than imagining

Kirsh and Maglio found that Tetris players rotate a shape on screen because it is quicker: about 100 milliseconds to turn it plus about 200 to press the button, against about 1000 to turn it in the head.

Becausethese are the paper's only measurements and they are borrowed; players also rotate to find out whether a piece fits at all, not only to place it, so the action buys information as well as time.
LimitsOne task, one pair of measurements, borrowed from another laboratory; nothing here establishes that the saving generalises, and the same literature later found people offloading where the saving was zero.
PracticeAudit which of your offloads are genuinely cheaper and which only feel cheaper. Where there is a real measured saving, take it; where the saving is assumed, you are running Risko and Gilbert's biased estimate.
After AIThe timings are the honest version of the case for delegation: a measured saving on a specific operation. Most claims about assistant productivity are not that, which is what makes this a useful standard.

Influence, Robert B. Cialdini

evidencethe second half of Directed deference; figure 24.9

Admitting a real weakness first wins trust faster than listing strengths

Cialdini finds that naming a genuine weakness before making your case earns trust faster than piling up strengths. The move works just as well for someone with an interest to serve as for an honest reporter.

Becausethe pattern recurs across independent settings — trial lawyers conceding a weak point are judged more credible and win more often, Domino's advertising in 2009 that its pizza had been bad, Buffett opening annual reports with a mistake — and the chapter supplies its own counter-case in Vincent the waiter
LimitsThe evidence is field and commercial rather than controlled. Vincent shows the move is as available to a practitioner with an interest as to an honest reporter, which the chapter concedes and does not resolve.
PracticeCalibration log — record the weakness you stated alongside the confidence you claimed, and check later which was the real one.
After AIA model that opens with a caveat is not being candid; the hedge is a style feature of the output, and it buys the trust that a real admission would.
evidencethe closing passage of Truths are us; figure 24.6

Cialdini found that saying bad behaviour is common makes it worse

Cialdini found that telling people an unwanted behaviour is common makes more of them do it. Inside the complaint sits the message that everybody does it.

Becausea field experiment against a measured base rate of 2.95 per cent moved theft in both directions — a sign depicting three thieves nearly tripled it to 7.92 per cent, a sign depicting one cut it to 1.67 — and the reversal has been reproduced in three other prevention literatures
LimitsThe repair — a truthful trend where there is no majority — rests on a single student study. The newest example in the 2021 edition, the rise in adolescent suicides after a television series, did not survive reanalysis.
PracticeFailure-mode review — report the failure as a trend that is moving, not as a prevalence that is high.
After AITelling a team that everyone is shipping unreviewed model output is the Petrified Forest sign. The message that lands is the frequency, not the disapproval.
opinionthe closing chapter, Primitive consent for an automatic age

Cialdini says check whether a persuasion cue is honest, not ignore it

Cialdini's defence against automatic compliance is not to refuse the shortcuts. It is to check whether the cue that triggered one — scarcity, authority, liking — was reporting something real, and to resist only where the cue has been counterfeited.

Becausethe position is stated throughout and dramatised rather than tested — the television bought knowingly and the shelf checked the next morning — and the two authority questions are offered as prescriptions, not as interventions with outcomes
LimitsNo defence in the book was tested. The check is recommended to the same faculty that just failed to notice the cue, which the authority chapter's own prediction gap shows to be unreliable.
PracticeFailure-mode review — in the review, check the condition the cue reported rather than re-litigating the decision it produced.
After AIThe check does not run on a cue that is a property of training rather than a report about anything. There is no shelf to go back to the next morning.
contestedthe Milgram passage in Directed deference; figure 24.7

In Milgram's study people obeyed one recognised authority and stopped without it

Milgram's participants obeyed one authority they recognised, and stopped as soon as the order came from anywhere else. Nobody gave a further shock when the researcher said stop, nobody obeyed a fellow volunteer, and everyone stopped when two researchers disagreed.

Becausethe reversals are what identify the effect — not one further shock when the researcher said stop, none when a fellow volunteer gave the orders, and every participant stopping under two contradictory researchers — but the familiar sixty-five per cent is one of twenty-four conditions running from near zero to over ninety
LimitsGina Perry's archive work found the experimenter departing from the four scripted prods and many participants doubting the shocks were real. Burger's 2006 partial replication found 70 per cent continuing against Milgram's 82.5 in the matching condition.
PracticeCognitive forcing — put a second, independent source in front of the decision, because two contradictory authorities is the condition in which everyone stopped.
After AITwo assistants given the same question and disagreeing is the cheapest available version of the condition that stopped every participant.
contestedthe nurse study in Directed deference

Nurses followed a dangerous phone order they knew enough to refuse

A steep rank gap, an order that cannot be checked, and a person working alone together produce obedience to an instruction the subordinate is competent to refuse. Nearly all the nurses in the study Cialdini reports did exactly that.

Becausethe original is dramatic — 95 per cent of twenty-two nurses' stations set off for the patient's room with twice the stated daily maximum of an unauthorised drug — but the 1977 rerun with a familiar drug, an identifiable physician and colleagues available produced two of eighteen
LimitsThe book does not mention the Rank and Jacobson reversal. The three conditions were varied together, so their separate contributions are unknown.
PracticeAutomation ironies audit — audit where in your workflow an instruction arrives that cannot be verified and has nobody to check it with.
After AIA model is an unknown voice issuing an unverifiable instruction to a person working alone, at any hour. The reversal names the fix: identifiability, and a colleague to consult.
evidencethe chapter Truths are us; figures 24.3 and 24.4

People copy the crowd most when they are unsure what to do

The less sure people are, the more they take other people's behaviour as evidence about what to do. The worst case is a room where everyone is hesitating and each person reads the others' hesitation as a reason to do nothing.

Becausethe effect is largest exactly where knowledge is missing — unfamiliar customers were the ones most swayed by the popularity label, and Goldman's shopping cart sat unused from 1934 until he hired shoppers to wheel them — and it reverses under unambiguous injury, with help in 100 per cent of staged accidents
LimitsThe Genovese parable was a newspaper's construction and the book now says so. A 2019 study of real closed-circuit footage found intervention in about ninety-one per cent of public conflicts, and more bystanders making it likelier rather than less.
PracticeCognitive forcing — when you notice you are uncertain, force the check before you look at what everyone else did.
After AIUncertainty is the condition under which an assistant gets used most, which is exactly where its answer is treated as evidence about the world rather than as one more opinion.
evidencethe chapter Directed deference; figure 24.8

People obey a uniform or a title, not the expertise behind it

Cialdini finds that people defer to the outward signs of authority — a uniform, a title, a suit, an expensive car — rather than to any real qualification, and they underestimate how much those signs move them.

Becausefive independent manipulations of a token each moved compliance — a uniform from 42 to 92 per cent, half an inch of estimated height per academic rank, a suit tripling jaywalkers followed into traffic, a designer label, a luxury car — and in every study participants underestimated the effect on themselves
LimitsThese are field studies from the 1970s and 1980s on small samples. What has held best is the prediction gap — students guessed 63 per cent where the uniform got 92 — rather than any single effect size.
PracticeProjection log — log which token you were responding to, since your estimate of its effect on you is the part that is reliably wrong.
After AIAn assistant's fluency and formatting are tokens that cost nothing to produce and carry no credential behind them at all.
evidencethe chapter Levers of influence; figure 24.1

People respond to one cue, so anyone who fakes that cue wins

Cialdini shows that a single feature of a situation, not the situation as a whole, sets off a complete pattern of behaviour. Anyone who can fake that feature can set the pattern off.

BecauseLanger's photocopier queue gives the cleanest numbers — 60 per cent for the bare request, 94 with a real reason, 93 with an empty one — and the same rule shows up in the turquoise that sold at double price and the painkiller rated more effective at $2.50 than at ten cents
LimitsThe photocopier result holds for small requests; at higher cost people attend to the reason, which the book reports and its popular retelling drops. The turquoise and painkiller cases are single demonstrations.
PracticeCognitive forcing — make the check fire on the cue itself: ask what feature produced the assent before asking whether you agree.
After AIAn explanation attached to a model's answer is the empty because at scale, and it raises acceptance whether or not the answer is right.
evidencethe passage on number in Truths are us

Telling people what their neighbours do beats appealing to their values

Cialdini reports that telling households most of their neighbours were saving energy cut use more than appeals to the environment, to responsibility or to the power bill. A number about what others do makes an action look doable, not correct.

Becauseof four weekly household messages, the three appealing to the environment, to responsibility and to the power bill were beaten more than threefold by a truthful statement that most neighbours were conserving, and a scanner study separates acceptance from validity by finding more conformity to four people than to four computers rated equally reliable
LimitsAllcott's 2011 evaluation of the commercial deployment found savings of 1.4 to 3.3 per cent of household electricity, far less than a threefold advantage over other messages implies.
PracticeWitness practice in review — in review, say what the team actually does rather than what it should value.
After AIWhat a team believes its peers do is now partly what a model reports that teams do. The feasibility channel does not check where the number came from.

Studies of Independence and Conformity, Solomon E. Asch

evidenceThe majority effect

Asch's wrong majority captured about a third of people's answers

When a unanimous group announced an obviously wrong answer, about a third of the judgements made by Asch's subjects went along with it, on a task people get right more than 99 per cent of the time when alone.

Because123 subjects at three colleges made a mean of 4.41 errors out of twelve, 36.8 per cent of critical estimates, against 0.7 per cent among 37 controls judging individually and three errors in 738 neutral judgements.
LimitsMale American college students, tested in public, on a question with no stake attached; two thirds of judgements were independent and a quarter of subjects never yielded once.
PracticeForce your own judgement into the open before the room's is known — a written estimate, a committed position — because the effect is on the answer given, not on the answer held.
After AIAn assistant is a confident unanimous voice with no visible stake, available on every question. Asch's subjects could see that the majority was wrong, which is the condition that mostly does not hold with a model.
opinionForms of independence and yielding

Counting wrong answers hides why a person agreed with the group

Asch found three different reasons for going along with the group and three for holding out, and counting a person's wrong answers cannot tell them apart. Someone who thinks the majority is right but reports what he sees scores the same as someone untroubled.

Becausethe individual interviews, conducted before debriefing and read from the extremes of the distribution, separate the kinds; Asch is explicit that distortion of perception, if it occurred at all, was the rarest form and cannot be established from the data.
LimitsInterview evidence from a small number of subjects at the extremes of the distribution, interpreted by the experimenter; Asch himself says the perceptual-distortion category cannot be established from his data.
PracticeIn review, watch what you are doing as you do it: holding a position, suppressing a doubt, or having no doubt at all. The behaviour is identical from outside and the three are not the same act.
After AIAccepting a model's output and agreeing with it are indistinguishable in the record you leave behind. Only attention at the time can tell them apart, and only you can supply it.
contestedSince 1956

How much people conform changes with the decade and the country

How much people conform depends on when and where the study was run, as much as on the person. Conformity in the United States fell steadily after the 1950s, and it is stronger in countries that value fitting in with the group.

BecauseBond and Smith's 1996 meta-analysis pooled 133 studies in seventeen countries and found both patterns, while Perrin and Spencer recorded one conforming response in 396 trials with British engineering students in 1980 and large effects with unemployed West Indian men facing white majorities — which points at what the subject has to lose.
LimitsContested: the cross-national comparison confounds culture with decade and with the populations tested, and the Perrin and Spencer results point at stake rather than at nationality.
PracticeAudit the conditions rather than the people. If dissent is rare on your team, the finding to act on is what standing apart costs here, not who is compliant.
After AIWhat a person has to lose by disagreeing is the moving part, and it has not gone anywhere. Disagreeing with a system the organisation has invested in has its own cost, and nobody has measured it.
evidenceThe majority effect (Table 3)

In Asch's experiment most people held out and a minority gave in

Asch's result is not that everyone gave in a little. 24 per cent of people never agreed with the wrong majority, 27 per cent agreed eight to twelve times, and the most common score was zero.

Becausethe J-shaped distribution is in the paper's own table, and Friend, Rafferty and Bramel documented in 1990 how textbook after textbook inverted the emphasis Asch insisted on.
LimitsThe split is observed in one paradigm on one kind of judgement; nothing here establishes that the independent quarter are independent elsewhere, and Asch's own interviews found three different routes to the same error count.
PracticeKeep a list of the judgements you will not delegate to a room or a tool, and treat independence as a disposition you can hold rather than a statistical exception. A quarter of Asch's subjects held it throughout.
After AIThe finding everyone cites — people conform — is not the finding. The one that matters for supervision is that resistance is common, unevenly distributed, and evidently a property of persons.
opinionStructure of the experimental conditions

In Asch's study the pressure came from the subject, not the group

The majority in Asch's experiment only stated answers; they did not argue, urge, reward or punish. Whatever pressure the subject felt he produced himself, out of what he thought standing apart would say about him.

Becausethe fifteen structural properties in the closing section are offered as an argument against reading the results as suggestion or uncritical acceptance, and the conflict is characterised as irreconcilable and, unusually, unintelligible.
LimitsAn argument from the structure of the situation rather than a manipulation of it; the claim that the pressure is self-generated is an interpretation of the interviews, and Cialdini reads the same phenomenon as social proof operating on the subject.
PracticeIn review, separate what the situation contains from what you have added to it. Asch's majority did nothing but say numbers, and a third of the judgements moved anyway.
After AIA model applies no pressure at all, by construction. If you find yourself deferring to it, the deference is yours — which is the most useful thing in this monograph and the least cited.
evidenceVariations of the experimental conditions

One dissenter mattered more in Asch's study than the majority's size

What made people give the wrong answer in Asch's experiment was that everyone else agreed, not how many they were. Three opponents produced the full effect and fifteen produced no more. One ally cut errors sharply, even when the ally was also wrong.

Becausethe partner results come from Asch 1951, reported in the monograph's discussion rather than in its own experiments, and when the partner defects to the majority the errors climb back toward the level of a man alone.
LimitsThe partner effect is reported from earlier work rather than tested here, and the relevant condition is that unanimity is broken — which says nothing about whether the dissent is informative.
PracticeArrange for one dissenting voice before a decision rather than more reviewers. A single ally who breaks unanimity is the cheapest intervention in this literature, and it works even when the ally is also wrong.
After AISeveral assistants agreeing is not several opinions; they were trained on overlapping data by overlapping methods. The unanimity is manufactured upstream, and the partner effect has no analogue inside a model.
evidenceVariations of the experimental conditions

People in Asch's study decided in the first trials and stayed

In Asch's study people settled early: over half of those who ever gave a wrong answer did so by the second trial, only 7 per cent first erred in the second half, and with 36 trials no one new gave in after the eighth.

Becausemore than half of those who ever erred did so by the second critical trial and only 7 per cent first erred in the second half, and tripling the series to 36 critical trials produced 37.6 per cent with no new defectors after the eighth.
LimitsEstablished on a repetitive perceptual task where nothing changed between trials; a setting in which evidence accumulates would not be expected to behave this way.
PracticeSpend your attention on the first exchange rather than on endurance. Whatever stance you take in the first minute of a review, with a room or with a model, is the stance you will keep.
After AIThe first answer an assistant gives sets your posture for the session. Deciding once, early, whether you are checking or accepting is a larger choice than it feels like at the time.
evidenceVariations of the experimental conditions (sixth experiment, Table 21)

People resisted the majority more when its error was obvious

In Asch's sixth experiment, as the majority's wrong answer moved from a quarter of an inch off to three quarters, errors fell from 56.7 per cent to 25.7. The more obvious the error, the easier it was to resist.

Becauseeighteen subjects across the discrepancy range give a monotone fall, and errors also rose with the length of the standard — 30.5 per cent at three inches to 48.1 at nine — which Asch names unquestionability and cannot explain.
LimitsEighteen subjects in one experiment, and the second pattern — more errors on longer standards — is reported without explanation by the author himself.
PracticeReview the near misses rather than the disasters. An output that is slightly wrong is the one you will accept, and the size of the error is inversely related to your chance of catching it.
After AIA model's plausible-but-wrong answer is precisely the small discrepancy. The obvious failures are the safe ones, and the failure rate you experience is concentrated where your resistance is lowest.
evidenceVariations of the experimental conditions (seventh variation)

People stop copying the group once they write their answer down

In Asch's experiment, letting people write their answer down instead of saying it aloud cut wrong answers from 36.8 per cent to 12.5 per cent, and no one gave a wrong answer many times.

Becausethe subjects insisted the change made no difference to them, and since all assumed the experimenter would compare their answers with the group's, the fully private case was never run.
LimitsEven the written condition was not private — every subject assumed the experimenter would compare — so 12.5 per cent is an upper bound on what privacy removes, not a measurement of the residual.
PracticeHave people write their estimate before anyone speaks. It is the same intervention as a cognitive forcing function, it costs a minute, and it removed the extreme errors here entirely.
After AICommitting to your own answer before reading the model's is the same manipulation. It is also the one users reliably dislike, which is why it has to be built into the process rather than left to intention.
evidenceForms of independence and yielding

People who went along with the group forgot how often they did

People who agreed with a wrong majority underestimated how often they had done so, by about four trials. Some who went along ten or twelve times reported two.

Becausethe interview totals set against the trial records show the gap, and confidence tracked performance elsewhere: 87 per cent of the wholly independent said a ruler would vindicate them against 41 per cent of those who erred eight to eleven times.
LimitsRetrospective self-report against a trial record in one session; the underestimate may be a repair of a conflict the subject felt rather than a failure of memory, and the design cannot separate these.
PracticeLog how often you took the tool's answer, as a count, at the time. Your memory of how independent you were will be about a third short, and the direction of the error is known.
After AINobody keeps this count with an assistant. The one measurement we have — developers 19 per cent slower while believing themselves faster — suggests the gap is at least as large as Asch's.

Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, Joel Becker and others

evidenceTwenty-one ways to be wrong

Developers reject most AI suggestions and spend real time fixing the rest

In METR's trial, developers accepted fewer than 44 per cent of what the model wrote. Reviewing and cleaning up the code they did accept took 9 per cent of their working time when AI was allowed.

Becausethe acceptance rate comes from Cursor's own logs and the review share from the hand-labelled recordings; three developers in four report reading every accepted line and more than half often rewrite it substantially.
LimitsAcceptance rates are tool-specific and move with model quality; the 9 per cent is an average over a small sample of recordings. Nothing here says review time is wasted — only that it is not free.
PracticeFailure-mode review — budget review and repair as a line item rather than assuming generated code arrives finished, and record what you had to change.
After AIAcceptance rates have risen since 2025, which moves the number and not the structure: whatever is accepted still has to be read by someone who could have written it, and that person's ability to read it is what the next claim in this chain is about.
evidenceThe forecasts and the result

Developers' estimates of AI's effect on their speed get the direction wrong

The same developers predicted AI would make them 24 per cent faster, and said afterwards it had made them 20 per cent faster. Measured, they were 19 per cent slower. Months of using the tool did not shrink the error.

Becausethe same people forecast 24 per cent faster before the trial and reported 20 per cent faster after months inside it, against 19 per cent slower measured; the error is a constant offset rather than noise, and it did not shrink with Cursor hours.
LimitsThe offset is measured on one kind of work by sixteen people. The developers were not bad estimators in general: their forecasts correlate with actual times at about 0.6, and only the AI term is inverted. Whether the same offset holds for greenfield work is untested.
PracticeCalibration log — record the estimate before the work and the clock afterwards, because the estimate does not repair itself through use.
After AIThe paper's method — fix the task before the coin, measure the time, and do not ask the person afterwards how it went — outlasts the model generation it was built to test. Any claim about an assistant's value that rests on how the work felt is now the weakest kind of evidence available.
evidenceThe forecasts and the result

Experts predicting the trial were more wrong than the developers in it

Experts who predicted the METR trial's result from outside were wrong in the same direction as the developers taking part, and by a wider margin: economists predicted 39 per cent faster and machine learning researchers 38, against 19 per cent slower measured.

Becausethirty-four economists and fifty-four machine learning researchers were given the design, the repositories and the participants' AI background in advance, and still missed by roughly twice the participants' margin.
LimitsTwo convenience samples of forecasters answering a single question. Nothing here separates a bias about AI from a general optimism about any intervention described in advance.
PracticeCalibration log — write down what you expect a tool to do for a team before it is deployed, with a date and a number, and score it; expertise in the field does not substitute for the record.
After AIThe forecasters were not lay observers but the professions that advise on AI deployment. Their miss is the reason an organisation's expectations of an assistant should be treated as a hypothesis to be scored rather than a premise to plan against.

How AI Impacts Skill Formation, Judy Hanwen Shen and Alex Tamkin

evidenceWhat the quiz found

Assisted workers found the work easier and the test just as hard

In Shen and Tamkin's study the people who used the assistant said the task felt easier, then rated the quiz afterwards exactly as hard as everyone else did.

Becausethe control group reported higher learning on a seven-point scale, the assisted group rated the task easier and the quiz no easier, and one assisted participant wrote afterwards, "I feel like I got lazy".
LimitsSelf-report on seven-point scales from twenty-six people per arm. The control group's higher reported learning could be effort justification rather than accuracy.
PracticeCalibration log — treat ease during the work as information about the interface and not about what you now know; test the knowledge separately and unaided.
After AIThe feeling of ease is the assistant's most reliable product, and it is the one thing that cannot be used to judge the assistant. That the assisted group rated the quiz no easier suggests the illusion is about the session rather than about the knowledge.
contestedWhat the quiz found

Programmers using an AI assistant lost most ground on debugging questions

In Shen and Tamkin's study the group that used an AI assistant scored furthest behind the unassisted group on the debugging questions and closest on the code-reading questions. This breakdown was exploratory, not planned in advance.

Becausethe by-question-type analysis is exploratory; the proposed mechanism is that both arms read comparable amounts of code but only the unassisted arm met and resolved errors.
LimitsNot pre-registered, and drawn from fourteen questions split across three abilities, so the sub-scores rest on a handful of items each. The direction is consistent with the error-count data but is not independent of it.
PracticeManual flying hours — take the debugging yourself even when you delegate the writing, because diagnosis is the capacity that lets you supervise what the model produced.
After AIIf it holds, the skill that decays first is the skill the supervision model depends on. An organisation that delegates the writing and keeps the reviewing is relying on a capacity that its own delegation is eroding.

Peak, Anders Ericsson and Robert Pool

evidenceMental representations

A chess master's memory advantage disappears on a randomly arranged board

Ericsson argues the mental patterns that make someone an expert work only on what they trained on. Faloon's memory system for digits did nothing for letters, and a chess master's advantage vanishes on a board arranged at random.

BecauseChase and Simon found a master replaces two-thirds of a real position after five seconds and two or three pieces of a random one, the same as a novice.
LimitsThe chess evidence is strong and old; the generalisation from digit spans and chessboards to professional judgment is the authors', not the experiments'. Nothing here fixes how narrow a domain has to be before representations stop transferring.
PracticeDomain audit — list the domains where you actually hold representations and the ones where you are a confident novice, and set the checking effort by that list rather than by seniority.
After AIA model's competence is also uneven across domains, but not along the same seams as a person's, and neither party can feel where the other's boundary lies. The audit has to be done twice.
evidenceThe power of purposeful practice, and The gold standard

Ericsson says a plateau means your method has run out, not you

When progress in a skill stops, Ericsson holds that the method being used has reached its limit. The way past the plateau is a different method, not more hours of the same practice.

BecauseElio stalled near twenty digits on mnemonics invented on the fly and never passed it, while Donatelli, taught Faloon's method, stalled at thirty, built his own retrieval structure and passed a hundred; Faloon's own limit was located at a single faulty group by giving him strings ten digits too long.
LimitsCase studies of a handful of digit-span subjects, generalised to skill at large. The diagnostic move — overload the performer to find the failing component — depends on a task whose components can be isolated, which most professional work is not.
PracticeFailure-mode review — when progress stops, push past the current limit to find which component fails first, and change that component rather than adding hours.
After AIThe assistant is a new method, and on this account a new method is what breaks a plateau. That is the strongest case for delegation the chapter contains, and it holds only where the plateau is in output rather than in understanding.
evidenceHarnessing adaptability

Ericsson says adaptation stops once the new demand feels comfortable

Ericsson argues that body and brain rebuild themselves only while they are pushed past what is comfortable, so getting better requires raising the demand again each time it stops being hard — and only a little each time.

Becausecells work to hold their chemistry steady and rebuild only while out of range — 112 genes switch on in an overloaded rat muscle — and in Maguire's four-year study the posterior hippocampus grew only in the forty-one trainees who qualified.
LimitsThe homeostasis account is a physiological analogy carried into skill, and the size of the increment that keeps adaptation going is never specified. Maguire's study is observational: the trainees who qualified may have differed before they began.
PracticeManual flying hours — raise the difficulty of the unassisted block as soon as it stops being uncomfortable, rather than repeating it at the level that has become easy.
After AIAn assistant's first effect is to make the work comfortable. On this account comfort is the signal that adaptation has stopped, which makes the assistant's most attractive property the one to watch.
contestedThe gold standard

Ericsson says hard practice with feedback builds skill, not years spent

Skill is built and kept up by practice that is hard, aimed just past what you can already do, and followed by feedback. Years spent near the work do not do it.

Becausethe Berlin violinists had logged 3,420 hours by eighteen for the future teachers, 5,301 for the very good and 7,410 for the best, and doctors twenty to thirty years in do worse on objective measures than doctors three years out; the 2019 replication failed to separate the two upper groups.
LimitsMacnamara and Maitra's 2019 replication, double-blind where the original was not, found the merely good had logged as many solitary hours as the best. Their 2014 pooling of eighty-eight studies put practice at 26 per cent of variance in games and under 1 per cent in the professions; the argument is now described as settled in the middle.
PracticeManual flying hours — put the hours where the work is hard and the feedback is quick, rather than counting the hours the job supplies on its own.
After AIExposure is what a delegated workflow supplies: hours in the vicinity of the work, with the effortful part performed elsewhere. Even in its narrowed form, the claim says supervising a model is not practice at the thing supervised.
evidenceHarnessing adaptability

Retired taxi drivers lost the brain tissue the job had built

Ericsson argues that a skill you stop practising decays in the brain as well as in performance. Retired London taxi drivers had less grey matter at the back of the hippocampus than drivers still working.

Becauseretired taxi drivers had less grey matter in the posterior hippocampus than working ones, on the same imaging measure that showed the growth.
LimitsCross-sectional comparison of retired against working drivers, with age and health as obvious confounds. The imaging finding is about volume, not about any measured decline in navigation performance.
PracticeManual flying hours — schedule the unassisted block; a skill kept only as a credential is not kept.
After AIDelegation is retirement from a task without the retirement. The decay clock starts on the day the tool takes the work, and nothing in the workflow reports it.
contestedHarnessing adaptability

Trained London cabbies remembered a complex drawing worse than untrained people

Getting better at one thing can make you worse at another. Maguire found that London taxi drivers who had qualified remembered a complex drawing worse than untrained people who had matched them four years earlier.

Becausethe four-year design makes the decline hard to explain by selection, but it is one measure in one study and has not been replicated.
LimitsA single delayed-recall measure in a study designed for something else. The mechanism — that the posterior hippocampus grows at the anterior's expense — is inferred from the same imaging data rather than tested.
PracticeThe stays-human list — when you decide to specialise, name what you are giving up and decide whether it belongs on the list of things that stay yours.
After AIThe trade is usually described as a cost of specialisation. The relevant version now is the trade made by specialising in supervising a model: what grows is the ability to judge output, and what may go is the ability to produce it.

Make It Stick, Peter C. Brown and others

evidenceLearning is misunderstood, and Mix up your practice

How well you do while practising does not show what you learned

How well someone performs during practice does not show how much they have learned. The conditions that raise practice scores fastest are not the ones that leave knowledge that lasts.

Becausein the volumes experiment blocked practice averaged 89 per cent during practice and 20 a week later, while interleaved practice averaged 60 during practice and 63 later; the Bjorks' separation of retrieval strength from storage strength names the same gap.
LimitsLaboratory tasks with delays of days to weeks. Steven Pan and Timothy Rickard's 2018 meta-analysis found the benefit of testing transfers only modestly and inconsistently to changed formats and new inferences, which is more cautious than the book.
PracticeCalibration log — never read a training metric as a learning metric; measure later and unaided, or do not claim the learning.
After AIEvery productivity dashboard for AI-assisted work is a performance-during-practice measure. Robert Bjork and Nicholas Soderstrom formalised the distinction in 2015 as a warning against reading a training metric as a learning metric, and it is now the sharpest objection available to the field studies of assistants.
evidenceLearning is misunderstood

Reading a text twice in a row adds nothing and wastes time

In Make It Stick, 148 students at two universities got no benefit from reading a passage twice in a row, in any condition tested. Over 80 per cent of college students name rereading as their main study method.

BecauseTulving's six prior exposures produced learning curves indistinguishable from no exposure, and 148 students across two universities got no benefit from reading passages twice in succession in any condition tested; over 80 per cent of college students name rereading as their main method.
LimitsThe result is about massed rereading in immediate succession; spaced rereading is a different condition and is not what these studies tested.
PracticeManual flying hours — replace a second pass over the documentation with an attempt to use it from memory.
After AIScrolling an assistant's explanation of the same system a second time is the modern form of the same method, and it is fluent in exactly the way the book warns about.
evidenceAvoid illusions of knowing, and Mix up your practice

Students mistake easy practice for learning and stick with the worse method

Learners judge how much they have learnt by how easy the practice felt, so they prefer the method that works less well. They keep preferring it even after they are shown the test results that prove otherwise.

Becauseblocked practisers were markedly overconfident predicting next-day performance while interleaved practisers were accurate, and students went on preferring massed practice after taking the test that showed them they were wrong.
LimitsPreference data from classroom and laboratory studies; the persistence after disconfirmation is reported in a handful of experiments and has not been the subject of a meta-analysis.
PracticeCalibration log — treat your preference between two working methods as evidence about which one feels better, and settle the question with a delayed unaided test instead.
After AIIt explains why the METR developers kept using a tool that was costing them time. The preference is not irrational on its own terms — the assisted session really is easier — it is only uninformative about what was learned.

Superforecasting, Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner

evidenceKeeping score

A forecast without a number and a date cannot be graded

Tetlock shows that people read phrases like "serious possibility" as different odds: Sherman Kent meant 65 to 35; his own analysts read it as 80/20 or 20/80. A forecast with no number and no deadline cannot be scored, and the vagueness protects reputations.

BecauseSherman Kent meant 65 to 35 by "serious possibility" and his own analysts read it as 80/20 and 20/80; the 2010 letter to Bernanke set no date and hedged on "risk", and its signatories told Bloomberg in 2014 they would not change a word.
LimitsThe Kent finding is about intelligence analysts reading a specific phrase; how much of ordinary professional hedging is strategic rather than imprecise is not measured. The wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy is a critique of readers as much as of forecasters.
PracticeCalibration log — write the number and the resolution date before the work, because a judgment you cannot score is a judgment you cannot learn from.
After AIModel evaluations inherit the problem in full. A claim that an assistant is "generally reliable" for a task is Sherman Kent's serious possibility, and it protects the same reputations.
evidencePerpetual beta

One hour of training made forecasters about ten per cent more accurate

Tetlock found that spending an hour reading a short set of forecasting guidelines raised a forecaster's accuracy by roughly ten per cent, and the gain lasted about a year.

Becausethe tournament's training module was tested against untrained forecasters on identical questions over identical periods, which is a randomised comparison rather than an observed difference.
LimitsSweller holds that generic cognitive skills cannot be taught and cites the failure of attempts to teach them; this is the randomised far-transfer result his position has to absorb, in a domain he would not count. Ericsson's strict definition of deliberate practice excludes a field with no agreed standard of superior performance, which is the field this was measured in.
PracticeCalibration log — read the guidelines once, then keep the log; the training is cheap and its effect decays, so repeat it.
After AIIt is the most encouraging result in the vault: the capacity you need in order to supervise a model is trainable in an hour and measurable afterwards. The training has to be repeated, because the effect lasts about a season.
evidenceKeeping score

Single-idea experts forecast worst in their own specialty

Tetlock found that hedgehogs, experts who explain everything through one big idea, were less accurate forecasting inside their own specialty than outside it. More information through one lens brings more confidence and no more truth.

Becausethe comparison is within-subject, between forecasts made inside and outside the expert's speciality; fame ran inversely to accuracy, since producers hunt for people who tell tight confident stories.
LimitsKlein's evidence runs the other way in domains with valid cues and fast feedback; the 2009 settlement with Kahneman says the conditions decide, not the setting. Which regime a given professional judgment belongs to is not something either book supplies a classifier for.
PracticeFailure-mode review — raise the checking effort on judgments inside your own speciality, not lower it.
After AIIt is the closest thing in the literature to a mechanism for the METR result, where the slowdown was largest exactly where the developers' repository knowledge was deepest.
evidenceSupersmart, superquants, supernewsjunkies

Superforecasters lose accuracy when their odds are rounded to the nearest five

When Mellers rounded everyone's forecasts to coarser numbers, superforecasters' accuracy got worse while ordinary forecasters' barely changed. The extra digits in a superforecaster's estimate are real information, not false precision.

BecauseMellers rounded everyone's forecasts and recalculated: superforecasters lost accuracy from rounding to the nearest five points, while regular forecasters barely lost anything from rounding four times as coarsely, and a third of superforecaster judgments used single percentage points.
LimitsThe test shows that the granularity carried information for these forecasters on these questions; it does not show that a novice's single percentage points mean anything. The regular forecasters' insensitivity to coarse rounding is the other half of the same result.
PracticeCalibration log — record the probability you actually hold rather than rounding to a decade, and let the score tell you whether the extra digits were real.
After AIIt is the argument for asking a model for a number rather than a hedge, and for scoring the number. Whether a model's fine-grained probabilities survive the same rounding test is a measurement anyone can now run.
opinionSupersmart, superquants, supernewsjunkies

Tetlock says look at the general rate before the specific case

Tetlock says a forecaster should first ask how often such things happen in general, and only then look at the details of the particular case. Whichever number you see first becomes the anchor your final estimate stays near.

Becausethe ordering is a recommendation drawn from anchoring research and from what superforecasters were observed doing — David Rogg counted six attacks in five years, set the base rate at 1.2 a year, lifted it to 1.8 for the rise of ISIS against tightened security, and scaled it to the 69 remaining days for 34 per cent — rather than a randomised comparison of the two orders.
LimitsThe ordering has not been tested against the reverse in a controlled comparison; the case for it is anchoring plus observed practice. Klein's evidence says the expert's first recognition is usually right in domains with valid cues, which is the opposite prescription.
PracticeCalibration log — find the reference class and its base rate before you look at the details of the case in front of you.
After AIAn assistant supplies the inside view instantly and in fluent prose, which makes it the first number you see. The outside view now has to be taken before the prompt, not after the answer.
evidenceKeeping score

Tetlock's experts forecast no better than chance and thinking style separated them

Tetlock scored 284 professionals on some 28,000 dated predictions made between 1984 and 2004. The average forecast was no better than chance. What told the better forecasters from the worse was how they thought, not their credentials, access or politics.

Because284 professionals, some 28,000 dated predictions between 1984 and 2004, half with doctorates; foxes beat hedgehogs on calibration and on resolution both.
LimitsTwenty years of political and economic questions, scored on the researchers' own resolution criteria. The fox and hedgehog division comes from a questionnaire, and the trait psychology around it has fared badly in the replication decade.
PracticeCalibration log — stop weighting a judgment by the seniority of the person making it and start weighting it by their score on comparable questions.
After AIThe finding transfers directly to the question of whether to trust a model's judgment: ask for its record on comparable questions, not for its confidence or its reasoning.
evidenceSupersmart, superquants, supernewsjunkies

Tetlock's forecasters revise often in small steps and dump a bad source

Tetlock found that good forecasters change their estimates often and by small amounts. The exception is when the report a forecast rests on is visibly failing, in which case they throw it out rather than nudge the number.

BecauseTim Minto's thirty-four revisions on the Syrian refugee question averaged three and a half points and scored 0.07, while Lorch swung from 55 to 95 per cent on one month-old sea-ice report and the ice stopped melting; most superforecasters are Bayesians who do not use Bayes's theorem.
LimitsTwo cases and an aggregate pattern; the rule for when to discard rather than nudge is stated by example. Klein's account of the expert who abandons a whole frame at once is the opposite prescription in a domain with valid cues.
PracticeCalibration log — log every revision with its size and its reason, so that an oversized swing shows up as an event rather than as a new opinion.
After AIA model will revise to whatever the last message implied, which is the failure mode this rule is written against. Frequent small updating is a virtue in a person and a pathology in an assistant that has no stake in the previous number.
opinionAre they really so super?

Tetlock's forecasting tournament says nothing about rare disasters

Tetlock's tournament scored questions that resolve within months or a few years. It shows nothing about rare catastrophes, because scoring forecasts of those would take decades or thousands of years.

Becauseit is Tetlock's own concession to Taleb, and the supporting fact is that accuracy decayed towards chance between three and five years out in the 1984–2004 data, with no evidence supporting forecasts a decade ahead.
LimitsAn admission rather than a finding, and Tetlock notes the loose definition of a black swan that makes the disagreement hard to settle. The Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament of 2022 put forecasters and domain specialists on catastrophic-risk questions out to 2100 and they finished about as far apart as they began.
PracticeIf you believed it you would stop citing forecasting expertise in arguments about tail risk, and you would treat a superforecaster's number on a 2050 question as an opinion with no track record behind it.
After AIIt applies directly to forecasts about AI. The instrument that works on months has no demonstrated reach into the horizon on which most claims about model capability are made.
evidenceThe tournament

Tetlock's superforecasters stayed ahead across years, so forecasting is a skill

Predicting world events months ahead is a skill rather than a run of luck. Tetlock's best forecasters extended their lead in the tournament's second and third years instead of drifting back toward average.

Becausethe test is regression to the mean, and the superforecasters extended their lead across the second and third years instead of regressing; the year-to-year individual correlation is about 0.65, with roughly 70 per cent staying in the top two per cent.
LimitsConsistency was measured on questions the tournament chose, resolving within months. Accuracy decayed towards chance between three and five years out in the 1984–2004 data, so the skill is demonstrated only on the tournament's own horizon.
PracticeCalibration log — keep the record long enough for persistence to show, because a single good quarter is indistinguishable from luck.
After AIIt is the cleanest available template for evaluating a model: the same questions, the same resolution dates, a score, and a benchmark. Nothing about the instrument requires the forecaster to be human.
evidencePerpetual beta

Willingness to change your mind beats intelligence at predicting forecasting accuracy

In Tetlock's tournament, how committed a forecaster was to changing their mind and improving predicted their accuracy about three times as strongly as their intelligence did.

Becauseit was the strongest predictor the project found of who rises into the top ranks; superforecasters scored above about 80 per cent of the population on fluid intelligence against 70 per cent for the other volunteers, so the large jump is from the public to the volunteers rather than within them.
LimitsA correlation within a self-selected volunteer pool, measured by questionnaire. The traits the chapter reaches for — grit and growth mindset — have both been cut down since 2015, which weakens the explanation without touching the tournament's own measurements.
PracticeCalibration log — treat every scored miss as the material, and record what you changed your mind about, not only what you predicted.
After AIIt is the property an evaluation of a model cannot have on the model's behalf. The updating that matters is the reviewer's, and it only happens if the misses are recorded.

The Upanishads, translated by Eknath Easwaran

opinionKatha: death as teacher — Katha 2.5 and 2.9

The Upanishads warn about half-learned confidence, not ignorance

The Upanishads do not condemn ignorance. What they warn against is the confidence that comes with a little learning: the Katha describes the blind being led by the blind, and says reasoning alone will not settle the question.

BecauseKatha 2.5 has the blind led by the blind, repeated almost word for word in the Mundaka, and 2.9 says that *tarka*, reasoning, does not terminate here; both are assertions, and the psychological claim in them is the part that has since been measured elsewhere.
LimitsThe text's remedy is a teacher who has been up the path, and nothing in it is scored or scoreable. The Dunning and Kruger pattern that supplies the modern evidence has itself been contested on statistical grounds.
PracticeCalibration log — treat the arrival of confidence as the moment to check, and score the check.
After AIA middling amount of learning is what an assistant reliably produces in a hurry, and it arrives with the fluency that the text says is the danger. The remedy the vault can actually run is Tetlock's score rather than the Katha's teacher.

Sources of Power, Gary Klein

evidenceStories, and the problem of hyperrationality

Experience only builds expertise in fields that are steady and give feedback

Klein, following Shanteau, holds that years of experience turn into real expertise only where the field stays stable, gives feedback, does not depend on predicting what people will do, and repeats often enough to build a sense of what is typical.

Becausethese are Shanteau's conditions, which Klein extends to legislators, whose experience is expertise in the procedures of the job and not in its judgments; where cause and effect cannot be traced, what fills the gap is ritual.
LimitsA list of conditions with no threshold on any of them, and no classifier for a domain that partly meets them. Klein's 2009 settlement with Kahneman rests on the same conditions, which makes them the durable part of his answer and also the untested part.
PracticeDomain audit — classify the domain before you trust anybody's fast judgment in it, your own included.
After AISoftware with a model in the loop fails the stability condition: the tooling changes every few months, so the sense of typicality is being rebuilt continuously. On Shanteau's own terms that is a domain in which experience accumulates more slowly than it used to.
evidenceThe recognition-primed decision model

Experienced fire chiefs recognise a situation instead of weighing up options

Klein found that experienced fire commanders under time pressure do not weigh options against each other. They recognise the kind of situation they are in, and the action to take arrives with the recognition.

Because156 decision points from non-routine fireground incidents were coded by two researchers with a third arbitrating and doubtful cases pushed into the comparative bin, giving 127 recognitional against 18 comparative — and half of the comparative came from one fire where the chiefs were novices.
LimitsInterviews coded by the researchers who ran them, which Klein says plainly. The 2009 settlement with Kahneman narrows it: recognition is worth trusting when the environment offers valid cues and the person has had a fair chance to learn them, and both conditions fail in most of Kahneman's settings.
PracticeDomain audit — list the domains where your first judgment has been trained by feedback, and stop demanding option comparisons there while insisting on them everywhere else.
After AIIt names what the model does not have. A model's fluent first answer looks like recognition and is not backed by a history of cases in this environment, so the surface behaviour is the same and the warrant is absent.
evidenceThe power to see the invisible

Experts describe the signs they use only when asked about specific cases

Klein found that experts can name the signs they act on if you ask them about particular past cases rather than about their method. A large share of the signs they name appear nowhere in the professional literature.

BecauseCrandall's neonatal nurses had nothing to say about detecting sepsis until asked for particular babies and shifts; almost half the compiled cues were not in the medical literature and several ran opposite to the adult signs.
LimitsThe critical decision method extracts what one person can recall about cases they chose to report. Beane's objection is that it records what has been lost rather than substituting for the transmission.
PracticeFailure-mode review — ask a colleague for the last three times they caught something, not for how they catch things.
After AIIt is the cheapest way to get undocumented knowledge into a form a model could be given. The neonatal cues became a training programme and then a monitor that catches the deterioration earlier than a person can — which is the whole arc in one example.
evidenceThe power of intuition

Experts often react to something that did not happen

What tips an expert off is often an expected event that did not occur. Because there is nothing there to point at, they cannot say what they noticed, and the judgement gets called a sixth sense.

Becausethe lieutenant evacuated a house fire because the living room was too hot, it was too quiet and the water did nothing — the seat of the fire was in a basement he did not know existed — and the *Gloucester* officer read altitude off a radar that does not measure it.
LimitsReconstructed after the fact from interviews with the people involved. An absence noticed in hindsight is the easiest kind of cue to over-report, and the method cannot separate it from a story built afterwards.
PracticeWitness practice in review — when something feels wrong in a review, ask what you expected to see and did not, before you ask what is there.
After AIGenerated code is missing things rather than containing wrong things, which makes this the right shape of attention to bring to it. A model has no expectations to be violated, so the absent-cue channel exists only on the human side.
evidenceThe recognition-primed decision model

Experts test one option by imagining it play out, not by comparing

People judge a single option by imagining it being carried out and watching for what goes wrong, not by setting it against a rival option.

Becausein the overpass rescue a lieutenant cycled through a harness, the harness reversed and a rescue strap in about a minute, finding a fault in each and never comparing two; the pattern is Simon's satisficing observed in the field.
LimitsField cases, not experiments. In domains where the cues are weak, Klein conceded in 2009, consistent rules beat consistent people — and comparison is what rules amount to.
PracticeFailure-mode review — evaluate a proposed change by walking it forward step by step until something breaks, rather than by lining it up against alternatives.
After AIReviewing a generated diff is exactly this operation: one option, arriving whole, to be run forward in imagination. The difference is that nobody chose it, so there is no intent to reconstruct when the simulation snags.
contestedThe recognition-primed decision model

Klein says formal weighing of options is what beginners do, not experts

Klein argues that comparing options on paper is not the ideal that experienced judgment approximates. It is what people fall back on when they do not yet recognise what to do.

Becausetank platoon leaders on their first course fell below 50 per cent recognitional, and the volunteer chiefs at the oil tank farm produced the study's strongest comparative decision because they were, for that fire, novices; but Klein conceded in 2009 that where cues are weak, consistent rules beat consistent people.
LimitsThe claim does not survive the 2009 settlement in domains where the cues are weak; Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein's case for rules as noise reduction runs directly against it. Klein describes this as the part of the book that reads weaker now than it did in 1998.
