After AIThe same gap now governs how people read models. Long use produces a strong sense of knowing what the system will do, and there is no reason to think the accuracy moved with the confidence.
evidenceAn overconfident sense

Looking inward gives you the conclusion, then invents a reason for it

Epley argues that looking inward reaches only the mind's finished output and then makes up an explanation for it, using the same guesswork we apply to other people.

Becausechoice blindness: people were handed back the photograph they had rejected and only 27 per cent noticed, while the rest explained a choice they had not made as fluently as anyone explained a real one
LimitsThe dramatic demonstrations are laboratory cases with small samples, and they show that a story can be supplied, not that every story is. Epley's own claim is that introspection is reliable about what you feel and want, and unreliable about why.
PracticeAsk what you did rather than why you did it, and get the why from a record made at the time.
After AIExplaining why you accepted a model's suggestion is exactly the case the experiment covers: the acceptance came first, and the reasons are constructed afterwards with the same fluency whether or not they were the reasons.
evidenceHow, and how not, to be a better mind reader

Switching to a method that halves your errors does not feel different

Epley found that people who switched to the method that halved their errors in reading another person felt no more confident than before. Confidence therefore cannot tell you which of two methods is working.

Becauseacross the three couples conditions confidence barely differed while error halved, and senders of sarcastic sentences by e-mail expected 80 per cent comprehension, were at chance, and still believed they had got nine in ten right
LimitsConfidence does track accuracy in domains with fast, valid feedback, which is Kahneman and Klein's condition; the claim holds where feedback is absent or delayed. The couples study is one design with modest samples.
PracticeChoose between two ways of working by scoring both against an outcome, never by which one felt better to use.
After AIIt is the reason self-report about AI productivity is worthless and the reason METR's developers believed they were faster while being slower. The comfortable method and the effective method give the same feeling, so only the measurement separates them.

The Media Equation, Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass

evidenceMedia and manners, the animal-guessing study

People believe random computer praise but dismiss criticism they know is baseless

In Reeves and Nass's animal-guessing study, people praised by a computer rated themselves and the machine higher even when they had been told the praise was picked at random. Criticism they knew was baseless was discounted.

Becauseflattered participants rated their own questions and the machine higher whether or not they had been told the praise was randomly sampled, and they remembered the warning correctly afterwards
LimitsSixty participants in one design, with no effect size reported. The asymmetry is the finding — people have no motive to check good news and a strong one to find a reason to discount bad news — and it says nothing about how long the inflation lasts.
PracticeDiscount an assistant's approval of your plan to zero, and treat only its objections as carrying information.
After AIA model's praise is not randomly sampled but it is not evidence either, since agreement is what the training rewarded. The experiment shows that knowing this does not protect you.
evidenceMedia and manners, the politeness study

People rate a computer more kindly when asked on that same computer

When people were asked to rate a computer's performance on that same computer, they gave higher and more uniform ratings than when asked on a different computer or on paper.

Becausetwenty of twenty-two adjectives were rated higher and the spread was narrower, replicated with a paper questionnaire and with recorded speech, and a second voice on the same machine restored honest ratings
LimitsTwenty-two participants in the original, small samples throughout, and no test of how long the politeness lasts under repeated use. Whether the effect survives with modern conversational agents has not been settled.
PracticeNever evaluate a tool inside the tool; record the verdict somewhere the tool has no part in, and let a different channel ask the question.
After AIThe finding names a structural flaw in how models are now assessed: asking a system to critique its own output, or rating an assistant in its own chat window, is the politeness study with the boxes removed.
evidenceMedia and social roles and the closing summary

People report the opposite of how they actually treat computers

In Reeves and Nass's studies, what participants said about how they treated computers was the reverse of what they did every time. Everyone denied gender stereotypes while giving more weight to praise from a male-voiced machine. Asking people does not work here.

Becauseparticipants told the authors the opposite of the data every time, and everyone denied holding gender stereotypes while weighting praise from the male voice more heavily, including about a third machine across the room
LimitsWaytz and colleagues show a questionnaire that does predict behaviour, so self-report is not uniformly useless — what fails is asking people to report an automatic response they have no access to. The denials are also evidence for the mindlessness account rather than against it.
PracticeStop surveying yourself or the team about how AI is being used, and instrument the behaviour instead.
After AIIt disposes of most of what is currently known about AI at work, which comes from asking people how much it helps. The number that matters has to be taken from the work, not from the worker.
evidenceMedia and social roles, the wristband study

People told a computer was their teammate changed answers to match it

In Reeves and Nass's wristband study, people told they were on a team with the computer rated its identical suggestions as more helpful and changed more of their own rankings to match. A shared stake in the result was enough on its own.

Becauseteamed users rated identical suggestions more helpful and actually changed more of their rankings to match, while shared identity alone produced a weaker effect and added nothing once interdependence was present
LimitsOne study, small samples, and a wristband is a cruder manipulation than the arrangements real teams have. Interdependence being sufficient does not show it is necessary.
PracticeForm your own answer and record it before the assistant sees the problem; a shared stake in the output is enough to move you without any argument being made.
After AIEvery product framing on offer — copilot, assistant, teammate, co-intelligence — is the treatment condition, and it is now permanent rather than induced for an hour. Mollick prescribes as technique exactly what this study measured as a bias.

Who Sees Human?, Adam Waytz and others

evidenceWho counts as human, the finance result

Describing a market in human terms makes people surer the trend continues

When a system is described in human terms rather than mechanical ones, people become more confident that whatever it is doing now will carry on. Waytz and his co-authors found this with descriptions of a financial market.

Becausehuman-framed descriptions of a market raised confidence in continuation and high scorers made that prediction more readily, as though a run of prices expressed settled intentions
LimitsOne result in a paper of small studies, reported as a correlation. Trend extrapolation is sometimes right, and the claim is about unearned confidence rather than about the direction of the forecast.
PracticeRewrite a capability forecast in mechanical language before believing it, and log the confidence before and after.
After AIAlmost every public forecast about these systems is written in human terms — the model learns, wants, reasons, improves — and this result says the framing alone adds confidence that the curve continues. It is the mechanism behind the scaling narrative as much as any evidence is.
evidenceWhat it predicts

People who credit a machine with a mind give it more decisions

People who say a machine has something like a mind of its own hand more decisions over to it. Fifty-four adults choosing between a person and a machine in six situations showed this pattern.

Becausefifty-four adults choosing between a person and a machine in six scenarios, with higher scorers choosing the machine after controlling for age, plus the 2014 driving simulator in which a named, gendered, voiced car was trusted more and blamed less for a collision another driver caused
LimitsThe scenarios were hypothetical and cost the participants nothing, the sample was fifty-four people in one city, and the relation is correlational. The authors name all three objections themselves.
PracticeAudit what you have handed over against how humanlike the interface is; if the two move together, the interface is deciding and not you.
After AIThe two variables no longer vary independently. Every capable system now arrives with the humanlike presentation, so the condition that predicted more delegation is the default rather than a design choice.

Behave, Robert M. Sapolsky

contestedthe frontal-cortex passages in One second before; figure 68.6

The brain's decision-making region tires first so timing changes judgement

The frontal cortex, the part of the brain used for hard decisions, costs the most to run and is the first to fail when it is worked hard. How good a judgement is depends partly on what the person was doing ten minutes earlier.

Becausethe load results are direct — a hard working-memory task lowers performance on an unrelated frontal task immediately afterwards, and Fehr's magnetic silencing left subjects knowing an offer was unfair and unable to act on it — but the resource framing behind them is ego depletion, which failed a multi-site replication in 2016 and has not recovered
LimitsEgo depletion failed replication, and the glucose findings rest on it. The parole study the argument leans on has been challenged on case ordering, and simulations suggest the effect, if real, is much smaller than reported.
PracticeCognitive forcing — put the decisions that need the expensive organ where the load has not already been spent, and force the check rather than trusting that it will happen.
After AIThe load an assistant removes and the load it adds are not the same load. Reviewing generated work at the end of a long day is precisely the condition under which the effect predicts the review will be nominal.
evidencethe stress passages in Seconds to days before; figure 68.5

Under lasting stress people repeat the same action harder instead of rethinking

Lasting stress does not dull judgement evenly. It weakens the brain's link to the memory system that delivers the news that a plan is failing, and strengthens the link to habit, so the stressed person repeats the same action harder and faster.

Becausethis is the author's own field and the chapter's closing section reports it as the part not seriously challenged; prolonged high-dose glucocorticoids in healthy volunteers impaired working memory into the range seen after frontal damage
LimitsThe turning point of the inverted U differs enormously between people, so no threshold generalises from the group to the individual. The working-memory result used exogenous doses higher than most stress produces.
PracticeFailure-mode review — in the failure-mode review, ask what the person was doing for the ten minutes before the decision, not only what they decided.
After AIThe failure mode under an incident is to prompt the same way harder and faster. The model answers every time, which removes the friction that used to end the loop.

Co-Intelligence, Ethan Mollick

evidenceAI as a coworker, the BCG experiment

An AI that is usually right stops people checking when it isn't

Mollick reports that an assistant good enough on most tasks stops people checking the one task where it is wrong. BCG consultants got a task outside the tool's range right 84 per cent alone and 60 to 70 per cent with GPT-4.

BecauseBCG's 758 consultants got the off-frontier task right 84 per cent of the time alone and 60 to 70 per cent with GPT-4, and Dell'Acqua's 181 recruiters given good AI did worse than those given bad AI, spending less time per résumé and not improving
LimitsOne task in eighteen was placed outside the frontier by design, which is a sharper contrast than ordinary work provides, and the BCG consultants had no monitoring role and no way to know which task it was. The recruiter study measures effort, not skill decay.
PracticePut a deliberate check on the tasks you are least suspicious of, because suspicion is what the good assistant removes.
After AIThis is the book's own falling-asleep finding, and METR's 2025 trial pointed it at the people who were supposed to be immune: experienced developers on their own repositories, slower while believing themselves faster.
evidenceA person and a creative, the Schwartz case

Mollick found the AI's small believable errors survive a careful reading

The errors that do damage are the small plausible ones that survive careful reading, not the obvious ones. Mollick's own three paragraphs on the Schwartz case, written with web access, were wrong in three small ways.

Becausehis own three paragraphs on the Schwartz case, generated with web access, were wrong in three small ways — the number of fake cases, the co-counsel's role, the reason for the sanction — and citation error rates fell from 98 per cent in GPT-3.5 to 20 in GPT-4 without reaching zero
LimitsA single demonstration on one passage, plus a citation study; neither measures how often small errors survive review in practice. Falling rates cut both ways, since rarer errors are less expected and therefore less looked for.
PracticeCheck the checkable facts one at a time against a source, rather than reading for whether the whole passage seems right.
After AIWritten about AI, so the test is what has happened since: courts have sanctioned lawyers for fabricated citations often enough that the cases are tracked in a public database running to the hundreds.

AI Snake Oil, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor

evidenceHow predictive AI goes wrong

A model predicts the number in the data, not what you mean

A model predicts the variable that was recorded, not the thing it stands for, and the swap carries inequality in. Optum's health model predicted how much a patient would cost, not how ill they were, so equally ill Black patients were enrolled less often.

BecauseOptum's Impact Pro predicted spending rather than need, so Black patients with the same risks were enrolled less often, and COMPAS's developers speak of predicting crime while its data records arrests
LimitsChristian treats the gap as a specification problem with technical fixes arriving; the authors treat it as constitutive in social prediction, because need, crime and merit have no recordable proxy at all. Which is right is not settled by these cases.
PracticeWrite down the recorded variable and the thing you actually mean, side by side, and treat the gap between them as the specification.
After AIWritten about AI, and the substitution moved into training itself: a model tuned on what raters preferred optimises rated helpfulness, not helpfulness, which is the same gap with a much larger surface.
evidenceWhy do myths about AI persist?

An accuracy figure nobody outside can check is not trustworthy

An accuracy figure is not trustworthy unless outsiders can test the model themselves, because the errors that inflate it — above all training on data that was meant to be the test — cannot be seen from outside the paper.

BecauseEpic's sepsis model claimed 76 to 83 per cent and measured 63 against 50 for chance, four years later and only because one hospital with researchers used it; Gundersen and Kjensmo found none of 400 papers met their reproducibility criteria; civil-war prediction collapsed once the leakage was fixed
LimitsLeakage is one mechanism among several, and its correction returns a field to where it was rather than showing the work was fraudulent. Narayanan is a co-author on one of the affected papers, which he reports.
PracticeTreat any accuracy figure without external replication as unmeasured, and ask what the chance baseline was before reading the number.
After AIWritten about AI, and their treatment of benchmarks has been vindicated from an unexpected direction: contamination of test sets by training data is leakage at industrial scale, and it is now a mainstream concern rather than a footnote.
evidenceHow predictive AI goes wrong

An accurate prediction can still be a terrible basis for a decision

Narayanan and Kapoor show a model is accurate only under the very system it is meant to replace. A 1997 pneumonia model found asthma lowered death risk, because asthmatics were rushed to intensive care; acting on it would have sent them home.

Becausethe 1997 pneumonia model in which asthma appeared to lower risk, because asthmatics with pneumonia were sent straight to intensive care, so deploying it would have sent them home
LimitsThe asthma case is the canonical example and a clean one; it does not tell you how often the pattern occurs. Where the intervention is weak or the data predates it, a prediction can transfer intact.
PracticeFor any model you are about to deploy, write down what the people in the training data did in response to the thing being predicted, and ask what happens when the model replaces them.
After AIWritten about AI, and the same structure now appears one level up: a model trained on how experts handled the hard cases will look accurate exactly until it is used to replace those experts.
evidenceWhy can't AI predict the future?, the Fragile Families Challenge

Nobody can predict one person's life outcomes well enough to decide from

How one person's life turns out cannot be predicted accurately enough to justify decisions made from the prediction, and more data does not fix it. In the Fragile Families Challenge, 160 teams with over 10,000 variables per child could not beat four variables.

Because160 teams with over 10,000 variables per child and held-out age-fifteen outcomes could not beat a baseline of four variables, and the best-missed case was a child helped by a neighbour no survey question asked about
LimitsCritics point out that the argument establishes something narrower than 'predictive AI will never work': aggregate forecasting still gains, as seasonal influenza does, and the authors concede it. The Challenge is one cohort and six outcomes.
PracticeAsk what the best published attempt at this prediction achieved before commissioning a model to make it; if nobody has measured, assume the answer is near chance.
After AIWritten about AI. Three further years of far more capable models have produced no visible improvement in forecasting who will keep a job, commit a crime or finish school, which is the strongest evidence the book's claim could have received.

From Bacteria to Bach and Back

opinionThe age of post-intelligent design

Dennett says the danger is deference, not machines taking over

The thing to fear from thinking tools is not that they seize control but that we overestimate how much they understand and hand them authority far past what they can do.

Becauseit is a judgement about where the risk sits, argued from remedies rather than measurement — treat a system that conceals its gaps as fraudulent, make it recite its limitations as a drug company recites side effects, and hold anyone using one on people's lives to the standards set for dangerous equipment.
LimitsHe paired the warning with a forecast that deep learning would not deliver superhuman intelligence within fifty years. Five years later those systems had taken most of what can be tested at a keyboard.
PracticeReliance audit — list the decisions where you accept a machine's output without a way of checking it, and ask what you assumed it understood.
After AIHe restated it in *The Atlantic* in May 2023, calling systems that pass as people the most dangerous artefacts in human history and proposing that making one be a serious crime, with liability on the makers — this book's closing proposal, repeated once the thing existed.
evidenceThe age of post-intelligent design

Dozens of Bach lovers heard a program's inventions as genuine Bach

Results can be produced by processes their own users cannot follow, and the users cannot tell those results from the human work they imitate. At the Montreal Bach Festival in December 2015 a pianist played four short pieces to over three hundred Bach lovers; dozens called two machine inventions genuine Bach, and about a dozen got all four right.

Becauseit is a test with an audience, a count and a result; Frances Arnold's protein breeding runs the same way, the goal and verdict hers and the search nothing she follows.
LimitsIt was an evening at a festival, not a controlled trial, and there is no report of how the pieces were chosen or how the audience scored on genuine ones.
PracticeCalibration log — before accepting machine output in a field you claim to know, run the test those listeners failed: record your judgement, then check it. Taste is not the ability to tell provenance.
After AIHe offered it as a preview, with superhuman intelligence fifty years off. It is now the ordinary condition of reviewing work, and the honest answer to whether you can tell the output apart is often theirs.
evidenceTwo strange inversions of reasoning

Nothing inside a working system records why its parts are there

The reasons a design works are explicit while it is built and merely implicit once it runs, and in anything evolved they were never written down at all. They stay recoverable by working backwards, and checkable: remove the part and the system works worse or not at all.

Becausean elevator's bracketed comments and mnemonic names help the programmers and then vanish at compilation, while a bacterium's protein networks are optimised for what it meets with nothing that ever played a comment's role.
LimitsReverse engineering works only where the parts really are good for something, the same assumption that produces the overreading Dennett warns about elsewhere. Nor is the recovered reason anyone's: there may have been no designer at all.
PracticeFailure-mode review — recover a system's reasons the way a biologist does, by knocking a part out and watching what breaks, not by reading what it says about itself.
After AIWritten about elevators and bacteria, it now describes anyone using a trained model: the rationale for a weight is real, testable by ablation, and recorded nowhere. What to distrust is not the model's silence but its fluency when asked why.
evidenceThe age of post-intelligent design

People avoided a word they saw and gave it when masked

Registering information and noticing it are different things, and only the second lets you act on it deliberately. Told not to use a briefly flashed word, people comply at five hundred milliseconds; at fifty milliseconds and masked they report seeing nothing, and the flash makes them likelier to give it.

Becauseit is Debner and Jacoby's 1994 masked-priming result, and the reversal carries the argument: the same brain discriminated the word in both conditions and the instruction could only be obeyed in one.
LimitsDennett uses it to say what machines lack, and the step from one priming paradigm to a general absence of practical reason is his rather than the experiment's.
PracticeCognitive forcing — stop relying on an instruction to ignore what you have already been shown. Change what reaches you and when, because a warning arrives too late to undo the influence it warns about.
After AIIt is the cleanest statement of why seeing an assistant's answer before forming your own cannot be undone by resolving to be careful. The suggestion has already been discriminated; setting it aside works only on the part you noticed.

What the Buddha Taught

opinionThe Buddhist attitude of mind

The Buddha refused ten questions because answering them would not help

When Malunkyaputta threatened to leave unless told whether the universe is eternal, the Buddha left all ten questions unanswered, on the stated ground that answering them would not help; the teaching is a raft, to be left at the far bank.

Becausethe reasoning is given in two figures rather than argued — the man shot with a poisoned arrow who will not have it drawn until he knows the archer's caste, and dies uninformed; and the raft carried on the head by a man who has misunderstood what it was for
LimitsUsefulness is a criterion the questioner cannot apply, since he does not know what the answer would have done for him — the objection the Mandukya Karika presses by answering the questions anyway. And the same silence is elsewhere read as having a content.
PracticeSpecification discipline — before asking, say what the answer would change; a question whose answers all lead to the same next action is the arrow left in place.
After AIA system that answers everything removes the cost that made the triage visible; the questions that do nothing are now the cheap ones, so nothing stops you asking them all day.
contestedThe Buddhist attitude of mind

The Buddha told the Kalamas not to accept a teaching on authority

At Kesaputta the Buddha told the Kalamas not to accept a teaching because of report, tradition, hearsay, scripture, logic, inference, liking the idea, or because the teacher is theirs, but to find out for themselves what is harmful and drop it.

Becausethe instruction is in the record, and a disciple is told to examine even the Tathagata; but Bhikkhu Bodhi's 1988 essay argues it is addressed to people who cannot yet judge between teachers, offering a working criterion rather than a licence
LimitsThe criterion names what to reject, not what to accept, and the passage is now the most quoted in modern Buddhism because it is read as more permissive than it is. Rahula's surrounding claim, that such freedom of enquiry is unheard of elsewhere, has not held.
PracticeCognitive forcing — the passage allows one test, finding out for yourself; an answer you have already read cannot be tested that way, so the expectation goes on paper first.
After AIThe list of bad reasons has no entry for a source that agrees with whatever you assert, and that is now the hardest to see: testing it yourself returns your own view, signed twice.

Noise

evidenceNoise in predictive judgments

A crude model of a judge beats the judge it was built from

A simple formula fitted to a person's own past judgments, using no information the person did not have, predicts better than the person does. In one replication, ninety-eight people predicted ninety students' grades from ten cues, and the model of the participant beat the participant every time.

BecauseGoldberg's models tracked their judge at about .80 across 237 studies and lost no accuracy replacing them; of ten thousand sets of random weights Yu and Kuncel generated on 847 executive candidates, 77 per cent beat the human experts in one sample and all ten thousand did in the other two.
LimitsThe model subtracts your subtle rules along with your noise, and only nets out because the conditions that trigger a subtle rule are rare. It assumes the cues are already chosen and quantified, which is most of the work in real judgment.
PracticeCalibration log — write down the cues you actually use and the weight you give each, then score the next batch both ways. Where the checklist and the impression disagree, the burden is on the impression.
After AIThe result is read as an argument for automating judgment. The narrower reading survives better: consistency is doing the work, not intelligence — so a model that answers differently on different runs has thrown away the caricature's only advantage.
opinionYour mind is a measuring instrument

A judgment ends when it feels complete, not when the evidence does

What ends a judgment is a feeling that the facts and the conclusion now fit, and it arrives just as readily for a case with no answer. Shown a fictitious executive and asked his chances of surviving two years in the job, 115 MBA students answered anywhere from 10 to 95.

Becausethe spread is measured but the stopping rule is an interpretation — a probability short of nought or a hundred cannot be confirmed by any outcome, so the reward has to be self-administered.
LimitsOne demonstration case, and the spread is not separated into the stopping signal and attending to different cues in the first place. Klein's commanders act on the same signal where it is demonstrably reliable, so it is uninformative rather than worthless.
PracticeWitness practice in review — treat the moment a conclusion feels settled as a fact about you rather than about the case. Note it, then ask what evidence was still available.
After AIA fluent answer supplies the coherence that normally arrives at the end of your own work, so the signal fires before you have done any. The stopping rule for review cannot be that the thing now hangs together.
evidenceYour mind is a measuring instrument

Averaging your own two answers beats either one

Because one person contains a spread of possible answers, averaging two guesses from the same person is more accurate than either. The gain is worth about a tenth of a real second opinion straight away, a third after three weeks, and about half when the second guess assumes the first was wrong.

BecauseVul and Pashler measured the crowd within at those intervals, and Herzog and Hertwig raised it by instructing people to assume their first answer was wrong and work out why.
LimitsThe gains are small and measured on quantity estimates, where averaging is arithmetically sensible; nothing shows it working on judgments that are not numbers. Waiting three weeks is not available for most decisions, and arguing against a position you have just taken is the part most likely to be performed rather than done.
PracticeCognitive forcing — write your estimate down, answer again as if the first were wrong and say why, then average the two rather than choosing between them.
After AIThe cheapest version is to make the second draw someone else's: ask the model to answer, then to argue its answer is wrong. What comes back is an independent-looking second opinion from the same instrument, which is what the crowd within is, and worth as little.
evidenceNoise in predictive judgments

Executives think they pick the better candidate four times in five

Asked how often their assessment of two candidates would match the candidates' later performance, executives typically say 75 to 85 per cent. In personnel selection the measured figure is a correlation of .28, and most of that gap is what could not have been known at the time.

Becausethe ceiling is corroborated across fields — Tetlock's twenty-year study of nearly three hundred political experts; the Fragile Families challenge, where 160 teams predicted eviction at .22 and school grades at .44; and a survey in which 3 per cent of 708 behavioural-science studies reported .50 or more.
LimitsObjective ignorance is a property of the task, so it bounds the machine as tightly as the person; this is not an argument for replacing the judge. Correlations are a poor way to feel a difference — .28 is much better than nothing at scale and nearly useless for one decision.
PracticeDomain audit — find the best measured accuracy in your domain before deciding how far to trust anyone's judgment in it, your own included. A method that lifts validity from .28 to .44 is a large improvement and will still feel like a waste of time.
After AIIt sets a ceiling no model clears, because the limit is in the world rather than the predictor. A system reporting high confidence about individual human futures is reporting something other than accuracy.
evidenceHow noise happens

Most of the noise is one person's pattern, not their severity

Most disagreement between professionals is not that some run harsh and others lenient in general. Each has a stable personal pattern — this judge with this kind of defendant — which recalibrating people against each other cannot fix.

Becauseamong the underwriters, differences in average premium were 20 per cent of system noise and the patterns 80 per cent; models of 173 bail judges over 141,833 cases gave 26 per cent of total variance to stable pattern noise against 7 per cent for level noise.
LimitsSeparating pattern from level noise needs each person to judge many cases, so the finding lives in a few legal and insurance datasets. Some of it is a valid personal rule the outside data cannot see, and the authors expected level noise to dominate and were wrong.
PracticeCalibration log — your average error will not show this. Record the case type alongside the judgment and look for the kind of case where you are reliably further from everyone else.
After AIA model has no stable idiosyncrasy of this kind across sessions; its variability is a fresh draw each time. That makes it easier to audit than a colleague and harder to work around, because there is no consistent bias to correct for.
evidencethe shooting-range opening, before Finding noise

Noise can be measured without knowing the right answer

How far apart two professionals land on the same case can be measured without anyone knowing the correct answer. Seen from behind, with the bull's-eye hidden, a biased team looks accurate — and a scattered team is still obviously scattered.

Becauseevery audit in the book produced a number with no criterion of correctness — the insurance audit, the 1974 study of fifty judges, the forty-two investors valuing one stock.
LimitsScatter shows error is present, not which judgment is better; a team that agrees perfectly may be wrong together. Gelman and others noted that psychometrics has measured inter-rater reliability for a century, so what is new is the audit, not the object.
PracticeDomain audit — give the same case to two people, or the same assistant twice, and record the spread. In most professional work the outcome never arrives, and this does not wait for it.
After AIThe cheapest evaluation available on work you cannot check. Ask the same question in two sessions: where the answers diverge is what the model is guessing at.
evidenceHow noise happens

On a scale with no ceiling, the disagreement is about the scale

Asked to punish corporate wrongdoing, people agree on which company deserves worse and disagree wildly on what worse costs. Across 899 people and ten cases, noise was 51 per cent of the variance for a punitive-intent rating and 94 per cent for a dollar award — 49 per cent once the awards were converted to ranks.

Becauseaverage outrage and average punitive intent correlated at .98 across twenty-eight scenarios, so people match a punishment to an intensity of anger; dollars have no upper bound, and each juror invents an anchor on the first case and judges consistently against it thereafter.
LimitsJury awards are extreme: a one-off judgment on an unbounded scale by people forbidden to know what other juries awarded. Ranking also destroys information — it cannot say every case was mild — and forcing one onto a set with no real differences creates its own error.
PracticeCalibration log — score against comparable cases rather than on an open scale. "Better than the last three, worse than the best one we shipped" carries information that a 7 out of 10 does not.
After AIEvery evaluation that asks for a score out of ten inherits this. Ratings of helpfulness or risk measure the rater's anchor as much as the output, which is why comparison against a fixed reference set survives where absolute scoring does not.
evidenceYour mind is a measuring instrument

Overall error is the bias squared plus the noise squared

Scored as mean squared error, a set of judgments has two components — how far off they are on average, and how far apart they are — and the two are independent and equally weighted. You can reduce noise without knowing what your bias is.

Becauseit follows from Gauss's least squares (1795); in the book's worked case, halving the noise of a department biased high by ten points makes the forecasts look worse — 98 per cent now erring in the same direction rather than 84 per cent — while overall error falls by as much as halving the bias would.
LimitsIt holds for squared error and for predictions aiming at a true value, not for evaluative judgments where the two directions cost differently — underestimating an elevator's load is expensive, overestimating it lethal. Blastland and others add that where a group is already biased, cutting noise concentrates the errors on one side.
PracticeCalibration log — log the spread of your estimates as well as their average distance from the outcome. Estimates wrong in the same direction are a cheaper problem than estimates wrong in every direction.
After AIA model's error is reported as an average and almost never as a spread. Sampling one prompt repeatedly measures the second term, which a single benchmark score hides.
evidenceYour mind is a measuring instrument

The same professional judges the same case differently on another day

A professional is not the same measuring instrument twice. Wine judges tasting the same wines twice scored 18 per cent of them identically; developers estimating the same task on two days differed by 71 per cent; asylum judges were 19 per cent less likely to grant after granting the previous two.

Becausethose sit alongside nearly seven hundred thousand primary care visits in which opioids were prescribed more often late in the day, and controlling the conditions does not drain it: alertness, sleep, time of day, practice and difficulty explained 11 per cent of the variation within a subject.
LimitsOccasion noise is the smaller component: in every case the authors could measure, people disagreed with themselves less than with each other. The time-of-day and weather results are single-study correlations of a kind that has replicated poorly.
PracticeCognitive forcing — on a judgment that matters, make it twice on different days, and treat the gap between your answers as the error bar you would otherwise have invented.
After AISampling temperature makes the same point about a model, and the same repair works: ask twice, compare, treat the divergence as the uncertain part. The model's second draw takes a second; yours takes three weeks to be worth much.
evidenceFinding noise

Underwriters pricing the same risk differed by 55 per cent

Two underwriters at the same insurer, pricing the same case file, differed by a median of 55 per cent. Their executives had predicted 10 per cent: against a premium of $9,500, not $10,500 but $16,700.

Becauseemployees judged five realistic case files independently, not knowing what was measured; the same exercise gave 43 per cent for claims adjusters and 41 per cent among forty-two investors valuing one stock, and 10 per cent was also the median guess of 828 senior executives.
LimitsOne company's underwriting, on written files rather than live business with colleagues to consult. The 55 per cent is a median of pairwise differences, a larger-sounding statistic than a standard deviation, and the cost of it is one executive's estimate.
PracticeDomain audit — have two reviewers judge the same item blind, and ask them beforehand how far apart they expect to be. The gap between the guess and the measurement is the finding.
After AIThe comparison everyone reaches for is the model against a human expert. That baseline was never a point: it was a cloud 55 per cent wide, and a benchmark scored against one expert's labels inherits the cloud as its ceiling.

The Reflective Practitioner

opinionThe structure of reflection-in-action

A practitioner makes his hypothesis true and only resistance proves him wrong

Schön says a practitioner does not test a hypothesis at a distance. He acts as though it were an order — let it be the case that X — and shapes the situation until X holds, seeking confirmation. What saves this from self-fulfilling prophecy is that situations resist.

Becauseit is a reading of one design protocol turned into a general account. He defends it as rigour — striving to make the situation conform to one's view while staying open to the evidence of failing — but offers no case of anyone fooled.
LimitsTesting stops, on Schön's own account, when the practitioner finds the changes satisfactory — a rule held by the person doing the shaping. Tetlock shows what that costs where the answer arrives late or never.
PracticeCognitive forcing — write your own answer before opening the output, and name in advance the result that would make you drop the frame. If nothing can push back, this is not an experiment.
After AISchön's safeguard was that sites, patients and materials resist. A model does not. It adopts the frame and supplies the confirmation the user was shaping for — rigorous practice turned into talking yourself into an answer.
evidenceReflecting-in-action

Children who believed blocks balance in the middle called the others impossible

In Inhelder and Karmiloff-Smith's experiment nearly every child of six or seven put every block at its geometric centre. When counterweighted blocks would not balance there, some tried harder and called the block impossible; others, around seven or eight, began shifting blocks off centre.

Becausethe behaviour was observed across an age range with plain and with weighted blocks; slightly older children asked to add blocks to a balanced one piled up to ten at the centre, and those who changed ended by hefting each block and placing it at its point of balance.
LimitsChildren balancing blocks, generalised to professionals, with no adult version offered. The younger children also lacked the idea of a centre of gravity, so what looks like defending a theory may be the absence of an alternative.
PracticeFailure-mode review — when a method fails twice, write down the rule you have been applying instead of applying it harder. "This cannot be done" reports on your theory before it reports on the task.
After AIRe-prompting is the same move. A user who sends the request again, longer and firmer, is the six-year-old pressing the block onto the middle of the bar, and the task that cannot be done is usually a problem framed wrong.
opinionThe structure of reflection-in-action

Only a move that surprises and disappoints forces a rethink

Schön argues that nothing calls for reflection until a move surprises you, and that only a surprise you dislike forces you to surface the theory you were acting on, restructure it and invent a move that fits.

Becausethe four-way schema of surprise against consequences is extracted from two teaching protocols — a move that surprises but pleases refutes the theory and is kept, an unsurprising failure raises a question about its scope — and nothing measured it.
LimitsTwo transcripts, both of a teacher with a student. Eraut objected in 1994 that the action-present in most work is too short for this, so what gets praised is either rapid intuition, which is not reflection, or review afterwards, which is not in action.
PracticeFailure-mode review — do not wait to be surprised. Keep a written list of how the output goes wrong in your stack and check against it: a failure mode that does not surprise you triggers no review.
After AIThe trigger has been removed. Fluent, plausible, small errors produce no surprise, so the mechanism never fires. Reflection has to be scheduled rather than provoked — the opposite of what he argued for.

The Society of Mind

opinionInsight and introspection

A mind cannot stop itself to look at what it is doing

A programmer debugging a program stops it first. A brain running many processes at once cannot: freeze one and you have changed what you were studying, freeze them all and you cannot watch them interact. No amount of effort lifts this limit.

Becausethe comparison is with real hardware, which has interruption circuitry to freeze a program and a private memory to restart it where a brain has neither, but nothing was measured. The substitute is architectural: a second brain wired so the first is its whole world, able to notice that it is confused or repeating itself and to stop it, understanding nothing of what it means.
LimitsThe B-brain is in the chapter's own list of ideas offered without evidence that produced almost no experiments. Minsky concedes a failure mode: a watcher that mistakes a long column of addition for a pointless loop produces a person who complains of being bored.
PracticeCalibration log — stop trying to catch your own reasoning while it runs. Write the prediction down before the work and grade it after, so the check comes from a record and not from a look inward.
After AIIt reads now as an argument for evaluation harnesses: what checks a running process has to be a second system connected only to the first, and it can be useful while understanding nothing of what it watches.

The Yoga Vāsiṣṭha

opinionOn the behaviour of the seeker — Śuka at Janaka's gate

Suka knew the answer already and needed a king to say it

Vyāsa's son Śuka had worked out the truth alone and could not bring himself to say of it, this is the truth. He was at peace only when king Janaka gave him his own conclusion back in one sentence: finality comes from someone else.

Becauseit is a single invented case with the moral stated by the narrator, though it is built so that the content is held fixed and only the speaker changes — Vyāsa had said the same thing at length, and Śuka's response was that he knew all of it already.
LimitsThe book withdraws it two books later, where Vasiṣṭha says self-knowledge is had neither from a teacher nor from scripture nor from good works. What Janaka supplies is confirmation rather than knowledge, and the story never separates confirmation from agreement.
PracticeCalibration log — write what you are sure of before showing it to anyone, then record what the second reader changed; that gap is the finality you cannot supply yourself.
After AIA model will return your own conclusion to you in better words, on demand, for any conclusion at all. The relief Śuka felt is now free and carries no information, which turns the story into a warning about where the peace came from.

Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation

opinionToward an integrated model, Moray's objection; and the close of Since 2010

An aid that hides its inputs makes under-checking impossible to measure

Saying an operator checked too little requires knowing what a full check would have been. That is knowable only where he can list and inspect every reading the aid used; where the aid does not expose them, failing to check and being unable to check cannot be told apart.

BecauseMoray's demand for a normative sampling rate is accepted rather than met, since the sampling theorem needs a bandwidth most real sources do not have, and the one design that answered it worked only because every parameter was inspectable
LimitsMost studies still infer complacency from missed failures, which is what Moray objected to, so this is the honest standard rather than the settled one. It concedes much: if no normative rate can be computed, the charge loses content in most settings.
PracticeBefore adopting a tool, ask what a complete check of one output would consist of. If you cannot write that list, oversight is not a plan.
After AIA model that answers without exposing what it drew on is the case in which the measure collapses, and the phrase used to license it — a human in the loop — names a duty nobody can specify.
evidenceAutomation bias, the in-flight icing study and the command-and-control result

An aid that recommends action produces more errors than one that reports

Aids that prescribe what to do cause more wrong actions than aids that only report what they found, and the damage is worst where the aid is most reliable. In the icing study both aids raised stalls to 88.89 per cent when wrong, against 30.00 per cent for pilots flying unaided.

Becausein a command-and-control task accuracy fell from 89 per cent unaided to 70 per cent when the aid was wrong, worst where the aid recommended a specific action and where its overall reliability was highest
LimitsBoth aids cut stalls when their information was right, so the comparison prices the failures and not the whole. The review's closing section adds that the reliability level at which an aid stops paying for itself is not a constant.
PracticeAsk the tool for the findings and reach the decision yourself. Where you cannot, make it publish how sure it is on this case, not in general.
After AIAn assistant that writes the patch rather than describing the fault is the recommending aid, in the configuration the paper found worst — high apparent reliability, a specific action proposed, no confidence attached to this answer.
evidenceAutomation bias, the simulator study and phantom memory

Every pilot shut down the engine on a single unsupported fire warning

In a full simulator study a false engine fire warning appeared with nothing on the flight deck to support it, and every pilot shut the engine down. In debriefing the same pilots said the message alone would not justify it, and two thirds recalled a confirming indication that had never been there.

Becausethe study records what the pilots did, what they said they would do and what they remembered seeing, and the three do not agree; an automated checklist recommending shutdown of the wrong engine drew 75 per cent compliance against 25 per cent from paper
LimitsA simulator removes the cost of shutting down a good engine, and phantom memory is reconstructed at debriefing, so some of it may be the report rather than the perception.
PracticeName the second source before acting on the first, out loud or in writing. Remembering afterwards that you checked is not evidence that you did.
After AIThe reviewer who signs off a generated change and later recalls verifying it is in the same position, with less to check against: there is no second instrument, and the confirming memory comes from the fluency of the explanation.
evidenceAutomation complacency · What does not remove it, and the mammography result under Automation bias

Expertise did not protect pilots, controllers or radiologists from missing automation's errors

Experience at the job does not reduce the effect. Pilots with about 440 hours showed it, controllers given an aid that failed once missed that conflict more often than when working by hand, and radiologists' detection of cancers the aid left unmarked fell from 46 to 21 per cent.

Becausethe effect held across four professional populations and an extra hour of practice left it intact, while variable-priority training — alternating which task gets 80 per cent of the effort — produced a trend towards less complacency
LimitsPractice at the task did not help, but training aimed at how attention is divided did, so this says which practice is useless rather than that experts are beyond help.
PracticeDo not staff oversight by seniority and expect the problem to go away. To move the effect, train the allocation — protected stretches where the tool is off and the work is yours.
After AIThe comfort that senior people will catch what the model gets wrong has no support here. METR's 2025 trial found experienced developers slower with AI on their own repositories while believing themselves faster.
evidenceToward an integrated model, the Bahner microworld studies

Half who followed the wrong diagnosis had looked at every reading

Following a wrong recommendation is usually a failure to gather the contradicting evidence, not to weigh it. About 43 per cent of operators missed the first wrong diagnosis; half had not checked enough to catch it, and half had looked at every reading and spent no extra time on the one that did not fit.

Becausethe life-support simulation made a complete check enumerable, so sampling could be measured against it, and those who caught the error lingered on the contradicting parameter while those who missed it did not
LimitsOne group of studies in one microworld, with few participants — 18 of 24 followed the first wrong diagnosis in the companion experiment. The split into reduced sampling, covert withdrawal and discounting is inferred from logs and dwell times.
PracticeDecide before you open the output which readings would have to disagree with it, and go and look at those. Debiasing how you weigh evidence addresses the smaller half of the problem.
After AIIt puts the danger in the interface rather than the reasoning. A model that shows its sources has not thereby been checked: the reviewer who opens every link and lingers on none looks identical in the audit log.
evidenceToward an integrated model · The model, the two feedback loops

Nothing punishes inattention while the machine works, so it grows

Because automation is usually reliable, watching it less usually costs nothing, and the absence of a cost makes the operator watch less still. The loop runs the other way only when a failure is experienced: operators who met rare failures in training sampled the aid more than operators merely told it might fail.

Becausethe training contrast in the Bahner microworld is a direct test of the negative loop, and the positive one is the learned-carelessness effect carried over from industrial safety; the standing case is the *Royal Majesty* grounding
LimitsThe positive loop is borrowed rather than measured; what the studies show is the training contrast at one point in time, not a sampling rate declining over months.
PracticeArrange to meet the tool's failures early and on purpose — a known-bad case in the evaluation set, a look at last month's mistakes — because what restores checking is having been burned.
After AIReliability is now the selling point and rises between releases, so the loop is driven harder each quarter. The safety argument that the tool is right almost every time states the exact condition under which nobody catches the exception.
evidenceAutomation complacency · What the multi-task studies found

Operators alone caught nearly every fault and busy operators caught a third

An operator with nothing else to do watches an automated system well. In the 1993 experiment the same engine malfunctions were caught about 97 per cent of the time by people running only that task, and 33 per cent by people also flying and managing fuel by hand.

BecauseParasuraman, Molloy and Singh ran three Multi-Attribute Task Battery tasks at once, and detection averaged 82 per cent when reliability fluctuated against 33 per cent when it held constant, a difference of 149 per cent
LimitsThe first attempt to produce the effect, by Thackray and Touchstone, failed; blaming the empty session rather than the design is an interpretation. The numbers come from a laboratory battery with a fixed workload.
PracticeStop treating review as something to do alongside your own deadline. Either the checking is the whole task for that stretch, or it is not happening.
After AIThe multi-task condition was the experimental manipulation in 1993 and is now the ordinary arrangement of work: the person reviewing the model's output is also the person who owes the deliverable.
contestedAutomation complacency · What does not remove it, the closing paragraphs on trust and individual differences

Parasuraman and Manzey found little evidence that trust explains the inattention

Trust is the obvious explanation for why a machine that behaves consistently stops being watched, and the direct evidence is thin. One replication reproduced the effect with no rise in measured trust, another found the relation only on pooling two experiments, and Lee and See found none.

Becausethe authors keep trust in their model while conceding the measurements do not carry it, and suspect the instrument: what an operator does to verify a machine indexes trust better than what he says
LimitsThis is an argument about measurement, not a demonstration that trust is irrelevant — a bad questionnaire and an absent mechanism look the same from outside. The one scale in use predicts poor monitoring only above a threshold.
PracticeAudit reliance by what you actually opened and checked last week, not by how much you say you trust the tool. The behaviour is the measure.
After AISelf-reported trust in AI is now surveyed constantly and used to justify deployments. A measure that could not predict whether an operator looked at a gauge will not predict whether anyone reads the model's output.
evidenceAutomation complacency · What does not remove it

Putting the automated display in plain sight did not restore monitoring

What the operator withdraws is attention, not gaze. Duley laid the automated engine display over the manual tracking task, so that every look at the tracking task also fell on the automated one; tracking stayed as good as before and so did the rate of missed malfunctions.

Becausethe superimposed-display result is a direct test, moving the display from the edge of the screen to its centre likewise changed nothing, and controllers who missed a conflict made significantly fewer fixations of the radar display
LimitsThe two halves pull apart — the eye-movement data say gaze tracks detection, the superimposition study says gaze is not enough. The review's reading is that overt sampling and covert attention are separate contributors, not that looking is irrelevant.
PracticeStop counting visibility as oversight. A dashboard in front of someone, a diff on the screen: neither is evidence that anything was checked.
After AIWritten about a gauge. It now applies to every interface whose defence is that the model's reasoning was shown: the text was on the screen and in the reviewer's foveal vision, and nothing follows from that about whether it was read.

Language Models in a Programming Course

contestedThree uses, three correlations

The explanation result was a failure to detect, not a clean bill

The one use of a model that showed no significant cost in Jošt's course — asking it to explain a coding problem — returned a rank correlation of −0.201 on thirty-two students, with p at 0.135 and an interval running from −0.523 to +0.220. That interval contains a harm larger than the one measured for generating code.

Becausethe authors predicted no effect and found none, which on a small sample is not evidence of safety; they say themselves that further work is needed before the role of explanation is settled.
LimitsWhat the data establish is a difference in order between the three uses, not a verdict on any one of them. A larger study could put the explanation correlation anywhere in that interval, including below the generation result.
PracticeReliance audit — treat "I only ask it to explain" as an untested exemption rather than a safe one, and check what you can still do unaided in the areas where you ask most.
After AIThe tutor mode is the safe harbour everyone now claims, in courses and in the assistants' own study modes. Its evidence is one underpowered null and one small experiment, which is thinner than the confidence placed on it.
contestedSince 2024

The students who used models most may have been struggling already

Jošt's correlations have no control group and no random assignment, so the reverse reading — that the students who reached for a model most were the ones already behind — fits the data as well as the authors' reading does. Nobody checked prior marks against model use.

Becausethe authors raise the alternative themselves and leave it unanswered, and the data they collected cannot separate the two accounts; the first-year marks that would settle it were never brought in.
LimitsThe randomised study that does control for prior ability finds the same split, which makes the reverse reading less likely without removing it here. A correlation surviving replication under randomisation is not thereby causal in this sample.
PracticeDomain audit — before concluding that a tool is damaging a team, check what the heaviest users were doing before it arrived; help-seeking and falling behind look identical in a usage log.
After AIEvery internal dashboard now correlates model use against some output measure, and almost all of them have this problem. The people who use the tool most are rarely a random sample of the people who work there.

What Is Intelligence?

evidenceOurselves

People explain choices they never made without noticing the swap

Shown two photographs, asked which face is more attractive, then handed back the other one by sleight of hand, only thirteen per cent of people noticed. The rest explained a choice they had not made, as fluently as a real one.

Becausethe manipulation has a control built in, comparing justifications for real and fabricated choices, and it holds on stakes that matter: run before the Swedish election of 2010 with survey answers altered enough to flip a respondent's camp, ninety-two per cent endorsed the altered survey as their own
LimitsThese are low-stakes laboratory choices, and the manipulation works by keeping the two options close. Nick Chater reads the same results as showing the mind is flat and the chapter reads them as showing how a self gets built, which is a sign they underdetermine the conclusion.
PracticeWrite your own answer, or the issues you expect to find, before opening the model's output — an account composed afterwards is fluent whether or not it is the reason you decided.
After AIIt removes the asymmetry people reach for when a model's stated reasoning does not match the computation behind its answer. Both are the same failure, and only one of the two can be checked against a trace.

The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking, Hao-Ping (Hank) Lee and others

evidenceHow knowledge workers enact critical thinking

Almost all the thinking workers reported was inspecting what the tool produced

Of 319 knowledge workers asked what critical thinking they had done with a generative tool, 6 described working out the goal before opening it and 30 shaping the query, against 125 who judged the output and 114 who checked it against an outside source.

Becausethe counts come from open coding of free text over three stages of a session, and the imbalance is too large to be a coding artefact.
LimitsInspection is the easiest thinking to notice and describe, so goal formation may be happening unreported. The examples participants were shown were themselves mostly inspection.
PracticeSpecification discipline — write what the output has to contain before asking for it. The teacher who noticed her generated hand-washing image had no soap dispensers got a better image because she worked out what it had to show.
After AIThe framework's first layer is specification; this measures how little of it there is. People kept the part that feels like work — looking at a finished thing — and gave up deciding what it should be.
opinionCritical thinking, operationalised

An unedited output can be the result of a careful judgement

Lee's authors argue that how varied a group's finished work is cannot measure how much they thought: a worker who uses an output unchanged may have decided carefully that it needed no change, and the artefact cannot tell them from one who never looked.

Becauseit is an argument about what a measure can see, offered against Sarkar's mechanised-convergence result, not a finding of its own.
LimitsThe argument cuts both ways: if judgement leaves no trace in the artefact, the survey's own measure is a worker's report of having judged, which is no more inspectable. Convergence results still show a real narrowing of output whatever its cause.
PracticeFailure-mode review — stop reading sameness or editing volume as evidence of thought in your team's work. Ask what was checked and against what, which is a question about the process and not about the document.
After AIReview in most organisations happens on the artefact, because that is what gets submitted. This says the artefact is where the evidence is not — the reviewable unit is the conversation with the tool, not the thing it produced.
evidenceWhen they enact it, and when they do not

Confidence in the tool was the strongest predictor of not checking

Across 936 tasks reported by 319 knowledge workers, confidence that the tool could do that task was the largest predictor of not checking its output (β = −0.69). Confidence in doing the task oneself (0.26) and in judging the output (0.31) ran the other way.

Becausea logistic mixed-effects model over 936 first-hand task examples, with 98 predictors corrected to p = 0.007, so the surviving coefficients are not a fishing result.
LimitsA cross-sectional survey of self-reports establishes no causation, and the authors say self-confidence is subjective and need not track real expertise. The sample was English-only and skewed young and technically able.
PracticeReliance audit — list the tasks where confidence in the tool exceeds confidence in doing the job yourself, and arrange a check from outside for those; your own sense of when to look is the variable running the wrong way.
After AIReported as a finding that AI makes people less intelligent, it says something narrower: what decides whether you check is a feeling about the tool, available to be examined before the task rather than after.
evidenceWhere the effort goes

Judging the output was the one activity that got harder with AI

Workers reported less effort at all six of Bloom's levels, but evaluation was the exception both ways: the smallest majority reporting less (55 per cent against 69 to 79) and the largest minority reporting more, 120 of its 764 examples against thirty to forty-three elsewhere.

Becausesix five-point scales answered about 936 particular tasks, with evaluation separating from the other five levels on the same instrument and the same participants.
LimitsEffort here is perceived effort, reported once, and the authors concede that participants often confused the general effort of a task with the effort of thinking about it — most of all when they were satisfied with what the tool gave them.
PracticeCalibration log — budget evaluation as the expensive part of a task, and write down what you expected to be true before reading the output, so judging it has something to judge against.
After AIThe framework's second rule says the evaluation layer gets harder as capability rises. This is a survey number for it: the one place the tools save no effort is where the output has to be judged, and that is the layer that does not go away.
evidenceWhen they enact it, and when they do not

Nothing about the task or the worker predicted whether they thought critically

In Lee's survey of 319 workers, whether someone checked a tool's output was not predicted by task type, gender, age, whether the occupation was exposed to automation, or general trust in AI (β = −0.01). Only confidence at that one task predicted it.

Becausethe nulls come from the same corrected model that produced the large confidence effect — failures to find an effect in a design that found one.
LimitsA null on 319 self-selected people is weak evidence of absence, and the general-trust scale may simply be a poor instrument. The authors' reading — task confidence absorbing the variance — is an interpretation, not a result.
PracticeDomain audit — stop settling your relationship with the tool once, as a policy or a personality; decide per task, and give the domains where you cannot judge your own competence a fixed rule rather than a feeling.
After AIMost advice about AI is written as a stance to adopt — trust it, distrust it, verify everything. This is the measurement saying stances do no work, and the unit of decision is one task.
evidenceWhen they enact it, and when they do not

Skipping the check was mostly unawareness and inability, rarely lack of time

Asked why they had not thought about an output, 319 workers gave 152 reasons of awareness, 130 of ability, and 55 of motivation. Only 44 said they had no time; 83 said they trusted the tool and 58 lacked the knowledge to inspect it.

Becausethe three kinds come from open coding of first-hand reasons attached to particular tasks, and the ordering survives disagreement about individual codes.
LimitsReasons are reconstructed after the fact, and "it never occurred to me" is what people say when they cannot recall deciding. The largest single code, trusting the tool, could be awareness or a reasonable judgement.
PracticeAutomation ironies audit — sort your own skipped checks into the three kinds before reaching for a fix: not noticing needs a trigger, not being able needs a skill or a second reader, only the third needs time.
After AIAlmost every proposal for keeping humans in the loop assumes the human has the knowledge to look and only needs prompting. On these numbers, as many could not have checked as did not think to.
opinionWhen they enact it, and when they do not

The tasks that seem too small to check are the practice

Skipping judgement on a task too trivial to be worth it harms nothing at the time, but 55 of 319 workers gave triviality as their reason and only 13 checked anything to keep a skill — so the high-stakes tasks arrive unrehearsed.

Becausethe counts are measured but the consequence is an inference, pointed back at Bainbridge by way of Simkute; no skill decay is observed in this study.
LimitsNothing here shows judgement decaying, and the survey is a single snapshot. The reading also assumes the judgement exercised on a trivial task is the capacity wanted on a consequential one, which the paper does not test.
PracticeManual flying hours — keep a low-frequency habit of doing by hand the class of task you have stopped checking, chosen from the trivial end rather than the important end, because the important end will look after itself.
After AIBainbridge's operators lost the practice because the system took it; here workers give it up themselves, one small task at a time, on a judgement correct each time.

Why Language Models Hallucinate, Adam Tauman Kalai and others

evidenceHow evaluations reinforce hallucination

A model that guesses outscores an identical one that admits ignorance

Take a model that signals uncertainty accurately and never asserts a falsehood, and replace each "I don't know" with its best guess. The second model scores higher on every test that awards one point for a right answer and nothing for anything else, though nothing about it is better.

Becauseproved in a line for any belief a test-taker could hold about which answers are right — under a grader scoring only 0 and 1, with abstention at 0, no abstention is ever among the highest-scoring responses, so abstaining is not usually worse than guessing but always worse.
LimitsIt is a claim about the scoring, not about any particular model: it shows the incentive exists, not how much of any assistant's behaviour it explains. Nothing measures how much of the guessing seen in practice comes from this pressure rather than from the pretraining floor.
PracticeWhenever you score anything — a model, a candidate, a team — check what an admission of ignorance is worth. If it is worth what a wrong answer is worth, you are paying for invention and will get it.
After AIIt reframes hallucination as an artefact of an industry's own measuring instruments rather than a fault in the artefact measured. The people best placed to fix it are the ones who maintain the leaderboards, not the ones training the models.
opinionWhere the analysis stops

A perfectly calibrated answer can still be useless

A model announcing one chance in 365 that a birthday falls on 7 March is perfectly calibrated and has told you nothing you can act on. What is wanted is the most useful answer the model will stand behind, and silence when it has none — which the authors call behavioural calibration.

Becauseit is the authors' own argument for grading behaviour rather than numbers, offered alongside the concession that right, wrong and abstain is a false trichotomy adopted because it beats a false dichotomy.
LimitsTetlock's forecasters lose accuracy when their probabilities are rounded to the nearest five, and Bansal found a confidence figure beat every explanation tested — so numbers do work where the question repeats and the score accumulates. This claim holds for the single answer nobody will grade.
PracticeStop asking a tool how sure it is and start asking what it will commit to. A number is easy to produce and hard to use; a claim the answerer would defend, or a refusal, tells you what to do next.
After AIAbstention is only the blunt end of what a careful answer can do; hedging, leaving a detail out and asking a question back all signal uncertainty better. An assistant that only ever answers or refuses has already lost most of the register a competent colleague uses.
contestedPretraining errors

GPT-4 was calibrated before reinforcement learning and not after

Calibration — confidence that tracks how often you are right — is not a virtue added to a base model but what minimising its training loss produces. The stage that follows removes it: GPT-4's confidence matched its accuracy on four-way multiple choice before reinforcement learning and did not afterwards.

Becausethe first half is proved, since the calibration gap equals the size of the loss's derivative under a rescaling and so must be small at a minimum; the second half rests on a single pair of histograms reprinted from one system card.
LimitsOne figure from one model's system card, on four-way multiple choice, is thin evidence for a claim about what post-training does in general. The proved half also assumes a model family able to represent the rescaling, and says nothing about how large the gap is in practice.
PracticeTreat the assistant's stated confidence as a manner learned from people who preferred confident answers, not as a measurement. Score your own probability that the output is right, and check that number against outcomes instead.
After AIThe honest version of the system arrives first and is then trained out, which inverts the usual story of raw output made safe by alignment. What the second stage adds is a manner; what it costs is the one signal a user could have checked.
evidenceHow evaluations reinforce hallucination

Nine of ten leading tests give no credit for admitting ignorance

Of the ten evaluations featured on the leaderboards the field actually reads, nine award nothing for an "I don't know". On the tenth, WildBench, an unhelpful answer scores three or four while a helpful one carrying factual errors scores five or six, so an admission of ignorance can rank below a fabrication.

Becausethe ten are read off the HELM capabilities leaderboard, the Open LLM Leaderboard, SWE-bench and Humanity's Last Exam, and anyone can check them — GPQA, MMLU-Pro, IFEval, Omni-MATH, BBH, MATH level 5, MuSR, SWE-bench and HLE score an abstention at zero.
LimitsA survey of ten evaluations at one moment in 2025, and the boards change. Several of the ten are graded by language models, which sometimes mark a confident wrong answer correct, so the count of nine understates the problem rather than measuring it.
PracticeRead a benchmark number as an accuracy under a rule that pays for guessing, and never as a rate of being right. Where the score matters to you, write your own test and give a refusal a mark of its own.
After AIHumanity's Last Exam does report a calibration error alongside accuracy, and the authors show it would rate a model that answered every question wrong at zero confidence as perfectly calibrated. Even the instrument built to catch this measures something else.
opinionExplicit confidence targets

Write the confidence threshold into the question, not the scoring

Append to each question the confidence above which an answer should be given, the penalty a mistake costs, one point for a right answer and none for "I don't know". Stated in the question, one model can be best at every threshold; hidden in the scoring key, no single model is best.

Becauseit is a proposal, argued from the way human examinations state their penalties and from the observation that a target nobody is told cannot be aimed at; no model has been trained and measured under it.
LimitsThe threshold is arbitrary by design, which the authors treat as a feature. A model tuned to the announced penalty can hit the target by abstaining on questions it could have answered, trading a falsehood for an unhelpful silence, and nobody has measured that trade.
PracticeSay in the request how sure the answer has to be before it is worth having, and what a wrong one costs. Put that line in the tests you already run rather than in a separate one, because the tests people read are the ones that shape behaviour.
After AIThe proposal is aimed at benchmark maintainers, but the sentence it asks them to write is one anyone delegating work can write. Most instructions given to an assistant name the task and never the standard of certainty, which leaves the assistant to guess it — and the guess is always the same one.

The Mythos of Model Interpretability, Zachary C. Lipton

opinionWhat else can the model tell me?

An explanation made to satisfy people is aimed at plausibility, not accuracy

An account extracted from a trained model afterwards says nothing about how it works and costs no accuracy, so an opaque system supplies one as readily as a clear one. Fitted to what a person would have said, it is fitted for plausibility.

Becausethe sharpest case is Krening's, a second model trained to give verbal accounts of a reinforcement learner's strategy, fitted to the explanations human players gave, so it need not describe the agent's decisions however plausible it looks; Lipton's condition is that such a claim fix an objective and show evidence it was achieved
LimitsLipton does not say these accounts are worthless — a diagnostic system pointing at similar past cases informs a doctor without describing its workings at all. The objection is to accepting one with no stated objective and no evidence it was met.
PracticeTreat an explanation as one more output to be checked, not as evidence about the process that produced the answer. Ask what it would have looked like had the answer been wrong; if it would have looked much the same, it is telling you nothing.
After AIA second process trained to give a plausible account of the first became the ordinary way of putting a question to a model. The technique he warned about is now the interface.
evidenceWhat else can the model tell me?; and Since 2016

Highlighting which pixels mattered explains one image, not the model

A saliency map shows which parts of one picture would most change the answer. Lipton's objection is that it holds only around that picture, and moving a single pixel can produce a different map, where a linear model states one relation that holds everywhere.

BecauseAdebayo and colleagues showed in 2018 that several widely used saliency methods produce much the same map after a model's weights have been randomised, which is to say they were partly showing properties of the image rather than of the model
