LimitsThe objection is to reading a local picture as a global account, not to the method. Adebayo tested image models, and the result does not carry to every attribution method; the comparison is with a linear model's global relation, which Lipton has already shown is not free either.
PracticeAsk any attribution method for a control before you read its picture: what does it produce on an untrained model, or on a neighbouring input? If the picture barely moves, it is describing the input and not the system.
After AIThe lesson survived the technique. Work on large models validates a claimed internal mechanism by intervening on it and reports how often the method shows nothing, which is the control he was asking for.

GPS and the Cognitive Map, Louisa Dahmani and Véronique D. Bohbot

evidenceFifty drivers

Drivers who felt most dependent on GPS corrected themselves least

How dependent a driver felt without the device predicted rigidity, not just weakness: with self-rated sense of direction held constant, the dependence score tracked the second probe at −0.33 — the probe on which people generally recover after the first one has misled them.

Becausethe second probe is scored as a gain over the first, and the mean gain was 0.73 of a point, so failing to improve measures not correcting rather than not knowing; the effect survives partialling out sense of direction.
LimitsOne correlation of −0.33 on a scale the authors built for this study, in fifty people. The related finding that confident navigators learned faster and were then more rigid is incidental and undefended.
PracticeTreat the feeling of being unable to work without the tool as a signal about correction, not only about skill. Where you feel most dependent, build in the step that makes you revise: a second pass with the first answer set aside.
After AIWhat matters in supervising a model is not raw ability but whether the first answer can be revised. Here the people most reliant on the tool were the ones an early wrong turn kept wrong.
evidenceWhich way the arrow runs

Heavy GPS users scored worse but felt no worse at directions

The drivers whose measured spatial memory was worst rated their own sense of direction no lower than anyone else: lifetime GPS hours and self-rated sense of direction were unrelated, r = 0.07, and over three years the measures fell while the self-rating stayed put.

Becausethe Santa Barbara sense-of-direction scale was in the battery to test the opposite account, that poor navigators buy a device and use it constantly, and it came back flat against both lifetime hours and daily reliance.
LimitsA null result on one self-report scale, in fifty people; the separate sense-of-dependence scale did track feeling badly oriented, at −0.58, which the authors treat as close to a restatement of what that scale asks.
PracticeDo not use your own sense of whether you have lost a capacity as evidence about whether you have. Put the question to a task you pass or fail without the tool present, on a schedule.
After AIRisko and Gilbert argued that a tool changes both the ability and your estimate of it. Here the two come apart, which is the worse case: the faculty that decides how closely to check is the one reporting no change.

Why Are There Still So Many Jobs?, David H. Autor

opinionPolanyi's paradox: will it be overcome?

A learning machine cannot tell its makers why it did that

Learning from examples does not dissolve the problem that people cannot state the rules they use; it moves the problem. A system that inferred its rule from labelled cases cannot tell its programmers why it does what it does either.

BecauseAutor names it as an irony of the method rather than demonstrating it, from his own description of the method as atheoretical brute force needing only training data, processing power and software; the unevenness he reports is consistent with it — IBM's Watson won at *Jeopardy* and in the same winning match answered Toronto to a question in the category of US cities.
LimitsStated as an aside and not investigated. It was also too pessimistic in one direction: interpretability work has since traced parts of what a model does internally, though Anthropic's own tracing method succeeded on only about a quarter of the prompts tried.
PracticeFailure-mode review — do not accept an explanation from the system as evidence that it worked. Keep a list of the failures you have actually seen and check against that instead.
After AIAutor offered it as a curiosity about a promising method. It is now the standing condition of the tools most people use, which means the whole burden of knowing whether an answer is right falls on checking the answer rather than on understanding the process that produced it.

The Consciousness of Self, William James

opinionThe mutations of the self

The stories we tell other people replace the memories they came from

James says the commonest source of false memory is the account we give other people of what happened: we make it simpler and better than the truth until the fiction expels the reality and reigns alone, and the error is made in entire good faith.

Becauseone case carries it — a friend of Frances Power Cobbe's who described a table rapping with nobody within a yard of it, then found her own note of ten years before recording that the hands of six persons had rested on it — with James asserting, rather than showing, that such errors are ordinary
LimitsA single anecdote, and one with a written record only by luck. Nothing in it says how often this happens or which memories are vulnerable; Bartlett in 1932 and Loftus from 1974 supplied that, four decades and more after James guessed it.
PracticeCalibration log — write down what you expected before you check, in the form you will be graded on. Any account reconstructed later has been through the telling, and yours will have improved.
After AIThe account you give of a session is now given to a machine that keeps it and works from it, so the improved version becomes the input to the next round rather than fading. Where the record matters, save what happened, not what you said about it.

What to keep and what to hand off

Ironies of Automation, Lisanne Bainbridge

evidenceTasks after automation · Manual control skill

An operator who only watches loses the skill to take over

Bainbridge says the routine work is what keeps a manual skill alive. An operator who has only monitored an automated system for months performs like a beginner when they have to take control.

Becausestep-change studies separate the experienced operator from the inexperienced one, and the skill that separates them is the one monitoring stops exercising
LimitsThe paper is a review; the step-change studies are cited a sentence each and the numbers have to be fetched from the skill-retention literature directly. It also assumes the skill the rare case demands is the one the routine work rehearsed, which is often but not always true.
PracticeKeep a share of the delegated work in your own hands on a fixed schedule, not because the output needs you but because the skill does.
After AIThe delegate is now a model that takes the routine work in every domain at once, so the decay is no longer confined to one plant and one operator. What is new is that there is usually no moment of takeover to expose it, only a decision about how closely to read.
opinionThe two ironies

Automation leaves people the jobs nobody could write down

Bainbridge argues that the tasks left to a human after automation are not a random leftover. They are exactly the ones nobody could write a specification for: the rare, the abnormal and the poorly understood.

Becausethe second irony is argued from what designers choose to automate rather than from a survey of what operators were left with
LimitsIt is a claim about designers' intentions, not a measured remainder, and it assumes the automation boundary is drawn by specifiability rather than by cost or convenience.
PracticeKeep an explicit list of what stays human, derived from what you could not specify, and treat every item on it as needing more support rather than less.
After AIA model does not need a specification to take a task, so the boundary is now drawn by what the model happens to do well, and the remainder is no longer reliably the hard part. What is left may be the part nobody thought to check.
contestedOperator attitudes

Bainbridge says watching a machine is stressful and the stress causes errors

Bainbridge argues that cutting an operator's job down to watching an automated system removes the control and the standing that made the responsibility bearable. The stress that follows is itself a cause of operating errors.

Becauseit rests on one plant where management had to be present on the night shift and one control-room survey linking controllability to low stress and good health
LimitsTwo observations, one of them anecdotal, carrying a causal claim about stress and error. The survey is cross-sectional and cannot separate controllability from everything else that differs between control rooms.
PracticeCount the human cost of a monitoring role as an operating cost. If the job has responsibility without control, expect errors from that alone and change the job, not the person.
After AIThe review seat is the deskilled job: full accountability for the output, no hand on the work that produced it. Self-determination theory and the job-crafting literature both predict the resentment Bainbridge only observed.
evidenceTasks after automation · Cognitive skill

Skills fade when unused and grow only through practice with feedback

Bainbridge argues that what you know fades when you stop using it, because recall depends on how often you use it, and it grows only through use plus feedback. Teaching an operator without letting them practise leaves someone who neither understands nor remembers.

Becauseshe rests it on the memory literature on retrieval frequency, and offers the reader a check they can run on any school subject they have not thought about since
LimitsThe supporting studies are cited rather than reported, and the claim is about long-term memory in general rather than about process knowledge specifically.
PracticeDo not count instruction as preparation. If someone is expected to handle a case, they have to have handled cases and been told how it went.
After AIHer warning that the automated plants of 1983 were riding on the skills of former manual operators reads now as a description of every team whose seniors learned the work before the model arrived. The next generation is the one she said could not be expected to have it.
opinionApproaches to solutions

The more reliable an automatic system the more operator training it needs

Bainbridge argues that the automated systems which almost never need a person to step in are the ones whose operators need the most training. The rarer the manual case, the more practice it takes to stay ready for it.

Becauseshe calls it the final irony and derives it from the argument rather than from any training study
LimitsIt is a deduction, not a measurement, and it runs against the cost logic of every organisation that buys automation to reduce headcount and training. Aviation is the one industry that has acted on it.
PracticeSet the training budget from how rarely the manual case arises, not from how often. The better the tool, the more you have to spend keeping people able to work without it.
After AIThe more reliable a model becomes, the more expensive it gets to keep anyone able to catch the case it misses — and the harder it is to justify that expense to anyone looking at the success rate.

The Design of Everyday Things, Donald A. Norman

opinionHuman error? No, bad design

Investigators stop asking why as soon as they can blame a person

Norman argues that accident investigations stop as soon as a human error is found, and that the fix is to keep asking why past that point. After the 2010 F-22 crash the Inspector General asked about oxygen deprivation and the Air Force restated pilot error.

Becausethe 2010 F-22 crash is the case — the Inspector General asked about oxygen deprivation and the Air Force restated pilot error — and Toyoda's Five Whys is offered as the procedure
LimitsNorman says himself that the number is not five, that the method guarantees nothing, and that the word why implies a single cause where complex events have many. His own utility case shows the procedure defeated by a culture rather than by a technique.
PracticeIn any review, when the answer is that someone made a mistake, ask why at least twice more, and do not close the item until the answer stops naming a person.
After AIThe new stopping point is that the model got it wrong, which closes an investigation as effectively as blaming the operator did. Keep asking why past that and you reach the objective, the data and the interface that showed the answer first.

Thinking, Fast and Slow, Daniel Kahneman

evidencePart III: overconfidence

Better estimates come from looking up how similar past projects went

Estimating from the details of the job in front of you cannot allow for what you do not know about it. The fix is a procedure: find out how comparable past projects turned out and start from those numbers, not a resolve to be realistic.

Becausehis own textbook team estimated two years against a reference class of seven to ten and took eight; the Scottish Parliament ran from about forty million pounds to about four hundred and thirty
LimitsReference class forecasting needs a reference class, and Kahneman's own team had one member who knew it and was ignored. Where the class does not exist, the procedure has nothing to offer.
PracticeBefore estimating, find the outcomes of comparable past cases and start from their distribution. Adjust from there, and record the adjustment.
After AIThe reference class for work done with a model is a few years deep and moving, and the METR result — developers slower while believing themselves faster — is the case where the inside view and the measurement point in opposite directions.
opinionConclusions

Training yourself out of bias barely works, changing the procedure does

Kahneman concludes that people cannot train their own biases away; his own thinking stayed as overconfident as before. What works is changing how a group decides: written positions before discussion, independent judgments, a premortem, and judging a decision by how it was made.

BecauseKahneman concedes that decades of study left his own intuitive thinking as overconfident and as prone to the planning fallacy as before
LimitsIt is a concession rather than a finding — no study is offered that debiasing training fails — and the organisational remedies are argued from the same source. The book's own remedy would have caught the chapters that did not replicate.
PracticeStop trying to be less biased and start changing the procedure: written positions before discussion, decorrelated error, a premortem, and judging a decision by how it was made.
After AIThe remedies survive the arrival of a capable assistant and the personal resolution does not. Buçinca's result is the same shape: what works is a change to the interface, and people dislike it.

Conditions for Intuitive Expertise, Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein

evidenceAlgorithms

A premortem gets people to say the doubts they were suppressing

Klein's premortem tells a team to assume the plan has already failed, spend two minutes writing why, then go round the table starting with the leader. It brings out the doubts people stop voicing once a decision is being made.

Becauseit rests on the finding that people generate more reasons for an outcome once told it is certain, which is what the exercise exploits
LimitsThe underlying finding is about reason generation, not about decision quality; no study here shows premortems improving outcomes. Going round the table starting with the leader is a procedural guess at the social problem.
PracticeBefore committing, have everyone spend two minutes writing why the plan has already failed a year from now, then go round the table starting with the most senior person.
After AIThe exercise is cheap to run against a plan a model produced, and it is one of the few checks that does not require you to follow the reasoning faster than it was written. It asks what would have gone wrong, not whether the argument holds.
evidenceAlgorithms

Kahneman and Klein list five conditions a usable formula must meet

Kahneman and Klein argue a formula can replace human judgement only where five things hold: everyone agrees which variables matter, the outcome can be measured, enough similar past cases exist, the gain is worth the cost, and conditions will not change in response.

Becausethe paper lists the conditions a usable algorithm has to meet, and the naturalistic objections hold wherever one of them fails
LimitsThe supervision half of the paper's argument is cited rather than shown: the automation-bias literature is named as such, and the evidence that operators become passive belongs to Bainbridge rather than to this paper.
PracticeRun the five conditions as a checklist before automating a judgement, and treat a failure on any one of them as a reason not to.
After AIThe last condition is the one that has failed. Conditions do change under a deployed model, and they change because it is deployed — the behaviour it is scoring shifts once people know they are being scored by it.

Crafting a Job, Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane E. Dutton

opinionThe model · three qualifications

Job crafting helps the worker but not necessarily the employer

Reshaping your own job is done for the worker's benefit, not the organisation's. A line worker who changes tasks may raise the quality of the work or may wreck the flow of it.

Becausestated as a qualification of the model, with the observation that a line worker who changes tasks may wreck the flow of work or may raise its quality, and that crafting is often invisible and unrewarded
LimitsIt is a caveat rather than a finding, and the later survey literature has mostly measured crafting against outcomes the organisation wants, which quietly reverses the qualification the original paper insisted on.
PracticeDo not sell crafting to management as a productivity measure. It is what people do to keep the work bearable, and sometimes that costs the organisation something.
After AIThe invisible, unrewarded extra work is the first thing to disappear when a tool makes the visible part cheap, and nobody notices because it was never in the job description.
opinionManagers and limits

Managers cannot order people to reshape their jobs, only make it likelier

Managers cannot order employees to reshape their own jobs. They can only affect it indirectly, through rewards, how the work is organised, and who is let into conversations about what the organisation is for.

Becausethe cleaners used the hospital's stated mission to legitimate framing cleaning as care, which is the one lever the paper can show working
LimitsOnly one of the three levers is illustrated, and the illustration is a single case. The paper's own list of open questions includes whether managers should encourage crafting at all, since it may harm the organisation.
PracticeIf you want people to own their work, change rewards, the organisation of tasks, and who is in the conversation about what the work is for. Do not ask them to feel differently.
After AIAdmission to the conversation about what the organisation is trying to do is the lever that matters most when the tasks themselves are being reassigned, and it is the one usually closed while the reassignment happens.
contestedSince 2001

The job crafting studies cannot show which way the cause runs

The research that followed the job crafting paper asks people to rate themselves at a single moment, and the effects are moderate. Studies of that kind cannot show whether crafting causes engagement or engaged people craft.

Becausethe meta-analyses associating crafting with engagement, satisfaction and rated performance rest on self-reported, cross-sectional designs with moderate effects
LimitsContested because the reversal of the arrow is now the default assumption in the field, which means the weakest part of the evidence supports the part everyone has accepted. Berg and colleagues' 2010 return to the original model is the nearest thing to a test.
PracticeRead any crafting-and-engagement finding as a correlation between two self-reports taken at the same moment, and ask what a longitudinal version would have to show.
After AIThe same design weakness runs through most of the early evidence about working with models: people reporting their own engagement and their own productivity in the same questionnaire. METR's result is what happens when the two are measured separately.
opinionThe model

Watched and tightly scheduled workers have little room to reshape their job

How much room someone has to reshape their own job depends on how tightly their tasks depend on other people's timing and how closely they are watched. A cleaner or hairdresser has plenty; an assembly-line worker or a monitored telemarketer has almost none.

Becausethe moderator is argued from the contrast between a cleaner or hairdresser with many degrees of freedom and an assembly-line worker or closely watched telemarketer with few
LimitsThe two moderators are asserted from contrasting occupations rather than measured, and the paper notes the modern workplace pulls both ways at once, which makes the prediction hard to test in either direction.
PracticeBefore telling someone to take more ownership of their work, count how tightly their tasks are yoked to others' timing and how closely they are watched.
After AISurveillance and flexibility have both increased since, and a new form of both has arrived: work that passes through a tool that logs it. That tightens interdependence and monitoring at the same time.

Does the Whole Exceed its Parts?, Gagan Bansal and others

opinionInformative rather than convincing

AI explanations make people agree rather than think, emptying their sign-off

Bansal and colleagues argue that explanations as currently designed make people go along with the AI rather than judge it. The human sign-off that is meant to catch errors then has nothing behind it.

Becauseit is the authors' reading of their own result, with the doctor who is soothed rather than informed as the case
LimitsAn interpretation rather than a measurement: the study shows acceptance rising and accuracy flat, not that the sign-off has been emptied. The requirement that a doctor sign off may be doing other work the study does not measure.
PracticeWhere a person is required to sign off for legal or moral reasons, check that the sign-off could go the other way. If nothing in the interface supports disagreement, it cannot.
After AIBainbridge's impossible task and this paper's empty sign-off are the same claim measured forty years apart, and the second supplies the numbers the first argued for.
evidenceThe test nobody had run

Human plus AI must beat both the human and the AI alone

Bansal and colleagues argue an AI decision aid is only worth deploying if the person and the AI together do better than either alone. In all eight studies offered as evidence for explanations, the model alone beat the team.

BecauseTable 1 assembles eight studies offered as evidence for explanations and adds the column they omitted: deceptive review detection at 51.1 per cent for workers, 87 for the model and 74.6 for the best team; house prices out by $331k, $200k and $232k
LimitsThe standard is accuracy alone, and the authors say so: a team might be complementary in speed or effort instead. It is also a standard for deployment decisions rather than for legal or moral requirements that a person sign off.
PracticeBefore keeping a person in a loop, measure all three: the person alone, the machine alone, and the pair. Two of those numbers are usually missing.
After AIThe three-number comparison is almost never run on the tools in daily use, and the eight papers in Table 1 are the reminder that publishing an improvement over unassisted work says nothing about whether the person should be there.

High Output Management, Andrew S. Grove

opinionManagerial leverage (the peer-group syndrome, the peer-plus-one remedy, the six questions, figure 26.6)

A group of equals stalls until someone senior joins the decision

Grove found that a meeting of people at the same level goes round in circles without settling anything until a senior person steps in. Stepping in helps at the moment of deciding and harms during the discussion.

Becauseobserved at Intel and offered as a remedy; the timing rule is a judgement about when authority helps, never tested against a control.
LimitsThe same senior presence that unlocks a decision is what Edmondson's managers responded to by withholding corrections when the boss's boss was present. Grove's rule says which stage helps but gives no way to tell, inside the room, which stage you are at.
PracticePut a senior person in the room for the decision and keep them out of the discussion, and settle the six questions — what, when, by whom, consulted, ratified, told — before the meeting starts.
After AIA model in the discussion is a peer with no standing, so it does not break the circling. Asked to arbitrate, it agrees with whoever framed the question, which is the peer-group syndrome with a more confident voice.
opinionThe players (the sales manager moved into a plant; the sergeant of the quiet camp)

A proven worker needs close direction again when the job changes

How ready someone is to work unsupervised applies to one task, not to the person. When the task or the pace changes, that readiness drops, and a manager who had stepped back has to go back to close, structured direction.

Becausetwo illustrative cases, offered as something that should have been predictable, with nothing measured.
LimitsGrove notes that the mode managers most dislike is the one they most often reach for too late, and that friendship makes the return to structure harder. The evidence is two anecdotes chosen to make the point.
PracticeKeep the structured mode available instead of treating a move to minimal involvement as permanent, and keep enough hands-on contact to use it. Manual flying hours is what makes the return possible rather than merely intended.
After AIA model's competence shifts with releases and with what is in its context, so the fall in maturity is not announced by a visible change of job. The manager has to detect it from the output, which is the thing the delegation was meant to stop requiring.
opinionManagerial leverage; the gate-or-monitor rule in The breakfast factory (figure 26.3)

Check delegated work at the rough draft, not the finished version

Grove argues that you should check work you have handed over at its cheapest stage, the rough draft rather than the polished report, because that is where a mistake costs least to catch.

Becausecarried over by analogy from factory inspection, and the London embassy case shows what sampling saves rather than what it catches.
LimitsThe gate is right where a defect is catastrophic rather than merely expensive, and Grove says so. A rough draft from a delegate whose competence is unknown also carries less information than a finished one.
PracticeAsk for the outline before the document and the plan before the diff, and spend the review budget there. Failure-mode review turns that early look into a fixed list of what to look for.
After AIA model produces a polished draft at the first stage, so the cheap early signal Grove relies on no longer exists in the work's natural shape. The low-value stage has to be created deliberately — an outline, a plan, a stated approach — before there is anything to monitor.
opinionManagerial leverage (the output equation, figure 26.4)

Grove counts a manager's output as what his teams produce

Andrew Grove defines a manager's output as the output of the teams he supervises or influences. So an activity that raises nobody else's output is worth nothing, however well it is done.

Becauseit is a definition Grove derived from running Intel, not a finding anyone tested.
LimitsIt is an accounting identity rather than a measurement: it gives no way to attribute an output among several influences, and the time offset between a manager's work and its result can be years. Grove's 1995 introduction concedes that the shared building and the long career the model assumes have gone.
PracticeStop counting hours spent and start asking which of them raised someone else's output. The stays-human list is where the answer gets written down for the firm rather than for one manager.
After AIWhen part of the unit is a model, the output still counts as the manager's, but the leverage term now includes work nobody on the team did. Reviewing a draft the model wrote is activity that raises no one's output unless it raises the next draft.
opinionThe players (the review; the potential trap; the light of distant stars)

Grove rates no manager higher than the team's actual result

Andrew Grove holds that a manager's performance rating must never be higher than the result his organisation achieved, however well he personally performed. Otherwise the company learns that acting like a manager is what counts.

Becausea rule Grove adopted after misrating a manager whose superb year was work done years earlier; one case, stated as policy.
LimitsThe time offset Grove names cuts both ways: this year's result may be the light of distant stars in either direction. Rating on the organisation's result alone punishes sound judgement that met bad luck, which is Edmondson's objection to rewarding outcomes.
PracticeRate the result, then ask separately what part of it was this year's work — and write the prediction down first so the offset is visible. Calibration log is that habit applied to any judgement you will later rely on.
After AIThe offset has shortened — a team's output can move within a quarter of adopting a tool — so a rating tracks the tool's arrival rather than the manager's work, and the distant-stars error runs in reverse.
opinionThe breakfast factory (indicators and the black box, figure 26.2)

Grove says every measure needs a second measure beside it

Grove argues that any number a team is pushed to improve needs a second number beside it that catches the damage. Cut inventory without counting shortages and the shortages rise unseen.

Becausea rule of thumb from running a factory; the examples — inventory against shortages, vouchers processed against errors found — show the failure mode without saying how often it occurs.
LimitsPairing assumes the counter-effect can be named in advance, which is exactly what is hard about a new measure. Self-determination evidence adds that the pair is itself a contingency, and contingent measurement shifts regulation from autonomous to controlled whatever it counts.
PracticeNever introduce a measure without naming, in the same sentence, the thing it will be gamed against. Failure-mode review supplies the counter-measure for delegated work: what got through, not how much got produced.
After AIOutput generated per person is the easiest thing to count and the counter-indicator — defects reaching production, hours spent verifying work nobody wrote — is the hard one. Without the pair, what gets reported is the gain people already believed they were getting.
opinionThe players, closing section (the training arithmetic, figure 26.11)

Grove says managers should teach their own people, not hire trainers

Andy Grove argues that a manager should run the training himself instead of hiring a trainer. Only someone the team sees as doing the work day to day can tie the lessons to how the job is actually done.

Becausethe arithmetic establishes leverage — twelve hours against ten people's twenty thousand working hours — and the authority claim is asserted from experience.
LimitsWeinberg's own classroom result cuts against the emphasis on the teacher: lecturing on the errors his students made moved them from 87 per cent to 83, and the exercises did the rest. The one per cent gain in his arithmetic is never measured.
PracticeTeach the thing yourself, as a series rather than an event, using this week's work as the material. Dreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule decides who needs which part.
After AIWhat a manager now owes his team is training in how to use and check a model, the one domain where he is least likely to be a practising authority. The arithmetic still holds and the authority does not.
opinionA team of teams (the three modes of control and the CUA factor, figure 26.8)

Grove says shared values are the only control when work is uncertain

Grove argues that where work is complicated, uncertain and unclear, the only thing that keeps people acting well is a set of values they share. Rules and contracts cannot be written fast enough to cover what comes up.

Becausea two-by-two derived from a commuting anecdote; the empty quadrant is an inference about why senior outside hires fail, not a count of them.
LimitsCulture needs shared experience to transmit, which is why Grove starts new employees in low-CUA jobs; where turnover is fast there is no time to build it. For the fourth quadrant — self-interest in a complex environment — his own answer is that no control works at all.
PracticeWhere the work outruns the rules, spend the effort on what the group will not do and why, rather than on another procedure. The stays-human list is that statement in its shortest form.
After AIAn agent has no shared values to fall back on when the contract runs out. What it has is a specification, which is the mode Grove says fails in exactly this quadrant, and that is the alignment problem stated in management vocabulary.
contestedThe players (motivation; the ring-tosser; the two levers, figure 26.9)

Grove sets targets a person reaches only half the time

Grove says goals should be set so that even someone working hard reaches them about half the time. High achievers left to themselves pick targets they are already certain of, because at that level the fear is of failing.

Becausethe rule rests on Maslow's hierarchy, which Grove adopted because his observation of working life confirmed it and which has not held up as psychology, though the distinction between needs that get people to work and needs that make them perform survives without it.
LimitsSelf-determination evidence says a target set for someone rather than with them shifts regulation to controlled whatever its difficulty. A fifty-fifty objective inside a company that rates on attainment is the potential trap Grove names two chapters later.
PracticeSet the target where failure is a real possibility, and then make sure nothing in the rating system punishes the person for taking it.
After AIWhen the delegate is a model, failure costs it nothing, so the even-odds rule loses its point for the agent and keeps it for the person who has to review the half that fails.
contestedThe players (the task-relevant maturity table and figure 26.10)

How closely to supervise depends on the person's experience at that task

Grove says how closely a manager should supervise is set by how experienced the person is at that particular task, not by what the manager prefers. None of the three styles is kinder than the others.

BecauseIntel's rotation of managers between similar groups was suggestive rather than controlled, and the construct is Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership renamed.
LimitsMaturity is specific to the task and falls when the job or the pace changes. Managers also misjudge their own position on the dial: about nine in ten saw themselves as more delegating than their people did.
PracticeSet the dial per task rather than per person, and write the mapping down so it can be argued with. Dreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule does exactly that.
After AIA model's competence is jagged across tasks and can move with a release, so the dial cannot be carried per delegate the way Grove carries it per person. It has to be reset for each task, and reset again when the version changes.

The What and Why of Goal Pursuits, Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan

evidenceAt work, the section on pay

Bonuses raise output on simple work and damage complex work

Ryan and Deci report that rewards like pay and bonuses predict better performance where the job is about how much gets done, and worse performance where it is about quality and complexity.

Becausea meta-analysis found intrinsic motivation a moderate to strong predictor of performance and strongest where quality matters, a meta-analysis of public-sector pay for performance found it helped on simple tasks and hurt on complex ones, and the industrial laundry attendance award was gamed, improved the chronically late and lowered the efficiency of the already punctual at tasks outside the programme.
LimitsComplexity is graded after the fact in most of the pooled studies, and the public-sector meta-analysis covers tasks unlike software.
PracticeIncentivise the throughput of routine work if you must, and measure the complex work some other way. Failure-mode review is one of the other ways.
After AIA model makes quantity cheap and leaves the complex judgement with the person, so an incentive aimed at output now sits on exactly the half of the job the evidence says it damages.
contestedIntrinsic motivation (the 128-study meta-analysis; figure 28.2)

Paying people for work they already enjoy reduces their interest in it

When people are paid or given prizes for an activity they already found interesting, they want to do it less for its own sake afterwards. They come to see the reason for doing it as coming from outside them.

Becausea meta-analysis of 128 studies over three decades, answered by a behaviourist meta-analysis, with the dispute still open and behavioural economists reproducing the crowding-out effect on their own terms.
LimitsWhat a reward does depends on its functional significance, so the effect is not a property of rewards as such — the same performance-contingent reward enhances or undermines depending on how it is given.
PracticeDo not attach a bonus to the part of the job people already want to do; attach it, if anywhere, to the part nobody enjoys.
After AIPay that is contingent on output a model produced is contingent on nothing the person did, which is the clearest case of an external locus the literature describes.
contestedWhat a need is (the functional test; the plant analogy, figure 28.1)

Ryan and Deci say people need skill, connection and choice, all three

Ryan and Deci argue that people have three built-in psychological needs: being good at something, being close to other people, and having a say in what they do. Health requires all three, so meeting two of them is not enough.

Becausethe three held up as cross-cultural predictors of well-being in later meta-analyses, while the objection that autonomy is a Western value has continued in parallel.
LimitsThe theory does not study need strength, and reads an unusually strong wish as evidence of past thwarting, which makes it hard to falsify from individual differences. The cross-cultural objection to autonomy has not been withdrawn.
PracticeBefore moving work off a person, ask which of the three the move removes; competence is the one delegation takes first. The stays-human list is where the answer is made binding on the firm.
After AIDelegating the interesting part of a job to a model removes competence satisfaction while leaving autonomy and relatedness intact. That is the two-out-of-three case the theory says is not enough, and it looks like a well-run team from outside.
evidenceAt work (the Fortune 500 field intervention, figure 28.6)

Training managers to support employees' choices changes what employees experience

Managers can be taught to give their staff more say in how they work. In a Fortune 500 study the training changed what the subordinates reported experiencing over thirteen months, not only what the managers said about themselves.

Becausetrained managers became more autonomy-supportive than controls, subordinates' perceptions improved over thirteen months, the managers who changed most had subordinates who changed most, the company's own attitude surveys agreed, and a second randomised training study replicated it.
LimitsThe founding study is from the 1980s, and the surrounding literature is largely self-reported, often cross-sectional, drawn heavily from the authors' own network and light on effect sizes. The two randomised training studies are the exceptions.
PracticeTrain the three behaviours the study trained — take the other's perspective, give feedback that informs rather than judges, support initiative — and measure the change on the subordinates, not on the managers. The stays-human list is one place the third behaviour becomes concrete.
After AIThe three trained behaviours are the ones a manager stops performing when the review is of a model's output and the person is only the conduit. Nothing in the job description changes; the perspective-taking simply has no object.
evidenceAt work, the section on pay (figure 28.7)

What a bonus means to the person matters more than its size

What a reward does to someone's motivation depends on how they read it — as information about how well they are doing, or as pressure to perform — and not on how large it is.

Becausethe same performance-contingent reward enhanced intrinsic motivation given in an autonomy-supportive way and undermined it given controllingly, and the field results fall on either side of that line: non-contingent salary predicted autonomous motivation in Norwegian insurers where quarterly bonuses predicted controlled, and a telecom firm that moved sales staff to full commission lost three-quarters of them within a year.
LimitsThe field results are correlational and the firms that changed schemes changed other things too; the clean evidence is the experiment that varied delivery while holding the reward fixed.
PracticeSpend the argument on how a reward is delivered and what it is said to mean, not on its size; pay level predicted only whether pay seemed fair.
After AIAn output metric a model can move makes the reward informative about the tool rather than about the person, which is the controlling reading by default.
evidenceWhy and what

Why a person acts predicts persistence better than how motivated they are

The reason a person does something predicts how long they keep it up, how well they do it, and their health — separately from how motivated they are. Two people who look equally motivated can be headed in different directions.

Becausethe same pattern appears in schools across four countries, in a six-month supervised diet whose autonomy-supported patients had kept the weight off nearly two years later, in smoking cessation confirmed biochemically at thirty months, and in methadone patients' urine tests.
LimitsThe reasons are self-reported, and most of the field studies are cross-sectional; the direction of the effect rests on the longitudinal minority.
PracticeAsk why someone is still doing the work rather than how much they are doing, and treat the answer as the leading indicator it is. The stays-human list makes the why explicit for the work that stays.
After AIThe question survives the delegation of what is done. A person who keeps the work because they endorse it and one who keeps it because the tool would expose them are in different states by this measure, and produce the same output this quarter.
evidenceInternalisation (the three-facilitator experiment, figure 28.4)

Without freedom to choose, people follow rules out of guilt

Ryan and Deci found that support for belonging and for feeling capable makes people keep up a behaviour, but out of guilt or shame. Only when their freedom to choose is also supported do they come to hold the value as their own.

Becausein the experiment the correlation between how much people did and how much they valued it reversed sign according to how many supports were present, which is a result a weaker design could not manufacture.
LimitsThe introjected step is the hardest part of the continuum to separate cleanly in later measurement, and the demonstration rests on one uninteresting laboratory task.
PracticeWhen imposing a change, supply all three: a real reason, an acknowledgement that the task is unwelcome, and a genuine choice about how it is done. Two of the three buys compliance that costs the person something.
After AIAn engineer given a rationale and a choice integrates a new tool. Told only that the team now ships this way, he keeps shipping and administers the resentment himself — which is introjection, and is invisible in the output.

The Psychology of Computer Programming, Gerald M. Weinberg

opinionThe programming group (the syllogism; figure 30.4)

A programmer who owns his code cannot see its faults

Weinberg argues that a programmer who treats a program as part of himself cannot see its errors. A fault found in the code lands as news about him, not news about the program.

Becausethe syllogism is introspection stated out loud and the supporting cases are anecdotes; what is evidenced is the remedy, not the mechanism.
LimitsWeinberg's mechanism is one person's attachment to an artefact, which predicts variation between people; Edmondson's interpersonal account predicts variation between two units of one firm, and that is the version that replicated.
PracticeArrange the work so that no listing is anybody's. Witness practice in review handles the half the arrangement cannot reach.
After AICode a model wrote is not part of anybody, so the ego is absent at the moment of review. What takes its place is ownership of the decision to use the tool, and that defends itself the same way.
evidenceThe programming group (Bill G. and Marilyn B.; the 1998 comment)

Letting others read your code catches errors and steadies delivery dates

Weinberg argues that when nobody owns a piece of code, other people find errors its author cannot see. The gain shows up as delivery dates that vary less, not as work finishing faster on average.

Becausethe founding case is one afternoon — seventeen errors in thirteen instructions, and no further error in nine years across a dozen installations — but by 1998 Weinberg reports no shortage of evidence that technical reviews produce more reliable code more cheaply.
LimitsWeinberg claims nothing about the mean time to finish, so a team measuring throughput sees the cost and not the gain. Brooks would put the same effort into fewer designing minds instead.
PracticeMake reading each other's work the default rather than the exception, and judge the arrangement on the spread of delivery dates, not the average. Failure-mode review says what the reader should be looking for.
After AIThe reading Weinberg wanted is now cheap and has changed direction: the model reads the person's code. The arrangement in which nobody owns the listing arrives by default.
contestedProgramming as an individual activity; and Since 1971 (Prechelt's 1999 reanalysis)

The famous thirty-to-one gap between programmers came from comparing different tasks

The often-quoted claim that one programmer is thirty times better than another came from comparing the best person on one task with the worst on another. On large problems the real difference is two or three to one.

Becausetwo studies of the same population reported thirty-to-one differences depending on whether the problem rewarded attention to detail or the broad view, and Prechelt found the largest ratios came from comparing the best subject on one task with the worst on another, with about four to one surviving.
LimitsThe reanalysis went back over the same small old studies rather than collecting new data, so what survives is a correction to an artefact and not a measurement of the real spread.
PracticeDo not price a hire, a tool or a reorganisation off the thirty-to-one figure; ask which stage of the work the number came from.
After AIThe spread that now matters is in reviewing rather than producing, and nobody has measured it. The figure the industry still quotes was never about the work it is used to justify.
evidenceProgramming as an individual activity (the one-page experiment, figure 30.7)

Weinberg found programmers do what the specification asks not what they prefer

Weinberg's programmers did about whatever they were asked to do. What the written instructions asked for, not who was assigned, set how much the work cost and what kind of program came out.

Becausea controlled manipulation in which only the last page of the specification differed and nobody knew: the group told to finish fast used two-fifths of the machine time and a third of the personal time and produced programs about ten times slower, replicated on a second problem.
LimitsFour subjects, one shop and one era; a large effect in a tiny sample, replicated once by the same author and by nobody since at scale.
PracticeSpend the argument on the last page of the specification rather than on who is assigned. Specification discipline is that argument written down before the work starts.
After AIThe finding transfers to the delegate that takes instructions most literally. What the specification asks for is what arrives, and the difference between make this fast and make this work now shows up in minutes rather than months.
opinionThe programming project (Mark S. and Henry F.)

Weinberg says a programmer nobody can replace is a danger

Weinberg argues that a programmer no one else can replace puts the project at risk. His advice is to remove that person from the job as quickly as possible.

Becausetwo cases chosen to point in opposite directions — the man who was given a raise instead of a successor and quit, leaving a system delivered a year late and scrapped, against the man who trained his two best people and left a project that finished.
LimitsBrooks's answer to the same fact is to concentrate design in one or two minds and pay for them, which makes indispensability the design. Weinberg's maxim is about what an organisation should tolerate, not about what produces the best system.
PracticeTreat any place where only one person can check the work as the next thing to fix, and fix it by training rather than by retention. Manual flying hours keeps the second person actually able.
After AIIndispensability now attaches to whoever can still check the work by hand, and that is the capability the tool quietly removes. The successor Weinberg wants trained is the person who keeps the skill.
opinionThe programming project (the military project's report; figure 30.6)

Weinberg says a smooth progress report shows filtering, not progress

Weinberg argues that every level of a reporting chain removes the extreme items, and the extremes are the only ones carrying news. A report that looks smooth is therefore evidence of the filtering, not of the work going well.

Becausethe arithmetic of the dates is checkable — worked backwards through printing and review time, a team's submission was due four days before the month it described began — and the smoothing at each of six or seven stages is observed but never measured.
LimitsWeinberg puts the smoothing in each reviewer's judgement; Edmondson's evidence puts it in the reporter's calculation about a specific audience, which is where an intervention has to go.
PracticeTreat an unusually smooth report as the finding, and go to the extremes the chain removed. Failure-mode review is one way to make the extremes reportable again.
After AIA summary written by a model is one more filtering stage, and it smooths by construction: it reports the central tendency of what it was given, which is precisely the part carrying no news.
opinionThe programming team (the rule of thumb, figure 30.5)

Weinberg says three programmers do about twice the work of one

Weinberg's rule of thumb is that three programmers do about twice the work of one, and three such teams about twice the work of one team. So an eight-month job for one person is a two-month job for nine, and no less.

Becausea rule of thumb with no measurement behind it, defended by the observation that it is doubtful nine programmers can do anything useful in less time than it takes them to get organised.
LimitsThe numbers are asserted rather than observed. Brooks reaches the same conclusion from a combinatorial argument that does not flatten, and the two disagree about whether the cost is bounded.
PracticeGive the best people you can find enough time that you need the fewest of them, and treat the floor as real when a date is being negotiated.
After AIModel capacity adds none of the familiar coordination cost and adds a new one, since every output has to be read by somebody who is already the bottleneck. The floor moves; it does not disappear.
evidenceThe programming project (Asch imported; the six team leaders and George's six weeks)

When every team leader agrees the schedule is fine, they are bluffing

Weinberg argues that when a group reports everyone is on schedule, it is managing how it looks rather than reporting the work. One person admitting they are behind releases the rest to admit it too.

BecauseAsch's line-judging result is experimental and the meeting reproduces its structure, including the single dissenter who restores almost everyone's sight; the meeting itself is one observation.
LimitsAsch's subjects doubted their own perception; Weinberg's leaders knew perfectly well they were behind and were managing an audience, so the conformity evidence supports the shape of the remedy and not the mechanism.
PracticeWhen a status round comes back unanimous, let the silence run and ask again rather than recording it. Cognitive forcing is the same move applied to an output you are about to accept.
After AIA model asked to review a plan will agree with it, and its agreement counts in the room as another voice. That is the unanimity Weinberg says carries no information, now available on demand.

The Fearless Organization, Amy C. Edmondson

contestedThe underpinning (the two-hospital study, figure 31.1)

Better hospital teams reported more errors, not fewer

In Edmondson's two-hospital study the better-performing units reported more errors, not fewer, because people felt able to speak about mistakes. A low error count says something about the team's climate before it says anything about the work.

Becausethe independent and dependent variables were measured by different people, the correlation was significant and pointed the wrong way, and a blind observer found the units differed in whether people felt able to talk about mistakes — but the outcome is measured by a process the climate itself affects.
LimitsLater work separated the two: departments with higher safety reported more errors, and made fewer only where the department also genuinely prioritised patient safety. The original finding remains compelling as a story and awkward as evidence.
PracticeRead a falling error count as a question rather than an achievement, and find out which of the two things moved. Failure-mode review is where the errors get somewhere to be recorded.
After AIA tool that logs every rejected suggestion makes caught errors cheap to count and accepted-and-wrong ones invisible, which reproduces the original confound in a new instrument.
evidenceThe paper trail (Bradley on project teams; the French master's teams; figure 31.3)

Disagreement and mixed expertise help safe teams and hurt unsafe ones

Whether a team feels safe to speak up decides which way other things cut. Conflict, mixed expertise and working apart all help teams where people feel safe, and hurt teams where they do not.

Becausetwo independent samples show the sign reversal, and the long-standing inconsistency in the demographic diversity literature is what a missing moderator looks like.
LimitsThe reinterpretation of the diversity literature is a suggestion rather than a re-analysis, and the two supporting studies are of project and student teams.
PracticeBefore adding a dissenting expert to a team, find out whether the team can absorb disagreement; without that, the addition makes things worse rather than neutral.
After AIA model is expertise diversity with no interpersonal cost attached, so by this account it should help unconditionally. What still depends on the climate is whether anyone will say they disagree with it.
evidenceThe underpinning (the fifty-one teams; the seven-item measure)

Feeling safe to speak up is a trait of teams, not companies

How safe people feel to speak up is a property of the work group they are in, not of the person or the company. Two teams in one organisation, under the same policies, can differ sharply.

Becausethe group-level variation has been replicated repeatedly since 2018 on a measure whose reliabilities run from about .73 to .94.
LimitsMuch of the literature is cross-sectional survey work in which safety and outcomes are measured at the same time and often from the same respondents, so the causal arrow is argued rather than demonstrated, and estimates shrink as designs tighten.
PracticeStop looking for a company-wide programme and look at the two teams whose numbers differ; the difference is the leaders. The stays-human list is one thing a single team can decide for itself.
After AIThe unit whose climate matters now contains a delegate that cannot be embarrassed. What still varies between two teams with the same tools is whether a person will say out loud that the output is wrong.
evidenceThe underpinning, and Since 2018

Feeling safe to speak up matters most on uncertain, shared work

How safe people feel to speak up matters more the more uncertain the work is and the more people depend on each other. For routine tasks done alone, it barely matters.

Becauseit was stated as a prediction in 2018 and has since been found by meta-analytic work, which is a real test because it could have failed.
LimitsUncertain and interdependent is graded by the researcher after the fact in most studies, and the meta-analytic estimates of the effect on performance shrink as designs tighten.
PracticeSpend the effort on climate where the work is novel and shared, and stop apologising for not spending it on the routine parts. The stays-human list marks which parts are which.
After AIThe routine work is what the tool absorbs, so the human work that remains moves into exactly the quadrant where the climate carries the most weight.
evidenceThe paper trail (the neonatal quality-improvement teams at twenty-three hospitals)

Feeling safe to speak up predicts learning from colleagues, not from reading

In neonatal teams at twenty-three hospitals, how safe people felt to speak up predicted how much they asked, suggested and worked things out together. It had no relationship at all with how much they read on their own.

Becausethe activity was split between reading the literature alone and working things out together, and the null on the first half is what shows the mechanism runs through interpersonal risk and nothing else; a spurious climate effect would have moved both.
LimitsThe activity split is self-reported and the study is one setting. The null says something about the mechanism and nothing about how much either kind of learning was worth.
PracticeIf a team is not improving, do not send more reading; make it cheap to ask the question in front of colleagues. Failure-mode review is one place that asking becomes routine.
After AIReading what a model produces is learning what, which the climate does not touch. Saying in front of the team that its answer is wrong is learning how, which is entirely what the climate decides.
opinionMaking it happen (the blame gap, figure 31.6)

Managers blame far more failures than they think deserve blame

Edmondson asks managers how many of their organisation's failures are truly blameworthy: they answer one to four per cent. She then asks how many are treated as blameworthy: seventy to ninety per cent.

Becausetwo answers Edmondson has collected from the same rooms of managers for years: audience polling, not a study, and she presents it as such.
LimitsThe respondents are self-selected audiences at her own talks, both figures are impressions, and the gap is between two beliefs rather than between a belief and the record.
PracticeSort failures before responding to them — deviation from a known process, a novel combination of ordinary events, a considered foray into new territory — and let the sort decide the response. Failure-mode review is where the second kind gets caught.
After AIWhen a failure came out of a model there is no obvious object for blame, and the organisation finds one anyway — usually the person who accepted the output rather than the person who chose the tool.
evidenceMaking it happen (Morath's question); and The fearless workplace (Rustenburg and the lekgotla)

Open questions get people talking where explanations produced silence

Edmondson finds that a specific question people cannot answer with yes or no brings out information that an explanation does not. At Rustenburg mine, where explaining had produced silence, deaths fell from forty-four in 2006 to seventeen in 2011.

Becausein both cases the explanation had already been given and had produced silence, and only the change of question moved anything; at Rustenburg fatalities fell from forty-four in 2006 to seventeen in 2011.
LimitsBoth are single organisational cases in which many things changed at once; the fall at Rustenburg followed a shutdown, a restructuring and a new chief executive as well as a new question.
PracticeReplace was everything fine with was everything as safe as you would have liked this week, and wait. The stays-human list is built from the same kind of question asked about delegation.
After AIThe rule applies to what one asks a model as well. A question it can answer yes or no gets agreement; a concrete one that cannot gets the part of the answer worth reading.
opinionMaking it happen (the 2017 Google memo case, worked through without taking a side)

Punishing a clear violation is fair; vague rules are what silence people

Edmondson argues that punishing someone for breaking a rule everyone knew does not make a workplace less safe to speak up in. What teaches people to stay quiet is not knowing where the line is.

Becausea distinction drawn from one contested case in order to separate a broken clear policy from an unclear boundary, offered as an analysis rather than as a rate.
LimitsWhether a boundary was clear is decided after the sanction and mostly by the people who imposed it, which is the part of the claim that cannot be checked from inside the organisation.
PracticeWrite the boundary down before you need to enforce it, and enforce it visibly when it is broken; the vagueness is what costs, not the severity.
After AIThe boundaries most often left unwritten now are the ones about tool use — what may be generated, what must be disclosed, what must be checked by hand. By this account leaving them vague costs more than writing them strictly.
evidenceThe paper trail (the terms-of-trade table; the vignette studies; the technician with children in college)

Telling people to speak up fails because silence pays them better

Speaking up helps the organisation later and uncertainly, while staying quiet helps the person now and for certain. Because the trade is one-sided, telling people to be braver changes nothing.

Becausean interview finding in which eighty-five per cent could name an occasion they had felt unable to raise a concern, and a vignette study in which managers were significantly more likely to offer an important correction when the boss's boss was absent.
LimitsThe vignettes measure stated intention rather than behaviour, and the eighty-five per cent figure is a recall question with no base rate for how often the withheld concern was right.
PracticeChange what silence costs rather than telling people to be brave; make the contribution requested by name and the silence the awkward option. The stays-human list is one such structure.
After AIThe same terms of trade were trained into a model by optimising on human approval. There the fix is in the reward signal rather than in the climate, because the model has no stake to protect.
opinionMaking it happen (responding productively; the surfactant the nurse did not raise)

Thanking someone before judging their point decides if they speak again

Edmondson argues that whether a person who raised a concern raises another one depends on being thanked for raising it before being told whether they were right.

Becausea prescription drawn from a counterfactual reading of one case, consistent with the rest of the evidence and not tested on its own.
LimitsGrove's remedy for the same moment lives inside the review — level, listen, leave yourself out — and neither version has been compared with the other. Good process and good outcome come apart, which is why rewarding outcomes alone punishes sound judgement that met bad luck.
PracticeThank the person for raising it before saying whether they were right, every time, including when they were wrong. Witness practice in review is what makes that possible when the correction stings.
After AIA model thanks the user for every correction and it buys nothing, because there is no next time in which it will be braver. Appreciation is an instrument that works only on someone who is keeping score.

The Mythical Man-Month, Frederick P. Brooks, Jr.

contestedThe mythical man-month (the worked twelve-man-month example; figures 33.2, 33.3)

Adding people to a late software project makes it later

Brooks argues that adding people to a late software project makes it later: newcomers must be trained by the people already working, the number of conversations grows as n(n-1)/2, and splitting the work again throws away finished parts.

Becausethe mechanism is arithmetic and the worked example is airtight, but Abdel-Hamid and Madnick, modelling with a learning curve, found that adding always costs more and does not always make it later.
LimitsBoehm's sixty-three projects give a cost-optimum schedule as the cube root of expected effort, with hardly any project succeeding in under three-quarters of it, which bounds the schedule from below without the law. Brooks kept the bald statement.
PracticeReschedule or trim the task rather than adding people late, and take no small slips. The stays-human list records what extra capacity will not be asked to do.
After AIModel capacity is added late by default and costs nothing to train, so the first two terms vanish. What remains is repartitioning and the review of work nobody on the team wrote.
opinionSince 1975 (the chapter heading Parnas was right, and I was wrong; the ten-thousand-page OS/360 workbook)

Brooks admits Parnas was right that hiding information beats showing everything

Brooks says he was wrong and Parnas was right: software design improves when each part hides its inner workings from the others, not when every programmer can see everything.

Becausea retraction argued from what happened afterwards — Parnas's encapsulated module became the abstract data type and then the class, which is the only way found to compose programs out of chunks larger than a statement.
LimitsThe documentary hypothesis survives with should see everything softened to should be able to see it, so the retraction concerns a mechanism and not openness. Weinberg's case for reading each other's code is untouched by it.
PracticeDesign the interface so that a person can work on one part without holding the whole, and stop treating total visibility as a virtue in itself.
After AIA model reads across every hidden boundary at once, so encapsulation is not what limits the machine. What it protects now is the human's ability to reason about a part without the whole.
opinionWhy did the tower of Babel fail? (the audit of the project; the tree and the network)

Brooks judges an organisation by the talking it makes unnecessary

Brooks says the point of an organisation chart is to cut down the talking that dividing up the work makes necessary. A structure should therefore be judged by how much communication it removes, not by who it puts in charge.

Becausea definition of the purpose of organisation, illustrated by a parable and by Brooks's own project, with the dotted lines named as what makes up the difference between the tree and the network.
LimitsGrove's dual reporting deliberately adds a path so that standards and priorities stay live at once, so this criterion files as failures organisations Grove would call correct.
PracticeJudge a reorganisation by which conversations it makes unnecessary, and count the ones it adds. The stays-human list names the conversations that must stay whatever the structure.
After AIAn agent sits on neither the tree nor the network and is reachable by everyone at once, so the structure removes nothing on its behalf. Whatever it produces still has to pass through the same human paths to be believed.
opinionThe tar pit (the two boundaries, figure 33.1)

Brooks puts finished software at nine times the cost of a program

Brooks estimates that turning a working program into a product a team can sell and run costs about nine times as much. Making it general, tested and documented costs three times; fitting it into a larger system costs three times again.

BecauseBrooks's own arithmetic, offered as the gap between what a programmer believes he can do — estimating from the thing that came out of the garage — and what his employer needs.
LimitsBoth factors of three are estimates and their independence is assumed rather than shown; nothing in the book measures either.
PracticeWhen something works in a demonstration, multiply by nine before promising a date. Failure-mode review covers the testing third of it.
After AIWhat now comes out of the garage in an hour is still the corner of the diagram that costs one. The factor of nine is the distance between a demonstration and something a team can run.
evidenceNo silver bullet (essence and accident, figure 33.6; the accident ceiling, figure 33.7)

Brooks says no one tool will make programming ten times faster

Brooks argued that no single development will make software work ten times faster within a decade. The hard part is the thing itself, its complexity, its need to fit other systems, its constant change and its invisibility, and tools only ease the writing down.

Becausethe prediction was stated so that it could fail, has run four decades rather than one without a candidate producing the gain by itself, and rests on an arithmetic claim nobody has disputed.
LimitsThe accidental fraction is Brooks's own estimate — half or less by 1995. The prediction is about a single development within a decade, so a compound of many gains over forty years neither falsifies nor confirms it.
PracticeAsk of any tool which part it attacks, and price the promise against the fraction of your effort that part actually consumes. Domain audit is that question asked domain by domain.
After AIThe current candidate attacks representation, which is the accidental half by Brooks's own division. What it does not do is decide what to build, and the measured results so far land where the arithmetic says they should.
opinionAristocracy, democracy, and system design (Reims; OS/360 against the PDP-10 time-sharing system; figure 33.5)

Brooks says one mind must own the shape of a system

Brooks argues that the most important thing in designing a system is that it hangs together as a single idea. That requires the design to come from one mind, or from a very few minds that agree.

Becausean aesthetic judgement about systems, supported by one costly natural experiment of his own — giving the OS/360 external specifications to a hundred and fifty implementers, which he estimates added a year of debugging.
LimitsThe counterfactual was never run and the year of debugging is Brooks's own estimate. Weinberg's arrangement distributes across every mind exactly what Brooks concentrates in one, and claims the same defect count as the payoff.
PracticeName the one person who owns the shape of the thing, separately from the person who owns the schedule, and let everyone else raise their effectiveness. Specification discipline is what that owner produces.
After AIGeneration is now cheap and agreement is not, so the constraint Brooks names is the binding one. Many minds can produce many designs in a day; the thing that cannot be parallelised is the single view that makes them one system.
opinionSince 1975 (the flat withdrawal; figure 33.8; Microsoft's nightly rebuild, Bell Northern's weekly)

Brooks withdrew his advice to plan on throwing the first build away

Brooks withdrew his own advice to build a first version and throw it away. Instead, get a bare working version running, add one piece at a time, and put it in front of users from the start.

Becausean author's retraction, supported by the industry practice that followed rather than by any comparison of the two approaches.
LimitsThe incremental build became the default and was never tested against the thing it replaced. What recommends it is the ordering — user test before full construction — rather than any measured gain.
PracticeGet a running skeleton first and keep it running, so that user testing starts before full construction has been paid for. Failure-mode review is what each increment gets checked against.
After AIA running skeleton is now the cheapest artefact in the project, so the discipline moves from producing one to deciding what the first working system must do. That is the part the tool does not supply.
opinionNo silver bullet (the case for rapid prototyping; the objection to program verification)

Deciding exactly what to build is the hardest part of software

Brooks argues that the hardest single part of building a software system is deciding exactly what it should do. Clients cannot describe a modern product correctly until they have built and tried some version of it.

Becausean assertion from experience, sharpened by the observation that verification establishes at best that a program meets its specification, whereas much of the essence of the work is debugging the specification.
LimitsHardest is not measured against anything. What the argument establishes is that the part is essential and not removable, not that it dominates the effort.
PracticeBuild something small and wrong on purpose so the client can say what they actually want, and treat the specification as the artefact under test. Specification discipline is how it gets written once they can.
After AIImplementation is the part that got cheap, so the ratio moved in the direction Brooks predicted and the residue is the specification — which is also the part an agent satisfies literally rather than queries.
opinionThe mythical man-month (the scheduling rule of thumb)

Half a software project is testing and the delay shows up last

Brooks says half a software project's time goes on testing, and the delay surfaces only at the end. The project looks on schedule until system testing, then discovers its slip when it is fully staffed and costing the most per day.

Becausea rule of thumb from examining conventionally scheduled projects, few of which allowed half the schedule for testing and most of which spent half, running on time until system test.
LimitsBrooks withdrew the model this rule sits inside. The incremental build he put in its place moves testing forward, so the allocation is right about where the effort goes and wrong about when the trouble can be discovered.
PracticeBudget the testing half explicitly, and treat on time before system test as no information at all. Failure-mode review gives the testing half something specific to look for.
After AICoding, the sixth Brooks allotted, is the part that collapsed. Testing and the verification of work nobody wrote did not, so the schedule is more lopsided now than when he drew it.
opinionNo silver bullet (the last attack, on people); and Since 1975, where he calls it the part still least acted on

Organisations develop managers on purpose and designers not at all

Brooks argues that organisations recruit and develop managers on purpose while doing nothing of the kind for designers, even though the quality of the people doing the designing is the single largest factor in whether a system succeeds.

BecauseBoehm's cost model found team quality the largest success factor by about four times, but the claim about what organisations do is offered without a count.
LimitsThe order-of-magnitude spread Brooks cites from Sackman, Erikson and Grant is what Prechelt's reanalysis found to be an artefact of cross-task comparison, so the gap is not the size he thought. The claim about neglect survives the correction.
PracticeBuild a route into design as deliberate as the route into management, with stages and the practice that moves people along it. Dreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule is that map.
After AIThe neglected skill has changed shape: it is now the judgement to specify and to verify. The pathway Brooks never proposed is what an organisation must build if it wants that judgement in ten years.

Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, Joel Becker and others

evidenceWhere the time went

Developers using AI spend a fifth of their time prompting and reviewing

METR found that about a fifth of working time in AI-allowed sessions went to prompting, waiting and reviewing. That time came out of writing code (36 to 24 per cent) and reading (24 to 16), not out of debugging.

Because74 hand-labelled screen recordings covering 84 hours show active coding falling from about 36 to 24 per cent of the session and reading and searching from 24 to 16, while testing and debugging barely moves and idle time rises from 6 to 10.
LimitsThe recordings cover 29 per cent of the study's time before filtering and 84 hours after it, at a labelling resolution of about ten seconds. The activity split is descriptive and cannot say which displacement causes the slowdown.
PracticeReliance audit — account for where an assisted hour actually goes before claiming the assistant saved one; the recovered time comes out of the activities that build the knowledge you will need to check its output.
After AIThe three activities that exist only in the assisted condition — prompting, waiting, reviewing — are the ones that grow as tools become agentic. The displacement of reading is the part to watch, because reading the system is how the reviewer stays able to review.
evidenceWhat the earlier studies measured, and Twenty-one ways to be wrong

Developers wrote more code in the condition where the work took longer

How much work appears to be produced can move in the opposite direction from how long the work takes. In METR's trial developers wrote 47 per cent more code per estimated hour while the same issues took them 19 per cent longer.

Becausethe two quantities are measured on the same issues in the same trial and move in opposite directions, which is what the field studies reporting 14 to 51 per cent gains could not have detected, because lines, commits and pull requests were all they measured.
LimitsThe 47 per cent figure sits among the ten factors the authors leave unresolved: it looks like scope creep, except that developers who report scope creep were slowed less than those who do not. The claim is about what output measures cannot show, not about what they always show.
