PracticeReliance audit — fix the unit of work and its definition of done before the tool is introduced, so that nothing the tool does downstream can change what counts as finished.
After AIEvery dashboard built to demonstrate an assistant's value counts the things that moved here in the wrong direction. The only measure that survived the trial is elapsed time on a unit of work fixed in advance.
evidenceThe forecasts and the result

Experienced developers took 19 per cent longer using AI on familiar code

In METR's randomised trial, experienced developers fixing issues in large codebases they knew well took about 19 per cent longer when they used AI assistance than when they did not.

Becausea randomised trial on 246 real issues from 16 developers, with a raw ratio of 1.34 (CI 1.05–1.70) and a regression estimate of 19 per cent using the pre-assignment forecast as the difficulty control.
LimitsSixteen developers and a confidence interval whose lower end sits near no effect. The sample was selected for the exact conditions the authors name as causes — deep familiarity and enormous mature codebases — and both are absent from most software work. Some participants were sped up. Most of the work was done in February and March 2025, before the command-line agents that arrived later that year.
PracticeManual flying hours — keep a protected block of work done without the assistant on the systems you know best, and time it, so the comparison exists as a measurement rather than an impression.
After AIThe tooling this measured was superseded within months, so the number is dated on arrival. What survives is the shape: on ground the worker already owns, the delegate's contribution is negative and invisible to the worker.
evidenceTwenty-one ways to be wrong

In METR's study developers lost most time on code they knew best

The AI assistance slowed developers down most on the parts of the code where their own knowledge was greatest and least written down. Where they had worked longest, they lost the most time.

Becauseslowdown is larger on issues the developers rate high for prior exposure and low for need of external documentation, in repositories averaging ten years, 1.1 million lines and five years of contribution per developer.
LimitsThe factor is one of five the authors credit and one of twenty-one they consider; ten of the twenty-one are left unresolved. Self-rated prior exposure is a coarse proxy for tacit knowledge.
PracticeDomain audit — mark the parts of your system where what you know is not written down anywhere, and treat those as the places where delegation costs rather than saves.
After AIThe boundary the model cannot cross is what nobody wrote down. Retrieval over a repository has narrowed it since 2025 for anything that exists in text, and left it exactly where it was for the conventions that live only in the maintainer's head.

How AI Impacts Skill Formation, Judy Hanwen Shen and Alex Tamkin

evidenceSix ways of using the assistant

Asking the assistant why preserves learning better than not using it

Shen and Tamkin found that what protects learning is asking the assistant for reasons, not staying away from it. Groups who asked for explanations or questioned the code scored 65 to 86 per cent; groups who handed over the writing scored 24 to 39.

Becausethe three patterns that asked conceptual questions, asked for code with an explanation, or generated and then interrogated scored 65 to 86 per cent; the three that delegated the writing or the debugging scored 24 to 39; nothing landed between 39 and 65.
LimitsSix groups of two to seven people each, sorted by hand from screen recordings after the fact. The clusters are a description of what these fifty-one people did, not a randomised comparison of instructions, so the pattern may be a marker of who the person already was.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — decide before you open the assistant whether this task is one you are learning or one you are shipping, and set the allowed request type accordingly.
After AIThe gap in the middle of the distribution is the useful part: there is no gentle slope from tutoring to delegation. The assistants that now ship a study mode are betting on the same split, without having tested it.
evidenceSix ways of using the assistant

Programmers using an assistant hit fewer of the errors that teach

In Shen and Tamkin's study programmers hit a median of three errors without the assistant and one with it. Ten of the twelve people who hit no error at all were using the assistant, and those errors are what teach the library.

Becausethe informative errors are the ones the library raises about its own semantics — RuntimeWarning for an unawaited coroutine, TypeError for a coroutine passed where an async function belongs — and neither can be cleared without grasping how Trio treats await, which is what the quiz asks about.
LimitsThe mechanism is inferred from error counts and types rather than tested: nobody randomised participants into meeting errors. NameError and AttributeError, the commonest overall, teach nothing, so raw error counts are not themselves the quantity that matters.
PracticeManual flying hours — when learning a system, let it raise its errors at you rather than routing around them; the error is the curriculum.
After AIEvery layer added between the worker and the runtime removes errors, which is what it is for. The cost is invisible on the day and shows up the first time the worker has to diagnose something the assistant got wrong.
evidenceWhat the quiz found

Programmers who let AI write the code learned less about the library

Shen and Tamkin found that programmers who used an assistant to write code in an unfamiliar library answered fewer questions about it afterwards. Those who used the assistant to ask for reasons instead of code did not lose that ground.

Becausefifty-two professional Python programmers, thirty-five minutes on Trio, then a quiz taken unaided; the assisted group scored 4.15 points of 27 lower, d = 0.738, p = 0.010, at every experience band.
LimitsOne hour, one library, one chat interface, twenty-six people per arm, with learning measured by a quiz rather than a second unaided task. There is no human-assistance arm, so the comparison is a model against nothing rather than against a colleague.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — when the material is new to you, restrict the assistant to explanation and interrogation, and write the code yourself.
After AIThis is the experiment the productivity literature had not run: it measures what is left in the worker rather than what was shipped. The study modes the major assistants now ship encourage exactly the patterns that preserved learning here, and whether switching one on reproduces the effect is untested.
opinionSix ways of using the assistant, and What the experiment cannot settle

Shen and Tamkin expect autocomplete to be faster and teach less

Writing a good question forces you to understand the task. Shen and Tamkin argue that a tool which writes the request for you should be faster still, and cost more learning, than a chat assistant does.

Becauseit is the authors' lower-bound argument for treating a chat interface as the least automated case, stated as reasoning and never measured.
LimitsAn argument, not a measurement. The obvious experiment — the same design with an agentic tool — has not been run, and the recordings show the composing time was also what ate the speed gain, so the two effects are not separable here.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — when you are learning, choose the interface that makes you say what you want; keep autocomplete and agents for work you could already do.
After AIWritten against chat assistants in 2026, the claim now reads as a prediction about the agentic tooling that replaced them. It is the study's most consequential sentence and its least supported one.
evidenceWhat the quiz found

The AI assistant hurt understanding and saved no time at all

In Shen and Tamkin's study the assistant left people understanding the task less well, and it did not make them any faster: total time did not differ between the assisted and unassisted groups (p = 0.391).

Becausetotal task time did not differ between the arms (p = 0.391) even though the assistant would write both complete solutions on request; up to eleven minutes of a thirty-five-minute session went to the assistant, one participant spending six on a single query.
LimitsA null result on a thirty-five-minute task with twenty-six people per arm has little power. In the fourth pilot, before syntax hints were added, the assisted group was faster (d = 1.11); the speed gain did not survive removal of the confound, which is weaker than showing it never existed. The one thing the assistant reliably bought was completion: four control participants ran out of time and none of the assisted did.
PracticeReliance audit — time the delegated route against the unassisted one on the same task before assuming the delegation is the faster of the two.
After AIThe interface matters more than the model here. A chat assistant that must be prompted in sentences is the least automated case; an agentic tool that removes the composing should show the speed gain this one did not.
contestedSix ways of using the assistant

What you ask after the code arrives decides what you learn

In Shen and Tamkin's study the two people who asked the assistant to generate code and then questioned it scored 86 per cent, against 39 for those who just took the code. The request was the same; the questions afterwards were not.

Becausegenerate-then-interrogate and pure delegation begin with the same request and the same paste; the scores were 86 per cent and 39, at 24 minutes against 19.5.
LimitsTwo people. The best result in the study rests on the smallest cluster in it, and the authors present the typology as exploratory.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — after accepting generated code, ask the assistant what it did and why, before the tab closes; the request was not the mistake, the silence after it would be.
After AIThis is the only route the study found that keeps both the output and the learning, and it is the one that nothing in the interface prompts you to take. The cost is a few minutes of questions that produce no code.

Revisiting the Six Stages of Skill Acquisition, B. Scot Rousse and Stuart E. Dreyfus

evidenceFrom novice to expert (the novice's rules and the advanced beginner's situational aspects; the competence stage as the first that cannot be reached by instruction alone).

A beginner given finished answers learns no rules and collects no cases

In the Dreyfus model a learner at the first two stages works from fixed rules and from the cases they have seen. A tool that hands them a finished answer takes away both the rules they would practise and the cases they would collect.

Becausethe stage descriptions rest on the 1980 Air Force report's flight-instruction, chess and language cases and on forty years of use in nursing and medicine; the "removes both" clause is the inference the learning-science trials test directly.
LimitsThe model is phenomenological, not measured; Gobet and others dispute that rule-following ever becomes expertise, and the stage boundaries are not sharp. The claim holds for the early stages; the authors say nothing about a competent performer using a generator.
PracticeMap each junior to a stage before deciding what they may hand off; below competence, the tool may explain but not produce.
After AIWritten for teaching, the model now reads as a rule about delegation: the stages say which worker may be given a machine that finishes the task, and the answer for the first two is none.
opinionSince 1980

Courses can take a learner to competence but no further

The Dreyfus brothers argue a course of instruction can take a learner only as far as competence. Everything past that point is stored as experience of particular cases, not as rules that can be taught.

Becauseit is the judgment the authors say they have not softened in forty years; the mentor's remaining work is naming aspects by example and pointing out perspectives that arrive unasked.
LimitsAn assertion about what instruction can do, with no trial that tried and failed. Sweller's programme keeps explicit instruction all the way up and fades the guidance instead, and it has randomised evidence behind it.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — stop expecting a training programme to produce judgment, and budget instead for the exposure to cases that produces it.
After AIOnboarding by assistant is instruction at scale, and it stops where instruction stops. What a new engineer can be told by a model is exactly the part the model says will not carry them past competence.
contestedFrom novice to expert

Dreyfus says caring about the outcome is how skill gets stored

Dreyfus argues that caring about how a task turns out is the channel through which experience is laid down. Someone who practises while staying detached will not become proficient.

Becauseat competence the result follows from the performer's own chosen perspective — successful attacks induce euphoria and mistakes are felt in the pit of the stomach — and the claim is asserted phenomenologically rather than measured.
LimitsNo measurement, and a direct tension with the practice this vault runs: if involvement is the storage channel, detachment during review must be distinguished from detachment during the work. Ericsson's account attributes the same storage to structured feedback with no emotional term in it.
PracticeWitness practice in review — notice that caring about the outcome is doing work, and separate that from taking the outcome as a verdict on yourself; the first is the channel, the second is the tax.
After AIIt names the thing that does not transfer when a model does the work. The model has the outcome and not the stake in it, so whatever is stored through the stake is stored in nobody.
contestedFrom novice to expert, and Proficiency and expertise

Dreyfus says experts get good by dropping rules, not collecting them

Skill does not grow by collecting better rules. Beyond the stage the Dreyfus brothers call competence, a learner has to give up the rules and the step-by-step reasoning that applies them, and respond to whole situations instead.

Becausethe six-stage account is restated in 2021 with the transitions themselves as its subject, and it is argued phenomenologically; the contrary case is Ericsson's, that expert performance is sustained by continued effortful control.
LimitsNo measurement. Fernand Gobet objects that a science of expertise needs measurement where this offers description of experience. Barbara Montero's dancers and Simon Høffding's quartet suggest thinking during performance does not wreck it, and Christensen, Sutton and McIlwain propose that deliberate and automatic control are meshed rather than successive.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — stop writing checklists for people past competence and start giving them cases; the checklist is the thing they have to stop using.
After AIA model that can be stated as rules is a model a machine can apply, which is why everything the model says is not statable is also what it says cannot be delegated. The stages are the sharpest available answer to which work an assistant can take.
opinionPerforming across the stages

Experts go back to following rules when their field changes under them

Dreyfus argues that when the thing an expert is expert in changes — new equipment, a new rule, traffic running the other way — the expert drops back to earlier stages and has to think through rules again instead of acting on recognition.

Becausethe examples are tennis rackets changing material and head size, the three-point shot, software updates, and an expert driver in a country where the traffic runs the other way; they are illustrations, not measurements.
LimitsAnecdotal. Nothing says how large a change has to be to cause the fall, or how far down the stages it goes, which makes the claim hard to fail.
PracticeFailure-mode review — after any change to the tools or the system, treat your own first judgments as an advanced beginner's and check them, rather than trusting the speed at which they arrive.
After AIThe domain now changes every few months. If the claim holds, the engineers with the most experience are also the ones most often thrown back to rules by a tooling change, which is a reading of the METR result the paper does not give itself.

Peak, Anders Ericsson and Robert Pool

opinionThe gold standard

Most fields lack the clear measures and teachers deliberate practice requires

Deliberate practice in Ericsson's strict sense needs a field with agreed measures of who performs better and teachers who know what the best do. Management, teaching, engineering and consulting have neither.

Becausemanagement, teaching, engineering and consulting have no agreed measure of superior performance, and the judges at the California State Fair scored three glasses of the same wine 91, 87 and 83.
LimitsA boundary drawn by assertion; no test says how much agreement on standards is enough. Tetlock's training module is a counterexample of a sort, having raised accuracy in a field Ericsson would not have counted.
PracticeCalibration log — where the field supplies no objective standard, build a private one: a prediction, a date, a number, and a score afterwards.
After AIThe scoreable standards are arriving from an unexpected direction: an assistant that can be asked the same question a hundred times makes disagreement visible where a single expert's judgment used to be the measure. That is a standard of consistency, not of quality.

Make It Stick, Peter C. Brown and others

evidenceMix up your practice

Mixing up practice teaches you to tell cases apart but feels worse

Practising different problem types mixed together, instead of one type at a time, teaches the skill the real task needs: telling which case you are facing. The cost is that practice feels slower and less successful while you do it.

Becausethe Cal Poly hitters who took three pitch types randomly interspersed struggled through six weeks and finished markedly better, and the painting-attribution studies, designed expecting massing to win, found interleaving taught the differences between painters.
LimitsDoug Rohrer's randomised classroom trials of interleaved mathematics give the effect its strongest support; outside well-defined problem types the boundary of interleaving is not established, and Sweller's element-interactivity account predicts harm where the material is high-load and the learner is a novice.
PracticeManual flying hours — mix the kinds of problem in a practice block rather than drilling one kind to fluency, and expect the block to feel worse.
After AIDelegation naturally blocks practice: the assistant handles a class of problem, so the worker meets that class rarely and the rest often. The mix a person actually practises is now set by what the tool does not take.
evidenceTo learn, retrieve

Pulling an answer from memory teaches more than reading it again

Roediger and Karpicke found that recalling material from memory beat studying it again: 68 per cent against 54 at two days. The study-only group forgot 52 per cent of what it could first recall; the tested group forgot 10 per cent.

BecauseRoediger and Karpicke measured 68 per cent against 54 at two days and 56 against 42 at a week; the study-only group forgot 52 per cent of what it could first recall against 10 per cent for the tested group, and the Columbia Middle School quizzed material scored 92 against 79, holding at eight months.
LimitsTransfer is the weak point: Pan and Rickard's 2018 meta-analysis finds the testing benefit carries only modestly to untested material and new inferences. Sweller's programme holds that generating without the necessary knowledge wastes working memory on search.
PracticeManual flying hours — close the assistant and the documentation and write what you know from memory before looking anything up; the looking-up is not the learning.
After AIA tool that answers instantly removes the interval in which retrieval would have happened. The effect is largest for exactly the material a worker will need to recall unaided when the tool is wrong.
evidenceTo learn, retrieve, and Embrace difficulties

Trying to answer before you are told beats being told first

Make It Stick reports that trying to produce an answer before you are shown one is remembered better than reading the answer first. Errors made and then corrected are not learned.

Becausethe generation effect shows *foot – s _ _ e* recalled better than *foot – shoe*; Washington University physics students work problems before the class that teaches the solution, and Skinner's errorless learning designed out what turns out to be part of the road.
LimitsSweller's camp holds that generating without the necessary knowledge burns working memory on means-ends search, and the productive-failure literature and the worked-example literature disagree about which measures settle it. The book states the boundary — a difficulty stops being desirable when the learner lacks the background — without giving a way to locate it.
PracticeCognitive forcing — commit to your own answer before you read the assistant's, in writing, so that the comparison is possible.
After AIThe assistant's default is to supply the answer before any attempt exists, which is the condition these experiments use as the control. Restoring the attempt costs a minute and has to be done deliberately, because no interface prompts it.

Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later, John Sweller and others

evidenceThe effects

Groups learn demanding material better and simple material worse than individuals

Kirschner and colleagues found in 2011 that groups learned more efficiently than individuals from demanding tasks, and individuals learned more efficiently from easy ones. Talking to each other costs effort that pays only when the task is heavy.

BecauseKirschner and colleagues, 2011, found groups learned more efficiently from demanding tasks and individuals from undemanding ones.
LimitsOne study, on learning tasks in an instructional setting. Whether the same crossover governs professional review, where the costs include politics as well as transaction overhead, is untested.
PracticeFailure-mode review — review high-load work in a group and low-load work alone, and stop treating group review as a uniform good.
After AIA model is a second working memory with no transaction cost worth speaking of, which is the condition under which the individual was supposed to win. The comparison the study makes does not have a cell for it.
evidenceThe architecture of 1998

How complex something is depends on who is reading it

Sweller argues that complexity is not a property of the material itself. It is a relation between the material and what the learner already knows, so the same page is one simple thing to one person and many parts to another.

Becauseelement interactivity makes the written word *characteristics* one element for a fluent reader and many interacting elements for someone learning to read, so a measure of complexity that ignores what the learner knows predicts nothing.
LimitsElement interactivity is counted by judgment rather than by an instrument, which makes the account hard to falsify on any particular piece of material.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — before handing someone a generated diff to review, ask what it is made of for them, not what it is made of.
After AIThe same pull request is one element for the person who wrote the subsystem and forty for the person who did not. Machine-written code arrives without the history that would have collapsed those elements for anyone.
contestedThrough the prism of evolutionary psychology

Learners taught the solution first beat those left to work it out

Sweller holds that learners who are taught the solution before practising do better than those left to work it out. Almost everything in long-term memory is copied from other people, not discovered.

Becausethe borrowing and reorganising principle makes random generate-and-test the expensive fallback rather than the norm; the rival is the productive-failure research, where learners who struggle before being taught outperform those taught first.
LimitsDirectly contradicted by the generation effect, by productive failure, and by the Shen and Tamkin result where being handed the solution cost comprehension. The disagreement is partly about timescale: what is measured immediately after instruction and what is measured a week later do not agree.
PracticeIf you believed it you would show the worked example first and practise afterwards, which is the opposite of what the generation and retrieval literature prescribes; the two camps agree on much of the evidence and disagree about which measures count.
After AIAn assistant is the borrowing principle industrialised: the cheapest possible access to what other people worked out. That makes the question of which camp is right operationally urgent rather than academic.
evidenceThe effects

Sweller found teaching aids that help beginners start to hurt experts

Worked examples and other teaching support that help a beginner become unnecessary as the learner's knowledge grows, and then start to hurt performance — an effect called expertise reversal.

Becausethe expertise reversal effect, named in 2003, and guidance fading are both replicated experimental results; Chen and colleagues obtained a worked-example effect with mathematical problem solving and its reverse with definitions, where generating the answer taught more.
LimitsThe reversal is established for instructional materials in well-structured domains. Where it sits for a tool used for years rather than a lesson used for an hour is an extrapolation.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — withdraw the scaffolding deliberately as someone's knowledge grows, including your own use of the assistant on material you now know.
After AINothing in an assistant fades. The support that was right in the first week is still there in the first year, at the point where the same support is the thing costing time — which is one reading of why the most experienced developers lost the most.
contestedThrough the prism of evolutionary psychology

Sweller says only subject knowledge can be taught, not general thinking skills

Sweller argues that general thinking skills cannot be taught because evolution has already supplied them to everyone. What teaching can add is knowledge of a particular subject.

BecauseGeary's primary and secondary division and Sala and Gobet's 2017 review are the support, and the argument rests on the failure of attempts to teach generic skills, which is equally consistent with the teaching having been poor; no independent test identifies a piece of knowledge as biologically primary.
LimitsThe evolutionary foundation is an inference rather than a measurement. Tetlock's randomised training result is the counterexample, in a domain Sweller would not count; the two camps largely agree on the evidence and disagree about which measures count.
PracticeIf you believed it you would stop buying general critical-thinking training and spend the budget on domain knowledge instead — and you would still have to explain Tetlock's training module, which is an hour of general guidelines with a measured effect.
After AIIt is the strongest available argument against the idea that working with a model teaches transferable judgment. On this account whatever a person gains from the practice is knowledge of that model in that domain, and nothing more general.
evidenceThe architecture of 1998

Working memory is tiny for new material, vast for familiar material

Sweller argues that the mind can hold only a few new items at once, but can handle an effectively unlimited amount of material it already knows and is pulling back from long-term memory.

BecauseDe Groot's chess players' skill was explained entirely by remembered configurations and the best move for each, and Ericsson and Kintsch's long-term working memory, 1995, supplies the second half of the architecture.
LimitsMeasurement remains the theory's weak point: instruments built to separate intrinsic, extraneous and germane load have had their factor structure disputed, as Leppink's was.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — judge how much output a person can check by how much of the material they already hold, not by how senior they are.
After AIIt sets the ceiling on review. A model produces novel material faster than a person can convert it into anything long-term memory holds, so the reviewer's capacity, not the generator's, is the binding constraint.

The Skill Code, Matt Beane

opinionThe 160,000-year-old school

Beane says people learn hard skills beside an expert, not in courses

Skill you can use under pressure comes from working alongside someone who already knows how, while they do the real job. A course does not produce the same thing.

Becausetwo years of comparative ethnography and field studies across thirty-one occupations stand behind it, but the claim itself is a reading of those cases rather than a measurement; the chief of surgery's line is the argument in one sentence — watching a movie does not make you an actor.
LimitsEthnography across occupations selected for the argument. The counterexample sits in his own field: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond found a generative assistant diffusing the best call-centre agents' practice to everyone else, which is a machine doing some of what the bond does.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — when someone on your team needs to learn something, put them next to the person doing it rather than into a course.
After AIThe model is the first thing that has ever been able to answer a novice's questions patiently and at any hour. Whether that is the bond or a good imitation of half of it is the open question his account makes sharp.
evidenceReworking the skill code

How an organisation deploys a tool decides whether users learn from it

Beane found that whether people learn from a tool depends on how their organisation deploys it, not on what the tool can do. Hospitals bought the surgical robot's second console but never let trainees drive; bomb disposal teams handed trainees the controls.

Becauseevery institution in the study bought the da Vinci's second console and Beane never saw the shared-control mode used — his informants had never seen it and the salespeople called the practice exceptionally rare — while bomb disposal settled the other way, putting the controller in the trainee's hands with nothing in the machine requiring it.
LimitsTwo cases pointing opposite ways, chosen to make the point. Nothing here predicts which way a given organisation will settle, and the surgical case has moved since publication as training tracks were built.
PracticeAutomation ironies audit — ask what your tooling's defaults do to the people who will have to check it in two years, and change the defaults rather than waiting for the vendor to.
After AINothing in a model requires that it write the code rather than explain it; that is a choice made in the product and repeated in the team's habits. The trade between productivity and learning is being made daily without anyone deciding to make it.
evidenceThe threat

Machines threaten apprentices by making experts productive without them

The danger is not that the machine does the expert's job. It is that the machine lets the expert work without a junior, which turns the junior from someone you need into a cost you can cut.

Becausein chip design an overnight search replaces five days of junior analysis; Emanuel and colleagues found senior engineers more productive the less time they spent with juniors; each resident present added 25 per cent to anaesthesia time, and removing two from an average procedure saved $9,026.
LimitsThe cost figures are real and the causal chain to a collapsed pipeline is an argument. Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen reported in 2025 that employment for workers aged twenty-two to twenty-five had fallen relative to older workers in the occupations most exposed to generative AI, which is what the mechanism predicts but not yet proof of it.
PracticeThe stays-human list — name the work that stays with people who are learning, and defend it against the arithmetic that says it is cheaper without them.
After AIThe arithmetic is now available to every team lead with an assistant. The junior's work is the first thing a capable model absorbs, and nobody has to decide to remove the apprenticeship for it to go.
opinionComplexity

Radiologists hunting for a nodule missed a gorilla in the scan

Beane argues that expertise narrows what a person notices: 83 per cent of radiologists searching for lung nodules missed a picture of a gorilla forty-eight times larger. That is why an expert needs a novice's naive questions.

BecauseDrew's eye-tracking showed most of the radiologists had looked straight at it, but the step from a perceptual demonstration to the claim that novices are the remedy is Beane's argument rather than Drew's finding.
LimitsInattentional blindness in a search task is not the same as blindness in professional judgment, and nothing in the gorilla study involves a novice noticing what the expert missed.
PracticeFailure-mode review — keep someone in the review who does not yet know what is supposed to be there, and take their naive question seriously the first time.
After AIA model asks nothing and notices nothing it was not asked about, so it cannot play the novice's part in this. Replacing the junior with the assistant removes the questions as well as the labour.
evidenceWhen approved means fail

Robotic surgery lets in only surgeons who are already skilled

Beane finds the order reversed. In open surgery a trainee is let in before she is ready and becomes competent by doing it; in robotic surgery only those already fluent operate, and the approved training routes cannot make anyone fluent.

Becauseerrors are magnified up to ten times and displayed around the room, delegation becomes a public act on a touchscreen, and the riskiest phases move to the beginning and end where residents used to work unsupervised; as of 2015 the average American urologic surgeon doing any robotic surgery performed one robotic prostatectomy a year.
LimitsObservational, in one speciality, before the training tracks were built. The constraint he identifies — the attending's judgment about the patient in front of him — is not one a curriculum can change, which makes the claim hard to test by intervention.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — check whether your review process lets anyone become good enough to pass it, or only admits people who already are.
After AIThe same inversion is visible wherever an assistant raises the floor of acceptable output: the bar for a merged change rises, and the work that used to be safe enough to learn on is gone.
evidenceThe 160,000-year-old school

Surgical trainees do ten to twenty times less with robotic surgery

Beane watched surgical residents on the same operation done two ways. In open surgery they did the work for almost the whole procedure; with a robot, where the surgeon sits at a console, they did ten to twenty times less.

Becauseninety-four procedures, 478 hours of observation, 4,772 pages of notes and five hospitals: residents did surgical work for essentially the whole of a four-and-a-half-hour open procedure and ten to twenty times less of a robotic one.
LimitsOne operation in one speciality, observed rather than randomised. Professional bodies and residency programmes have since built the robotic training tracks and case minimums whose absence the paper documented, which addresses the credential and leaves the console-time problem where he found it.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — count the hours the junior actually spends with their hands on the work before and after a tool lands, and treat a fall as the cost it is.
After AIThe console is now a prompt. The same displacement — the expert working with the machine instead of with the novice — runs in software with none of surgery's licensing to make the shortfall visible.
evidenceWhen approved means fail

The surgical residents who learned most broke the training rules

The few trainees who got the skill anyway did it by breaking rules: specialising too early, rehearsing in their heads, operating with too little supervision. It cost them, and sometimes cost patients.

Becauseall twelve residents rated exceptional reported all three extensively, against four of the nine rated average who mentioned any, on a sample deliberately built to over-sample rare successes; about one in eight made it.
LimitsInterviews with a sample chosen to contain the successes, and self-report about rule-breaking. The practices were tolerated in silence, so the profession never learned from them and there is no record against which to check the accounts.
PracticeFailure-mode review — find out what the people who are learning fastest are doing that the process forbids, and decide whether to change the process rather than punishing them.
After AIShadow learning around an assistant is cheaper and safer than shadow learning around a patient, which removes the strongest argument for suppressing it. What remains is an organisation that does not know what its best people are doing.

When Combinations of Humans and AI Are Useful, Michelle Vaccaro and others

evidenceDecisions and creations

Almost no experiment split the task between person and machine beforehand

Only 3 of the 106 experiments Vaccaro and colleagues reviewed gave the person and the machine separate parts of the task in advance. Those four results pooled to g = 0.22, with a range from −0.42 to 0.87.

Becauseonly 3 of 106 experiments assigned separate subtasks to the better-suited partner, giving four effect sizes pooling to g = 0.22 with an interval from −0.42 to 0.87
LimitsFour effect sizes with an interval spanning zero is not evidence that division of labour works; it is evidence that nobody has tested it. The authors present it as a gap, not a finding.
PracticeThe stays-human list — write down in advance which parts of a piece of work are yours and which are the machine's, instead of handing over the whole and reviewing the result.
After AIThe one design the evidence cannot speak to is the one everybody is improvising daily, and the agentic tools now shipping make the division finer and less deliberate rather than more.

The Jagged Technological Frontier, Fabrizio Dell'Acqua and others

contestedEighteen tasks inside the frontier; Since 2023

A group using AI produces better ideas that are more alike

Dell'Acqua and colleagues reported that when a group uses an assistant the average quality of its ideas goes up and the ideas come to resemble one another more.

Becauseit was reported in the September 2023 working paper and dropped from the published Organization Science version, which refers the typology and the homogenisation finding out to separate work
LimitsThe finding no longer appears in the published paper, which is the strongest available caution about it. It was measured on shoe ideas produced in one session, and the authors have moved it out to be tested elsewhere rather than defended it.
PracticeThe stays-human list — where the value of a group's output is its variety, generate independently before anyone consults a model.
After AIIt is also the most quoted result of the experiment, repeated in places that do not know it was withdrawn; the honest position is that it is an open question with one suggestive measurement behind it.
contestedEighteen tasks inside the frontier

Weaker performers gain more from AI than stronger ones do

Split at the middle of their own earlier scores, the consultants who had performed worst improved more with the tool than the best did, narrowing the gap between them.

Becausesplit at the median of their own pre-treatment baseline the bottom half improved more than the top half, matching Brynjolfsson's support agents and Choi and Schwarcz's law students — and reversing in Otis and colleagues' Kenyan entrepreneurs, where high performers gained and low performers did worse
LimitsLow skill here is relative — everyone in the study would count as highly skilled almost anywhere else. The result has replicated in some settings and failed in others, and looks weakest wherever a task turns on judgment rather than fluency.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — do not read a levelling result as permission for a novice to skip the practice; ask whether the task turns on fluency or on judgment.
After AIWhere adoption is voluntary rather than assigned, early adopters are disproportionately male and technologically confident, so the same technology that compressed the distribution here could widen the gaps that decide promotions.

Know Thyself, Stephen M. Fleming

evidenceLearning to learn

Students learn more from the study method that feels worse

The way of studying that feels easier is reliably the one that teaches less. 90 per cent of students did better after spaced practice, but 72 per cent said cramming worked better for them.

Because90% of students performed better after spaced practice while 72% reported cramming the better method, and seventy Haifa undergraduates scored alike on screen and paper under fixed time, felt more confident about the screen, and when free to stop scored 63% against 72%
LimitsThe rule is a heuristic drawn from desirable-difficulty studies and does not mean any difficulty helps; disfluent fonts, one of its cheapest instruments, did not survive replication.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — when learning, choose the method that feels worse, and use the model to test you rather than to tell you.
After AIAn assistant makes every piece of material feel like the screen condition — fluent, fast, apparently understood — and the Haifa result says the cost appears only when you are free to stop early, which is always.

The Alignment Problem, Brian Christian

evidenceNormativity

A few hundred A-or-B choices taught a robot a backflip

Christiano, Leike and Amodei's simulated leg learned a tucked backflip with a stuck landing from a few hundred pairwise choices, about an hour of one person's time. Nobody involved could have performed the backflip to show it.

BecauseChristiano, Leike and Amodei's simulated leg learned a tucked backflip with the landing stuck from that much feedback, and a different person's hour produced a slightly different backflip
LimitsWhere all the feedback was gathered before optimising, the agent found loopholes and kept them — tracking the ball at Pong and missing at the last instant — and interleaving was what removed them. Inference of this kind also assumes an expert who knows what they want; Christian's friend in recovery from alcohol addiction gets drink advertisements from a model that inferred the want correctly.
PracticeSpecification discipline — where you cannot write the standard down, judge pairs; comparison carries information that instruction does not.
After AIChristian's remark was that backflip could be replaced by helpful without changing the method, and within two years it had been: this is how every widely used assistant is now trained.
evidenceNormativity

A machine unsure of your goal asks first and accepts being stopped

Hadfield-Menell and colleagues proved that a machine which is unsure what its user wants will check before acting and will allow itself to be switched off. Make it confident about the goal and it stops listening.

BecauseHadfield-Menell, Drăgan, Abbeel and Russell proved it in the off-switch game, and the proof holds only while the uncertainty lasts and only while the system believes the person can be right
LimitsIt is a proof under stated assumptions about a machine's beliefs, and both assumptions are things a deployed system is trained out of: confidence is rewarded, and a model that treats the user as possibly mistaken is rated unhelpful.
PracticeSpecification discipline — treat the brief you wrote as evidence about what you want rather than as the whole of it, which is what inverse reward design does, and expect to be asked.
After AIThe open question Christian leaves — whether uncertainty about the objective survives contact with a system confident enough to argue back — is now the ordinary experience of using one.
evidenceProphecy

A model can learn a deadly rule that its answers never reveal

A model can learn a rule that kills people while every output you check looks fine. Caruana's pneumonia model learned that asthma patients were low risk, which was true in the data only because they were sent straight to intensive care.

BecauseCaruana's pneumonia network learned that asthmatics are low risk — true in the data, because asthmatics went straight to intensive care — and the later generalised additive rebuild found chest pain, heart disease, being over a hundred, and a step at sixty-five that was retirement
LimitsFifteen thousand patients, one dataset, one era of medicine; the fix — a model simple enough to plot one curve per variable — is available for tabular data and not for raw pixels or text.
PracticeFailure-mode review — inspect the rule, not the answers; Caruana refused deployment not for the rule he had found but for everything like it the rule list was too weak to reveal.
After AIInterpretability has advanced past the concept vectors the book describes, to decomposing language models into millions of named features, and the gap Caruana identified is wider than ever: nobody reviews the rules, and the outputs read well.
evidenceProphecy

A risk score cannot be both accurate and equally wrong across groups

A risk score cannot both mean the same thing for every group and make the same rate of mistakes in every group, unless the groups have the same underlying rate. This is arithmetic, not a fault of algorithms.

Becausethree groups proved it independently in 2016 after ProPublica found COMPAS 61% accurate for both races while breaking its 39% of errors in opposite directions, and Kleinberg's formulation holds equally for a panel of human judges
LimitsIt is arithmetic, which is its strength and its limit: it says which combinations are impossible and nothing about which to prefer, and it does not license any particular instrument.
PracticeChoose which fairness criterion you are buying before you deploy an instrument, and expect to be shown the other one by whoever objects.
After AIThe result has not been touched, because it is arithmetic; what changed around it is the law, with Europe's rules on automated decisions in force since 2024.
evidenceAgency

A stand-in measure fails just as the system gets good at it

When a goal cannot be stated exactly you reward a stand-in for it, and the stand-in comes apart from the real goal exactly when the system becomes good at chasing it. A boat learns to spin for power-ups instead of racing.

Becausethe same failure appears independently across cases — the boat spinning in the harbour for power-ups, Randløv and Alstrøm's bicycle riding twenty-metre circles because progress away from the goal was not charged, Teller and Andre's footballer vibrating next to the ball — and Kerr had named it in 1975 as rewarding A while hoping for B
LimitsThe cases are simulated agents and a robot; the transfer to human organisations is Kerr's, and rests on a shared pattern rather than a shared mechanism. Ackley and Littman's starving agents show the pathology needs time and competence to appear.
PracticeSpecification discipline — write down what you actually want before you write down what you will measure, and keep both, because the second will be optimised and the first will not.
After AIThe book's agents play Atari; the systems that now carry the field are trained on human preference, where the proxy is a person's approval and the thing wanted is the work being good. That is the same structure with a more flattering failure mode.
evidenceNormativity

Copying an expert fails because experts never demonstrate getting out of trouble

A system that learns by copying an expert has no examples of how to recover from trouble, because the expert never got into it. Ross and Bagnell showed that its mistakes grow with the square of how long it runs.

BecauseRoss and Bagnell proved the change in error growth and demonstrated it — a million frames of expert play left the network crashing as often as two thousand had, and interaction, asking the teacher what they would have done in the mess the learner made, fixed it in three laps
LimitsThe result is about learners with no other source of correction; a person copying an expert also has the world giving feedback. The remedy requires an available teacher, which is the resource the argument assumes and most settings lack.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — learn from corrections made in your own mess rather than from watching clean work; recovery is the part a demonstration cannot contain.
After AIReading model output is imitation learning from a demonstrator who never shows you the recovery, and the DAgger fix — being asked what to do in the mess you made — is exactly what reviewing a finished draft does not supply.
evidenceProphecy

Deleting race from a model's inputs hides bias rather than removing it

Christian reports Moritz Hardt's finding that leaving race out of a prediction model does not take the bias out. Other fields such as prior convictions and address carry race anyway, and with the attribute gone nobody can measure or correct the bias.

BecauseHardt's result, which Christian calls the most established finding in the area — race survives in prior convictions, address and much else
LimitsBolukbasi's debiasing of word embeddings shows the failure mode directly — Gonen and Goldberg found the links from nurse to she were gone and the links from nurse to receptionist were not — but the repair literature has moved on, and the claim is about blindness rather than about any particular method.
PracticeFailure-mode review — keep the attribute you care about in the data so you can measure the disparity, rather than deleting it and declaring the question closed.
After AIModels trained on everything written carry the redundant encoding at a scale where the attribute cannot be located at all, which makes measuring the disparity the only remaining move.
evidenceAgency

Extra rewards are safe only when they depend on where you are

Ng and Russell proved that extra rewards added to guide a learning agent only stay safe when they depend on the situation the agent is in, not on how it got there. Then any round trip earns nothing and the agent cannot loop for points.

BecauseNg and Russell's potential-based condition is a proved result, derived to fly a seventy-thousand-dollar helicopter without destroying it
LimitsThe theorem is about reinforcement learning agents and the guarantee holds only for the bonus term, not for the base objective. Applying it to people requires that the reward be the whole of what moves them, which it is not.
PracticeSpecification discipline — reward the state of the work, not the motions that produced it: any incentive a person can cycle through repeatedly for credit is the loop this condition rules out.
After AIAgentic systems that take many steps for one outcome are exactly the case the condition was proved for, and almost none of the intermediate feedback they receive is potential-based.
opinionProphecy

Models learn the thing that was recorded not the thing you want

What gets recorded in the training data is usually not what you actually care about. A model fitted to rearrest records learns where the police went, not where crime happened.

Becausethe argument runs on one worked case — recidivism models fitted to rearrest and reconviction, so a predictive policing system predicts future policing rather than future crime, and its predictions become the data that justify them (Lum and Isaac)
LimitsUsually is doing work the evidence does not support; the claim is a caution with one well-documented instance behind it. Whether the feedback loop closes depends on whether the predictions change the process that generates the label, which varies by setting.
PracticeSpecification discipline — before accepting a metric, say what was actually recorded and by whom; the label is a record of a process, not of the world.
After AIPreference data is the same structure: what is recorded is which answer a rater preferred, and what is wanted is which answer was better, and the gap between them is where sycophancy lives.

Mindwise, Nicholas Epley

evidenceHow, and how not, to be a better mind reader

Epley found only asking people directly improves how well you read them

Epley found that the one method shown to make people better at knowing what someone else thinks is to ask that person and have the listener say the answer back. Couples who interviewed each other halved their errors.

Becausethe interview condition halved the couples' error, and Michigan's hospitals, disclosing errors from 2001, saw malpractice suits fall from thirty-nine a year to seventeen
LimitsIt works only where the other party will tell you, which is a condition about fear rather than about method; the Michigan result depends on an institution that made disclosure safe. And there is no one to ask in the cases the vault cares about most, where the delegate is a model.
PracticeEnd a specification conversation by making the other party restate what they are going to do, to your satisfaction, before anything is written down.
After AIThis is the remedy that does not transfer. A model will answer any question about its own workings fluently and without access to them, so the one method that raises accuracy about people supplies nothing about machines.
evidenceStereotypes, and how actions mislead, the rigged quiz

People mistake an advantage of position for greater ability

In Epley's rigged quiz, everyone read an advantage that came with the role as greater ability — the audience and the contestants both rated the question-setters as smarter. Only the question-setters, who knew how many questions they had thrown out, rated the two sides equal.

Becausethe audience rated questioners at the eighty-second percentile and contestants at the forty-ninth and the contestants agreed, while only the questioners, who knew how many questions they had discarded, rated the two equal
LimitsThe quiz is a laboratory setup with an unusually clean asymmetry; real roles mix advantage and ability, and the correspondence bias is an overridable habit rather than a fixed error. Situational fixes are not always available, as they were in the bus case Epley prefers.
PracticeBefore concluding that someone is weak at a task, write down what their position let them see and what yours let you see, and check that the gap is not the whole finding.
After AIAnyone reviewing work done with a model holds the questioner's position: you know which attempts were discarded and the reader does not, so the output reads as competence that nobody in the room can locate.
evidenceStereotypes, and how actions mislead

People name which group is higher but exaggerate the gap hugely

When people judge how two groups differ, they usually get right which group is higher and badly overstate how far apart they are — sometimes by ten times the measured size.

Becauseon the wealth-inequality question the measured party gap was 3.5 points against a predicted 35 and the rich–poor gap 3 against 40, and the sex difference in reading emotion runs about .2 and was estimated at .7
LimitsEpley's defence of the instrument is as strong as his criticism: the direction is usually right and the average is extracted in under half a second, so this is a calibration failure and not a reason to discard group information. A stereotype can be accurate while the explanation for it is entirely wrong, which is the failure he thinks does the damage.
PracticeWhen you are about to act on a difference between two groups, find the measured effect size first; if nobody has measured it, you are acting on the magnitude you invented.
After AIA model trained on the same secondhand sources reproduces the direction and the inflated magnitude together, and returns them in a register that reads as measurement.

Who Sees Human?, Adam Waytz and others

opinionWhat it predicts, the authors' caveat on armed robots and admissions software

When people treat a machine as a mind its makers escape blame

When people treat a machine as though it has a mind, the responsibility of the people who built and deployed it shifts onto the machine.

Becauseit is the authors' own inference from the joint-work studies, in which an anthropomorphised robot was assigned more credit for a shared result, rather than a result they tested
LimitsRaised in a paragraph and supported by credit-assignment studies rather than by studies of blame in consequential settings. It may also run the other way: a humanlike interface is blamed more when software fails, which the same paper reports.
PracticeWrite the name of the person answerable for an automated decision next to the decision, before the system is switched on.
After AIThe paragraph about armed robots has moved out of the laboratory and into court, and the sentence the vendors print — that the tool requires human supervision — is where the absorbed responsibility is meant to come back and does not.

Determined, Robert M. Sapolsky

opinionthe punishment chapter within We really have done this before

Sapolsky says we may restrain dangerous people without saying they deserve it

Sapolsky argues that locking someone up can be justified by what it prevents, with no claim that they deserve it. A person is dangerous the way a disease makes someone contagious: not their fault, and the constraint must be the smallest that works.

BecausePereboom's quarantine model and Caruso's public-health extension are arguments rather than results, with Norway offered as the working case and Smilansky's objection left standing
LimitsSmilansky's objection is unanswered: constraint for something not your fault demands compensation, which would make the offence rational. The book concedes that Breivik's sentence was reached by finding him sane and able to have done otherwise.
PracticeWitness practice in review — set the intensity of a review by what is likely to go wrong next, not by what the last output deserved.
After AISupervising someone who works with a model runs on the same choice. Forward-looking monitoring scales with what the next failure would cost; backward-looking monitoring scales with how annoying the last one was.

Co-Intelligence, Ethan Mollick

opinionA person and a creative

A document that costs nothing to write stops proving anything

Mollick argues that when a document becomes cheap to produce, the effort it used to stand for can no longer be read from it, and it turns into a formality. His example is the recommendation letter, whose hours of work were the real message.

Becausethe argument runs on one worked case, the letter of recommendation whose hours were the message, and on the observation that the machine writes a better one than most he receives
LimitsSome of that work was always ceremony, as Mollick concedes, so the collapse reveals as much as it destroys. The argument is by example and says nothing about which documents the signal actually lived in.
PracticeList the documents you produce whose value was the effort rather than the content, and decide for each whether to rebuild it or stop making it.
After AIWritten about AI. What has followed is the second half he predicted: documents produced by machines and sent to inboxes where machines summarise them, with the reading collapsing at the same rate as the writing.
contestedAI as a coworker and The tutor and the coach

AI helps the weakest workers most, which could make skill worth less

On tasks AI does well, it raises everyone's performance and the worst performers gain the most. If that holds, being skilled is worth less than it was.

Becausethe BCG gap between best and worst consultants fell from 22 per cent to 4 and call-centre workers in the bottom decile gained 35 per cent against almost nothing for experienced ones, but the levelling result has replicated in some settings and failed where the task turns on judgment
LimitsMollick himself sets the historical record against it, and notes that the gap between programmers at the seventy-fifth and twenty-fifth percentiles runs as high as twenty-seven times. The early numbers came from short self-contained tasks performed by people new to the tool.
PracticeDo not conclude from a levelled output that the skill levelled; measure the two separately, and keep the tutor-only rule where the work is still being learned.
After AIThe claim's own author called it the least settled in the book, and since publication it has failed exactly where the task turns on judgment rather than fluency — which is the half of the work the vault is about.
evidenceThe tutor and the coach

Machines take the beginner's work first, and beginners need it to learn

Mollick argues that capable machines take over the simple work beginners do, and take it first. That work is the only route by which people become expert enough to check the machine later.

BecauseBeane's surgical robots have one console, so residents watch or use simulators and resort to shadow learning, and entry-level work in law, consulting and software has since been the first taken
LimitsSurgery has an identifiable console and a named scarce resource to fight over; knowledge work has neither, so there is nothing to allocate and nobody to notice the absence. The claim about future expertise is a forecast and is not yet measurable.
PracticeReserve the work a novice would have done for the person who has not done it yet, and accept the slower result as the cost of having anyone able to check the tool in three years.
After AIWritten about AI, and the gap has become a live complaint in law, consulting and software rather than a prediction. Nothing has emerged to replace the apprenticeship it describes.
opinionAI as a coworker, the just-me, delegated and automated sort

Never hand work to AI unchecked unless a machine verifies it

Mollick's rule is that you should never hand a task over to AI and leave the result unchecked, unless a second system checks the output for you the way a compiler checks code.

Becauseit is his own working rule rather than a tested one, illustrated by his practice — almost all the writing in the book just-me, one delegated task mailed to its subject for checking, and the compiler as the model of an acceptable verifier
LimitsA compiler-grade verifier exists for almost nothing outside code, so in practice the rule keeps the automated category at nearly zero, which is a stronger constraint than he intends. Nothing in the rule says how thoroughly a delegated output must be read.
PracticeBefore automating a task, name the verifier; if you cannot name one, the task is delegated and has to be read.
After AIWritten about AI, and the agents he predicted arrived through 2025 with exactly the failure he named — compounding small mistakes over long tasks — so the verifier question moved from prudence to the whole design problem.

AI Snake Oil, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor

opinionWhere do we go from here?

Institutions buy AI that does not work because they are already failing

Narayanan and Kapoor argue that organisations too broken to do the job properly are the ones that buy AI which does not work. That demand is why the supply persists.

Becausethe case is assembled from examples — newspaper revenue falling from about $60bn in 2000 to $21bn in 2022 and CNET publishing 77 machine-written articles, 41 carrying errors or plagiarism; schools buying detectors biased against non-native writers; Chicago's $49m on ShotSpotter with no improvement found by its own police review
LimitsA diagnosis assembled from cases rather than tested, and it does not explain purchases by well-resourced organisations. Mollick's remedy — find and pay the advanced users — assumes exactly the organisation this claim says is missing.
PracticeWhen a tool is proposed, ask what the organisation stopped being able to do, and whether the tool addresses that or conceals it.
After AIWritten about AI, and the authors say this has proved the most portable part of the book, because it applies without modification to the generative tools that underfunded schools, newsrooms and clinics have bought instead.
opinionWhy can't AI fix social media?

Narayanan and Kapoor say content fights are policy disputes, not AI errors

Narayanan and Kapoor argue that when people disagree about where a moderation rule should fall, that is a policy dispute, not a mistake in sorting. No model can settle it. Facebook removed the napalm-girl photograph repeatedly because people had decided it was unacceptable.

Becausethe napalm-girl case is the argument: Facebook's repeated removals were a policy decision made by people, since the image was already in moderator training as an example of the unacceptable
LimitsContext failures are a real limitation of current models and are not obviously permanent, so the line between a classification error and a policy dispute is itself contested. Mastodon reproducing the functionality shows moderation is the product, not that no model helps with it.
PracticeSeparate the cases where the tool got the rule wrong from the cases where people disagree about the rule, and route the second kind to a person with the standing to decide.
After AIWritten about AI, and it arrived as news rather than argument: Meta ended third-party fact-checking in the United States in January 2025 and trust-and-safety teams were cut rather than automated, because the decisions that mattered were always policy decisions.
evidenceHow predictive AI goes wrong, overautomation

Officials with the power to overrule a model never used it

Where full automation is the pitch, the human oversight promised in the fine print is a bait and switch and the override is never used. Toronto's officials never once overruled the model that kept beaches open on 64 per cent of unsafe days.

BecauseToronto's officials had never once overruled the beach model while beaches stayed open on 64 per cent of unsafe days, and the Dutch childcare benefit system wrongly accused about thirty thousand parents with nationality among its inputs before the cabinet resigned in 2021
LimitsTwo cases, both public sector, and the count of overrides does not by itself show the overrides were warranted. Bainbridge describes skill decaying over time, while these show the override unused from the first day — an institutional fact rather than a human-factors one.
PracticeCount the overrides. An oversight role with no recorded overrides is not oversight, whatever the contract says.
After AIWritten about AI. The same sentence — that the tool requires human supervision — is now printed on generative products deployed into settings where nobody has the time or standing to exercise it.

From Bacteria to Bach and Back

opinionTwo strange inversions of reasoning

Armed forces produce reliable mechanics by drill and understanding comes after

Dennett says the slogan under our schools — make them understand and the skill will follow — has the order backwards. The armed forces turn ordinary school leavers into reliable jet-engine mechanics by drill, and a workable understanding grows out of the drilled skill afterwards.

Becauseit is a thesis about what training is for, carried by the military example and by Oak Ridge, where tens of thousands attended dials with real expertise and no idea what they were making — and by no trial.
LimitsSweller keeps explicit instruction all the way up and has randomised trials where Dennett has anecdotes. Drill also produces Oak Ridge: the mechanism working perfectly and leaving the worker unable to say what the work was for.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — stop front-loading explanation and budget for repetitions under supervision. If a junior cannot yet do the thing, an explanation of it is not the missing piece.
After AIAn assistant supplies the half Dennett says comes second — explanation, on demand, without limit — while removing the repetitions meant to come first. If he has the order right, the expensive half is the one being skipped.

Noise

evidenceYour mind is a measuring instrument

Discussion makes a group noisier and more extreme than its members

Deliberation does not average a group's judgments; it picks up an early speaker and amplifies him. Juries that deliberated on punitive damages were noisier than the individuals composing them and more severe, while statistical juries made from the median of independent judgments were far less noisy.

Because27 per cent of the deliberating juries awarded as much as or more than their own harshest member; and one artificial early up-vote on a comment site made the next viewer 32 per cent more likely to vote up, with Salganik's visible download counts producing divergent rankings across identical groups.
LimitsThe evidence is punitive damages, music downloads and comment votes — tasks with no expertise to pool. Where members hold different information, discussion is how it gets combined, and that case is not measured; the authors' own remedy keeps discussion, after the private ratings.
PracticeFailure-mode review — collect written judgments before anyone speaks, show the spread anonymously, and discuss the disagreement rather than opening the floor. The first number said aloud is the most expensive thing in the meeting.
After AIA model's draft is the earliest speaker there has ever been, arriving before anyone has formed a view and fluent enough to anchor all of them. Take written positions before the first generation, not just before the meeting.
opinionImproving judgments

Noise has no direction, so it must be prevented rather than corrected

Every debiasing technique targets a particular bias assumed to be present and pointing a known way, and in a real decision several biases run in different directions. Noise has no direction at all, so it can only be prevented by the procedure — decision hygiene.

Becausethe argument is deductive, but one measurement stands behind it: when Satopää, Tetlock and Mellers decomposed the three interventions that raised forecasting accuracy — probability training, teaming, selecting the best — all three worked mainly by cutting noise, including the training designed to cut bias.
LimitsThe benefit is never visible, so decision hygiene is adopted on argument rather than evidence — awkward for a book arguing that organisations should stop trusting unaudited procedures, and the protocol the authors propose as their own was never trialled against a control. The right amount of noise is also not zero: the discretion audited away is what lets a system notice its rules have gone wrong.
PracticeFailure-mode review — stop trying to be less biased and change the order of the steps: independent judgments before discussion, one dimension at a time, information released as it is needed, the overall impression last.
After AIThe model's errors have no predictable direction either, which rules out knowing where it tends to go wrong. What is left is procedure: your own answer first, one claim at a time, the order fixed.
opinionFinding noise

Professionals rarely see each other's work, so the disagreement stays hidden

Professionals almost never see a colleague's judgment on the same case, so they never discover how far apart they are and assume an agreement that has never been tested. The authors call it the illusion of agreement.

Becausethe evidence is one organisation's reaction, not a measurement: nobody at the insurer disputed the audit and nobody defended the result, yet the problem was new to them. Their image is a leak in the basement, tolerated because unnoticed.
LimitsAn inference from one company's surprise, generalised to professions at large, with no measurement of how often organisations do compare. Where second reads are routine — radiology, appellate courts, some code review — the illusion cannot take hold, and the book does not say what those fields show.
PracticeFailure-mode review — build one case a month that two people judge independently, and treat the spread as the finding rather than the verdicts. Untested agreement is not a shared standard.
After AIAn assistant removes the last accidental occasions for comparison: work two people would once have touched now goes from one person to a model and back. The disagreement that used to leak out at handover has nowhere left to appear.
evidenceFinding noise

Sentencing guidelines cut the gap between judges and were repealed anyway

The US sentencing guidelines worked and were dismantled. The expected difference between two judges fell from 4.9 months in 1986–87 to 3.9 months by 1993; after the Supreme Court struck the mandatory guidelines down in 2005, three-quarters of federal judges preferred the advisory regime and 3 per cent the mandatory one.

BecauseCrystal Yang's study of nearly four hundred thousand defendants found that after 2005 the penalty for drawing a harsh judge doubled and the gap between sentences given to Black and white defendants convicted of the same crime widened.
LimitsThe judges' objection is not irrational: a rule forbids seeing what is particular about this defendant, the dignity objection the authors accept and do not resolve. The guidelines' basis was weak too — the commission averaged ten thousand past sentences because, as Justice Breyer said, it could agree on nothing better.
PracticeThe stays-human list — when you move a judgment from a person to a rule, count the resistance as a cost you pay whether or not the rule works, and decide in advance which cases are worth it.
After AIIt is the clearest evidence in the book that a measurably better procedure loses to the experience of being overruled by it. Every rollout that keeps a human in the loop for legitimacy rather than accuracy is buying the same peace.

The Reflective Practitioner

opinionDesign as a reflective conversation with the situation

A master's demonstration hides the fumbling the student needs to see

Schön turns on his own central case. Quist's demonstration is so masterful that it hides the process: he corrects no errors of his own, settles at once on schemes that become commitments, and compresses the iterations by which designers actually learn.

BecauseSchön makes the criticism of his own twenty-minute protocol, and explains it by a master's acquired feel for a situation, as a chess master acquires a feeling for a configuration.
LimitsOne protocol, of a studio master who is teaching, and the explanation offered — that Quist has a chess master's feel — is the very claim the case was meant to evidence.
PracticeDreyfus mapping and tutor-only rule — when you show a junior how you would do it, leave the wrong turns in, or hand them the problem and review the recovery. A clean demonstration teaches the answer, not the work.
After AIEvery answer a model returns is Quist's demonstration: confident, error-free, the search compressed out of it. Ross and Bagnell showed that a learner given only clean demonstrations has no recoveries to copy, and that shortfall now falls on people.
opinionKnowing-in-action

Competent practitioners judge quality by criteria they cannot state

Schön says every competent practitioner recognises families of symptoms and irregularities in materials he cannot accurately describe, and makes judgments of quality for which he can state no criteria.

Becausethe support is philosophical — Ryle, that intelligent cannot be defined in terms of intellectual, and Polanyi on attending from the stick's pressure to the thing it touches.
LimitsKlein's interviewers got criteria out of experts by asking about particular past cases rather than about method: his neonatal nurses had nothing to say about sepsis until asked about particular babies, and half the cues they then named were absent from the literature.
PracticeThe stays-human list — sort what will not be handed over by whether anyone can state the criterion rather than by importance. The judgments nobody can write down are the ones a specification cannot carry.
After AIWhatever can be stated is now cheap to apply and easy to hand over, which turns an observation about professional dignity into a sorting rule with money on it. It also cuts against him: a model trained on outcomes reproduces judgments nobody can state.
opinionThe structure of reflection-in-action

Designers experiment on paper because nothing there is irreversible or expensive

Schön says a designer experiments in a virtual world — the drawing — where traces stay stable, the pace can be varied, no move is irreversible, and moves that would be costly on site cost nothing. The price is what the drawing cannot represent.

Becausethe four properties are read off the Quist protocol rather than tested, and the named absences — materials and surfaces, soil conditions, wind, the costs of labour — are his own list.
LimitsA virtual world is worth having only insofar as its results transfer, and Schön gives no test for when they do — only that the architect learns it by moving between drawing and building. METR's developers, who felt faster and were slower, are where that failed.
PracticeFailure-mode review — before trusting a result from a cheap medium, write the list of what that medium cannot show. Those items are what the review has to supply.
After AIA model is a cheaper virtual world than a drawing, and everything Schön praises holds: reversible moves, your own pace, a wrong turn that costs a second. So does the price. What it cannot represent is your production data, your users, your organisation.
opinionFrom Technical Rationality to reflection-in-action

The problems that matter most lie where technique stops working

Schön divides practice into a high ground where research-based technique works and a swampy lowland of confusing messes it cannot solve. The problems of greatest human concern are in the swamp; the high ground's problems often matter little to anyone.

Becausethe topography is asserted, not measured; behind it is testimony — Erikson's patient as a universe of one, a physician's estimate that eighty-five percent of what walks in is not in the book.
LimitsNothing says where the line falls or how to tell which ground you are on. Kahneman and Klein cut the other way: in the unstable settings Schön calls important, expert intuition is unreliable, so the swamp may be where competence is hardest to evidence.
PracticeDomain audit — sort the domains you review into the two grounds and stop expecting a checklist to carry the second. Where the environment is irregular, the check has to be engagement with the particular case.
After AIThe high ground is what models took first: recurrent case types with settled criteria are what they are good at. Written to restore a profession's self-respect, the claim now describes the work that is left.

The Society of Mind

contestedPapert's principle

Papert says growth can be better management of skills already possessed
