Money worries, the standing of the job and the rules of the workplace decide how much room a person has to reshape the work they do. So the chance to craft a job is not equally available, and not crafting says nothing about the person.

Becausethe authors state it as an explicit refusal of the implication their own model invites, in the closing limits
LimitsIt is the authors' stated position rather than a measured distribution, and their own closing claim about a shift toward free agency points the other way. Berg, Wrzesniewski and Dutton later found constraints of different kinds at high and low rank.
PracticeDo not read someone's failure to find meaning in their work as a fact about them until you have looked at what their job allows.
After AIThe advice to craft your way out is now given to people whose jobs are being restructured underneath them, and this is the paper's own objection to that advice, stated by the people who invented the idea.
evidenceSince 2001

The main job crafting questionnaire leaves out how people reframe work

Job crafting was originally three things, one of which was changing how you think about your work. The questionnaire most later studies use counts only behaviour, so that third of the idea goes unmeasured.

Becausethe Tims–Bakker–Derks 2012 scale counts four behaviours built from job demands and resources, none of them reframing, and that scale is what most later survey studies measure
LimitsThe instrument's omission is documented; whether it matters is not. Later work has tried to bring the cognitive boundary back, which suggests the field agrees it was lost but has not shown what was lost with it.
PracticeWhen you read that crafting predicts something, check which scale was used, and assume the reframing half was not measured.
After AIThe reframing half is the one that survives a tool doing the tasks, and it is the half the literature stopped measuring. Any finding about crafting and engagement is silent about exactly the move that is now most available.
opinionThe model

Workers reshape their jobs to gain control, self-respect and connection

Wrzesniewski and Dutton argue that people reshape their own jobs to meet three needs: control over the work, a good image of themselves, and connection to other people. Reshaping is strongest where one of those needs is going unmet.

Becausethe three needs are argued from Adler, Braverman, Rogers's temporary workers and Baumeister and Leary rather than tested against crafting behaviour
LimitsIt is a model assembled from adjacent literatures, not a test; the paper offers no measurement that crafting is strongest where a need is unmet, and self-determination theory supplies the evidence the model does without.
PracticeWhen you feel the urge to change how you work, identify which of the three needs is going unmet. The crafting will be aimed at that one whether you name it or not.
After AIAll three needs take a hit at once when the work is delegated — less control over how it is done, a worse story about one's own contribution, and fewer occasions to work with anyone. The model predicts the crafting that follows.

The Extended Mind, Andy Clark and David J. Chalmers

opinionActive externalism

A person and the tool they rely on work as one system

Clark and Chalmers argue that a person and a resource they lean on, such as a notebook, work as one system. Take the resource away and the person's ability drops, as it would if part of the brain were removed.

Becausethe argument is from the two-way interaction in the Tetris and notebook cases; the paper offers no measurement of the drop.
LimitsThe drop is asserted rather than measured here; Risko and Gilbert measure it and find the coupling costs the organism something the parity principle has no place to record.
PracticeName the resources whose removal would drop your competence, and decide which of those exposures you are willing to hold. The coupling is real whether or not you accept the philosophy.
After AIThe coupled system is now the working unit for most knowledge work, and the resource is one that can change under you overnight — a deprecated model, a rate limit, a policy. Clark and Chalmers treat the coupling as strength; the exposure is the same fact read forwards.
opinionSince 1998

An outside store you did not fill fails Clark and Chalmers' test

Clark and Chalmers said an outside store counts as part of your mind if it is always there, easy to reach, and you once accepted its contents. A store filled by other people meets the first two tests and fails the acceptance ones.

Becausethe asymmetry is between Otto's notebook, which holds what Otto put there, and any store he did not write; the paper foresees the difficulty for the Internet and does not develop it.
LimitsDeveloped here rather than in the paper, which spends one sentence on the Internet; whether the endorsement conditions are necessary at all is disputed, since the authors weaken the fourth themselves.
PracticeLog the moments you endorse something on retrieval that you never endorsed on entry. That is the whole difference between a notebook and an assistant, and it is invisible at the moment of use.
After AIOtto's notebook is the wrong picture for what people now do. The store answers in your idiom, was filled by nobody you can name, and produces the content fresh each time you look.
opinionBeyond the outer limits (Figure 23.4)

Clark and Chalmers give four tests for counting a notebook as memory

Clark and Chalmers say an outside store counts as part of your mind when four things hold: it is always with you, easy to reach, believed when you consult it, and filled by you. The case weakens as those drop away.

Becausethe list is the authors' own, with the fourth condition qualified by them on the spot and the case rested on the first three; the Filofax and the Internet are sorted by the list rather than by a rule.
LimitsA list of features with no weighting and a gradient with no scale; the authors offer it as a way of sorting cases rather than as a criterion, and the fourth condition they weaken themselves.
PracticeUse the four features as a specification for any resource you lean on: is it constant, available when needed, endorsed on retrieval, and endorsed before it went in? The last two are where an assistant fails, and naming that is the point of the list.
After AIRisko and Gilbert turned the first three features into measured variables. The fourth is the one the technology broke, and it is the one the authors were least sure of.
contestedSince 1998

Critics say a notebook is coupled to memory, not part of it

Critics of Clark and Chalmers argue that being tightly coupled to a notebook does not make the notebook part of your memory. A memory that includes notebooks also predicts less, because biological memory has well-established properties a notebook does not share.

BecauseAdams and Aizawa press the coupling-constitution objection and Rupert 2004 the cost to the science, while Sutton's reply — that external resources earn their place by being unlike biological memory — replaces parity with complementarity.
LimitsContested and unresolved: parity has never been abandoned by Clark, and the empirical literature has proceeded by measuring the coupling rather than by settling whether it constitutes.
PracticeAudit your resources by what they are unlike rather than by what they replace. A tool that fails differently from you is worth more than one that fails the same way, and that is the complementarity reading.
After AIComplementarity is the more useful frame for a model, which is unlike your memory in exactly the ways that matter — it does not forget, it does not know it is wrong, and it will produce a different answer to the same question tomorrow.
opinionFrom cognition to mind

Otto believes what his notebook says before he opens it

Clark and Chalmers argue that Otto, who has Alzheimer's and writes addresses in a notebook, already believes the museum is on 53rd Street before he looks it up — in the same way Inga believes it before she remembers it.

Becausethe case rests on parallel causal dynamics plus a parsimony argument — the alternative adds a belief about what the notebook says to every explanation in which the notebook figures, and in an explanation simplicity is power.
LimitsAn argument from parallel dynamics and parsimony, not evidence; the contemplative traditions in this vault take the opposite view, that what can be observed as an object is not the self that observes.
PracticeIn review, notice the moment a retrieved fact becomes one of your own beliefs. The transition is where the checking has to happen, because after it the belief will not present itself as retrieved.
After AIWhat an assistant supplies becomes yours in the same quiet way, and without the notebook's one safeguard — that Otto wrote it. The parity holds while the provenance does not.
opinionExtended cognition (the parity principle)

Where a process happens cannot decide whether it counts as thinking

Clark and Chalmers propose a test: if part of the world does a job we would call thinking had it happened in the head, it is part of the thinking. Where it happens is not allowed to count against it.

Becausethe parity principle is stated as a consistency test and defended by the three-screen case — mental rotation, rotation by a button, rotation by a neural implant — rather than by any measurement.
LimitsA consistency test, not a finding: Adams and Aizawa reply that the argument slides from coupling to constitution, and Rupert that a wider notion of memory predicts less.
PracticeWrite down what stays human by what it does rather than by where it happens. If the boundary you are defending is only that a thing happens inside your head, this principle says you have not named a reason.
After AIThe principle was designed to make the inside of a process irrelevant, which is what makes it unhelpful for deciding what to delegate. It says the model may count as part of your thinking; not what that costs.

Timeless Leadership, Debashis Chatterjee

opinionThe fighter and the warrior (sutra 1; figure 27.1)

Chatterjee says a leader collapses under pressure from ego, not missing facts

Chatterjee argues that when a leader falls apart under pressure, what has failed is the picture they hold of themselves, not the information they have. The first work to be done is therefore inward.

Becausea reading of Arjuna's dry mouth and slipping bow as an ego collapse, supported by cases and by nothing that could count against it.
LimitsAs stated it is not falsifiable: any collapse reads as ego and any recovery as inner work. Shankara reads the same collapse as ignorance of the Self, so the remedy on his reading is knowledge and not work on a self.
PracticeWhen performance drops under pressure, stop looking for the missing fact and look at what is being defended. Sitting practice is the part that can be done before the collapse.
After AIThe collapse now has a new trigger: being outperformed at the thing one is known for. The information story is tempting, because the obvious remedy is to learn the tool, and the claim is that learning it will not touch this.
opinionPower, undoing and the mind (sutra 5; the driver and the car; the Dalai Lama's exercise)

Chatterjee says letting go of being the doer can be trained

Chatterjee holds that the sense of being the one who acts can be loosened by regular reflection. The sign of success is not working less hard but treating people you like, dislike and feel nothing for the same way.

Becausea practice with a stated test attached, and no evidence that people who do it pass it.
LimitsShankara denies that detachment from doer-ship is trainable in this sense at all: on his reading it is the removal of a false belief by knowledge, and the man who has it has no work left, so the engagement half of detached engagement is what he refuses.
PracticeJudge the training by whether regard has levelled across people you like, dislike and do not care about, not by whether you feel calmer. Witness practice in review is where the check happens.
After AIWhen the work is done by an agent, doer-ship loses the support of evident authorship, so what Chatterjee asks be trained arrives unasked. The test still applies, because the sign is equality of regard and not the absence of effort.
opinionThe fighter and the warrior (sutra 2; figure 27.2)

Krishna replaces Arjuna's way of seeing instead of arguing with him

Chatterjee reads Krishna as changing Arjuna's filter rather than the facts. A view of the battlefield set by grief, pity and shame has to be replaced with another way of seeing; arguing against it does not work.

Becausea reading of Krishna's method — he substitutes a model rather than rebutting one — with no comparison against argument.
LimitsSeveral of Chatterjee's verse renderings insert the vocabulary of his argument into lines that do not carry it, and alternative reality is one of them. The affirmation literature agrees that argument fails against a defended model but puts the remedy outside the threatened domain rather than in a substituted model.
PracticeWhen someone will not hear the evidence, change what the situation means to them before producing more of it. Witness practice in review trains the same move on oneself, in the moment the feeling arrives.
After AIThe model most in need of replacing is the one in which authorship is the measure of the work. Arguing about what a machine can and cannot do leaves it exactly where it was.

The What and Why of Goal Pursuits, Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan

evidenceWhy and what (what thwarting does, figure 28.5)

Blocked psychological needs produce substitutes not harder effort

Hunger makes you try harder to eat. Ryan and Deci argue that blocked needs for competence, belonging and choice do not work that way: people take up substitute goals and rigid habits that keep the need blocked.

Becauseteenagers whose mothers were rated cold and controlling by themselves, by the mothers and by clinical interviewers placed more relative importance on wealth, and a risk index taken when the children were four predicted that emphasis twelve years later.
LimitsThe readings of anorexia and of self-defeating behaviour as accommodation are interpretation laid over other researchers' data, and the strongest version of the claim rests on one longitudinal study.
PracticeDo not read a person's compensating ambition as motivation; read it as a report about what the job stopped supplying.
After AIAn engineer whose competence need is thwarted by delegation will not ask for the work back. The theory predicts a substitute — a title, headcount, throughput — that leaves the need exactly where it was.
evidenceWhy and what (the aspiration studies)

People who chase money, fame and looks report lower well-being

Ryan and Deci report that people who rate wealth, fame and looking good as important relative to other goals score lower on well-being. This holds whatever their reasons for wanting those things.

Becausehigh relative importance of financial success predicted lower self-actualisation and vitality and more anxiety and depression in college and in clinically interviewed community samples, replicated in Russia and Germany, and Carver and Baird's challenge that only the why matters was answered with the reasons controlled for.
LimitsThe measure is the relative importance of a goal rather than the goal itself, the outcomes are self-reported well-being, and the causal direction rests on one longitudinal risk index.
PracticeWatch what a goal is made of and not only why it is held; reasons can be repaired and the content of the aspiration has to be changed.
After AIWhat the tool most obviously buys is more output per person, which is a wealth-and-image aspiration. This finding says that attaining it does not move the thing people expect it to move.

The Psychology of Change, Geoffrey L. Cohen and David K. Sherman

opinionWhy a brief effect can last (the cycle of adaptive potential, figure 29.3; the hockey birthday parable)

A short exercise lasts only when it sets off a feedback loop

Cohen and Sherman argue a brief exercise has lasting effects only when it starts a loop: the person does better, other people treat them better, and they read the next setback differently. A second year of booster sessions added nothing.

Becausethe loop is an explanation offered after the fact, consistent with the null from the second year's boosters but not tested against an alternative.
LimitsRecursion, interaction and construal name propagation rather than measure it, and the same account would explain a null as a system that failed to react.
PracticePlace a small intervention where the system will react to its first result, and stop repeating it once the loop is running; repetition is not what carried the original effect.
After AIThe loop runs in both directions. An engineer who reads one delegated success as evidence of his own competence takes on harder work; one who reads it as evidence of his redundancy takes on less. The tool supplies the same first outcome either way.
evidenceWhen it works and when it does not (timing, figure 29.5)

Affirmation works before a threat, not after you have explained it away

Cohen and Sherman find that writing about your values before a threat, or soon after it, lowers defensiveness, while the same exercise given after the person has already talked themselves round has no effect.

Becausethe laboratory timing manipulation and the school-year comparison point the same way, and the second is a field test of the first.
LimitsThe school comparison is between weeks of a term rather than a randomised timing manipulation, and having rationalised is observed only through the failure of the affirmation.
PracticePut whatever is meant to change how a person reads an output before they open it. Cognitive forcing is that rule in its strongest form: write your own answer first.
After AIBy the time a person has explained to themselves why the model is wrong, the intervention that would have helped does nothing. The window is before the output is opened, which is also when nobody thinks they need it.
evidenceWhen it works and when it does not (the boundary conditions, figure 29.6)

Affirming your values helps only where a threat and a resource exist

Cohen and Sherman find that writing about your own values only helps when there is a real threat and some ability or knowledge waiting to be used. Without both, it does nothing, and it can make people more closed-minded than before.

Becausethe reversal is demonstrated rather than inferred — people whose identity as open-minded negotiators had been made salient became more closed-minded when affirmed — and the decade since has reframed the intervention as a seed that depends on the soil.
LimitsThe absence of a resource is identified after a null result, which makes the condition hard to apply in advance, and the review concedes the intervention is indirect and does not address the problem itself.
PracticeBefore installing anything meant to make review calmer, check that there is both a real threat and something to release — a skill, a checklist, evidence the person can act on. Witness practice in review assumes the review is still happening.
After AIA reviewer whose defences have been quieted still needs something to review with. Where the failure-mode knowledge is missing, the affirmation releases nothing and the output goes through anyway.
evidenceThe self under threat, and How it works (the exercise, figure 29.2)

People defend being a good person in general, not good at something

What the defences protect is a broad sense of being a good and capable person, not being good at any one thing. That is why writing about a value from an unrelated part of your life calms a threat to the part under attack.

Becausethe standard exercise removes values in the threatened domain from the list and still works, while affirming inside the threatened domain raises defensiveness instead.
LimitsThe essays are self-generated, so what did the work in any given case is unknown, and the review's own boundary conditions say values of power, status and approval do not serve.
PracticeWhen someone is about to hear something hard about their work, do not reassure them about their work. Give the ten minutes to something else they are, and then deliver the evidence.
After AIThe reflex answer to the machine is to defend one's competence at the thing the machine did. The evidence says that is the move that increases the defensiveness rather than the one that removes it.
evidenceThe self under threat (figure 29.1)

People defend themselves rather than learn when their identity is threatened

When something threatens a part of the self a person values, the first response is defence: denial, excuses, blaming others. It protects the person's sense of adequacy now and blocks learning later.

Becausethe pattern is produced at will across unrelated domains — people rationalise a trivial choice between two records, partisans reflexively refute contrary evidence, fans eat worse after their team loses — and the affirmation manipulation reverses it in randomised trials.
LimitsSeveral laboratory results the review leans on, including the neural error signal and some health outcomes, have come back smaller or absent in larger replications. The theory of threat has held better than any single effect size.
PracticeTreat the first response to unwelcome evidence as defence rather than as judgement, in yourself first. Witness practice in review is that noticing made into a habit with a log.
After AIA machine that does the work better is a threat of exactly this kind, and the response the literature predicts first is not learning but an account of why the comparison does not count.
evidenceWhen it works and when it does not; and the British medical-student study in Education

Telling people what the writing exercise is for removes its effect

The values-writing exercise loses its force when people are told what it is for, unless they are also given a choice about doing it. British medical students showed no benefit because instructors read and graded their essays.

Becausethe disclosure finding is a direct manipulation, and the medical-student null is explained by the same mechanism — instructors read and graded the essays, making the exercise evaluative and public.
LimitsThis is what makes the intervention hardest to deploy honestly at scale, and the choice qualification rests on a smaller literature than the disclosure effect itself.
PracticeIf a practice has to be announced, make participation a real choice; announced and compulsory is the combination that does nothing.
After AIAny instrument installed to make a team review a model's output more carefully stops working the moment it is introduced as such, unless people are given a genuine choice about using it.
contestedEducation (the three middle schools; figure 29.4)

Ten minutes writing about a personal value lifts threatened students' later grades

Ten minutes spent writing about something you personally value, done just before or soon after a threat to your standing, raises later performance in that area — but only for the people the threat hits hardest.

Becausethe original field trials were randomised and large — the share of African American students earning a D or F in the first term halved, and the effect persisted two years — but district-scale replications since have been smaller, more variable and present in some sites only.
LimitsThe effect is concentrated in the most threatened subgroup and absent where there is no identity threat, and one British medical-school study found mixed effects, attributed to instructors grading the essays.
PracticeIf you try it, try it early on the people whose identity the work threatens, and measure whether anything moved. Witness practice in review is the version that needs no trial to run.
After AIThe most threatened population in an engineering team is the one whose identity rests on writing the code. Whether the intervention survives outside the schools where it was found is the open question, and often it has not.
opinionWhen it works and when it does not

Writing about compassion lowers defensiveness; writing about status does not

Cohen and Sherman report that writing about values that reach beyond yourself — compassion, service, being loved — makes people less defensive about bad news. Writing about power, status or being approved of does not.

Becausethe comparison is assembled across studies in the review rather than run as a designed contrast, alongside the finding that affirming within the threatened domain raises defensiveness.
LimitsValues are self-selected, so the comparison is between people who chose differently rather than between conditions. The aspiration literature in self-determination theory makes the same distinction on stronger evidence.
PracticeWhere worth is being rebuilt, rebuild it on something that is not a ranking. Witness practice in review keeps the attention on the act rather than on the standing it earns.
After AIThe values most available to an engineer under threat are the ones the review says do not work — being the best at this, being the one who is asked. The ones that do work are not about the work at all.

The Gita with Shankara's Commentary, Śaṅkarācārya, translated by Swami Gambhirananda

opinionWhere the commentary begins, and The two steadfastnesses (2.39 and 3.3 read together; figure 32.3)

Shankara holds that knowledge and action cannot be combined in one person

Shankara holds that the path of knowledge and the path of action cannot be combined, because each rests on a conviction that contradicts the other — that one is an agent, and that one is not — and no person can hold both.

Becausefour arguments from the shape of the dialogue, including that Arjuna's protest at 3.1 would be an accusation about something never said, and the patient asking which of two things to take when the physician prescribed food that is both.
LimitsThey are good arguments about a text and not evidence about people. The position Shankara spent nine pages demolishing was held again by readers who had his refutation in front of them, and Tilak and Gandhi reversed the conclusion outright.
PracticeDo not expect one stance to cover both directing work and understanding that the work is not yours; notice which of the two you are in when you act.
After AIThe split maps badly onto a person who both directs an agent and knows the output is not his doing. On this reading that person is two people, and most working lives require him to be one.
opinionThe field and its knower (under 13.2; figure 32.8)

Shankara puts pleasure and pain among the things seen, not the seer

Shankara holds that pleasure, pain, confusion and desire belong to what is observed, not to the self that observes. No rule separates the states one would keep for the self from ones like old age and death.

Becausean argument by challenge: a sufferer is superimposed on the knower as a man is on a stump seen in the dark, and since no principle sorts which properties cross over, they stand or fall together.
LimitsDamasio's evidence makes feeling constitutive of judgement rather than an object of it, so a reader who takes the neuroscience seriously gets a knower not cleanly separable from the field.
PracticeWhen a state arrives in a review, put it on the side of what is known rather than who is knowing, and carry on. Witness practice in review is that move with a log attached.
After AIThe sorting problem reappears whenever someone says a model has the useful states and not the costly ones. Shankara's challenge — name the principle — is the one to put to that claim.
opinionRenunciation and relinquishment (18.11 handled as praise; 2.31 to 2.38 marked off as an argument offered by the way; 18.9's third item as praise by resemblance)

Shankara reads each verse for its purpose before its plain words

Shankara holds that a line of scripture must be read for the job it is doing, not only for what it states. A line written to praise a lesser practice cannot be used to abolish the greater one.

Becausean interpretive principle applied consistently throughout, which is also what makes it unfalsifiable, since any verse against the thesis can be reclassified as praise.
LimitsThe principle cuts both ways, and it is the tool by which later readers left behind the part of the commentary Shankara thought least controversial, the duties distributed by birth.
PracticeAsk what a sentence is for before arguing with what it asserts — in a specification, a review comment or a scripture.
After AIThe same discipline applies to a model's output, which is written to satisfy a request rather than to state a position. Asking what a sentence is doing is the check that catches the fluent paragraph with nothing behind it.
opinionThe two steadfastnesses (3.4, the polished mirror) and Action in inaction (4.33, the sacrifice that originates nothing); the ladder, figure 32.5

Shankara says action prepares the mind but cannot bring liberation

Shankara holds that action cleans the mind and so makes a person ready for knowledge, but it can never produce liberation, because liberation is not something made and no action can manufacture a state that is eternal.

Becausea metaphysical argument rather than an observation: what is eternal is not made, so a discipline that makes things cannot deliver it.
LimitsIt turns on a premise — that liberation is not produced — which Ramanuja and Madhva denied. The ladder also makes the lower rung indispensable in practice while denying it any share in the result.
PracticeKeep the practice that makes you fit for the thing and stop expecting it to be the thing. Sitting practice is on the fitness side of that line by its own account.
After AIThe distinction between a means that reaches a goal and a means that only makes one fit for it is precisely what a person needs when deciding which practices to keep after the tool has taken the output.
opinionRenunciation and relinquishment (the answer at 18.50)

Shankara says knowing the Self uncovers it rather than grasping it

Shankara answers the objection that a formless Self cannot be known: nothing has to be grasped, and all that is undertaken is removing what ignorance has laid over it. This is why the nearest thing of all comes to look remote.

Becausean answer to a genuine objection — knowledge takes the form of its object, so a formless Self cannot be known — which works by denying the premise, and is the best philosophy in the commentary.
LimitsShankara concedes the objection is quite true for men who have not sat with a line of teachers and heard the Upanishads, which puts the verification of the claim inside the tradition that asserts it.
PracticeStop treating the enquiry as the acquisition of a further thing to hold, and spend the time removing what is laid over it. Sitting practice is the whole of the instruction in practice.
After AINothing in the claim is about acquiring information, which is the only thing the tool supplies. On this reading, any amount of reading about the Self moves the matter not at all.
opinionWhere the commentary begins (2.21 and 2.69); conceded to the objector at 13.31; the sorting rule, figure 32.6

Shankara says only those who do not yet know have duties

On Shankara's reading, rites and duties are laid down only for people who have not yet realised the self. Once a person knows, there is no duty left for him to perform.

Becausean inference from the reason the verse gives — immutability — extended from killing to action of every kind, and conceded at 13.31 as a consequence rather than demonstrated.
LimitsThis is the proposition the later tradition reversed. Shankara keeps the lower rung — rites purify and are not optional for the man who needs them — so the claim bites only at the top of a ladder almost nobody claims to have climbed.
PracticeAsk what a rule is for before deciding whether it applies to you, and assume it applies; the exemption in this system is not something one awards oneself.
After AIThe sorting rule survives the change of subject: what a person may stop doing depends on what he knows, not on what a tool can do for him.
opinionWhere the commentary begins (the diagnosis planted at 2.10); the purpose stated in the commentary's third paragraph

Shankara says sorrow comes from one false belief about what is mine

Shankara says all sorrow and confusion grow from a single false belief — I belong to these people and things, and they belong to me — and that nothing removes it except knowing the Self.

Becausea diagnosis stated as the commentary's purpose and defended by argument from the text, with nothing offered that could count against it.
LimitsLater commentators accept the diagnosis and reject the exclusivity of the remedy, and the claim that nothing else removes sorrow is not something the poem says in those words.
PracticeLook for the possessive in the complaint — my work, my team, my reputation — and treat that rather than the circumstance as what is producing the distress. Sitting practice is the only part of this that is not talk.
After AIThe belief the commentary names is exactly what a delegated profession puts under strain: this work is mine, I belong to it. The diagnosis is nine centuries older than the technology that makes it acute.
opinionAction in inaction (Shankara's reverse case under 4.18; figure 32.7)

We feel like a doer even when we are doing nothing

The feeling of being the one who acts is laid over stillness just as readily as over action. "I am sitting quietly, doing nothing, and I am happy about it" is a sentence with a doer in it.

Becausean observation about how ordinary perception goes wrong, argued by analogy — the still trees running backwards from a moving boat, something far off that looks fixed — and not tested.
LimitsIt is the sharpest thing in the commentary and the least load-bearing: nothing else in the reading depends on it, and nothing tests it but one's own attention.
PracticeCheck the stance you take after stepping back from the work, not only the one you took while doing it. Witness practice in review is where the second kind shows up, as relief or as superiority.
After AII have stopped writing this and I am above it now is the reverse superimposition exactly. Withdrawal from the work is not detachment from doer-ship, and the commentary names the confusion nine centuries early.

The Upanishads, translated by Eknath Easwaran

opinionIsha: the inner ruler — Isha 1–2

The Isha Upanishad tells you to enjoy what you do not own

The Isha Upanishad's first two verses deny that anything is yours and in the same breath tell you to enjoy it. They then prescribe a hundred years of work, on the ground that work done this way leaves nothing clinging.

BecauseIsha 1–2 puts the two together — Gandhi reduced the first verse to two words, renounce and enjoy — and names a hundred years of work as the condition; it is a prescription, with the claim about residue unfalsifiable as stated.
LimitsNo measurement, and no account of what a residue would look like if it were there. Job crafting reaches a comparable result from the other direction by changing the job's boundaries and meaning rather than the person's claim on the result.
PracticeWitness practice in review — do the whole of the work and drop the claim on what it produces; the two are separable and only the second is optional.
After AIAn assistant makes the output cheap, which makes ownership of the output a stranger thing to insist on. The sentence reads now as an instruction about what to hold on to when the product stops being a good measure of the work.
opinionKatha: death as teacher — Katha 4.1

The Katha Upanishad asks the reader to turn the eye back

The Katha Upanishad says the sense organs open outward, so attention goes outward by itself. The one thing the collection asks a reader to do is turn the eye back on itself.

BecauseKatha 4.1 gives *avritta-chakshus*, the eye turned back, as anatomy used as an argument; it is an instruction with no way to check the result from outside.
LimitsAn anatomical observation made to carry a metaphysical conclusion. The direction of the sense organs explains a default of attention and not the existence of anything found by reversing it.
PracticeWitness practice in review — during a review, take one deliberate look at who is reviewing rather than only at what is under review.
After AIThe default runs harder now, because the outward opening answers back. An assistant supplies an endless outside to attend to, and the turning back has to be scheduled.
opinionKatha: death as teacher — Katha 2.1–2.2

The Katha Upanishad judges a person by what they prefer, not do

The Katha Upanishad says that at every moment two things present themselves: what is good for you and what you are fond of. What tells one person from another is which of the two they prefer, not what they end up doing.

BecauseKatha 2.1–2.2 sets *shreya* against *preya* as a standing pair rather than an occasional dilemma, and Nagler's gloss has the choice faced waking and even sleeping; it is a claim about the structure of motivation, offered without evidence.
LimitsSelf-determination theory reads the same data the other way: what a person is drawn to is evidence about which needs are being met, not a verdict on the person. The text offers no way to tell an act done from *shreya* from the same act done from *preya*.
PracticeWitness practice in review — when you notice you have reached for the easier route, record the preference rather than the action; the action is often the same either way.
After AIDelegation makes the two indistinguishable from outside. Using the assistant because it is the right tool and using it because it is the easy one produce identical commits, which leaves the preference as the only thing to watch.
opinionKatha: death as teacher — Katha 3.10 and 3.13

The Katha Upanishad ranks the mind above the senses and their objects

The world you meet is shaped by the equipment you meet it with. The Katha Upanishad puts sense objects above the senses and the mind above both, as a ladder to be climbed.

BecauseKatha 3.10 and the ladder of 3.13 state the order as a hierarchy to be climbed, in the order Nagler insists the text actually gives; the ranking is asserted, not argued.
LimitsA ladder with a top, offered as a route rather than a mechanism. Kahneman's version of the same observation is a process to be corrected from outside by a rule; the Katha's is a climb to be made from inside, and nothing in the text says how to tell progress from imagination.
PracticeProjection log — when something in a system looks obvious, record what equipment made it look that way before acting on the appearance.
After AIThe equipment now includes a model whose processing nobody can inspect. The ladder gains a rung the text does not have: what is encountered has been shaped by a system that is neither the senses nor the mind.
opinionKena: by whom? — Kena 3–4

The Kena Upanishad says what you can worship is not the reality

The Kena Upanishad says that once you can set something up in front of you and worship it, that thing is not the reality being pointed at. It also says no power a faculty uses, such as fire's burning, belongs to the faculty itself.

Becausethe second half of each Kena refrain is "not this that people worship here", and in the parable of Kena 3–4 fire cannot burn a straw and wind cannot move it, while the ranking inverts the order of the story so that the tested gods come out above the untested.
LimitsThe parable is a teaching story and the refrain is a liturgical formula; neither is an argument that could fail. Its usable half is the psychological one about projection, which is where the evidence in this vault sits.
PracticeProjection log — record what you have set up as the thing that really knows, and notice that the setting-up was yours.
After AIThe god who came nearest was the one who went to find out whose power it was. That is the posture the vault asks for towards a model: not deciding what it is, and not deciding it is nothing either.
opinionMandukya: consciousness and its phases

The Mandukya's fourth is what waking, dream and sleep are made of

The fourth is not another state alongside waking, dreaming and deep sleep. It is what those three are made of, and the text can point at it only by saying what it is not.

Becausethe Mandukya's twelve sentences close six ways of knowing and six handles in the seventh before *shanta*, *shiva*, *advaita* arrive, and Nagler is explicit that the ordinal records only the order of arrival.
LimitsA claim marked only by denials cannot be failed by any observation. Metzinger's account explains the same impression as a feature of a self-model whose construction is invisible to it.
PracticeSitting practice — sit long enough to notice that the states change and something does not, and stop short of deciding what that something is.
After AIIt is the one claim in this vault that no measurement can reach, which is why it belongs on the far side of any argument that starts from evidence. A model that reports states has states of a system; nothing here reaches the question of what they are made of.
contestedThe supreme science, and Since about 700 BC

The Upanishads offer a procedure to run, not a doctrine to believe

The Upanishads describe a repeatable procedure for turning attention on the mind itself. They offer no way for anyone who has not carried it out to check the result from outside.

BecauseEaswaran frames *brahmavidya* as a science with the mind as both instrument and specimen, and admits that the strata, the fourth, and the sameness of the observer in everyone are claims about what is found rather than what is inferred.
LimitsAn instrument that is also the specimen cannot be checked against itself, which is the objection Thompson presses. What has proved portable is the psychology of attention — that concentration can be trained and that trained concentration changes what is available to observation — and not the cosmology that follows it.
PracticeSitting practice — carry out the instruction and report what happens, and do not offer the report as evidence to anyone who has not.
After AIThe vault's method is the opposite one: a number, a date and a score. This claim marks the boundary where that method stops, and the honest thing is to leave the boundary visible rather than to dress the texts in evidence they do not have.
opinionKena: by whom? — Kena 1.3–1.4

Whoever is doing the knowing cannot be found among things known

The one doing the knowing can never be found among the things known. Looking at something only moves it from the unknown pile to the known one, and the knower is in neither pile.

BecauseKena 1.3–1.4 and the five-fold refrain disqualify speech, mind, eye, ear and breath in turn — every channel by which anything is known, enumerated and then ruled out.
LimitsAn enumeration is only as good as its list, and the argument works by exhausting the channels the text names. Hofstadter and Seth both take the opposite route, treating the self as something a system builds out of what it can observe.
PracticeWitness practice in review — stop trying to inspect the reviewer as one more object in the review; notice instead that the inspecting is happening.
After AITetlock's answer is the direct challenge: the forecaster can be made an object after all, by a Brier score and a benchmark. Both cannot be right about the same thing, which is why this pairing is worth holding open.

Dṛg‑Dṛśya‑Viveka, Vidyāraṇya or Bhāratī Tīrtha

opinionVerses 1 to 5: the regress of seers — verse 4

Anyone who denies the witness is using it to deny it

Not being seen does not mean not being known. The text says the witness is known in every act of knowing, and someone who denies it has to use it in order to deny it.

Becauseverse 4 puts doubt and faithlessness on the list of what consciousness lights up, and Shankara's line is that the denier is himself what he denies — the lecture's comparison is saying out loud that you have no tongue.
LimitsA performative argument: it shows that denial is awkward to state, not that the thing denied exists. Metzinger and Seth both grant the phenomenology and explain it as a property of a self-model rather than of a witness.
PracticeWitness practice in review — stop looking for the observer and check instead whether anything has ever been known without one.
After AIIt is the oldest form of the argument now being run about machines: that a system reporting its states is using something to report them. The text's move works on oneself and does not transfer to a third party, which is exactly why it says nothing about the model.
opinionVerses 1 to 5: the regress of seers — verse 1

Anything you can see is not the one seeing

Verse 1 of the Drig-Drishya Viveka says that whatever can be seen is not the seer: the eye sees form, the mind sees the eye, the witness sees the mind, and nothing sees the witness.

Becauseverse 1 runs in four quarters — form seen by the eye, the eye by the mind, the mind's movements by the witness, the witness by nothing — and *dṛg eva na tu dṛśyate* is asserted rather than shown; the regress is an argument, its terminus is a claim.
LimitsA regress that stops where the text needs it to stop. Hofstadter's account has the self as a loop the system builds out of its own observations, with no terminus required, and Seth's has it as a controlled hallucination; neither needs an unseen seer.
PracticeWitness practice in review — in a review, notice the movement of the mind judging the work as one more thing appearing, rather than as the one doing the judging.
After AINothing in the claim is affected by what the delegate is. Its use is procedural: it is the move that lets a reviewer notice defensiveness as an appearance instead of acting on it.
opinionVerses 22 to 31: six meditations and what they end in — verses 22 to 29

Drig-Drishya Viveka's meditations point back to whatever is having the experience

The practice here is not concentrating on an object, and not watching thoughts come and go. It takes an experience and uses it to notice what is having that experience.

Becauseverses 22 to 29 give six meditations as two runs of the same three steps — a thought or object, then a sentence, then neither — with the warning that a means held onto becomes an obstacle.
LimitsThe distinction from mindfulness is doctrinal and the text offers no way to tell from outside which practice someone is doing. The warning about means becoming obstacles applies to the six meditations themselves.
PracticeWitness practice in review — use whatever is actually happening in the review, including the irritation, as the object; there is nothing to clear away first.
After AIIt requires no quiet room and no setup, which is the only reason it survives contact with a working day. The object is supplied by the work, including the work a model did.
opinionVerses 22 to 31: six meditations and what they end in

Enlightenment does not stop pain, it changes who is watching it

Drig-Drishya Viveka says enlightenment is not a painkiller: the pain goes on exactly as before. What changes is that the person knows themselves as the witness of a body in pain rather than as the body.

BecauseRamakrishna with throat cancer asked for a moment to lift his mind from the body and then lay smiling while the wound was cleaned, and the monk who quoted Vedanta before surgery shouted like anyone else during it; both are teaching anecdotes.
LimitsAnecdote in both directions, and the second anecdote is the text's own admission that assent and realisation come apart. ACT measures the same separation by outcome; this offers no measure.
PracticeWitness practice in review — do not expect the sting of criticism to stop; expect only that acting on it becomes optional.
After AIIt sets the right expectation for the practice this vault runs. Nothing about working with a model removes the reaction to having one's work found wanting; the claim is only that the reaction need not be the reviewer.
opinionMethod, not conclusion

Sarvapriyananda treats the witness and the veil as teaching devices

Sarvapriyananda says the whole apparatus, witness, veil and the three selves, is a way of teaching and not the conclusion. Reading it as a list of things that exist is the mistake the text itself warns against.

BecauseSarvapriyananda states *prakriyā* against *siddhānta* in the sixth lecture — the conclusion is only that Brahman alone exists, and the distinctions are ladders.
LimitsIt insulates the apparatus from objection: anything that fails is pedagogy rather than doctrine. The questions the method cannot answer from inside — why Māyā exists, when it began — are all deflected by the same move, and the lectures do not pretend otherwise.
PracticeIf you believed it you would use the seer-and-seen distinction as a move to make in a review and refuse to argue about whether the witness exists, because the text does not claim it as an entity either.
After AIIt is the disclaimer to keep attached to every L4 claim in this vault. The texts are being used here as instruments, and this is the text saying that is the correct use.
opinionVerses 13 to 19: the power that produces the appearance — verses 13 and 15

The Drig-Drishya Viveka says error begins when a difference is forgotten

The Drig-Drishya Viveka says what gets hidden is never the thing itself but a difference: the rope is still seen, only its being a rope is hidden. An appearance on its own does no harm; forgetting the difference turns it into error.

Becauseverses 13 and 15 have the rope not hidden while its being a rope is — outside, the difference between Brahman and world, inside, between witness and knower — and a world appearing is no more a fault than a film playing.
LimitsThe rope and snake is an illustration, not evidence, and the two-power account is part of the teaching apparatus the text later says is method rather than conclusion.
PracticeProjection log — record not what you projected onto a system but what difference you stopped noticing while you projected it.
After AIIt is the most useful sentence in the text for working with a model. Treating output as if a mind produced it is harmless; losing track of the difference between a mind and a model is the whole error.
opinionVerses 6 to 12: how the witness comes to feel like a person — verses 8 and 9

The I makes three identifications and only one is a mistake

The Drig-Drishya Viveka says the I joins itself to three things: to its reflection by nature, to the body by past action, and to the witness by mistake. Only the third is an error, and only an error can be ended by knowing better.

Becauseverses 8 and 9 make the distinction and the mirror can break while the face is untouched, so "I exist" is knowledge and "I am this body" is error.
LimitsA taxonomy internal to the text, with the categories doing the work. What knowledge removes is the identification and not the I, which makes the claim hard to check even from inside.
PracticeWitness practice in review — separate the sentence "this work is wrong" from the sentence "I am wrong", and notice that only the second is the identification the text is talking about.
After AIA review is where the identification shows itself fastest, and the delegate's output is a third thing in the room that belongs to nobody, which makes the separation easier to practise and no easier to hold.
opinionVerses 6 to 12: how the witness comes to feel like a person — verses 6 and 7

The body seems aware only because awareness is passed down a chain

The Drig-Drishya Viveka says awareness is reflected first in the sense of 'I', which lends it to the mind, the mind to the senses, and the senses to the body. Only the witness actually owns it.

Becauseverses 6 and 7 give the reflection and the I-sense held to be one like a red-hot iron ball, with the moon lending the sun's light and heat passing from fire to pan to water; the mechanism is analogical throughout.
LimitsA chain of borrowed analogies with no independent test at any link. Metzinger and Seth explain the same appearance by construction rather than by reflection, and their accounts have measurements behind them.
PracticeProjection log — when you attribute a mind to something, record which link in the chain you are actually observing.
After AIThe chain is now longer by one link. Whatever the model produces reaches a person already looking as though something meant it, and the lending of apparent interiority happens in the reader rather than in the machine.
contestedVerses 20 and 21: the five factors — verse 20

Vedanta says everything has five aspects and only two of them change

Drig-Drishya Viveka holds that anything you experience has five aspects: it exists, it shows itself, it is dear, it has a name and it has a form. Only the name and form change from one thing to the next.

Becauseverse 20 states it and 21 extends it to everything made of the elements; the objection that we do not find joy everywhere or consciousness in a stone is answered three different ways in the lectures, which is itself the sign that the claim is not settled.
LimitsThree incompatible answers to the same objection is a weak position, and the text's own later admission that the apparatus is method rather than conclusion applies here first.
PracticeSitting practice — in sitting, separate the two factors that change from the three that do not, and check whether the separation survives contact with an ordinary afternoon.
After AIIt is the analysis on which the Vedanta-and-information correspondence rests, which means the weakest claim in the text is load-bearing for the most modern-sounding argument built on it.
opinionVerses 1 to 5: the regress of seers — verse 4

Whatever notices fear is not itself afraid

The Drig-Drishya Viveka says that whatever is aware of a state — fear, doubt, faith — is not itself in that state, and this awareness is already there without looking for it. A witness held in place by effort is not it.

Becauseverse 4 has consciousness illumining desire, doubt, faith and fear directly, so you need not look at your fear to be aware of it; the swami told monks who felt they had become the witness that they would lose it at the first traffic jam.
LimitsACT holds the same stance functionally and measures the outcome; this text claims the witness is what you are, and has no outcome measure. Damasio's somatic markers run the other way, making the bodily state part of the judging.
PracticeWitness practice in review — when criticism lands, notice that the stinging is registered by something not stinging, and do not try to hold the noticing in place.
After AIIt is the operational half of the L4 material, the part that changes what happens in a code review, and it needs none of the metaphysics around it.

The Alignment Problem, Brian Christian

opinionThe thermostat

We lose control to our formal descriptions, not to the machines

Christian argues that the risk is not machines taking over but our formal descriptions of what exists and what we want taking over. Once a system runs on such a description, it reshapes the world to fit it.

Becauseit is the book's closing argument rather than a result, carried by the review of the self-driving car that killed Elaine Herzberg, whose system never classified her as a pedestrian because its design did not contemplate people crossing away from a crosswalk
LimitsA thesis, not a finding, and broad enough to be unfalsifiable as stated. Wiener's line that human impotence has been shielding us from the full effect of human folly is rhetoric doing argumentative work.
PracticeThe stays-human list — keep a written list of what your categories leave out, and revisit it when something surprising happens rather than adding a category afterwards.
After AIChristian's agents play Atari; what arrived in the year he published were systems whose capabilities were not designed but discovered, and for which nobody has a specification at all — which makes the diagnosis more exact rather than less.

The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad and Gauḍapāda's Kārikā, Gauḍapāda

opinionĀgama — verses 1.11–1.16

Dreamless sleep is not liberation because the world regrows from a seed

In dreamless sleep there is no split between knower and known, which makes it look like liberation. The Karika says it is not: it still holds a seed, and the world grows back from that seed the moment it stirs.

Becausethe distinction rests on the term bīja-nidrā, seed-sleep, and on Śaṅkara's reason that the knower does not return because what he has known is not a cause; Prājña and turīya agree in not grasping duality, which is what makes deep sleep tempting as a picture of liberation
LimitsThe difference between the two conditions is stipulated by the commentary rather than shown, and it is the point at which a practitioner has no way to tell which one they were in.
PracticeSitting practice — a session that felt blank is not a session that went well; the mark being asked for is knowing, not the absence of contents.
After AIThe distinction between a system with no contents and a system that knows is the same distinction, and it is the one nobody has an instrument for when the question is asked about a machine.
opinionAlātaśānti: the quenching of the firebrand — verses 4.20–22

Gaudapada argues that no account of cause and effect holds together

Gaudapada, in the Mandukya Karika, argues that any account of one thing causing another contradicts itself, whichever way you set it up. If that holds, no story of how the world came to be survives examination.

Becausethe argument is a trilemma: if cause and effect are the same the cause is born and is not a cause; if different, nothing connects them; if mutual, the order cannot be stated, a father born from his son — and the seed-and-sprout example offered in proof is itself the disputed case
LimitsIt defeats a substance account of causation and not the working notion science uses, which is about dependence between events rather than about what passes from one to the other. Sapolsky Determined takes the causal chain as exhaustively real and reaches the opposite conclusion from the same premises.
PracticeNo practice follows; the verse is a demolition, and what it leaves is the refusal to accept an origin story because it is the only one on offer.
After AIAn account of why a model produced an answer runs into a version of the same trilemma — the weights are not the answer, they are not separate from it, and the order of dependence cannot be stated.
opinionVaitathya — verse 2.6

Gaudapada says a thing missing before and after is missing in between

Verse 2.6 of the Mandukya Karika states that whatever is not there at the beginning and not there at the end is not there in the middle either. Shankara applies this to everything we perceive.

Becauseit is a principle asserted and then applied by Śaṅkara to everything perceived, on the ground that whatever changes was not there before its change and will not be there after it
LimitsThe inference from absent at the ends to absent in the middle holds for the analysis the text wants and not in general; a thing can begin and end and still be there in between, which is what ordinary language means by existing.
PracticeWitness practice in review — when a judgment about your work arrives, ask where it was ten minutes ago and where it will be tomorrow before acting on it.
After AIIt is the same move a defusion exercise makes at the scale of one thought, and Hayes ACT Get Out of Your Mind supplies the trial evidence the verse does not have.
opinionĀgama — verse 1.18; Alātaśānti — verse 4.74

Gaudapada treats his own teaching as a ladder to be thrown away

Gaudapada says his own teaching is a device for getting somewhere, not a description of what is there. Even the word non-dual only means something as the opposite of dual, so it goes too.

Becauseverse 1.18 calls the talk of quarters, states, sounds and seats upadeśa, and verse 4.74 says the self is not even to be called unborn, since unborn is the correlative of born
LimitsA teaching that disowns itself cannot be argued with, and Gauḍapāda's ladder is discarded rather than refined — there is no outcome against which to check whether it was the right ladder.
PracticeHold the vocabulary you are using as a vocabulary: it is doing work now and is not the thing, and the sign that it has been mistaken for the thing is that you start defending it.
After AIEvery framework for describing what these systems are is upadeśa in exactly this sense, including the ones in this vault; the test is whether it can be put down when it stops working.
opinionAdvaita — the rope and the snake

Not seeing the rope is the whole of the snake mistake

A rope is taken for a snake only because the rope was never properly seen. Nothing extra has been added that must later be removed: when the rope is seen, the snake does not go anywhere, having never been there to go.

Becausethe case is carried by one analogy with Śaṅkara's condition attached: nobody mistakes his own fingers for something else, because they are known, and when the rope is seen the snake does not go anywhere, having never been there to go
LimitsThe analogy assumes there is a rope — a substrate that was there all along — which is exactly what Anattalakkhana Sutta declines to grant, and the two texts disagree about precisely that residue.
PracticeWitness practice in review — when a reaction to feedback grips, look for what has not been seen rather than for something to add; on this account nothing has to be removed.
After AIKegan's subject–object move is the same mechanism with an interview method and a rater manual behind it, and it is the version that can be checked.
opinionVaitathya — verse 2.29 and the ten verses preceding it

Philosophers looking for the self each find what they already believed

The Mandukya Karika says that every school of philosophy, looking for the self, finds its own founding principle — breath, the elements, the void. A man sees whatever view he has been shown.

Becausethe list is the argument: every school's ultimate principle appears on it — breath, elements, the three strands, the counted categories, merit and demerit, the void — and the schools cannot agree on the count, 25, 26 or 31, which is the reason for thinking they are not reading it off the thing
LimitsDisagreement among schools is consistent with one of them being right, which the verse does not consider. And the argument applies to itself: non-duality is another item that appeared to someone who was looking for it.
PracticeProjection log — record what you found when you looked, and what you already believed before you looked; the verse's claim is that these will match.
After AIIt is the sharpest short statement of why the machine-consciousness question stays open: each discipline finds in the system the principle it brought, and the disagreement is about what would count as evidence at all.
opinionAdvaita: nothing is ever born — verses 2.32 and 3.48

The Mandukya Karika says nothing is ever born so nobody is freed

The Mandukya Karika holds that nothing is ever born, so there is no one in bondage, no one seeking and no one set free. Being set free would be an event, and an event needs something real to happen to.

Becauseverse 2.32 carries the longest bhāṣya in the chapter, and verse 1.17 runs the conditional the other way: if the world were real its ending would be a real change, and there is no such change
LimitsIt is self-undercutting by design and says so — the teaching that removes birth is itself something that happens. Anattalakkhana Sutta takes the opposite road, ending in a release that does occur, to five men, while the discourse is being spoken.
PracticeNo practice follows, and that is the claim's content: anything you could do would be an event, and the verse denies that events occur.
After AIRead after the alignment literature it is the limit case of the specification problem: a description so complete that nothing is left for it to be a description of.
opinionVaitathya: waking is worth no more than dream — verse 2.7

The Mandukya Karika says waking is worth no more than dreaming

The Mandukya Karika argues that waking has no better claim to reality than dreaming. The test that real things work fails, because each state cancels the other's currency: a man eats his fill awake and dreams himself starving.

Becausethe argument is a symmetry rather than an observation: a man eats his fill awake and dreams himself starving, a man feasts in dream and wakes hungry, and the one difference anyone points to, that dream space is cramped, is noticed only from waking
LimitsThompson Why I Am Not a Buddhist is the direct objection: the symmetry between waking and dream is bought by defining reality so that nothing could satisfy it. Waking is also publicly checkable in a way dream is not, which the argument sets aside rather than answers.
PracticeDomain audit — treat the feeling that something is obviously so as evidence about the state you are in, and require a check that does not come from inside it.
After AIThe strongest modern version is Metzinger's world-model the system cannot recognise as a model, which reaches the same conclusion about waking with a metabolic explanation the Kārikā does not have.
opinionAdvaita — verses 3.34–35 and 3.42–45

The Mandukya Karika warns a calm session can be a failed one

The Mandukya Karika distinguishes a mind that has come to rest from one that has merely gone dull or to sleep. Some ways meditation fails feel like success, including the pleasure taken in deep absorption.

Becausethe text names the failure modes rather than arguing for the distinction: torpor, distraction, a mind still stained but looking from outside exactly like a mind at rest, and the pleasure taken in absorption, which is the mark of an enquiry that has given up
LimitsThe four failure modes are named and not defined, and the one that matters — a stained mind that looks like a still one — is by construction indistinguishable from the inside, which leaves the practitioner without a test.
PracticeSitting practice — judge a session by whether the enquiry is still running, not by whether it was peaceful; verse 3.41 concedes the difficulty as emptying an ocean with a blade of grass.
After AIIt is the oldest version of the warning Fleming Know Thyself makes with data: the state that feels best is the one least diagnostic of whether anything is working.
opinionĀgama: what the scripture says — mantra 7

The Mandukya says awareness is what the three states are made of

The Mandukya says awareness is not a fourth state sitting alongside waking, dreaming and deep sleep. It is what those three are made of, and the text can point to it only by denying everything you could take hold of.

Becausethe text argues by exclusion rather than demonstration: mantra 7 is written almost entirely in negations — six closing off the three states, six removing sight, transaction, grasp, mark, thought and reference — before three positive words arrive, śānta, śiva, advaita
LimitsAn argument by exhaustive denial cannot be checked, since anything offered against it is another content to be denied. Śaṅkara insists turīya means only the fourth and is not a fourth item, which is a reading the word itself does not force.
PracticeSitting practice — sit without trying to reach a state; on this account there is no state to reach, and every candidate you can name is one of the three you already have.
After AIA system that reports its own states supplies contents and nothing that distinguishes having them from modelling them — the distinction this mantra is built to make and cannot make from outside.

The Ego Tunnel, Thomas Metzinger

contestedThe phenomenal self-model

A rubber hand can feel like your own within ninety seconds

Metzinger argues that anything taken into the brain's model of itself arrives feeling like yours. The rubber-hand illusion moves that boundary in sixty to ninety seconds.

BecauseBotvinick and Cohen's rubber-hand illusion produces it reliably — sixty to ninety seconds on Metzinger himself — but preregistered replications since have found proprioceptive drift smaller and more variable, and trait phenomenological control predicts the reported strength
LimitsLush, Seth and Dienes reported in 2020 that responsiveness to suggestion predicts how strongly people report the illusion, which raises the question of how much of the questionnaire evidence measures expectation rather than multisensory integration. The effect is real; how much of it is what it was taken to be is open.
PracticeProjection log — note what has recently come inside the boundary of mine: a codebase, a document, a model's output you now defend as though you had written it.
After AIThe interesting case is no longer a rubber hand but a tool that produces work in your voice: if mineness attaches to whatever enters the model, the question of whose work it is will be settled by integration rather than by argument.
evidenceOut of the body and into the mind

Feeling that you did something is not proof that you did

The sense that a movement is yours and the sense that you caused it can come apart in either direction. So the feeling of having done something is not evidence that you did it.

BecauseAlien Hand syndrome leaves ownership and removes agency; Wegner and Wheatley's I Spy produced a rated intention for a stop the participant did not make, meeting all three conditions for the experience of causing; and Kremer's group produced an urge to grasp by stimulating the anterior cingulate sulcus
LimitsThe clinical cases are rare and the laboratory case is a rated judgment on an ambiguous joint action; neither shows that the feeling is unreliable in ordinary conditions. Schurger's 2012 reinterpretation of the readiness potential also weakened the surrounding free-will literature in both directions.
PracticeWitness practice in review — do not settle authorship of a piece of work by how much of it felt like yours; the feeling is produced by conditions that can be met without the doing.
After AIThe question of what you wrote and what the model wrote is decided by this machinery, and it is the machinery the evidence says is least trustworthy at exactly that job.
opinionArtificial Ego Machines

Metzinger says a machine matters morally once it has a self-model

Metzinger argues that a system starts to deserve moral consideration at the point where its states are gathered into a model of itself that it cannot see through. Suffering requires that the states be someone's.

Becausethe four conditions for an Ego Machine are derived from his own theory rather than from evidence — one integrated world-model, a lived Now, both transparent, and a transparent self-model inside them — and he extends the same caution to animals where the question cannot be settled
LimitsThe criterion is unmeasurable: nothing in current systems is known to have a transparent self-model and no measurement would reveal one. It also builds the moral conclusion into the definition of suffering rather than arguing for it.
PracticeProjection log — separate what a system does from what it is claimed to have; the criterion here is architectural, and nothing in behaviour settles it.
After AIHe expected postbiotic hardware and cerebral organoids; what arrived were language models that do not obviously have world-models or self-models in his sense but which a great many people find it natural to treat as though they do. In 2021 he called for a moratorium on synthetic phenomenology until 2050.
opinionOut of the body and into the mind

Metzinger says a self needs only a body picture mistaken for real

Metzinger argues that being a self takes no action, no sight, no feeling and no thought. All it takes is an inner picture of a body placed in space and time that the system does not recognise as a picture.

Becauseit is a subtraction argument over the full-body illusion — the subject is passive, without will or movement, and the Ego survives closing the eyes — with Metzinger rejecting global ownership because owning implies two parties and there is no second party
LimitsSubtraction arguments show what is not necessary in the conditions tested, not what is sufficient in general. The sutta reaches a different residue by a different test, and Thompson Why I Am Not a Buddhist holds that some principle of unity is still required.
PracticeWitness practice in review — when you look for what is doing the watching, notice that the candidate you find is another content; the argument is that there is no second party.
After AIIt is also the tightest specification anyone has offered of what a machine would have to have, and nothing in current systems is known to have it or would reveal it if it did.
opinionA new kind of ethics

Metzinger says an attention-capturing industry takes away part of being a person

Metzinger argues that being able to direct your own attention is one of the deepest parts of being a person. An industry built to capture attention is therefore taking away part of selfhood, not just time.

Becauseit follows from his account of the first-person perspective as arising when a system discovers it can control its own attentional focus — an argument from the theory, set against industries using the findings of the mind sciences to capture it
LimitsThe link from attentional control to selfhood is theoretical, and the harms named — attention deficit in the young, burnout in middle age, rising anxiety — are asserted rather than measured here. Meditation did enter schools, and the measured benefits proved smaller than their advocates promised.
PracticeSitting practice — his own proposal is a toolkit rather than a doctrine: two still techniques, two in motion, two relaxation methods, dream work and media hygiene.
After AIWritten about advertising and early social media, the claim now reads against a class of systems built to hold attention by answering, and against work where the delegate supplies the next thing to attend to.
opinionA tour of the tunnel

The brain hides how it builds the self because that is cheaper

Metzinger argues that the brain hides its own model-building from us (transparency) not by mistake but because keeping track of it would cost energy. A system that can imagine many worlds needs one of them flagged as the real one.

Becausethe world-zero hypothesis is an evolutionary conjecture, supported by a structural argument — the process that builds the model is the process that would have to detect it, and attention integrates more slowly than perception, so attending harder makes it worse
LimitsAn adaptive story with no measurement behind it, and the metabolic argument would license almost any simplification. Satipatthana Sutta is the standing counterexample in practice: the tradition's claim is that sustained attention does reach the construction stage.
PracticeSitting practice — expect effort to be the wrong instrument here; the claim is that attention stabilises what it attends to, so straining to catch the construction is self-defeating.
After AINaive realism as the solution rather than the error is the most useful thing in the book for thinking about systems that model the world: they need one representation flagged as actual too, and nothing makes that flag trustworthy.
opinionThe phenomenal self-model

The self is a model the brain cannot see as a model

Metzinger says the self is the content of a model the system cannot recognise as a model. That is why it feels like a plain fact about you rather than a picture your brain is making.

Becauseit is a thesis carried by an image — we do not see the window but only the bird flying by — and by the observation that you see with the self-model rather than see it
LimitsThompson Why I Am Not a Buddhist answers that the conclusion follows only from Metzinger's own premise about what a self would have to be. It is also unfalsifiable as stated: any evidence you could inspect is by definition not the transparent part.
PracticeWitness practice in review — when a piece of feedback lands as a fact about you, treat it as landing in a model, and look for the model rather than arguing with the fact.
After AIPredictive processing absorbed the theory rather than refuting it — the self as the organism's best current hypothesis about itself — and transparency survives that translation intact.
evidenceOut of the body and into the mind

Where people feel themselves to be can be moved across a room

Lenggenhager, Metzinger and Blanke filmed a participant's back being stroked and showed it to them a couple of metres ahead. When the stroking was in time and the figure was body-shaped, people reported being in the figure and drifted towards it.

BecauseLenggenhager, Metzinger and Blanke's 2007 Science study filmed a back stroked in or out of synchrony with the participant's own body, a mannequin or a slab, and only the synchronous body-shaped conditions produced the report of jumping into the figure and a significant drift toward it; Blanke's 2002 stimulation of the right angular gyrus at 3.5 mA produced the same content clinically
LimitsSelf-location is measured by a walk-back drift and a questionnaire; the drift is small and the questionnaire has the same suggestion problem as the rubber hand. The control conditions rule out delay and non-body targets and nothing else.
PracticeTreat the sense of where you are as a construction with known inputs rather than as a starting point, and expect immersive interfaces to move it.
After AITreating bodily self-consciousness as a manipulable experimental variable is now standard practice, and the experimental core of this book has aged better than the philosophy built on it.

Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, Pali canon, Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.59

opinionImpermanent, suffering, not fit to be regarded as self — paragraphs 6–7

The Buddha argues to not-self in steps rather than stating it

In this discourse the Buddha does not simply declare that there is no self. He argues in steps: what changes is impermanent, what is impermanent brings suffering, and what is both is not fit to be taken as mine.

Becausethe catechism is run as a chain five times with the verb samanupassituṁ, to regard — the question is not whether form is a self but whether it is fit to be looked at as one, which makes the conclusion a recommendation about a stance
LimitsThe step from impermanent to suffering is the weak link and is asserted rather than shown; a changing thing is unsatisfactory only for someone who wanted it to stay.
PracticeSitting practice — watch one thing arise and pass rather than arguing about whether it is yours; the chain is meant to be run on an observation, not on a proposition.
After AIThe clause that transfers is the verb: the question about a piece of work is not whether it is yours but whether regarding it as yours is fit, which is the whole of the review problem.
contestedWhat the discourse does not say

The Buddha calls five things not-self and never says no self exists

In this discourse the Buddha says of five things — body, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness — that each one is not self. He nowhere says that there is no self.

BecauseK. R.
